(p-19) Surah al-Baqarah

Section on its virtue

Abu Hurairah narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Do not make your houses graveyards, for the house in which Surah al-Baqarah is recited, the Shaytan does not enter."

Abu Umamah narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Recite the two bright ones: al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran, for they will come on the Day of Resurrection as if they were two clouds, or two shades, or two flocks of birds in ranks, pleading for their companions. Recite al-Baqarah, for taking it up is a blessing, leaving it is a regret, and the idle (al-batalah) cannot master it."

What is meant by az-zahrawayn is "the two luminous ones" (al-muniratayn). It is said that everything luminous is zahir. Al-ghayayah is everything that shades a person from above his head, like a cloud or dust. It is said: "They shaded the people above so-and-so's head with swords," as if they had shaded him with them. Labid said:

"So I descended upon him, returning, and over the earth were the shades of the child."

The meaning of firqan is two parts. Al-farq is a portion of a thing. The Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿So every part was like a great mountain﴾ [ash-Shu'ara' 26:63]. As-Sawwaf means arranged in rows, pressed together, so as to shade its reciter. Al-batalah means the sorcerers.

**

Section on its revelation

Ibn Abbas said: it was the first thing revealed in Madinah. This is the view of al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ikrimah, (p-20) Jabir ibn Zayd, Qatadah, and Muqatil. Some people said it is Madani except for one verse, which is the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:281]. It was revealed on the Day of Sacrifice at Mina during the Farewell Pilgrimage.

Section on the explanation

As for His words: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾, the scholars differed concerning it and concerning all the disjointed letters at the beginnings of the surahs, into six opinions.

The first: they are among the ambiguous (mutashabih) matters whose meaning none knows but Allah. Abu Bakr as-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "For Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, there is a secret in every book, and the secret of Allah in the Qur'an is the beginnings of the surahs." To this view went ash-Sha'bi, Abu Salih, and Ibn Zayd.

The second: they are letters of names, and when they are combined in a certain arrangement they become names of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Ali ibn Abi Talib said: "They are disjointed names; if people knew how to combine them, they would know the name of Allah by which, when He is called upon, He answers."

Ibn Abbas was asked about "Alif Lam Ra," "Ha Mim," and "Nun," and he said: "It is the name ar-Rahman in disjointed form." To a similar view went Abu al-Aliyah and ar-Rabi' ibn Anas.

The third: they are letters by which Allah swore. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Ikrimah. Ibn Qutaybah said: It is possible that He swore by all the disjointed letters, and mentioned only some of them, as one says: "I learned alif ba ta tha," meaning all the letters, and as one says: "I recited al-Hamd," meaning the Opening of the Book, naming it by its first letter. He swore by the letters of the alphabet for their nobility, and because they are the building blocks of His revealed books, and by them He is mentioned and made One. Ibn al-Anbari said: The response to the oath is omitted, its estimate being: "By the letters of the alphabet, Allah has indeed made the path clear for you, and I have made the proofs clear for you through the revealed Book." It was omitted because the addressees know it, and because in His words: ﴿This is the Book, there is no doubt in it﴾ there is an indication of the response.

(p-21) The fourth: He indicated by what He mentioned of the letters to all the rest of them. The meaning is that since the letters are the foundations of composed speech, He informed that this Qur'an is only composed of these letters. This was said by al-Farra' and Qutrub.

If it is said: They already knew that it is letters, so what is the benefit of informing them of this?

The answer: He thereby alerted them to its inimitability, as if He said: "It is made of these letters from which you compose your speech; so why are you unable to oppose it?! When you are unable, know that it is not the speech of Muhammad, peace be upon him."

The fifth: they are names of the surahs. This is related from Zayd ibn Aslam, his son, and Abu Fakhitah Sa'id ibn Alaqah, client of Umm Hani'.

The sixth: they are from the symbolic code that the Arabs use in their speech. A man says to another: "Hal ta?" and he replies: "Bala," meaning "Hal ta'ti?" (Will you come?), and he suffices with one of its letters. They recited:

"We said to her: 'Stop (qifi) for us,' and she said: 'Qaf — do not think we have forgotten the haste.'"

He meant she said: "Aqif" (I stop). And similar to it:

"Call out to them: 'Alla, come!' 'Alla ta!' — they all said together: 'Alla fa!'"

He meant: "Alla tarkabun?" (Will you not ride?) They said: "Bala, so ride!" And similar to it:

"With goodness, goodnesses; and if evil, fa; and I do not desire evil except that ta..."

Its meaning: "And if evil, then evil; and I do not desire evil except that you will it." To this view went al-Akhfash, az-Zajjaj, and Ibn al-Anbari.

Abu Rawq Atiyyah ibn al-Harith al-Hamdani said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite aloud in all the prayers, and the polytheists would clap and whistle, so these disjointed letters were revealed; they heard them and remained bewildered." Others said: He addressed them with what they do not understand so that they would turn their attention to listening to it, for souls strain toward what its meaning has hidden from them. When they turn to it, He addresses them with what they understand, and that becomes like a means to conveying the message. However, there must be a meaning known to others, or known to the addressees; so this statement encompasses all the letters.

The exegetes specified His words ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ with five opinions:

The first: it is among the ambiguous matters whose meaning none knows but Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and its explanation has already preceded.

The second: its meaning is "I am Allah, the Most Knowing." Narrated by Abu ad-Duha from Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Mas'ud and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said the same.

The third: it is an oath. Narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, and Khalid al-Hadhdha' from Ikrimah.

The fourth: they are letters of names. Then there are two views. One: the alif from "Allah," the lam from "Jibril," and the mim from "Muhammad," said by Ibn Abbas.

If it is said: If the first letter of each name is taken to suffice, why is the lam taken from Jibril, which is the last letter of the name?

The answer: The beginning of the Qur'an is from Allah, the Most High, so He indicated this by the beginning with the first letter of His name; Jibril is the one through whom the revelation and recitation were concluded, so the last letters of his name were taken; and Muhammad is the beginning in the recitation, so the first letter in it was taken. The second view: the alif from "Allah" the Most High, the lam from "Latif" (Subtle), and the mim from "Majid" (Glorious), said by Abu al-'Aliyah.

The fifth: it is a name of the names of the Qur'an, said by Mujahid, ash-Sha'bi, Qatadah, and Ibn Jurayj.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 2:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That﴾ has two opinions.

One of them: it means "this," and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Kisa'i, Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash. Some of them argued with the verse of Khifaf ibn Nudba:

"I say to him while the spear bends its shaft: 'Consider, Khifaf, that I am that (dhalika).'"

That is, "I am this." Ibn al-Anbari said: he only meant, "I am that one whom you know."

The second: it is a reference to something absent.

Then, regarding it, there are three opinions.

The first: he meant by it what was previously sent down to him of the Qur'an.

The second: he meant by it what He promised to reveal to him, in His saying: ﴿Surely We shall send down upon you a weighty word﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 5].

The third: he meant by that what He promised to the People of the earlier Scriptures, because they were promised a Prophet and a Book.

And ﴿the Book﴾: the Qur'an. It was called a Book (kitab) because some of it is gathered to some of it. From the same root comes "al-katiba" (a military battalion), named so because some of its parts are gathered to others. And from it: "kataba al-baghla" (I gathered the mule's bridle/ I tied the mule's girth-strap together).

**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There is no doubt in it﴾. Al-raib: doubt. Al-huda: guidance. Al-muttaqun: those who guard themselves against what they fear.

Our shaykh 'Ali ibn 'Ubayd Allah distinguished between taqwa (god-consciousness) and wara' (scrupulousness), saying: taqwa is taking a shield (iddah), and wara' is repelling a doubt (shubha). So taqwa has a certain cause, and wara' has a presumed effect.

The scholars differed about the meaning of this verse in three opinions.

The first: its apparent form is negation, but its meaning is prohibition, and its estimate is: it is not fitting for anyone to doubt it, because of its perfection and firmness. Similar to it is: ﴿It is not for us to associate anything with God﴾ [Yusuf: 38], meaning: it is not fitting for us. And similar to it: ﴿so there shall be no obscenity nor wickedness﴾ [al-Baqara: 197]. This is the view of al-Khalil and Ibn al-Anbari.

The second: its meaning is: there is no doubt about it that it is guidance for the god-fearing. This was said by al-Mubarrad.

The third: its meaning is: there is no doubt about it that it is from God, said by Muqatil and others.

If it is said: a people have indeed doubted it. The answer: it is true in itself, and whoever examines it with verification will know it.

The poet said:

"There is no doubt in the truth, O Umama; doubt is only what the liar says."

If it is said: the god-fearing person is guided, so what is the benefit of restricting guidance to him? The answer is in two respects. First: he meant the god-fearing and the disbelievers, and he suffices with mentioning one of the two groups, as in His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], meaning: and the cold. Second: he specified the god-fearing because they benefit from it, as in His saying: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 45], and he was a warner to those who fear and to those who do not fear.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 3:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who believe in the unseen﴾. Iman (faith) linguistically means tasdiq (affirmation, confirmation). The Shari'ah confirmed it upon that meaning and added to it speech and action. The root of al-ghayb (the unseen) is a settled place in which something hides due to its descent away from what surrounds it, so every hidden thing is called ghayb.

Regarding the meaning of al-ghayb here, there are six opinions.

The first: that it is the Revelation (wahy). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj.

The second: that it is the Qur'an. This was said by Abu Razin al-'Uqayli and Zirr ibn Hubaysh.

The third: that it is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This was said by 'Ata' and Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The fourth: that it is what is hidden from the servants of the matters of Paradise and Hell, and similar things mentioned in the Qur'an. This was narrated by al-Suddi from his shaykhs, and Abu al-'Aliyah and Qatadah adopted this view.

(p-25) The fifth: that it is the divine decree (qadar) of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This was said by al-Zuhri.

The sixth: that it is faith in the Messenger regarding one who has not seen him. 'Amr ibn Murrah said: The companions of 'Abd Allah said to him, "Blessed are you, for you fought alongside the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and sat with him." He said: "The matter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was clear to those who saw him, but more amazing than that are people who find a written book and believe in it without having seen him." Then he recited: ﴿Who believe in the unseen﴾.

**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And establish the prayer﴾. Salah (prayer) linguistically means supplication (du'a'). In the Shari'ah, it is actions and statements upon specific characteristics. Regarding its being named salah, there are three opinions.

The first: that it was so named because of raising the sala, which is the place where the tail meets the horse's rump.

The second: that it derives from "salaytu al-'ud" (I straightened the wood) when I softened it, so the one who prays softens and becomes humble.

The third: that it is built upon supplication and request, and salah linguistically means supplication. In this context it is a generic noun (ism jins).

Muqatil said: he intended by it here the five daily prayers.

Regarding the meaning of establishing it, there are three opinions.

The first: that it is the completion of its performance in the manner commanded. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid.

The second: that it is maintaining its appointed times, its wudu', its bowing (ruku') and its prostration (sujud). This was said by Qatadah and Muqatil.

The third: that it is continuing it. The Arabs say of a regular thing, "qa'im" (standing/established), and "so-and-so establishes the stipends of the soldiers." This was said by Ibn Kaysan.

**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And from what We have provided them﴾, meaning: what We have given them. ﴿They spend﴾, meaning: they bring out. The root of infaq (spending) is bringing out. It is said: "nafaqat al-dabbah" (the animal died) when its spirit came out.

(p-26) Regarding the intended meaning of this spending, there are four opinions.

The first: that it is spending on family and dependents. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud and Hudhayfah.

The second: that it is the obligatory zakat. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah.

The third: that it is voluntary charity (sadaqat nawafil). This was said by Mujahid and al-Dahhak.

The fourth: that it is the spending that was obligatory before the obligation of zakat. Some exegetes mentioned this, and they said: it was obligatory upon a man to retain from what was in his hand an amount sufficient for his sustenance for his day and night, and to distribute the remainder to the poor. According to this view, the verse is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of zakat; but other than this view is affirmed. Know that the wisdom in combining belief in the unseen, which is the commitment of the heart, with prayer, which is an act of the body, and with charity, which is an obligation relating to wealth, is that there is no fourth category in obligation, since whatever is beyond these categories is a mixture of two of them, like Hajj and fasting and the like.

The Words of the Exalted: ﴿And those who believe in what has been sent down to you﴾. The scholars differed over who was meant, and there are two opinions.

The first is that it was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and his companions. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbās, and Muqātil chose this view.

The second is that it was revealed concerning the Arabs who believed in the Prophet (ﷺ) and in what was sent down before him. Ṣāliḥ narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbās. The exegetes (mufassirūn) said: [What was sent down to him is the Qur'an. Our shaykh ʿAlī ibn ʿUbayd Allah said: the Qur'an ] and other than it of what was revealed to him.

**

The Words of the Exalted: ﴿and what was sent down before you﴾. It means the earlier Books and the revelation. As for "al-ākhirah" (الآخرة, the Hereafter), it is the name for what comes after this world. It was called "ākhirah" because this world precedes it. It was also said that it was called ākhirah because it is the final outcome of the matter.

(p-27)

**

The Words of the Exalted: ﴿they are certain﴾. Yaqīn (certainty, يقين) is that by which trust is attained and the heart is set at rest, and it is the most intense form of acquired knowledge.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 5:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They are upon guidance﴾ means: upon right direction (rashad). Ibn ʿAbbas said: upon light and uprightness (istiqamah). Ibn Qutaybah said: "al-muflihun" (the successful ones) are those who attain the everlasting endurance (baqa' al-abad), and the original meaning of al-falah (success) is endurance (al-baqa'). The following verse of Labid bears witness to this:

"We alight in lands all of which were alighted in before us, and we hope for endurance after ʿAd and Himyar."

He means: endurance (al-baqa'). Al-Zajjaj said: "al-muflih" is the one who attains success by which the goodness of his condition is complete. Ibn al-Anbari said: from this comes the phrase "Hasten to al-falah" (hayya ʿala al-falah), meaning: come to the path of success and entry into Paradise.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 6:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved﴾ — regarding its revelation there are four opinions.

The first: it was revealed concerning the leaders of the confederates (al-Ahzab), related by Abu al-'Aliyah.

The second: it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl and five of his family, related by al-Dahhak.

The third: it was revealed concerning a group of the Jews, among them Huyayy ibn Akhtab, related by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The fourth: it was revealed concerning the polytheists of the Arabs, such as Abu Jahl, Abu Talib, Abu Lahab, and others who did not embrace Islam.

Muqatil said: As for its interpretation, kufr (disbelief) in the language means covering. One says: "I kafara the thing" when one covers it, so the disbeliever is called kafir because he covers the truth.

**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is the same for them﴾ — i.e., their being warned and their not being warned are equal to them. Al-indhar (warning) is informing together with frightening. And "Banu Fulan tanadhara this matter" means when some of them frightened one another about it.

Our shaykh 'Ali ibn 'Ubayd Allah said: This verse came in a general wording, but what is meant by it is particular, because it indicates that the disbeliever, at the time of his being warned, will not believe, while many of the disbelievers did believe upon being warned. Had it remained on its apparent generality, God's report about them would have been contrary to what He informed of, and therefore it was necessary to transfer it to the particular.

**The Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 2, Verse 7:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has set a seal upon their hearts﴾. *Al-khatm* means *al-ṭab'* (stamping, imprinting). The heart (*al-qalb*) is a piece of black, congealed blood, lodged in the chest. It is the house of the soul and the dwelling place of the intellect. It was named *qalb* because of its *taqallub* (constant turning and fluctuation).

It was also said: it is named so because it is the pure essence of the body. He specifically singled it out for sealing because it is the locus of understanding.

**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and upon their hearing﴾. He means: upon their *asmā'* (ears/hearing faculties). He mentioned it in the singular form, but its meaning is plural, so the singular was used to stand for the whole group. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then He brings you forth as a child﴾ [al-Hajj: 5].

They also recited, as an example of this:

*"Eat from the middle of your bellies, so that you may live, for your time is a lean time."*

That is, *fī anṣāf buṭūnikum* (in the halves of your bellies). This explanation was mentioned by Abu 'Ubayda and al-Zajjaj. There is another explanation: the Arabs treat *al-sam'* (hearing) in the manner of a *maṣdar* (verbal noun, i.e., a noun of action), and a verbal noun is used in the singular, as you say: "Your speech pleases me" and "Your striking pleases me." However, *al-baṣar* (sight) and *al-qalb* (heart) are nouns that do not function in the manner of verbal nouns in this sense. This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Qasim. 'Amr ibn al-'As and Ibn Abi 'Abla recited (*wa-'alā asmā'ihim*) in the plural.

**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and upon their sight is a covering﴾. *Al-ghishāwa* means *al-ghiṭā'* (covering).

Al-Farra' said: As for Quraysh and most of the Arabs, they pronounce the *ghayn* of *ghishāwa* with a kasra (*ghishāwun*). The tribe of 'Ukl pronounce it with a damma, and some Arabs pronounce it with a fatḥa, and I think that is the dialect of Rabi'a. Al-Mufaddal narrated from 'Asim that it was read *ghishāwatan* in the accusative, with the sense of: *ja'ala 'alā abṣārihim ghishāwatan* (He placed upon their sights a covering).

As for *al-'adhāb* (punishment), it is continuous pain. And *mā' 'adhb* (sweet water) is water which, when it continues in the throat, goes down smoothly.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 8:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in Allah"﴾ — the scholars differed concerning whom it was revealed, on two views.

(p-29) One of them: that it was about the hypocrites (munafiqun). This was related by al-Suddi from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, and Abu al-'Aliyah, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd also said so.

The second: that it was about the hypocrites among the People of the Book. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Sirin said: "They used to fear this verse." Qatadah said: "This verse describes the hypocrite: he recognizes with his tongue and denies in his heart, he affirms with his tongue and opposes with his deeds, he is in one state in the morning and in another state in the evening, and he sways like a ship: whenever a wind blows, he is blown along with it."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 9:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They seek to deceive Allah﴾.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy, Muʿattib ibn Qushayr, and al-Jadd ibn al-Qays, when they met those who believed, would say: "We believe, and we testify that your companion is truthful." But when they were alone, they were not like that. So this verse was revealed.

As for the explanation: al-khadiʿah (deception) is trickery and cunning, and it was called khadiʿah because it occurs in concealment.

Al-makhdaiʿ is a room inside a room in which a woman hides. A man is called khadiʿ (a deceiver) when he commits deception, whether or not his aim is achieved; when his aim is achieved, it is said: "He has deceived." And the man is ikhtadaʿa: he responded to the deceiver, whether he intended to respond or not. The Arabs call time (al-dahr) khidaʿ, because of its changing with what it conceals of good and evil.

Regarding the meaning of their deceiving Allah, there are five opinions.

The first: they used to deceive the believers, so it was as if they had deceived Allah. This is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn Qutaybah preferred it.

The second: they used to deceive the Prophet of Allah, so Allah made His Prophet stand in His place, as He said: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are actually pledging allegiance to Allah﴾ [al-Fath: 10]. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The third: among the Arabs, al-khadiʿ means "corrupt." They recited:

"White of hue, delicious of taste, good of saliva, when the saliva has spoiled [khada'a]."

That is, it spoiled. Muhammad ibn al-Qasim related this from Thaʿlab, from Ibn al-Aʿrabi. Ibn al-Qasim said: The interpretation of ﴿they seek to deceive Allah﴾ is: they corrupt what they display of faith by what they conceal of disbelief.

The fourth: they used to do in the religion of Allah what, if they had done it among themselves, would have been deception.

The fifth: they used to conceal their disbelief and display belief in Him.

**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But they deceive none except themselves﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, and Abu ʿAmr read (wa-ma yukhadiʿuna), while the Kufans and Ibn ʿAmir read (yakhdaʿuna). The meaning is that the harm of that deception returns upon them.

When does the harm of their deception return upon them? There are two opinions on this.

One: in the present world, and this is by two means. The first: by the respite and delay that increases their punishment. The second: by the Prophet and the believers becoming aware of their inner states that they concealed.

The second opinion: the return of the deception upon them is in the Hereafter. On this there are two views.

One: it returns upon them when a barrier is set between them and the believers, and this is His saying: ﴿It will be said: "Go back behind you and seek light." So a wall with a gate will be struck between them﴾ [al-Hadid: 13].

The second: it returns upon them when the people of Paradise look down upon them. When they see them, they will long for the comfort of those before them, and they will say: ﴿Pour upon us some water or some of what Allah has provided you﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 50], and they will be answered: ﴿Indeed, Allah has forbidden them to the disbelievers﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 51].

**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they do not perceive﴾, meaning: and they do not know. Regarding that of which they were unaware, there are two opinions.

One: it is Allah's disclosure of their lie to His Prophet. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: it is their secret self-concealment of their disbelief. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 10:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿In their hearts is a disease﴾. Al-maraḍ (disease) here means doubt; this was said by ʿIkrimah and Qatadah.

﴿So Allah increased their disease﴾. This is a report from Allah, the Exalted, that He did this to them. Al-alim (painful) is in the sense of al-mu'lim (causing pain). The majority recite (yukadhdhibun) with the doubled letter (shaddah), while the Kufans other than Aban, from ʿAsim, recited it with the single letter and an open yaa (fatḥ al-yaa).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 11:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption on the earth,"﴾ the scholars differed over who was meant by this, giving two views.

One of them: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites (munafiqun) who lived in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is the view of the majority (al-jumhur), including Ibn Abbas and Mujahid.

The second: what is meant by them are a people who had not yet been created at the time of its revelation. This was said by Salman al-Farisi.

Al-Kisa'i used to read with a damma on the qaf of "qil" (qīla), the ha of "hil" (ḥīla), the ghayn of "ghiḍa" (ghīḍa), the jim of "ji'a" (jī'a), and the sin of "si'a" (sī'a) and "si'at" (sī'at). Ibn Amir used to put a damma on three of these: "ḥīla," "sīqa," "sī'a," and "sī'at." Nafi' used to put a damma on "sī'a" and "sī'at" and kasra on the rest. The others read all of these with a kasra.

Al-Farra' said: the people of the Hijaz from Quraysh and those neighboring them from Banu Kinana pronounce the qaf of "qīla," "jī'a," and "ghīḍa" with a kasra, while many of Aqil and those neighboring them, and the general body of Asad, give these a sound mixed between damma and kasra (ishmam) in "qīla" and "jī'a."

(p-32) Regarding the meaning of corruption (fasad) here, there are five views.

One: it is disbelief (kufr), said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: acting in acts of disobedience (ma'asi), said by Abu al-Aliya and Muqatil.

The third: it is disbelief and acts of disobedience, said by al-Suddi on the authority of his teachers.

The fourth: it is abandoning the carrying out of commands and avoiding prohibitions, said by Mujahid.

The fifth: it is the hypocrisy by which they associated with the disbelievers and informed them of the secrets of the believers, mentioned by our teacher Ali ibn Ubayd Allah.

**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿"We are only reformers"﴾ there are five views concerning it.

One: its meaning is a denial of what they were accused of, and its implied sense is: "We have done nothing that would necessitate corruption."

The second: its meaning is: "We intend to bring reconciliation between the Muslims and the disbelievers." Both views are reported from Ibn Abbas.

The third: they meant that befriending the disbelievers is reform, not corruption, said by Mujahid and Qatada.

The fourth: they meant that this act of ours is the reform, and confirming Muhammad (ﷺ) is the corruption, said by al-Suddi.

The fifth: they thought that befriending the disbelievers is beneficial in the worldly life, not in religion, because they believed that if the dominion belonged to the Prophet (ﷺ), they had secured themselves by pledging allegiance to him, and if the dominion belonged to the disbelievers, they had secured themselves by their friendship with them, mentioned by our teacher.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 12:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Verily, it is they who are the corrupters﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "Ala" (alā, "verily, indeed"): a word with which a statement is begun, used to draw the attention of the addressee, and it indicates the soundness of what follows it. And "hum" (hum, "they") is an emphasis for the speech.

(p-33) Regarding His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But they are not aware﴾, there are two opinions.

One of them: they are not aware that God will inform His Prophet of their corruption.

The second: they are not aware that what they did is corruption, not righteousness.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 13:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe as the people have believed,"﴾ There are two opinions regarding those to whom it was said.

The first: they are the Jews. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Muqatil.

The second: they are the hypocrites (munafiqun). This was said by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd.

Regarding those who said it to them, there are two opinions.

The first: they are the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, but he did not specify any of the Companions.

The second: they are specific individuals, namely Saʿd ibn Muʿadh, Abu Lubaba, and Usayd. Muqatil mentioned this.

Regarding the belief to which they were called, there are two opinions.

The first: it is affirmation (tasdiq) of the Prophet (ﷺ). This is the view of those who said they were the Jews. The second: it is acting in accordance with what they had professed outwardly. This is the view of those who said they were the hypocrites.

Regarding the intended meaning of "the people" (al-nas) here, there are three opinions. The first: all the Companions. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and the Jews who embraced Islam with him. This was said by Muqatil.

The third: Muʿadh ibn Jabal, Saʿd ibn Muʿadh, Usayd ibn Hudayr, and a group of the notable Ansar, whom al-Kalbi enumerated.

Regarding those whom they meant by "the foolish" (al-sufaha'), there are three opinions. The first: all the Companions, said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: women and children, said by al-Hasan. The third: Ibn Salam and his companions, said by Muqatil.

Regarding what they meant by "the unseen" (al-ghayb) concerning the faith of those whom they claimed were the foolish, there are three opinions. The first: they meant the religion of Islam, said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Suddi. The second: they meant resurrection and recompense, said by Mujahid. The third: they meant the exposure of the two groups' enmity without considering the outcome. This last view and the one before it proceed on the basis that they are the hypocrites, while the first proceeds on the basis that they are the Jews.

Ibn Qutayba said: "al-sufaha'" means "the ignorant" (al-jahala). It is said: "Fulan made his opinion foolish (saffaha ra'yahu)" when he regarded it as ignorant, and from this comes the saying that obscenity is "safah," because it is ignorance.

al-Zajjaj said: The root meaning of safah in the language is lightness of forbearance (khiffat al-hilm). It is said: "a thawb safih" when it is thin and worn out, and "tasaffahati al-rih al-shajar" when the wind bent the trees. The poet said:

"They walk as spear-shafts sway, their tips bent by the passing of the gentle winds."

**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿But they do not know.﴾

Muqatil said: They do not know that they themselves are the foolish.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 14:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they meet those who have believed, they say, "We believe." But when they are alone with their evil ones (shayatin), they say, "Indeed, we are with you; we were only mocking."﴾

They differed about who this verse was revealed concerning, on two views. The first: it was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites and others among the People of the Book who used to show the Prophet ﷺ a faith that contradicted what they told their leaders, as said by al-Hasan.

As for the interpretation: "ila" (إلى) here carries the meaning of "maʿa" (مَعَ, "with"), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who are my helpers in (the cause of) Allah?﴾, meaning: with Allah. "Shayatin" is the plural of shaytan. Al-Khalil said: every rebellious one is a shaytan in the view of the Arabs. Regarding this word there are two opinions. The first: it derives from "shatana" (شَطَنَ), meaning he went far from good; according to this, the nun is original (part of the root).

Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said, describing Sulayman, peace be upon him:

Whichever rebellious one (shatin) disobeyed him, he bound him, then he is cast into prison and shackles.

"ʿakahu" means: he bound him. And al-Nabigha said:

Su'ad departed from you by a distant (shuttun) journey, so she parted, while the heart is held captive by her.

The second: it derives from "shaṭa yashiṭu" (شاطَ يَشِيطُ), meaning when one burns and is consumed, so the nun is added (extra). They recited:

And the champion is consumed (yashitu) upon our spears.

That is: he perishes.

Regarding the intended meaning of "their shayatin" there are three opinions. The first: they are their leaders in disbelief, said by Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, and al-Suddi. The second: their brethren among the polytheists, said by Abu al-ʿAliya and Mujahid. The third: their soothsayers (kahanatuhum), said by al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, we are with you (innā maʿakum).﴾

On this there are two opinions. The first: they meant, "We are with you in your religion." The second: "We are with you in support and backing." And al-Hazw (الهَزْءُ) means mockery (al-sukhriyya).

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 15:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾.

The scholars differed over the meaning of Allah's mocking of them, giving nine opinions.

The first: He opens for them a door to Paradise while they are in the Fire. They hasten toward it, and it is closed. Then another door is opened for them, and they hasten toward it, and it is closed. So the believers laugh at them. This was narrated from Ibn Abbas.

The second: When the Day of Resurrection comes, the Fire will harden for them as fat hardens in a pot. They will walk, and the ground will swallow them. This was narrated from al-Hasan al-Basri.

The third: The mocking of them is that a wall with a gate is set up between them and the believers. Its inner side contains mercy, and its outer side, facing them, contains punishment. They remain in darkness, and it is said to them: ﴿Return behind you and seek light﴾ [al-Hadid: 13]. This was said by Muqatil.

The fourth: The meaning is that He repays them for their mocking. The wording is matched with its like, though the meaning differs. It is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the recompense for an evil act is an evil act like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40], and His saying: ﴿So whoever has assaulted you, assault him in the same manner as he assaulted you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194]. Amr ibn Kulthum said:

Let no one among us act ignorantly toward us, lest we act with ignorance beyond the ignorance of the ignorant.

He meant: we will punish him with a punishment more severe than his.

The fifth: The mocking from Allah is a rebuke of them and a declaring of them to be ignorant. Its meaning is: Allah rebukes their action and declares them ignorant for persisting in their disbelief.

The sixth: His mocking is His leading them on gradually (istidraj).

The seventh: It is the bringing down of their mockery upon them, and the returning of their deception and scheming upon themselves. Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Anbari mentioned these opinions.

The eighth: The mocking of them is that one of them is told in the Fire, while in the utmost humiliation: ﴿Taste it; indeed, you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49]. Our shaykh mentioned it in his book.

The ninth: When they displayed in this world the rulings of Islam contrary to what was concealed within them, that became for them like mocking.

**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He extends them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾.

On this there are four opinions. The first: He grants them respite; this was said by Ibn Mas'ud. The second: He gives them time; this was said by Ibn Abbas. The third: He increases them; this was said by Mujahid. The fourth: He gives them a delay; this was said by al-Zajjaj.

Tughyan (transgression) means exceeding the measure and going beyond the limit of moderation in abundance. It is said: "The sea transgressed" when its waves surged, and "the flood transgressed" when it brought a great deal of water. Regarding the meaning of their transgression there are two views. The first: it is their disbelief; this was said by the majority. The second: it is their rebellion and arrogance; this was said by Ibn Qutayba. And "ya'mahun" (wandering blindly) means being bewildered. It is said: "a man is 'amah and 'amih," meaning bewildered.

(p-37) The rajaz poet said:

And a bewildered one, staggering in a barren desert, guided astray by the desert's haze, in a wasteland of confusion.

Blind to guidance, among the ignorant, the blinded ones.

Ibn Qutayba said: "Ya'mahun" means they ride their heads, so they do not see.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 16:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾.

Regarding its revelation there are three opinions. The first: it was revealed concerning all the disbelievers; this was said by Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas. The second: it concerns the People of the Book; this was said by Qatadah, al-Suddi, and Muqatil. The third: it concerns the hypocrites; this was said by Mujahid. "Ashtaraw" (they bought) means "istabdalu" (they substituted), and the Arabs treat one who prefers something over something else as a buyer of it and a seller of the other. "Al-dalalah" and "al-dalal" have the same meaning.

Concerning it, the commentators have three opinions.

The first: the intended meaning here is disbelief (kufr), and what is meant by guidance is faith (iman); this was narrated from al-Hasan, Qatadah, and al-Suddi.

The second: it is doubt (shakk), and guidance is certainty (yaqin).

The third: it is ignorance (jahl), and guidance is knowledge ('ilm).

Concerning the manner in which they substituted error for guidance, there are three opinions. The first: they believed and then disbelieved; this was said by Mujahid. The second: the Jews believed in the Prophet (ﷺ) before his mission, and when he was sent they disbelieved in him; this was said by Muqatil. The third: when the disbelievers received what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought of guidance, they rejected it and chose misguidance, so they were like one who exchanges one thing for another; this was mentioned by our shaykh 'Ali ibn 'Ubayd Allah.

**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So their trade did not profit﴾.

This is a figure of speech (majaz), for trade does not profit; rather, profit is gained through it. Similar to it is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Rather, the plotting of the night and the day﴾ [Saba': 33], meaning: rather, their plotting in the night and the day. Similar to it is ﴿And when the matter is resolved﴾ [Muhammad: 21], meaning: it was resolved upon. And they recited:

Harith, you have relieved my worry, so my night slept, and my grief was revealed (cleared).

The night does not sleep; rather, one sleeps in it. Such usage is employed only where the difficulty disappears and the speaker's intent is known. But when it is attributed to something that could rightly be described by it, and something else is intended, it is not permissible; for example, if you say: "Your slave profited," meaning: "I profited through your slave." This meaning was adopted by al-Farra', Ibn Qutaybah, and al-Zajjaj.

**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they were not guided﴾.

Concerning it there are five opinions. The first: they were not guided in the knowledge of God. The second: they were not guided out of error. The third: they were not guided to the trade of the believers. The fourth: they were not guided in buying error. The fifth: a merchant may not profit and yet be upon guidance in his trade, not deserving blame for what he undertook; so God, mighty and majestic, negated both matters from them, as an intensification of their censure.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿مَثَلُهم كَمَثَلِ الَّذِي اسْتَوْقَدَ نارًا﴾ .

Allah the Exalted says: "Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire" (2:17).

هَذِهِ الآَيَةُ نَزَلَتْ في المُنافِقِينَ. و"المَثَلُ" بِتَحْرِيكِ الثّاءِ: ما يُضْرَبُ ويُوضَعُ لِبَيانِ النَّظائِرِ في الأحْوالِ. وفي قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿اسْتَوْقَدَ﴾ قَوْلانِ. (p-٣٩)أحَدُهُما: أنَّ السِّينَ زائِدَةٌ وأنْشَدُوا:

This verse was revealed about the hypocrites. "Mathal" (a parable, or a likeness used to clarify the similarity of states) is that which is cited and set forth to explain the resemblance between conditions. Concerning His words ﴿istawqada﴾ (he kindled) there are two opinions. One is that the letter sīn is extra (zāʾida), and they cited:

؎ وداعٍ دَعا يا مَن يُجِيبُ إلى النَّدى فَلَمْ يَسْتَجِبْهُ عِنْدَ ذاكَ مُجِيبُ

*And a caller called, "O you who answers to generosity!" but no answerer answered him at that time.*

He meant: "fa-lam yujibhu" (he did not answer him). This is the view of the majority, including al-Akhfash and Ibn Qutayba.

والثّانِي: أنَّ السِّينَ داخِلَةٌ لِلطَّلَبِ، أرادَ: كَمَن طَلَبَ مِن غَيْرِهِ نارًا.

The second is that the sīn denotes seeking (ṭalab), meaning: like one who asked someone else for fire.

**

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿فَلَمّا أضاءَتْ ما حَوْلَهُ ذَهَبَ اللَّهُ بِنُورِهِمْ وتَرَكَهم في ظُلُماتٍ لا يُبْصِرُونَ﴾ .

Allah the Exalted says: "So when it lit up what was around him, Allah took away their light and left them in darkness, unable to see" (2:17).

وَفِي "أضاءَتْ" قَوْلانِ. أحَدُهُما: أنَّهُ مِنَ الفِعْلِ المُتَعَدِّي، قالَ الشّاعِرُ:

Regarding "aḍāʾat" there are two views. One is that it is transitive, and the poet said:

؎ أضاءَتْ لَهم أحْسابُهم ووُجُوهُهم دُجى اللَّيْلِ حَتّى نَظَّمَ الجِزْعَ ثاقِبُهُ

*Their noble lineages and their faces lit up for them in the darkness of night, until the borer strung the onyx beads.*

وَقالَ آَخَرُ:

And another said:

؎ أضاءَتْ لَنا النّارُ وجْهًا أغَرَّ ∗∗∗ مُلْتَبِسًا بِالفُؤادِ التِباسًا

*The fire lit up for us a bright face, clinging to the heart with a close clinging.*

والثّانِي: أنَّهُ مِنَ الفِعْلِ اللّازِمِ. قالَ أبُو عُبَيْدٍ: يُقالُ: أضاءَتِ النّارُ، وأضاءَها غَيْرُها. وقالَ الزَّجّاجَ: يُقالُ: ضاءَ القَمَرُ، وأضاءَ.

The second is that it is intransitive. Abu 'Ubayd said: it is said "aḍāʾati al-nār" (the fire lit up), and "aḍāʾahā ghayruhā" (something else made it light up). al-Zajjaj said: it is said "ḍāʾa al-qamar" and "aḍāʾa" (the moon shone).

وَفِي "ما" قَوْلانِ. أحَدُهُما: أنَّها زائِدَةٌ، تَقْدِيرُهُ: أضاءَتْ حَوْلَهُ. والثّانِي: أنَّها بِمَعْنى الَّذِي. وحَوْلَ الشَّيْءِ: ما دارَ مِن جَوانِبِهِ. والهاءُ: عائِدَةٌ عَلى المُسْتَوْقَدِ. فَإنْ قِيلَ: كَيْفَ وحَّدَ، فَقالَ: ﴿كَمَثَلِ الَّذِي اسْتَوْقَدَ﴾ ثُمَّ جَمَعَ فَقالَ: ﴿ذَهَبَ اللَّهُ بِنُورِهِمْ﴾ ؟ فالجَوابُ: أنَّ ثَعْلَبًا حَكى عَنِ الفَرّاءِ أنَّهُ قالَ: إنَّما ضُرِبَ المَثَلُ لِلْفِعْلِ، لا لِأعْيانِ الرِّجالِ، وهو مَثَلٌ لِلنِّفاقِ. وإنَّما قالَ: ﴿ذَهَبَ اللَّهُ بِنُورِهِمْ﴾ لِأنَّ المَعْنى ذاهِبٌ إلى المُنافِقِينَ، فَجُمِعَ لِذَلِكَ. قالَ ثَعْلَبٌ: وقالَ غَيْرُ الفَرّاءُ: مَعْنى الَّذِي: الجَمْعُ، وُحِّدَ أوَّلًا لِلَفْظِهِ، وجُمِعَ بَعْدُ لِمَعْناهُ، كَما قالَ الشّاعِرُ:(p-٤٠)

Regarding "mā" there are two views. One is that it is extra, the sense being "aḍāʾat ḥawlahu" (it lit up around him). The second is that it means "alladhī" (that which). "Ḥawl" (around) of a thing is what surrounds it from its sides. The pronoun (hāʾ) refers back to the one who kindled. If it is asked: how did He use the singular, saying ﴿kamathali alladhī istawqada﴾ (like one who kindled), and then the plural, saying ﴿dhahaba Allahu bi-nūrihim﴾ (Allah took away their light)? The answer: Tha'lab related from al-Farra' that he said: the parable was struck for the act, not for the individual men, and it is a parable for hypocrisy. He said ﴿dhahaba Allahu bi-nūrihim﴾ because the meaning turns toward the hypocrites, so it was made plural accordingly. Tha'lab said: others than al-Farra' said: the meaning of "alladhī" is plural; it was made singular first for its wording and plural afterward for its meaning, as the poet said:

؎ فَإنَّ الَّذِي حانَتْ بِفَلْجٍ دِماؤُهم ∗∗∗ هُمُ القَوْمُ كُلُّ القَوْمِ يا أمَّ خالِدٍ

*Indeed those whose blood was shed at Falj, they are the people, all the people, O mother of Khalid.*

فَجَعَلَ "الَّذِي" جَمْعًا.

Thus he made "alladhī" plural.

فَصْلٌ

اخْتَلَفَ العُلَماءُ في الَّذِي ضَرَبَ اللَّهُ تَعالى لَهُ هَذا المَثَلَ مِن أحْوالِ المُنافِقِينَ عَلى قَوْلَيْنِ. أحَدُهُما: أنَّهُ ضَرَبَ بِكَلِمَةِ الإسْلامِ الَّتِي يَلْفِظُونَ بِها، ونُورُها صِيانَةُ النُّفُوسِ وحَقْنُ الدِّماءِ، فَإذا ماتُوا سَلْبَهُمُ اللَّهُ ذَلِكَ العِزَّ، كَما سَلَبَ صاحِبَ النّارِ ضَوْءَهُ. وهَذا المَعْنى مَرْوِيٌّ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ. والثّانِي: أنَّهُ ضَرَبَ لِإقْبالِهِمْ عَلى المُؤْمِنِينَ وسَماعِهِمْ ما جاءَ بِهِ الرَّسُولُ، فَذَهابُ نُورِهِمْ: إقْبالُهم عَلى الكافِرِينَ والضَّلالُ، وهَذا قَوْلُ مُجاهِدٍ.

Section

The scholars differed about what Allah struck this parable for, from among the states of the hypocrites, in two views. One is that it was struck for the word of Islam which they utter; its light is the preservation of their lives and the safeguarding of their blood, but when they die Allah strips them of that honor, just as He stripped the owner of the fire of its light. This meaning is related from Ibn 'Abbas. The second is that it was struck for their turning toward the believers and their listening to what the Messenger brought; so the taking away of their light is their turning toward the disbelievers and misguidance. This is the view of Mujahid.

وَفِي المُرادِ بِـ "الظُّلُماتِ" هاهُنا أرْبَعَةُ أقْوالٍ. أحَدُها: العَذابُ، قالَهُ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ. والثّانِي: ظُلْمَةُ الكُفْرِ، قالَهُ مُجاهِدٌ. والثّالِثُ: ظُلْمَةٌ يُلْقِيها اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِمْ بَعْدَ المَوْتِ، قالَهُ قَتادَةُ. والرّابِعُ: أنَّها نِفاقُهم قالَهُ السُّدِّيُّ.

Regarding what is meant by "ẓulumāt" (darknesses) here, there are four views. The first is punishment, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second is the darkness of disbelief, said by Mujahid. The third is a darkness Allah casts upon them after death, said by Qatada. The fourth is that it is their hypocrisy, said by al-Suddi.

فَصْلٌ

وَفِي ضَرْبِ المَثَلِ لَهم بِالنّارِ ثَلاثُ حِكَمٍ.

Section

In striking the parable for them with fire there are three wisdoms.

إحْداها: أنَّ المُسْتَضِيءَ بِالنّارِ مُسْتَضِيءٌ بِنُورٍ مِن جِهَةِ غَيْرِهِ، لا مِن قِبَلِ نَفْسِهِ، فَإذا ذَهَبَتْ تِلْكَ النّارُ بَقِيَ في ظُلْمَةٍ، فَكَأنَّهم لَمّا أقَرُّوا بِألْسِنَتِهِمْ مِن غَيْرِ اعْتِقادِ قُلُوبِهِمْ، كانَ نُورُ إيمانِهِمْ كالمُسْتَعارِ.

The first: one who is lit by fire is lit by light from another source, not from himself; when that fire goes out, he remains in darkness. So, since they confessed with their tongues without belief in their hearts, the light of their faith was like something borrowed.

والثّانِيَةُ: أنَّ ضِياءَ النّارِ يَحْتاجُ في دَوامِهِ إلى مادَّةِ الحَطَبِ، فَهو لَهُ كَغِذاءِ الحَيَوانِ، فَكَذَلِكَ نُورُ الإيمانِ يَحْتاجُ إلى مادَّةِ الِاعْتِقادِ لِيَدُومَ.

The second: the light of fire needs fuel to continue, which is its sustenance like the food of a living creature; likewise the light of faith needs the sustenance of conviction in order to endure.

(p-٤١)والثّانِيَةُ أنَّ الظُّلْمَةَ الحادِثَةَ بَعْدَ الضَّوْءِ أشَدُّ عَلى الإنْسانِ مِن ظُلْمَةٍ لَمْ يَجِدْ مَعَها ضِياءٌ، فَشَبَّهَ حالَهم بِذَلِكَ.

(p-41) The second [wisdom, as stated in the text]: the darkness that comes after light is harder on a person than a darkness in which he never found any light; so He likened their condition to that.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 18:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind﴾.

Al-samam (deafness) is the blocking of the openings of hearing, and it is more severe than al-taresh (partial deafness). Regarding al-bukm (dumbness) there are three opinions. The first: it is al-khares (muteness), said by Muqatil, Abu 'Ubayd, and Ibn Faris. The second: it is a defect in the tongue that prevents one from speech; it was said that khares is acquired (lit. "is produced anew") from it. The third: it is a defect in the heart that prevents one from taking in something so as to understand it, thereby combining corruption in the locus of understanding and the locus of speech. Our shaykh mentioned these two opinions.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So they do not return﴾.

On this there are three opinions. The first: they do not return from their misguidance, said by Qatadah and Muqatil. The second: they do not return to Islam, said by al-Suddi. The third: they do not return from deafness, dumbness, and blindness. He attributed the returning to them because they turned away by their own choice, due to the dominance of their desires over examining guidance with the instruments of examination; they were not actually deaf or dumb. And because, when they turned away from hearing the truth and speaking it, they became like the deaf and dumb. The Arabs call one who turns away from a thing "blind," and one who turns away from hearing it "deaf." Miskin al-Darimi said:

؎ What harm does it do to my neighbour, whom I live beside, that his door has no curtain?

؎ I am blind when my neighbour comes out, until the curtain covers my neighbour.

؎ And my ear is deaf to what is between them, until it is as though it were heavy (deaf).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 19:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or like a rainstorm from the sky﴾

"Aw" (or) is a particle referring back to His saying: ﴿Their likeness is like the likeness of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17]. The scholars differed concerning it in six opinions.

The first: that it is here for choice (takhyir). The Arabs say: "Sit with the jurists or the grammarians," meaning: you are free to sit with whichever of the two groups you wish. It is as if He gave us the choice between presenting them the first parable or the second.

The second: that it is for indefiniteness (ibham) concerning what Allah knows to be realized, so that what they do not seek to have detailed is left vague for them. It is as if He said: "Their likeness is like one of these two." A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Then they are like stones, or harder in hardness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74]. The Arabs leave vague what has no benefit in being detailed. Labid said:

"My two daughters wish that their father would live, and am I anything but of Rabi'ah or Mudar?"

That is: am I anything but from one of these two groups? Both of them have perished, so my way is to perish as they perished.

The third: that it means "bal" (rather). Al-Farra' recited:

"She appeared like the sun's horn in the brightness of forenoon, and her form, or you are more graceful in the eye."

The fourth: that it is for distribution (tafsil). Its meaning: some of them are likened to the one who kindled a fire, and some of them to the people of the rainstorm. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Be Jews or Christians﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135]; its meaning: some of them said, namely the Jews: "Be Jews," and the Christians said: "Be Christians." Likewise His saying: ﴿Our punishment came upon it by night, or while they were resting at midday﴾ [al-A'raf: 4]; its meaning: some of them had Our punishment come upon them by night, and some of them had Our punishment come upon them at the time of midday rest.

The fifth: that it means "waw" (and). A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿that you eat from your houses or the houses of your fathers﴾ [al-Nur: 61]. Jarir said:

"He attained the caliphate, or it was for him a decree, just as Moses came to his Lord at an appointed time."

The sixth: that it is for doubt regarding those addressed, since doubt is exalted above the Truth, mighty and majestic. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿and it is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27]; he means: restoration is easier than initiation, according to what you suppose.

As for the explanation of the meaning of the speech: "or like the people of a rainstorm," the word "people" (ashab) is omitted, because His saying ﴿they put their fingers in their ears﴾ is evidence for it.

Al-sayyib: the rain. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is fay'al from "saba yasoub," when it descends from the sky. Al-Zajjaj said: whatever descends from a height to a lower place has "saba yasoub." The poet said:

"As if a cloud had struck upon them, whose lightning bolts are a crawling for their birds."

Concerning thunder (al-rad) there are three opinions.

The first: that it is the voice of an angel who drives the clouds. This meaning has been related as a marfu' report to the Prophet (ﷺ), and Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said so. In one narration from Mujahid, it is the voice of an angel who glorifies (Allah). 'Ikrimah said: it is an angel who drives the clouds as the driver drives the camels.

The second: that it is wind confined between the sky and the earth. It has been related from Abu al-Jild that he said: "al-Ra'd: the wind." Abu al-Jild's name is Jilan ibn Abi Farwah al-Basri, and Qatadah narrated from him.

The third: that it is the collision of the bodies of the clouds, related by our shaykh 'Ali ibn 'Ubayd Allah.

Concerning lightning (al-barq) there are three opinions.

The first: that it is whips (makhariq) with which the angel drives the clouds. This meaning has been related as a marfu' report to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is the saying of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. In one narration from 'Ali he said: it is a striking with an iron whip. And from Ibn 'Abbas: it is a striking with a whip of light. Ibn al-Anbari said: al-makhariq are cloths that are wrapped, with which children strike one another, so he likened the whip with which the clouds are struck to that makhraq.

'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

"As if our swords among us and among them were makhariq in the hands of our playing youths."

Mujahid said: al-barq is the angel's striking and shaking, and al-mas' is striking and moving.

The second: that al-barq is water; this was said by Abu al-Jild, and Ibn Faris related that al-barq is the glitter of water.

The third: that it is fire struck out from the collision of the bodies of the clouds as they move and strike one another; related by our shaykh.

As for al-sawa'iq, it is the plural of sa'iqah, which is a severe sound from the sound of thunder, accompanied by a piece of fire that burns whatever it strikes. It was related from Shahr ibn Hawshab that the angel who drives the clouds, when his anger intensifies, fire flies from his mouth, and that is the sawa'iq. Others said: they are fire that sparks from the collision of the bodies of the clouds. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is called sa'iqah because when it strikes it kills; one says "sa'aqathum," meaning, it killed them.

**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and Allah encompasses the disbelievers﴾.

Concerning it there are three opinions.

The first: that none of them escapes Him, so He will gather them on the Day of Resurrection. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿He has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ [al-Talaq: 12]; this was said by Mujahid.

The second: that ihata (encompassing) means destruction, like His saying: ﴿and its fruit was encompassed﴾ [al-Kahf: 42].

The third: that nothing they do is hidden from Him.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 2, verse 20:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾. *Yakādu* means "it approaches" (nearly). It is a word which, when affirmed, negates the action, and when negated, affirms the action. One of the later scholars was asked, and it was said to him:

؎ Is it the grammarian of this age who says, "What is this word that has run on the tongues of Jurhum and Thamud?"

؎ "When you negate it, and God is witness, it affirms; and when it is affirmed, it takes the place of denial."

[p. 45] Evidence for its affirmation when negated is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They almost do not understand any speech﴾ [al-Nisa': 87], and His saying: ﴿When he extends his hand, he almost does not see it﴾ [al-Nur: 40]. Similar to this is ﴿and he can hardly express himself clearly﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 43]. Evidence for its negation when affirmed is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The lightning nearly [yakādu]﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20], ﴿The brilliance of His lightning nearly [yakādu]﴾ [al-Nur: 43], and ﴿Its oil nearly [yakādu] gives light﴾ [al-Nur: 35].

Ibn Qutayba said: *kāda* means "he intended but did not do." It has also come with the meaning of affirmation. Dhu al-Rummah said:

؎ "Even if Luqman the Wise had encountered, before his eyes, a woman unveiled, he would nearly [kāda] be dazzled."

That is, if she had presented herself to him, he would have been dazzled, meaning he would have been astonished and bewildered.

I say: Dhu al-Rummah has also used the negated form in a way that shows it is used for affirmation, in his saying:

؎ "When distance has changed the lovers, the trace of passion does not nearly [yakad] depart from love of Miyya."

He meant: it did not depart.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿snatches away their sight﴾.

The majority read it with a *fatḥa* on the *yā'*, a *sukūn* on the *khā'*, and a *fatḥa* on the *ṭā'*. Abān ibn Taghlib and Abān ibn Yazid, both on the authority of 'Asim, read with a *fatḥa* on the *yā'*, a *sukūn* on the *khā'*, and a *kasra* on the *ṭā'*, lightened. Al-Ju'fi related from Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, a *fatḥa* on the *yā'*, a *kasra* on the *khā'*, and a shadda on the *ṭā'*; this is also the recitation of al-Hasan in this form, except that he put a *kasra* on the *yā'*. And from him (al-Hasan) also: a *fatḥa* on the *yā'* and the *khā'* with a *kasra* on the shadda-ed *ṭā'*.

The meaning of *yakhṭifu* is "seizes/plunders." The original sense of *ikhtiṭāf* is seizing. What the bucket is drawn with is called *khuṭṭāf* (a pulley-wheel), because it snatches up what is hung from it. al-Nabigha said:

؎ "Pulleys, hooked, in ropes of twisted fiber, which hands pull toward you, drawing them."

*Ḥajn* means "curved/hooked," and a *khayṭaf* camel is one that moves swiftly; that swiftness is called *al-khaṭfā*.

**

[p. 46] His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whenever it lights up for them﴾.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is said *ḍā'a al-shay'u yaḍū'u* and *aḍā'a yuḍī'u*, and this second dialect is the preferred one.

**Section**

The scholars differed over what resembles the thunder among the matters connected with the conditions of the hypocrites, in three opinions.

The first: it is the frightening (*takhwīf*) found in the Qur'an. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it is what they fear of calamities that might befall them if the Prophet and the believers came to know of their hypocrisy. This was said by Mujahid and al-Suddi.

The third: it is what they fear from the call to jihad and fighting those whose friendship they feign. This was mentioned by our shaykh.

They also differed over what resembles the lightning among their conditions, in three opinions. One: it is what becomes clear to them of the admonitions and wisdom of the Qur'an. Two: it is the light of their Islam, which they display, that shines for them. Three: it is a parable for what they gain by displaying Islam, namely the preservation of their blood, which, compared with what has been stored up for them at their term, is like the lightning.

They differed over the meaning of His saying: ﴿They put their fingers in their ears because of the thunderbolts﴾, in two opinions. One: they used to flee from hearing the Qur'an, lest it command them to jihad and to face death. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Suddi. Two: it is a parable for their turning away from the Qur'an out of aversion to it. This was said by Muqatil.

They differed over the meaning of ﴿Whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾, in four opinions.

One: its meaning is that whenever the Qur'an brings them what they love, they follow it. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi.

[p. 47] Two: the lighting of the lightning is the attainment of what they hope for, namely the safety of their souls and property, so they hasten to follow it. This was said by Qatada.

Three: it is their speaking with Islam and their walking in it, their being guided by it; and when they abandon that, they stand in error. This was said by Muqatil.

Four: its lighting for them is their being left without trial or test, and their walking in it is their remaining in peaceful coexistence through displaying what they display. This was mentioned by our shaykh.

As for

**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when it darkens over them﴾: whoever says that its lighting is its bringing them what they love, says that its darkening is its bringing them what they hate. And all the other opinions we have mentioned follow the reverse of this.

The meaning of *qāmū* ("they stood"): they halted.

**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Had God willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight﴾. Muqatil said: its meaning is: had He willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight as a punishment for them. Mujahid said: at the beginning of al-Baqarah there are four verses describing the believers, two verses describing the disbelievers, and thirteen describing the hypocrites.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 21:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, that you may become righteous.﴾

The scholars differed about who is meant by this address, giving four opinions. The first: it is general, addressing all of mankind, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. The second: it is addressed to the Jews alone, to the exclusion of others; this was said by al-Hasan and Mujahid. The third: it is addressed to the disbelievers, from among the polytheists of the Arabs and others; this was said by al-Suddi. The fourth: it is addressed to the hypocrites and the Jews; this was said by Muqatil. "Al-nas" (mankind) is the name for the human animal. They were so named because of their movement in their desires; al-nawS (al-nawsu) means movement. It was also said that they were named unas (ünās) because of the forgetfulness that overtakes them. (p-48)

Regarding the meaning of worship here, there are two opinions. One: monotheism (tawhid). The second: obedience (ta'a). Both were narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-khalq means creation and bringing into existence. He mentioned "those before you" because it is more forceful in reminding, more decisive in refuting denial, and more careful in establishing proof. It was also said that He mentioned those before them so as to alert them to take warning from their circumstances: the reward of the obedient and the punishment of the disobedient.

Regarding "la'alla" (perhaps / so that), there are two opinions.

One: it carries the meaning of "kay" (in order that), and they cited in support of this:

"You said to us, 'Cease the wars, so that perhaps we may cease, and you pledged to us every binding pledge.'
But when we ceased the war, your covenants were like the glint of a mirage shining in the open plain."

He means: "so that we may cease." This is the view of Muqatil, Qutrub, and Ibn Kaysan.

The second: it carries the meaning of hope (tarajji), and its meaning is: worship Allah, hoping for righteousness, and that through worship you may protect yourselves from the punishment of your Lord. This is the view of Sibawayh. Ibn 'Abbas said: "that you may become righteous of shirk (associating partners with Allah)." al-Dahhak said: "that you may guard against the Fire." Mujahid said: "that you may obey."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 22:

Allah's statement: ﴿Who made the earth for you a bed﴾.

The earth (al-ard) was so named for its vastness (si'ah), from the saying of the Arabs: "aridat al-qurhah" (the sore spread out), meaning when it expands.

It is also said: it was named so for its being lowered (inhitat) below the sky, and everything that is low is "ard." It is also said: it was named so because people trample it (yarudduna) with their feet. The sky was named sama' (sky) for its height (ulluw). Al-Zajjaj said: everything that rises above the earth is called "bina'" (building/structure). Ibn 'Abbas said: "al-bina'" here means the ceiling (saqf).

**

Allah's statement: ﴿And sent down from the sky﴾, meaning from the clouds.

﴿water﴾, meaning: rain.

**

(p-49) ﴿So do not set up rivals (andad) to Allah﴾, meaning: partners, equals. It is said: "hadha nidd hadha" (this is the rival of that), and "nadidahu." Regarding what is meant by "andad" here, there are two opinions. The first: idols, said by Ibn Zayd. The second: men whom they obeyed in disobedience to Allah, said by al-Suddi.

**

Allah's statement: ﴿while you know﴾.

On this there are six opinions.

The first: "while you know" that He created the sky, sent down the water, and did what is described in these verses. This meaning is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and Muqatil.

The second: "while you know" that this is not in your books, the Torah and the Gospel. This is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and it follows the view of those who say the address is to the People of the Book.

The third: "while you know" that He has no rival, said by Mujahid.

The fourth: that knowledge here means intellect ('aql), said by Ibn Qutaybah.

The fifth: "while you know" that no one other than Him can do what He mentioned, mentioned by our shaykh 'Ali ibn 'Ubayd Allah.

The sixth: "while you know" that they (the idols) are stones, which I heard from the shaykh Abu Muhammad ibn al-Khashshab.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 23:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you are in doubt﴾.

The occasion of its revelation was that the Jews said: "This which Muhammad brings to us does not resemble revelation, and indeed we are in doubt about it," so this verse was revealed. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Muqatil. The "in" (inna) here is not for [expressing] doubt, because Allah, exalted is He, knew that they were skeptical; rather, this is a custom of the Arabs, as a man says to his son: "If you are my son, then obey me." It was also said that it here carries the meaning of "idh" (when). Abu Zayd said: among its examples is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And leave what remains of interest, if you are believers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 278].

**

(p-50) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then produce a surah like it﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: the word "surah" is pronounced with a hamza and without a hamza. Whoever pronounces it with a hamza takes it from "asʾarat," meaning "afdalat" (it surpassed), because it is a portion of the Qur'an; and whoever does not pronounce it with a hamza takes it from "surat al-bina'" (the rank of a building), i.e., one station after another. al-Nabigha said about al-Nu'man:

Have you not seen that Allah has given you a surah, by which you see every king below it swaying?

The "surah" in this verse is the surah of glory, and it is borrowed from the surah of building. Ibn al-Anbari said: Abu ʿUbayda said: the surah was only called a surah because one rises in it from one station to another, like the surah of building. The meaning of "He gave you a surah" is a station of honor by which you rose above the stations of kings. Ibn al-Qasim said: it may also be that it was named a surah for its nobility; the Arabs say: "He has a surah in glory," meaning nobility and elevation; or because it is a portion of the Qur'an, from your saying "asʾartu suʾran," meaning "I left a remainder." Regarding the pronoun in "mithlihi" there are two views. One: it refers to the revealed Qur'an, said by Qatadah, al-Farra', and Muqatil. The second: it refers to the Prophet ﷺ, so the meaning becomes: "then produce a surah like this unlettered servant," mentioned by Abu ʿUbayda, al-Zajjaj, and Ibn al-Qasim. According to this view, "min" is for the beginning of the limit; and according to the first view, it is superfluous (zaʾidah).

**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and call your witnesses besides Allah﴾.

Regarding this there are two views. One: its meaning is "seek help" (istaʿinu, from al-maʿunah), said by al-Suddi and al-Farra'. The second: "seek aid" (istughithu, from al-istighathah), and they recited:

When our horsemen and their men met, they called "O family of Kaʿb!" and we claimed affiliation with ʿAmir.

This is the view of Ibn Qutaybah.

(p-51) Regarding "their witnesses" there are three views.

One: they are their gods, said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Suddi, Muqatil, and al-Farra'. Ibn Qutaybah said: they were called witnesses because they bring them along and present them. Others said: because they worshipped them so that they would bear witness for them before Allah.

The second: they are their helpers, also related from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: its meaning is "then produce people who will testify that what you bring is like the Qur'an," related from Mujahid.

**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿if you are truthful﴾, i.e., in your claim that this Qur'an is not from Allah, said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 24:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But if you do not⟩ — in this verse there is an implied, understood element, which the sense requires to be placed before it: namely, that when He challenged them with what is in the preceding verse of challenge, and they remained silent without answering, He said: ﴿But if you do not⟩. And in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and you will never⟩ there is a greater proof of the soundness of the prophethood of our Prophet, because He informed that they would not do it, and they did not do it.

**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So fear the Fire whose fuel is men and stones; it has been prepared for the disbelievers⟩.

Al-wuqud (الوَقُود), with a fatḥa on the waw, is the firewood, and with a ḍammah it is the act of kindling (al-tawaqqud); it is like al-wuḍū' (الوَضُوء) with a fatḥa meaning the water, and with a ḍammah meaning the verbal noun, which is the name for the actions of the one performing ablution. Al-Ḥasan and Qatada read wuqūduhā (وقُودُها) with a ḍammah on the waw, but the preferred reading is with a fatḥa. "The people" (al-nās) are those who kindled it in the way of punishment, and "the stones" are mentioned to show its strength and intensity, since it burns even stones. Regarding these stones there are two views. The first: they are the idols they worshipped, as stated by al-Rabi' ibn Anas. The second: they are sulphur stones, which are the hottest of things; when heated, they are used to punish them. The meaning of "prepared" (u'iddat) is "made ready."

The warning with the Fire is given because they did not bring anything like the Qur'an: when they denied it and were unable to produce its like, the proof was established against them, and their opposition became obstinacy, and the recompense of the obstinate is the Fire.(p-52)

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 25:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And give good news to those who believe﴾.

Bishara (good news): it is the first report that reaches a person, and it is called bishara because it affects the skin (bashra) of the one who receives it. If it is good, its effect is the manifestation of joy and expansion; if it is bad, its effect is contraction and grief. In common usage, bishara is most often used for good news, though it may also be used for bad news, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Give the hypocrites the good news that there is a painful punishment for them﴾ [al-Nisa': 138].

**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾.

It encompasses every righteous deed. It has been related from Uthman ibn Affan that he said: "Make your deeds sincere." And from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Establish the obligatory prayers."

As for ﴿gardens﴾ (jannat), it is the plural of jannah (garden). The garden was named jannah because its land is concealed (istitar) by its trees. The jinn were named jinn because they are concealed, and the embryo (janin) is from this root. The shield is called junna, and "the night concealed (janna al-layl)" when it covered everything. It is related from al-Mufaddal that the jannah is every orchard containing palm trees. Al-Zajjaj said: every plant that grows thick and abundant, with its parts covering one another, is a jannah.

**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾, meaning: beneath its trees, not beneath its ground.

**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿This is what we were provided with before﴾. There are three opinions concerning it:

The first: its meaning is "This is what we were fed before," since the provision of the morning is like the provision of the evening. This was related from Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, and Muqatil.

The second: "This is what we were provided with before" in the world. This was said by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd.

The third: when the fruit of the Garden is plucked, its like is produced in its place; and when they see what has replaced what was plucked, it appears similar to them, so they say: ﴿This is what we were provided with before﴾. This was said by Yahya ibn Abi Kathir and Abu Ubayda.

**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and they will be given it in resemblance﴾.

There are three opinions concerning it.

The first: that it resembles in appearance and color but differs in taste. This was said by Mujahid, Abu al-Aliyah, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, and Muqatil.

The second: that it resembles in its excellence, with no inferiority in it. This was said by al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj.

The third: that it resembles the fruits of this world in form and name, but is better in appearance and taste. This was said by Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. If someone says: what is the point of the favor in its resemblance, when the more varied the foods and the more diverse their colors, the better they are? The answer: if we say it resembles in appearance but differs in taste, it is more wondrous to the creation and better; for if you saw an apple containing the taste of all other fruits, that would be the utmost in wonder. If we say it resembles in excellence, it may differ in colors and tastes. If we say it resembles the form of the fruits of this world while the meanings differ, it would be more novel and more marvelous, and all of these are compelling considerations.

**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And for them therein are spouses purified﴾, meaning: in their nature, for they do not menstruate, nor do they urinate, nor do they defecate. And in their character, for they do not envy, nor are they jealous, and they do not look at anyone other than their husbands.

Ibn Abbas said: "pure from filth and harm." Al-Zajjaj said: "purified" (mutahhara) is more emphatic than "pure" (tahira), because it denotes intensity. And khulud (eternity): lasting permanence that has no cessation.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 26:

Allah's words: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example (mathal), [even] of a gnat or what is above it.﴾

There are two reports about the occasion of its revelation.

The first: When Allah revealed ﴿A parable has been presented, so listen to it. Indeed, those you invoke other than Allah will never create a fly, even if they gathered together for it﴾ [al-Hajj 22:73], and revealed ﴿like the example of the spider, which takes a house﴾ [al-Ankabut 29:41], the Jews said, "What are these parables?" So this verse was revealed. This was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada, Muqatil and al-Farra'.

The second: When Allah struck the two earlier parables, namely ﴿like the example of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:17] and ﴿or like a rainstorm from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:19], the hypocrites said, "Allah is too exalted and too high to strike such examples." So this verse was revealed. Al-Suddi related it from his shaykhs, and similar was reported from al-Hasan and Mujahid.

Al-hayaa' (with a long vowel) means withdrawal and restraint (inqibad wa ihtishaam). However, the attributes of the Truth, mighty and majestic is He, are not to be grasped as to their modality; rather they are affirmed as they have come. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed your Lord is Shy (hayiyy) and Generous (karim)." It was also said that the meaning of ﴿is not ashamed﴾ is: "does not leave off." Ibn Jarir al-Tabari related from some of the linguists that the meaning of ﴿is not ashamed﴾ is: "does not fear." A parallel is Allah's words: ﴿and you fear the people, while Allah has more right that you fear Him﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:37], i.e., you feel shame before Him. Thus al-istihya' (shame) and al-khashya (fear) may each substitute for the other. Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin read it as ﴿la yastahi﴾ with a single ya', and this is a dialect.

Allah's words: ﴿to strike an example (mathal)﴾.

Ibn Abbas said: "to mention a likeness (shabah)." Know that the benefit of the mathal is that the matter for which it was struck becomes clear to the one to whom it is struck, so its obscurity is cleared away.

**

Allah's words: ﴿a gnat (ba'udah)﴾.

Ma here is superfluous (za'idah), and this is the choice of Abu Ubayda, al-Zajjaj and the Basrans. They cited for it the verse of al-Nabighah:

[She said]: Alas, would that this dove of ours [were exchanged] for her dove, or half of it, [then it] is lost.

Abu Ja'far al-Tabari mentioned that the meaning is "from a gnat up to what is above it," and then the mention of "from" (bayna) and "up to" (ila) was omitted, since the accusative of "gnat" and the entry of the fa' on the second ma indicate them, as the Arabs said: "We were rained upon from Mazabalah up to al-Tha'labiyyah," and "He has twenty she-camels, ma naqatan fa-jamalan" [meaning: from her head to her feet], and "She is the most beautiful of people, ma qarana fa-qadama" [meaning: from her horn to her foot]. Others said: the accusative of "gnat" is in apposition (badal) to "example."

Al-Asma'i related from Nafi': "ba'udatun" with a nominative, by supposing a pronoun ("huwa"). The ba'udah is the small gnat (saffirat al-baqq).

**

Allah's words: ﴿and what is above it﴾. Concerning this there are two views.

The first: its meaning is "and what is above it in size." This was said by Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Jurayj and al-Farra'.

The second: "and what is above it in smallness," so its meaning would be "and what is below it." This was said by Abu Ubayda.

Ibn Qutaybah said: "The fawq may also mean 'below' (duna), and it is among the words with opposite meanings (al-adhdad).
