Similar to it: al-jawn, which is said of both the black and the white; al-sarim, meaning both dawn and night; al-sudfah, meaning both darkness and light; al-hullal, meaning both the small and the large; al-nahil, meaning both the thirsty and the sated; al-mathil, meaning both the standing and the one lying flat on the ground; al-sarikh, meaning both the helper and the one seeking help; al-hajid, meaning both one who prays at night and one who sleeps; al-rahwah, meaning both elevation and descent; al-tal'ah, meaning both what is raised from the earth and what is lowered from it; al-zann, meaning both certainty and doubt; al-aqra', meaning both menstruation and purity; al-mufarra' fi al-jabal, meaning both the ascent and the descent; al-waraa', meaning both behind and in front; asrartu al-shay', meaning both I concealed it and I made it public; akhfaytu al-shay', meaning both I revealed it and I hid it; rataw al-shay', meaning both I tightened it and I loosened it; sha'abtu al-shay', meaning both I gathered it and I scattered it; bi'tu al-shay', meaning both I sold it and I bought it; shariytu al-shay', meaning both I bought it and I sold it; and al-hayy khulufun, meaning both absent and differing."

**

They differed concerning Allah's words: ﴿by it He misleads many and by it He guides many﴾, whether it is part of the speech of those who said ﴿What does Allah intend by this as an example?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:26], or whether it is a new beginning from the speech of Allah, mighty and majestic is He. There are two views.

The first: that it is the completion of the preceding speech. This was said by al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah. Al-Farra' said: "It is as if they said: 'What does Allah intend by an example that every person does not understand, by which this one is misled and by which that one is guided?!' Then the speech was resumed, and Allah's report was introduced, and He said: ﴿And He does not mislead by it except the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqin)﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:26]."

The second: that it is a new beginning from the words of Allah, mighty and majestic is He. This was said by al-Suddi and Muqatil.

As for al-fisq (defiant disobedience), linguistically it means "going out." It is said: "fasaqat al-rutabah" when the date came out of its skin. So the fasiq is one who goes out of obedience to Allah into disobedience to Him.

Concerning who is meant by al-fasiqin here, there are three views. The first: they are the Jews, said by Ibn Abbas and Muqatil. The second: the hypocrites, said by Abu al-Aliyah and al-Suddi. The third: all the disbelievers.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 27:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who break the covenant of Allah﴾.

This is a description of the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqin), and the three opinions about them have already been mentioned. Naqd (breaking) is the opposite of ibram (firm binding), and its meaning is undoing a thing after it has been tied. Naqd applies to each thing according to what suits it: the breaking of a building is the scattering of what was joined after it was made firm, and the breaking of a covenant is abandoning adherence to its terms.

Regarding this covenant there are three opinions.

The first: it is what was enjoined upon the People of the Book concerning the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the instruction to follow him. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Muqatil.

The second: it is what was enjoined upon them in the Qur'an, so they acknowledged it and then disbelieved. This was said by al-Suddi.

The third: it is the covenant that He took from them when He brought forth the offspring of Adam from his loins. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Although we have not mentioned that covenant, it has been established by the report of the Truthful (ﷺ), so belief in it is obligatory.

Regarding "min" (from) there are two views. The first: it is extra (za'ida). The second: it denotes the starting point (li-ibtida' al-ghayah), as if he said: the beginning of the breaking of the covenant is after its binding. Regarding the pronoun in "mithaqihi" (its binding) there are two views. The first: it refers to Allah, exalted is He. The second: it refers to the covenant, so its meaning is: after the firm establishment of the agreement concerning it.

Regarding "that which Allah commanded to be joined" there are three opinions. The first: it is the kinship ties and relatives. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and al-Suddi. The second: it is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), whom they severed by denying him. This was said by al-Hasan. The third: it is belief in Allah and not distinguishing between any of His messengers, so they believed in some and disbelieved in others. This was said by Muqatil.

Regarding their corruption on the earth there are three opinions. The first: it is their calling people to disbelief. This was said by Ibn Abbas. The second: it is acting in acts of disobedience. This was said by al-Suddi and Muqatil. The third: it is their cutting off the road to those who came as emigrants to the Prophet (ﷺ), in order to prevent people from Islam.

Al-khusran (loss) in the language means deficiency.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 28:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿How do you disbelieve in Allah﴾. Regarding "kayfa" (how) there are two views.

The first: it is an interrogative used in the sense of wonder (ta'ajjub), and this wonder is directed at the believers, meaning: be amazed at these people, how they disbelieve when the proof of Allah has already been established against them. This was said by Ibn Qutaybah and al-Zajjaj.

The second: it is an interrogative that serves the purpose of affirmation (taqrir) and rebuke (tawbikh). Its implied meaning is: "And [yet] how do you disbelieve in Allah?" Al-Ajjaj said:

Did you become merry, while you are an old man, and time, for man, is a turner [of affairs]?

He meant: Do you become merry while you are an elderly old man?! This was said by Ibn al-Anbari.

**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you were dead﴾.

al-Farra' said: meaning, "and you had been dead." Similar is ﴿or they come to you with their hearts restrained﴾ [an-Nisa: 90], meaning, "they had been restrained." Similar also is ﴿and if his shirt is torn from behind, then she has lied﴾ [Yusuf: 26], meaning, "then she had lied." Were it not for the implied "qad," such a construction would not be permissible in speech.

Regarding the two lives and the two deaths there are several views. The most correct of them is that the first death is their state of being drops of semen, clots, and lumps of flesh, and He gave them life in the wombs; then He causes them to die after they emerge into this world; then He gives them life again for resurrection on the Day of Resurrection. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, Muqatil, al-Farra', Tha'lab, al-Zajjaj, Ibn Qutaybah, and Ibn al-Anbari.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 29:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is He who created for you whatever is on the earth, all of it﴾, meaning: for your sake. Some of it is for benefit, and some of it is for reflection (i'tibar, taking lessons).

﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾, meaning: He intended its creation (ʿamada ila khuluqiha). The word "al-sama'" (heaven) is singular in its form, but its meaning is plural, as is evidenced by His saying: ﴿and He completed them as seven heavens﴾.

As for which of the two was created first, the earth or the heaven, there are two opinions. One is that the earth was first; this was said by Mujahid. The second is that the heaven was first; this was said by Muqatil.

They differed concerning the manner in which the creation of the earth and what is in it was completed. Ibn 'Abbas said: He began with the creation of the earth in two days, then He created the heavens in two days, and He measured within them their sustenance (aqwatiha) in two days. Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: He gathered the creation of the earth and what is in it into four consecutive days, then He created the heaven in two days.

As for "al-'Alim" (the All-Knowing), it is in the pattern of fa'il (fa'il), for emphasis in describing Him with the perfection of knowledge.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 30–31:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels﴾.

Abu 'Ubayda used to say: "idh" (when) is superfluous (mulghah), and the sense of the sentence is: "and your Lord said." Ibn Qutayba followed him in this, but al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Qasim criticized both of them for it. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "idh" is "the time," as though He said: "The beginning of your creation was when your Lord said to the angels."

"Al-malaika" (the angels) derives from al-ulook (الأُلُوك), which means message. Labid said:

"And a youth whose mother sent him with a message (bi-alook), so we gave what he asked."

The singular of "malaika" is "malak" (angel), and its original form is "mal'ak." Sibawayh recited:

"So I am not for a human, but for a mal'ak descending from the expanse of the sky, showering [rain]."

Abu Ishaq said: the meaning of mal'ak is "one who carries a message." It is said: ma'laka, ma'luka, and mal'aka. Ma'alik is the plural of ma'luka. The poet said:

"Convey to al-Nu'man on my behalf a messenger (ma'luka), that he has long kept me imprisoned and waiting."

Regarding these angels there are two views. The first: they are all the angels; this was said by al-Suddi, from his shaykhs. The second: they are those who were with Iblis when he was sent down to the earth; this was mentioned by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

It is related that there were beings on the earth before Adam, who caused corruption, so God sent Iblis with a company of angels, and they destroyed them.

They differed over what was intended by God, the Mighty and Majestic, informing the angels of the creation of Adam, in six views.

The first: God knew pride in the soul of Iblis, so He wished to reveal it to the angels and to manifest what had preceded in His knowledge. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, and by al-Suddi from his shaykhs.

The second: He intended to test the obedience of the angels. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: when He created the Fire, the angels were frightened and said: "Our Lord, for whom did You create this?" He said: "For whoever disobeys Me." So they feared the existence of disobedience among them, while they did not know of the existence of any creation other than themselves. So He said to them: ﴿Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a khalifa (successor)﴾ [al-Baqara: 30]. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: He intended to show their inability to encompass His knowledge, so He informed them until they said: ﴿Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein?﴾ Then He answered them: ﴿Indeed, I know that which you do not know﴾.

The fifth: He intended to magnify Adam by mentioning his caliphate before his existence, so that they would honor him if He brought him into being.

The sixth: He intended to inform them that He created him to settle him on the earth, even though the beginning of his creation was in the heaven.

The khalifa is the one who stands in place of another; it is said: "This is the successor (khalf) of so-and-so and his khalifa." Ibn al-Anbari said: the original form of khalifa is khalif, without a ta' marbuta, and the ta' was added for emphasis in praising him with this attribute, as they say: 'allama (very knowledgeable), nassaba (very knowledgeable of genealogies), and rawiya (great transmitter). There are two views regarding the meaning of Adam's caliphate.

The first: he is a khalifa on behalf of God, the Exalted, in establishing His law, the proofs of His oneness, and judgment among His creation. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and Mujahid.

The second: he is a successor to those who preceded him on the earth. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan.

**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein﴾.

There are three views concerning it.

The first: the apparent alif is interrogative, entering upon the meaning of knowledge so that certainty is established by it. Jarir said:

"Are you not the best of those who rode the mounts, and the most generous of the peoples in pouring out wine?"

Its meaning is: "You are the best of those who rode the mounts."

The second: they said it seeking to learn the wisdom behind it, not in the manner of objection. This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

The third: they asked about their own condition, so the sense is: "Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein, while we glorify You with Your praise, or not?"

Did the angels know that they would cause corruption through a revelation from God, or did they reason from the condition of those before them? There are two views.

The first: it was through a revelation from God. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Qutayba. al-Suddi narrated from his shaykhs that they said: "Our Lord, and what will that khalifa be?" He said: "He will have offspring who will cause corruption on the earth, envy one another, and kill one another." So they said: ﴿Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein﴾.

The second: they reasoned from the conditions of those who preceded Adam. A similar view is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliya and Muqatil.

**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and sheds blood﴾.

al-Jumhur read it with a kasra on the fa' (yafsiku). Ibn Musarrif and Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Abla read it with a damma, and both are dialects. It is narrated from Talha and Ibn Miqsam: "wa-yusaffiku," with a damma on the ya', a fatha on the sin, and a shadda on the fa' with a kasra, and this form indicates intensification and repetition of the action. Safk al-dam (shedding of blood) means pouring it out, spilling it, and spreading it. This is used for any wasted thing, except that safk is specific to blood, while sabb, saff and iraqa are said of blood and of other things.

There are four views concerning the meaning of their glorification (tasbih). The first: it is prayer; this was said by Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas. The second: it is their saying "Subhan Allah"; this was said by Qatada. The third: it is exalting and praising; this was said by Abu Salih. The fourth: it is submission and humbleness; this was said by Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Anbari.

**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and we sanctify You﴾.

The quds is purity. There are three views concerning the meaning of their sanctification. The first: its meaning is: "we purify ourselves for You from their deeds"; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: "we magnify You and declare You great"; this was said by Mujahid. The third: "we pray to You"; this was said by Qatada.

**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, I know that which you do not know﴾.

There are four views concerning it. The first: its meaning is: "I know what is in the soul of Iblis of rebellion and disobedience"; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi from his shaykhs. The second: "I know that there will come from that khalifa prophets and righteous ones"; this was said by Qatada. The third: "I know that I will fill Hell with jinn and men"; this was said by Ibn Zayd. The fourth: "I know the outcomes of affairs; I test those whom you think to be obedient, and the test leads them to disobedience like Iblis, and those whom you think to be disobedient, and they obey"; this was said by al-Zajjaj.

**

Indication of the creation of Adam, peace be upon him

Abu Musa narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed God, the Mighty and Majestic, created Adam from a handful He took from all of the earth, so the children of Adam came according to the extent of the earth: among them the red and the white and the black, and what is between that; and the easy and the hard, and what is between that; and the wicked and the good." al-Tirmidhi said: this is a sound hadith.

al-Bukhari and Muslim in their two Sahihs have related from the hadith of Abu Hurayra from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "God, the Exalted, created Adam; his height was sixty cubits." Muslim, in what he alone related, reported from the hadith of Abu Hurayra from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "God created Adam after the 'Asr on Friday, the last of creation, in the last hour of the hours of Friday, between 'Asr and night." Ibn 'Abbas said: when He breathed the spirit into him, the breath reached him from the direction of his head, and it did not move in anything except that it became flesh and blood.

**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾.

There are two views regarding the naming of Adam. The first: he was named so because he was created from the surface (adim) of the earth; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and al-Zajjaj. The second: it is from adma (brownness) in color; this was said by al-Dahhak, al-Nadr ibn Shumayl and Qutrub.

Regarding the names which He taught him there are two views. The first: He taught him all the names; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and Qatada. The second: He taught him the names of specific counted things. Then there are four views concerning these: the first, that He taught him the names of the angels; said by Abu al-'Aliya. The second, that He taught him the names of genera without their species, like your saying: insan (human), malik (angel), jinni (jinn), and ta'ir (bird); said by Ikrima. The third, that He taught him the names of what He created on the earth of beasts, creeping things and birds; said by al-Kalbi, Muqatil and Ibn Qutayba. The fourth, that He taught him the names of his offspring; said by Ibn Zayd.

**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then He presented them﴾.

He means the individual creatures, presented to the angels. Ibn 'Abbas said: "the angels here are specifically those who were with Iblis."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Inform me﴾ means "tell me."

**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿if you are truthful﴾.

There are two views. The first: "if you are truthful that I will not create a creature better and more knowledgeable than you"; said by al-Hasan. The second: "that I will place upon it one who causes corruption therein"; said by al-Suddi from his shaykhs.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 30–31:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels﴾.

Abu 'Ubayda used to say: "idh" (when) is superfluous (mulghah), and the sense of the sentence is: "and your Lord said." The second: He intended to test the obedience of the angels. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: when He created the Fire, the angels were frightened and said: "Our Lord, for whom did You create this?" He said: "For whoever disobeys Me." So they feared the existence of disobedience among them, while they did not know of the existence of any creation other than themselves. So He said to them: ﴿Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a khalifa (successor)﴾ [al-Baqara: 30]. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: He intended to show their inability to encompass His knowledge, so He informed them until they said: ﴿Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein?﴾ Then He answered them: ﴿Indeed, I know that which you do not know﴾.

The fifth: He intended to magnify Adam by mentioning his caliphate before his existence, so that they would honor him if He brought him into being.

The sixth: He intended to inform them that He created him to settle him on the earth, even though the beginning of his creation was in the heaven.

The khalifa is the one who stands in place of another; it is said: "This is the successor (khalf) of so-and-so and his khalifa." Ibn al-Anbari said: the original form of khalifa is khalif, without a ta' marbuta, and the ta' was added for emphasis in praising him with this attribute, as they say: 'allama (very knowledgeable), nassaba (very knowledgeable of genealogies), and rawiya (great transmitter). There are two views regarding the meaning of Adam's caliphate.

The first: he is a khalifa on behalf of God, the Exalted, in establishing His law, the proofs of His oneness, and judgment among His creation. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and Mujahid.

The second: he is a successor to those who preceded him on the earth. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan.

**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein﴾.

There are three views concerning it.

The first: the apparent alif is interrogative, entering upon the meaning of knowledge so that certainty is established by it. Jarir said:

"Are you not the best of those who rode the mounts, and the most generous of the peoples in pouring out wine?"

Its meaning is: "You are the best of those who rode the mounts."

The second: they said it seeking to learn the wisdom behind it, not in the manner of objection. This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

The third: they asked about their own condition, so the sense is: "Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein, while we glorify You with Your praise, or not?"

Did the angels know that they would cause corruption through a revelation from God, or did they reason from the condition of those before them? There are two views.

The first: it was through a revelation from God. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Qutayba. al-Suddi narrated from his shaykhs that they said: "Our Lord, and what will that khalifa be?" He said: "He will have offspring who will cause corruption on the earth, envy one another, and kill one another." So they said: ﴿Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein﴾.

The second: they reasoned from the conditions of those who preceded Adam. A similar view is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliya and Muqatil.

**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and sheds blood﴾.

al-Jumhur read it with a kasra on the fa' (yafsiku). Ibn Musarrif and Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Abla read it with a damma, and both are dialects. It is narrated from Talha and Ibn Miqsam: "wa-yusaffiku," with a damma on the ya', a fatha on the sin, and a shadda on the fa' with a kasra, and this form indicates intensification and repetition of the action. Safk al-dam (shedding of blood) means pouring it out, spilling it, and spreading it. This is used for any wasted thing, except that safk is specific to blood, while sabb, saff and iraqa are said of blood and of other things.

There are four views concerning the meaning of their glorification (tasbih). The first: it is prayer; this was said by Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas. The second: it is their saying "Subhan Allah"; this was said by Qatada. The third: it is exalting and praising; this was said by Abu Salih. The fourth: it is submission and humbleness; this was said by Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Anbari.

**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and we sanctify You﴾.

The quds is purity. There are three views concerning the meaning of their sanctification. The first: its meaning is: "we purify ourselves for You from their deeds"; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: "we magnify You and declare You great"; this was said by Mujahid. The third: "we pray to You"; this was said by Qatada.

**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, I know that which you do not know﴾.

There are four views concerning it. The first: its meaning is: "I know what is in the soul of Iblis of rebellion and disobedience"; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi from his shaykhs. The second: "I know that there will come from that khalifa prophets and righteous ones"; this was said by Qatada. The third: "I know that I will fill Hell with jinn and men"; this was said by Ibn Zayd. The fourth: "I know the outcomes of affairs; I test those whom you think to be obedient, and the test leads them to disobedience like Iblis, and those whom you think to be disobedient, and they obey"; this was said by al-Zajjaj.

**

Indication of the creation of Adam, peace be upon him

Abu Musa narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed God, the Mighty and Majestic, created Adam from a handful He took from all of the earth, so the children of Adam came according to the extent of the earth: among them the red and the white and the black, and what is between that; and the easy and the hard, and what is between that; and the wicked and the good." al-Tirmidhi said: this is a sound hadith.

al-Bukhari and Muslim in their two Sahihs have related from the hadith of Abu Hurayra from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "God, the Exalted, created Adam; his height was sixty cubits." Muslim, in what he alone related, reported from the hadith of Abu Hurayra from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "God created Adam after the 'Asr on Friday, the last of creation, in the last hour of the hours of Friday, between 'Asr and night." Ibn 'Abbas said: when He breathed the spirit into him, the breath reached him from the direction of his head, and it did not move in anything except that it became flesh and blood.

**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾.

There are two views regarding the naming of Adam. The first: he was named so because he was created from the surface (adim) of the earth; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and al-Zajjaj. The second: it is from adma (brownness) in color; this was said by al-Dahhak, al-Nadr ibn Shumayl and Qutrub.

Regarding the names which He taught him there are two views. The first: He taught him all the names; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and Qatada. The second: He taught him the names of specific counted things. Then there are four views concerning these: the first, that He taught him the names of the angels; said by Abu al-'Aliya. The second, that He taught him the names of genera without their species, like your saying: insan (human), malik (angel), jinni (jinn), and ta'ir (bird); said by Ikrima. The third, that He taught him the names of what He created on the earth of beasts, creeping things and birds; said by al-Kalbi, Muqatil and Ibn Qutayba. The fourth, that He taught him the names of his offspring; said by Ibn Zayd.

**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then He presented them﴾.

He means the individual creatures, presented to the angels. Ibn 'Abbas said: "the angels here are specifically those who were with Iblis."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Inform me﴾ means "tell me."

**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿if you are truthful﴾.

There are two views. The first: "if you are truthful that I will not create a creature better and more knowledgeable than you"; said by al-Hasan. The second: "that I will place upon it one who causes corruption therein"; said by al-Suddi from his shaykhs.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 32:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: Glory be to You﴾.

Al-Zajjaj said: There is no disagreement among the people of the language (ahl al-lughah, the lexicographers and Arabic linguists) that tasbih (glorification, declaring God free of imperfection) is: declaring God exalted above every evil. "Al-Alim" (the All-Knowing) means "al-alim" (the knower), and it came in the pattern "fa'il" for emphasis (mubalaghah, intensification). Regarding "al-Hakim" (the All-Wise) there are two views. One of them is that it means "al-hakim" (the judge), as said by Ibn Qutaybah. The second is: the one who makes things firm and precise (al-muhkim li-l-ashya'), as said by al-Khattabi.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 33:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Said, "O Adam, inform them of their names."﴾ That is, tell them. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he read "anbi'him" with a kasra on the ha' (anbi'hi-m). Abu 'Ali said: the reading of the majority (al-Jumhur) is on the original form (al-asl), because the original form of this pronoun is that the ha' is dammah, as you say: "darbahum" and "abna'ahum," and "hadha lahum." Whoever reads with a kasra makes the ha' follow the kasra of the ba' before it, which is the kasra of the ba'. The ha' and the mim refer to the angels.

Regarding the ha' and mim in "asma'ihim" (their names), there are two opinions. The first: they refer to the created things that He presented to them, as stated by most scholars. The second: they refer to the angels, as stated by al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

Regarding what they had revealed (abdaw), there are two opinions. The first: it is their saying, ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?﴾ This was mentioned by al-Suddi from his shaykhs. The second: it is what they displayed of hearing and obedience to Allah when they passed by the body of Adam. Iblis said: "This one's superiority over you, what will you do?" They said: "We obey our Lord." Iblis said to himself: "If I am preferred over him, I will destroy him, and if he is preferred over me, I will disobey him." This was stated by Muqatil.

Regarding what they had concealed (katamu), there are two opinions. The first: it is the belief of the angels that Allah, exalted is He, would not create a creation more noble than them. This was stated by al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliyah, and Qatadah. The second: it is what Iblis concealed of arrogance and disobedience, narrated by al-Suddi from his shaykhs, and said by Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, and Muqatil.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 34:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam"﴾.

The majority of reciters read the taa' in "al-malā'ikah" with a kasra, but Abu Ja'far and al-A'mash read it with a damma when connected (fi al-wasl). Al-Kisa'i said: it is a dialect of Azd Shanu'ah.

Regarding these angels there are two views. The first: they are all the angels; this was said by al-Suddi, from his shaykhs. The second: they are a group of the angels; this was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. The first is more sound.

Sujud (prostration) in the language means humility and submission, and they recited:

"Prostrate of the nostril, which does not raise it; with lowered gaze, deaf to the listener."

Regarding the manner of their prostration to Adam there are two views. The first: it was in the manner of the prostration of prayer, and this is the more apparent. The second: it was bowing and inclining, equal to the ruku' (bowing).

(p-65)

**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except Iblis﴾.

Regarding this exception there are two views.

The first: it is an exception from the genus (of the angels), so according to this view he was of the angels; this was said by Ibn Mas'ud in one narration, and Ibn 'Abbas. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he was of the angels, then Allah transformed him into a devil (shaytan). The second: he was not of the same genus, so he was of the jinn; this was said by al-Hasan and al-Zuhri. Ibn 'Abbas said: Iblis was one of the keepers of Paradise, and he managed the affairs of the lowest heaven. If it is said: how is it an exception when he was not of the same genus? The answer: he was commanded to prostrate along with them, so he was excepted from them, because he did not prostrate. This is as when you say: "I commanded my servant and my brothers, and they obeyed me except my servant." This is the saying of al-Zajjaj.

Regarding Iblis there are two views. The first: he is a non-Arabic proper name, not derived, and for this reason it is not declined (ghayr munsarif); this is the view of Abu 'Ubaydah, al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari. The second: it is derived from al-iblas, which is despair (al-yas); this was narrated from Abu Salih. Ibn Qutaybah mentioned it and said: it is not declined because it has no namesake, so it is considered heavy. Our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi said: the first is more sound, because if it were from al-iblas it would be declined. Do you not see that if you named a man "Ikhritit" or "Ijfil," it would be declined in the definite form?

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿refused﴾ means: he held back. ﴿and was arrogant﴾ is istaf'ala from al-kibr (pride). Regarding "and he was" (wa kana) there are two views. The first: it means "became" (sara); this was said by Qatadah. The second: it is in the sense of the past, so its meaning is: he was in Allah's knowledge a disbeliever; this was said by Muqatil and Ibn al-Anbari.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 35:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We said, "O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in Paradise"﴾. "His wife" is Hawwa' (Eve). Al-Farra' said: The people of the Hijaz say of a man's wife "zawj" and pluralize it as "al-azwaj," while Tamim and most of Qays and the people of Najd say "zawjah" and pluralize it as "zawjat."

The poet said:

"Indeed, the one who rushes to stir up my wife is like one who walks toward a lion of al-Shara, seeking to take her."

Abu al-Jarrah recited to me:

"O friend, convey to all the owners of wives: there is no union once the bonds of the marriage-tie are undone."

Regarding the Paradise in which Adam was made to dwell, there are two opinions. One is that it is the Garden of Eden (Jannat 'Adn). The second is that it is the Garden of Eternity (Jannat al-Khuld).

Al-raghad means abundant, wide provision. It is said: "Arghada fulan" when someone is in plenty and ease.

**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not approach this tree﴾, meaning: by eating, not by drawing near to it.

Regarding the tree, there are six opinions:

The first: that it is the ear of grain (al-sunbulah). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, Ka'b al-Ahbar, Wahb ibn Munabbih, Qatadah, 'Atiyyah al-'Awfi, Muharib ibn Ditar, and Muqatil.

The second: that it is the vine (al-karm). This was related from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Ja'dah ibn Hubayrah.

The third: that it is the fig (al-tin). This was related from al-Hasan, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, and Ibn Jurayj.

The fourth: that it is a tree called the "Tree of Knowledge," as said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fifth: that it is the camphor tree (shajarat al-kafur), reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.

The sixth: that it is the palm tree (al-nakhlah), reported from Abu Malik.

They have also mentioned a seventh view, reported from Wahb ibn Munabbih, that he said: it is the Tree of Eternity (shajarat al-khuld), and that the speech concerns its kind in general.

**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And thus you would be among the wrongdoers﴾.

Ibn al-Anbari said: Zulm (wrongdoing) is placing a thing in other than its proper place. It is said: "Zalama al-rajul siqa'ahu" when he gives it to drink before its butter has come out. The poet said:

"A true companion whose complaint has not harmed me: I wronged him, and in my wronging him, deliberately, there is a reward."

By "the companion" he meant the skin of milk, and his wronging it was giving it to drink before its butter came out.

The Arabs say: "He is more wrongdoing than a snake," because it comes to a hole which it did not dig and dwells in it. It is also said: "The water has wronged the valley" when it reaches a place it did not reach before.

If it is asked: what is the wisdom in singling out that tree for the prohibition? The answer is that it was a trial from Allah the Exalted with what He willed.

Abu al-'Aliyah said: It had a weight among the trees of Paradise. When he ate from it, it was said: "Go out to the abode that suits what has come from you."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 36:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then Satan caused them to slip from it and expelled them from that in which they had been.﴾

Azallahuma means istazallahuma (caused them to slip). Hamzah recited (fa-azalahuma), meaning: he removed them (nahhahuma). Abu Ali al-Farisi said: Since the meaning of ﴿Dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden﴾ is "remain in it," and they remained, Hamzah matched remaining (ath-thabat) with removal (az-zawal), which is its opposite, and his recitation is strengthened by ﴿and expelled them﴾.

Ash-Shaytan is Iblis, and the verb is attributed to him because he was the cause. Regarding the pronoun in (anha, "from it"), there are three opinions: first, that it refers to the Garden; second, that it refers to obedience; third, that it refers to the tree. The meaning then is: he caused them to slip by a lapse that proceeded from the tree.

Regarding the manner of his causing them to slip, there are three opinions. First: he devised a way until he entered the Garden to them, and it was the serpent that brought him in; this was said by Ibn Abbas and as-Suddi. Second: he stood at the gate of the Garden and called out to them; this was said by al-Hasan. Third: he whispered to them and placed the idea in their souls without address or being seen; this was said by Ibn Ishaq, though it is weak. Az-Zajjaj said: The better view is that he addressed her, due to His saying ﴿and he swore to them both﴾.

The scholars differed regarding Adam's disobedience by eating. A group said: he was forbidden a specific tree, and he ate from its kind. Others said: he interpreted the prohibition as disapproval (karahah) rather than prohibition (tahrim).

**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We said: Go down, some of you enemies to others, and for you on the earth is a place of settlement and provision for a time.﴾ Al-Hubut, with a dammah on the ha', is descending from a height; with a fathah on the ha', it is the place one descends to. To whom is this address directed? There are six opinions. First: it is directed to Adam, Eve and the serpent; this was reported by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. Second: to Adam, Eve, Iblis and the serpent; related by as-Suddi from Ibn Abbas. Third: to Adam and Iblis; said by Mujahid. Fourth: to Adam, Eve and Iblis; said by Muqatil. Fifth: to Adam, Eve and their offspring; said by al-Farra'. Sixth: to Adam and Eve only, the plural form being used for the dual, like His saying ﴿And We were witnesses to their judgment﴾ [al-Anbiya': 78]; mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari, and it is also the underlying reason in Mujahid's view.

The scholars differed: were they sent down all together or separately? There are two opinions. One: they were sent down together, but they landed in different lands; said by Ka'b and Wahb. The other: they were sent down separately. Iblis descended before Adam; Adam descended in India, Eve in Jeddah, and Iblis in al-Ubulla; said by Muqatil. It is reported from Ibn Abbas that he said: the serpent was sent down with two portions. He said: God the Exalted commanded Jibril to bring Adam down. He seized his forelock and freed him from the tree that had seized him, and Adam said: "O King, be gentle with me." Jibril said: "I am not gentle with one who disobeys God." Adam trembled and shook, and his speech departed, while Jibril rebuked him for his disobedience and enumerated God's blessings upon him. He said: he was admitted to the Garden in the forenoon and left it between the two prayers; he remained there for half a day, which is five hundred years by the reckoning of the people of this world.

Regarding the enmity mentioned here, there are three opinions. One: the descendants of some of them are enemies to others; said by Mujahid. Second: Iblis is an enemy to Adam and Eve, and they are his enemy; said by Muqatil. Third: Iblis is an enemy to the believers, and they are his enemies; said by az-Zajjaj.

Regarding al-Mustaqarr (the place of settlement), there are two opinions. One: it means the graves; related by as-Suddi from Ibn Abbas. The other: it is the place of settling; said by Abu al-Aliyah, Ibn Zayd, az-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutaybah, and this is the more sound view.

Al-Mata' is benefit. Al-Hin is time. Ibn Abbas said: "for a time" means until the end of the appointed term by death.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 37:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He accepted his repentance. Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾

Talaqqa (received) means akhadha (took) and qabila (accepted). Ibn Qutaybah said: It is as if Allah, exalted is He, inspired him to seek forgiveness from Him [and He would accept it] with words from Himself, and Adam did that, so He accepted his repentance. Ibn Kathir recited, "fataqqa Adama" with a fatha (nasb) on Adam, and "kalimatun" with a damma (raf'), on the basis that the words are the doer (al-fa'ila).

Regarding the words, there are several opinions.

The first: they are His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers.﴾ (Al-A'raf: 23). This was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Ata' al-Khurasani, Ubayd ibn Umayr, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and Ibn Zayd.

The second: He said, meaning: O Lord, did You not create me with Your hand? He said: Yes. He said: Did You not breathe into me of Your spirit? He said: Yes. He said: Did Your mercy not precede Your wrath toward me? He said: Yes. He said: Did You not make Your angels prostrate to me, and settle me in Your Paradise? He said: Yes. He said: O Lord, do You see that if I repent and amend, You will return me to Paradise? He said: Yes. This was related by al-Suddi from Ibn Abbas.

The third: He said: "Allahumma la ilaha illa Anta, subhanaka wa bihamdika, Rabbi inni zalamtu nafsi faghfir li, innaka khayru al-ghafirin. Allahumma la ilaha illa Anta, subhanaka wa bihamdika, Rabbi inni zalamtu nafsi farhamni, fa-Anta khayru al-rahimin. [Allahumma] la ilaha illa Anta, subhanaka wa bihamdika, Rabbi inni zalamtu nafsi fatub alayya, innaka Anta al-Tawwab al-Rahim." This was narrated by Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid. Sayings close in meaning to this, from the words of seeking excuse, have been mentioned.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He accepted his repentance.﴾

The root of tawba is return (ruju'). So Adam's repentance is his return from disobedience, and from Allah, exalted is He, it is His return to him with mercy; and the reward, which is such that whenever the servant's repentance is repeated, His acceptance of it is repeated. Hawwa' is not mentioned in the repentance only because no mention of her had preceded, not because her repentance was not accepted. Some people said: when the action of two is one in meaning, it is permissible to mention one of them while the meaning applies to both, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ (At-Tawbah: 62), and His saying: ﴿So let him not drive you both out of the Garden, [for then] you would suffer.﴾ (Ta-Ha: 117).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 38:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We said, "Go down from it, all of you. And when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance – no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve."﴾

Regarding the repetition of the mention of the descent (al-hubut), which has already been mentioned, there are two opinions.

One of them: it was repeated because Adam was made to descend twice, one descent from the Garden to the heaven, and the second from the heaven to the earth. And which of the two is the descent mentioned in this verse? On this there are two opinions.

The second: he only repeated the descent for emphasis.

(p-71) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿fa-immā﴾ (then, if). Al-Zajjaj said: this is the "in" (inna) of conditional, to which "mā" has been joined. The original in pronunciation is "in mā" separated, but it has been assimilated (idgham) and written according to the assimilation. When "mā" is joined to "in," the verb takes the heavy nun or the light nun. The nun is obligatory with it because "mā" enters as an emphasizer, and the nun also enters as an emphasizer, just as the lam of oath requires the nun in your saying: "By God, you will surely do it" (wa-Llāhi la-tafʿalanna). The response of the conditional is the fa (fa-).

Regarding what is meant by "al-hudā" (guidance) here, there are two opinions. One of them: it is the Messenger, said by Ibn ʿAbbās and Muqatil.

The second: it is the Book, related by some of the commentators.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿so no fear will there be concerning them﴾.

Yaʿqub recited "fa-lā khawfa" with a fatha on the fa without tanwin, and Ibn Muhaysin recited it with a damma on the fa without tanwin. The meaning: there is no fear for them regarding what they will face of punishment, nor will they grieve at death. Fear is for a future matter, and grief is for a past matter.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 39:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs — those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾ Regarding the meaning of the verse (āyah) there are three opinions.

The first: it means a sign (ʿalāmah), so the meaning of āyah is a marker separating the speech that precedes it from the speech that follows it. The poet said:

Ala abligh ladayka Banī Tamīmin bi-āyati mā yuḥibbūna al-ṭaʿāmā

And al-Nābighah said:

Tawahhamtu āyātin lahā fa-ʿaraftuhā // li-sittati aʿwāmin wa-dhā al-ʿāmi sābiʿu

This is the view chosen by Abū ʿUbayd.

The second: it was called āyah because it is a group of letters of the Qur'an, and a portion of it. Abū ʿAmr al-Shaybānī said: it is said, "The people went out with their āyāt," meaning with their group. And they recited:

Kharajnā min al-naqbayni lā ḥayya mithlunā // bi-āyātinā nuzjī al-liqāḥa al-maṭāfilā

(p. 72) The third: it was called āyah because it is a marvel, since its reciter, when he recites it, derives evidence of its distinction from the speech of created beings. This is like your saying, "So-and-so is an āyah among the āyāt," meaning a marvel among marvels. Ibn al-Anbārī mentioned this.

Regarding what is meant by these āyāt there are four opinions.

The first: the verses of the books that are recited. The second: the miracles of the prophets. The third: the Qur'an. The fourth: the signs of God in His creation. And "companions of the Fire" means its inhabitants; they were called companions (aṣḥāb) because of their constant association with it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you, and fulfill My covenant, I will fulfill your covenant, and fear none but Me.﴾

Isra'il (Israel): it is Ya'qub (Jacob), and it is a non-Arabic name. Ibn 'Abbas said: its meaning is "servant of Allah." The Arabs pronounced it in several forms: they said Isra'il, Isral, Isra'il, and Isra'in.

Umayyah said:

"Indeed I am the one who wears iron mail, over the people, coats of mail with flowing skirts. I see none who helps me in my life, other than myself, except the Banu Isra'il."

A Bedouin who had hunted a lizard (dabb) and brought it to his family said:

"The people of the market said when we came: 'This, by the Lord of the House, is Isra'ina.'"

He meant: this is one of those who were transformed from the Children of Israel.

Ni'mah (blessing): it means favor, and its like is al-Na'ma'. An-Ni'mah, with a fatha on the nun, means luxury and comfortable living. By "blessing" he meant the blessings, and he used the singular, because they are content with one of the collective, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the angels after that are a supporter﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4], meaning supporters.

Regarding what is meant by this blessing, there are three opinions. The first: it is what He promised them in the Torah, in which is the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: it is what He bestowed upon their fathers and forefathers when He saved them from the family of Pharaoh, destroyed their enemy, gave them the Torah, and similar things; this was said by al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj.

He bestowed the favor upon them by what He gave their fathers, because the pride of the fathers is pride for the sons, and the shame of the fathers is shame upon the sons.

The third: it is the plural of ni'mah according to the variations of states.

The meaning of remembering it is thanking it, for whoever does not give thanks has not remembered it.

**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fulfill﴾.

Al-Farra' said: the people of the Hijaz say "awfaytu," and the people of Najd say "wafaytu," without an alif.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is said "wafa bil-'ahd" and "awfa bihi," and he recited:

"As for Ibn Tawq, he fulfilled his pledge, just as the one who drives the camels of the star fulfilled his driving."

Ibn Qutaybah said: it is said "wafaytu bil-'ahd" and "awfaytu bihi," and "awfaytu al-kayl" only.

Regarding what is meant by His covenant, there are four opinions. The first: that when He charged them in the Torah with the description of Muhammad (ﷺ), narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: that it is the carrying out of commands and avoiding of prohibitions, narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. The third: that it is Islam, said by Abu al-'Aliyah. The fourth: that it is the covenant mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah certainly took the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We raised among them twelve leaders﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 12], said by Qatadah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I will fulfill your covenant﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: I will admit you into Paradise.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fear none but Me﴾, meaning: fear Me.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 41:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And believe in what I have sent down﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿confirming what is with you﴾, meaning the Torah or the Gospel, for the Qur'an confirms both of them, that they are from Allah, and agrees with them concerning the description of the Prophet ﷺ.

(p-74) ﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾.

He said "the first disbeliever" because the one who hastens to disbelief is greater in sin than one who disbelieves after that, since the one who rushes ahead did not reflect upon the proof, but hastened to obstinacy, so his condition is more severe. It was also said: "And do not be the first disbeliever in it after having believed," and the address is to the leaders of the Jews.

Regarding the pronoun in "bihi" (in it) there are two views. The first: it refers to the revelation (al-manzil), this was said by Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas.

The second: it refers to what is with them (ma ma'ahum), because when they concealed the description of the Prophet ﷺ while it was with them, they disbelieved in it. This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not exchange My signs for a small price, and fear Me alone﴾.

That is: do not exchange [My signs] for a small price. Regarding this there are three views. The first: that they used to take from the goods of this world. The second: the retention of their leadership over them. The third: taking a wage for teaching the religion.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 42:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not mix the truth with falsehood, nor conceal the truth while you know [it]﴾.

Talbisu (you mix/confuse): it means tukhalitu (you mingle/mix). It is said: labbastu al-amra 'alayhim, ulbisuhu, meaning I obscured the matter from them. Their mixing-up was that they said: "Indeed Allah has entrusted to us that we should believe in the Prophet the Unlettered, and it has not been mentioned that he is from the Arabs."

Regarding what is meant by "the truth," there are two opinions. The first: it is the command of the Prophet (ﷺ), said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Suddi, and Muqatil. The second: it is Islam, said by al-Hasan.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 43:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And establish prayer and give zakah﴾.

He means the five prayers (al-salawat al-khams), and here it is a generic noun (ism jins). As for zakah (obligatory almsgiving, purification), it is derived from zaka', which means growth and increase. It is said: "zaka al-zar'" (the crop grew), yazku zuka'an. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning of zakah in the speech of the Arabs is increase and growth, and it was named zakah because it increases the wealth from which it is taken out, makes it abundant, and protects it from calamities. It is also said: "This is more zakiy (purer, better) than that," meaning it has more excess in it than the other.

(p-75)

**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And bow with those who bow﴾.

That is: pray with those who pray. Ibn Abbas said: He means Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them). It was also said: He mentioned bowing (ruku') only because there is no bowing in their prayer, and the address is to the Jews. In this verse there is evidence that the disbelievers are addressed with the subsidiary rulings (al-furu', the detailed rulings of the Shari'ah), and this is one of the two reports from Ahmad (may Allah be pleased with him).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 44:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do you order the people to righteousness and forget yourselves, while you recite the Book? Will you not then reason?﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: It was revealed concerning the Jews. A man would say to his relative among the Muslims in private: "Hold fast to what you are upon, for it is the truth." The alif in "Ataʾmurūna" (Do you order) is the alif of interrogation (istifham), and its meaning is reproach (tawbikh).

As for "al-birr" (righteousness) here, there are three opinions. The first: it is adherence to their Book; they used to order others to follow it while not acting upon it themselves. The second: it is following Muhammad (ﷺ); both of these opinions are narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. The third: it is charity (ṣadaqah); they used to order it while being stingy. This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and forget﴾ means: you leave aside. As for "al-Kitab" (the Book) there are two opinions. The first: it is the Torah (al-Tawrah), as stated by the majority of scholars. The second: it is the Qur'an, and in that case the address would not be directed to the Jews according to this opinion.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 45:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer, and indeed it is difficult except for the humble before God﴾. The root meaning of ṣabr (patience) is restraint (ḥabs), so the one who is patient restrains himself from anxiety. The fasting person is called ṣābir because he restrains himself from eating, drinking and intercourse. Al-maṣbūrah is an animal that is tied up to be used as a target. Mujāhid said: "Ṣabr here means fasting."

Regarding what they were commanded to be patient in, there are three opinions. The first: it is the performance of the obligatory duties; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Muqatil. The second: it is abstaining from sins; this was said by Qatadah. The third: it is not seeking leadership (riʾāsah). This address is to the People of the Two Books. The way that prayer (ṣalāh) is a means of seeking help is that in it is recited what encourages one toward the Hereafter and turns one away from this world.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed it﴾. Regarding the pronoun referring back (to what is meant here), there are three opinions. The first: it refers to the prayer (ṣalāh); this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, and the majority. The second: it refers to the Kaʿbah and the qiblah, because when He mentioned the prayer, it pointed to the qiblah; this was reported by al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Muqatil also said it. The third: it refers to the act of seeking help, because when He said ﴿and seek help﴾, it indicated seeking help; this was mentioned by Muḥammad ibn al-Qasim al-Nahwi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿is difficult﴾ (la-kabīrah). Al-Ḥasan and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: al-kabīrah means heavy, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is hard for the polytheists what you call them to﴾ [al-Shura: 13], meaning burdensome. Khushūʿ (humility) in the linguistic sense means submissiveness and humbleness; it has also been said that it means stillness (sukūn).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those who are certain that they will meet their Lord, and that they will return to Him.﴾

Here "ẓann" (here translated as certainty) carries the meaning of yaqin (certainty). It has several senses, which we have mentioned in the book "al-Wujuh wa'l-Naza'ir" (Aspects and Parallels).

Allah's saying: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾. He means: over the worlds of their time. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliyah, Mujahid, and Ibn Zayd. Ibn Qutaybah said: "This is from the general (al-'amm) which is intended to be the particular (al-khass)."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (*Zad al-Masir*) on Surah 2, verse 48:

God's words: ﴿And guard yourselves against a Day on which no soul will avail another soul in anything, nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will any compensation be taken from it, nor will they be helped.﴾

al-Zajjaj said: The Jews used to claim that their forefathers, the Prophets, would intercede for them on the Day of Resurrection. God dispelled this hope for them through this verse.

God's words: ﴿And guard yourselves against a Day﴾ contain an ellipsis (*idmar*, an implied element). The implied sense is: "Guard yourselves against the punishment of a Day," or "against what occurs on a Day." By "the Day" is meant the Day of Resurrection. The word *tajzi* (﴿تَجْزِي﴾, "avail" or "suffice") means *taqdi* (to settle or discharge). Ibn Qutayba said: It is said *jazā 'annī al-amr yajzī*, without a hamza, meaning "it settled the matter for me." And *ajza'anī yujzi'unī*, with a hamza, meaning "it sufficed me."

God's words: ﴿no soul [will avail] another soul﴾. They said the word "soul" here means the disbelieving soul. On this reading, it is one of the general terms that is intended in a specific sense (*al-'amm alladhi ur'īda bihi al-khass*).

God's words: (And intercession will not be accepted from it.) Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with the *ta'* (feminine form, *tuqbalu*). The rest read it with the *ya'* (*yuqbalu*). Qatada, however, read the *ya'* with a fatha and put *al-shafa'a* in the accusative, so that the verb is attributed to God, Exalted is He.

Abu 'Ali said: As for the one who reads with the *ta'*, it is because the noun to which this verb is attributed is feminine, so the predicate must also take the feminine marker. As for the one who reads with the *ya'*, it is because the feminine in the noun to which the verb is attributed is not real (*haqiqi*), so the verb is construed according to the meaning, just as *al-wa'z* and *al-maw'iza* have the same meaning.

In the verse there is an ellipsis; its implied sense is: "No intercession will be accepted from it in it" (*la yuqbalu minha fihi shafa'a*).

*Al-shafa'a* (intercession) is derived from *al-shaf'* (the even number), which is opposed to *al-witr* (the odd number). This is because the request of the intercessor joins (*yashfa'u*) the request of the one for whom intercession is sought with his own.

As for *al-'adl*, it means ransom (*al-fida'*). It is called *'adl* because it equals (*yu'adilu*) the one ransomed. The philologists differed over whether *al-'adl* (with a fatha on the 'ayn) and *al-'idl* (with a kasra on the 'ayn) differ or not. Al-Farra' said: *al-'adl* with a fatha is what equals a thing from a different kind, while *al-'idl* with a kasra is what equals a thing from its own kind, so it is the like. You say: *'indi 'adlu ghulamika* (with a fatha), when you mean its value from a different kind; and *'indi 'idlu ghulamika* (with a kasra), when a slave is equal to a slave. Al-Zajjaj related from the Basrans that *al-'adl* and *al-'idl* mean the same as *al-mithl* (the like), and that the meaning is one, whether the like is of the same kind or not.

God's words: ﴿nor will they be helped﴾, that is, they will not be prevented from the punishment of God.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 49:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And [remember] when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and sparing your women; and in that was a tremendous trial from your Lord﴾. Its implied sense is: "Remember when We delivered you," and these blessings were bestowed upon their forefathers.

Regarding "the people of Pharaoh" (Al Fir'awn), there are three opinions. The first: they are the people of Egypt, said by Muqatil. The second: specifically his household, said by Abu 'Ubayda. The third: his followers in his religion, said by al-Zajjaj. As for whether al-Al (family) and al-Ahl (people) have the same meaning or differ, there are two opinions on this. I have explained the meaning of al-Al in my book "al-Nazair." Fir'awn is a non-Arabic name; it is said that it is his title. Regarding his name there are four opinions. The first: al-Walid ibn (p-78) Mus'ab, said by most scholars. The second: Fayatus, said by Muqatil. The third: Mus'ab ibn al-Rayyan, related by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari. The fourth: Mughith, mentioned by some exegetes.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿yasumunakum﴾ means: they subject you to (yuwallunakum). It is said: "So-and-so subjects you to humiliation," meaning he imposes on you disgrace and contempt. "Su' al-'adhab" means its severest form. Al-Zajjaj held that His saying, ﴿they slaughter your sons﴾, is an explanation of His saying, ﴿they subject you to the worst torment﴾. Some scholars rejected this, saying: God has distinguished between them in another place, when He said: ﴿they subject you to the worst torment and slaughter your sons﴾ [Ibrahim: 6]. The worst torment is merely their employing you in the most grueling labors. al-Farra' said: the place where the conjunction (waw) is omitted explains the qualities of the torment, while the place where the waw is present indicates that they inflicted upon you other forms of torment besides slaughter; it is as if He said: "they torment you without slaughter and with slaughter."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they spare your women﴾ means: they let your women live (yastabqunan nisa'akum), that is, your daughters. They only spared your women for the purpose of humiliation and service.

Regarding "al-bala'" (trial) here there are two opinions. One: it means a blessing (ni'mah), said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Abu Malik, Ibn Qutayba, and al-Zajjaj. The second: it means a calamity (niqmah), related by al-Suddi from his shaykhs. According to this view, "dhalikum" in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿that﴾, refers to their subjecting you to the worst torment, slaughtering your sons, and sparing your women; and according to the first view it refers to the deliverance from the people of Pharaoh. Abu al-'Aliya said: The cause of the slaughter of the sons was that the soothsayers told Pharaoh: "A boy will be born in Egypt this year by whose hands your destruction will come," so he killed the sons. al-Zajjaj said: How astonishing is the foolishness of Pharaoh! If the soothsayer was truthful in his eyes, what benefit is killing? And if he was lying, what is the meaning of killing?

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 50:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [remember] when We parted the sea for you and saved you and drowned the people of Pharaoh while you were watching﴾. Al-faraq is the separation between two things, and "bikum" means "lakum" (for you). He mentioned the people of Pharaoh without mentioning Pharaoh himself, because it was already known that he was among them. Regarding His saying ﴿while you were watching﴾ there are two views. The first is that it is from seeing with the eye, meaning: while you were seeing them drowning. The second is that it means knowledge, like His saying ﴿Have you not considered your Lord, how He extended the shade﴾ [25:45]. This was said by al-Farra'.

The reference to their story.

al-Suddi narrated from his shaykhs that God Exalted commanded Musa to set out with the Children of Israel, and He cast death upon the Copts, so the firstborn of every man among them died. They woke up and were burying him, and were occupied from pursuing them until the sun rose. ʿAmr ibn Maymun said: When Musa set out, this reached Pharaoh, and he said: "Do not follow them until the rooster crows, tonight." Abu al-Salil said: When Musa reached the sea he said: "Hihi, Abu Khalid," and he was seized by afkal (trembling), meaning a shaking. Muqatil said: the water parted to the right and to the left like two facing mountains, and in them were openings through which each tribe could see the other. al-Suddi said: When Pharaoh saw it split, he said: "Do you not see that the sea has split apart from me, opening up for me?!" Pharaoh's horsemen came but refused to plunge in. So Gabriel descended upon a mare (Madhyana), and the wind of the mare's scent stirred the stallions, so they plunged in after her. When the first of them wanted to exit and the last of them had entered, He commanded the sea to take them, and it closed over them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 51:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when We appointed for Musa forty nights﴾.

Abu Ja'far and Abu 'Amr read "wa'adna" (without an alif) here, and in (al-A'raf) and (Ta-Ha). Abан ʿan ʿAsim agreed with them in (al-Baqarah) specifically. The rest read "wa'adna" with an alif. The rationale for the first reading is the singling out of the promise as coming from Allah, Exalted is He. The rationale for the second reading is that when Musa accepted the promise of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, that became a mutual promise between Allah Exalted is He and Musa. A parallel is His saying: ﴿And do not promise them secretly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 235].

The meaning of the verse: We promised Musa the completion of forty nights, or the expiry of forty nights. "Musa" is a non-Arabic name; its original form in Hebrew is "Musha": "mu" means water and "sha" means tree, because he was found near water and trees, so it was Arabized with a sin (س).

Why was this promise made? There are two views. The first: for the receiving of the Torah. The second: for the speaking (with Allah). Regarding this period there are two views. The first: it is Dhu al-Qa'dah and ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah; this is the view of those who said the promise was for the giving of the Torah. The second: it is Dhu al-Hijjah and ten days of Muharram; this is the view of those who said the promise was for the speaking. The nights alone were mentioned rather than the days because the custom of the Arabs is to date by nights, since the first night of a month precedes its day, and the Arabs rely on the crescent moons, so the days became subordinate to the nights. Abu Bakr al-Naqqash said: He mentioned only the nights because He commanded him to fast these days and join them with the nights, and therefore mentioned the nights; but this is not correct.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 52:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then you took the calf [for worship] after him while you were wrongdoers﴾ ﴿Then We pardoned you after that, that you might be grateful﴾. "After him" means: after his departure to the mountain.

The reference is to their taking the calf.

Al-Suddi narrated from his shaykhs that when Musa departed and appointed Harun as his successor, Harun said: "O Children of Israel, indeed the spoils of war are not lawful for you, and indeed the ornaments of the Copts are spoils of war. So gather them, dig a pit for them, and bury them. If Musa makes them lawful, then take them; otherwise they will be a thing you did not eat." So they did this. Al-Suddi said: Jibril had come to Musa to take him to his Lord, and the Samiri saw him, recognized him, and said: "Indeed, this has a significance." So he took a handful of dust from the print of the horse's hoof and threw it into the pit, and the calf appeared. It was also said: the Samiri ordered them to throw those ornaments in, and said: "Musa's absence from you has only lengthened because of what you have of the ornaments. So dig a pit for them and offer them to God, and He will send you your prophet, for it was a loan." This is mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Regarding the cause of the Samiri's making a calf, there are two views. The first: the Samiri was from a people who worshipped cows, and that was in his heart; this is said by Ibn Abbas. The second: when the Children of Israel passed by a people who were devoting themselves to their idols, they were impressed by that; when they asked Musa to make for them a god and he denounced them, the Samiri produced for them, during his absence, a calf, because of what he saw of their admiration for that. This is said by Ibn Zayd.

Regarding the manner of making the calf, there are two views. The first: the Samiri was a goldsmith; he fashioned it and cast the handful into it; this is said by Ali and Ibn Abbas. The second: they dug a pit and threw into it the ornaments of the people of Pharaoh and their borrowed items, to rid themselves of them; the Samiri then threw the handful of dust, and it became a calf. This is also narrated from Ibn Abbas. Ibn Abbas said: it became flesh, blood and body. The Samiri said to them: "This is your god and the god of Musa, but Musa has come and gone astray," so they worshipped it and buried around it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 53:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion, that perhaps you would be guided﴾. "The Book" is the Torah (al-Tawrah). Regarding "the Criterion" (al-Furqan) there are five opinions.

The first: it is victory (al-nasr). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd.

The second: it is what is in the Torah of the distinction (al-farq) between truth and falsehood, so that "the Criterion" is a description (na't) of the Torah. This was said by Abu al-'Aliyah.

The third: it is the Book itself, and it is repeated with a different wording. 'Adi ibn Zayd said:

"So he cast her words as lies and falsehood"

And 'Antarah said:

"More strong and more impoverished after Umm al-Haytham"

This is the saying of Mujahid, and the choice of al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj.

The fourth: it is that He split the sea for them. This was mentioned by al-Farra', al-Zajjaj, and Ibn al-Qasim.

The fifth: it is the Qur'an. The meaning of the speech is: "Indeed We gave Moses the Book, and Muhammad (ﷺ) the Criterion." This was mentioned by al-Farra', and it is the saying of Qutrub.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 54:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [mention] when Moses said to his people, "O my people, indeed you have wronged yourselves by your taking of the calf [for worship], so turn in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves. That is best for you in the sight of your Creator." And He accepted your repentance. Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾ (p-82) "Al-qawm" (the people) is a term for men to the exclusion of women. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people, perhaps they may be better than them; and let not women ridicule [other] women, perhaps they may be better than them.﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11]. Zuhayr said:

Wa ma adri wa sawfa akhal adri / aqawmun Al Hisnin am nisa'?
(I do not know, and I will surely suppose I know: are the Family of Hisn a people, or women?)

They were called "qawm" because they stand up (yaqumuna) with affairs.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿fa-tubu ila bari'akum (so turn in repentance to your Creator)﴾. Abu 'Ali said: Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i pronounced the hamzah with a kasrah without ikhtilas (rapid vowel reduction) or takhfif (softening). Al-Yazidi and 'Abd al-Warith related from Abu 'Amr: "bari'akum" with the hamzah jazm (vowelless). Al-'Abbas ibn al-Fadl related from him: "bari'akum" with hamzah, not doubled (not with tashdid). Sibawayh said: Abu 'Amr used to perform ikhtilas of the vowel in "bari'akum" and "ya'murukum" and similar words in which vowels follow one another, so he would hear it as though he had made it sakin when he had not made it sakin.

Al-bari' means al-Khaliq (the Creator). The meaning of ﴿fa-uqtulu anfusakum (kill yourselves)﴾ is that some of you should kill others; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid.

They differed regarding those addressed by this on three views. The first: that it is an address to all; this was said by al-Suddi from his shaykhs. The second: that it is an address to those who did not worship [the calf], so that they might kill those who worshipped; this was said by Muqatil. The third: that it is an address only to the worshippers, who were commanded that some of them should kill others; this was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. Regarding the demonstrative "dha" in ﴿dhalikum (that)﴾, there are two views. One: it refers to the killing. The second: it refers to the repentance.

The reference is to their story in that matter.

Ibn 'Abbas said: They said to Moses, "How can fathers kill sons, and brothers kill brothers?" So Allah sent down upon them a darkness in which none could see another. They said, "What is the sign of our repentance?" He said: that the weapons stand upright so that they do not kill, and the darkness is lifted. So they killed until they waded in blood, and the children cried out: "O Moses, pardon, pardon!" Moses wept, and then repentance was revealed, the weapons stood still, and the darkness was lifted. Mujahid said: the number of the slain reached seventy thousand. Qatadah said: He made the killing a martyrdom for the one killed, and a repentance for the one who survived.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 55–56:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you said, "O Musa, we will never believe you until we see Allah openly," so the thunderbolt seized you while you were looking on.﴾ ﴿Then We revived you after your death that you might be grateful.﴾

Concerning those who said this to Musa (peace be upon him), there are two opinions. The first: they were the seventy chosen men (al-Mukhtarun), as said by Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas. The second: all of the Children of Israel except those whom Allah protected from among them, as said by Ibn Zayd. He said: That is because he brought them the Book of Allah, and they said: "By Allah, we will not accept your word until we see Allah openly; then He will say, 'This is My Book.'"

Regarding "jahratan" (openly), there are two opinions. The first: it is a description of their saying, meaning they said that statement aloud, as said by Ibn 'Abbas and Abu 'Ubayda. The second: it is clear sight, meaning He showed Him to us without anything concealing Him from us. It is said: "So-and-so openly commits sins (yatajahara bil-ma'asi)," meaning he does not hide himself from people, as said by al-Zajjaj.

The meaning of "al-sa'iqa" (the thunderbolt) is that by which they were struck senseless (yus'aqun), meaning they died. Among the evidence that they died is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We revived you﴾. This is the saying of the majority. A group claimed that they did not die, and they argued with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Musa fell down unconscious﴾. This is a weak opinion, because Allah, exalted is He, distinguished between the two passages: there He said ﴿when he regained consciousness﴾, and here He said ﴿Then We revived you﴾. Regaining consciousness is for one who has fainted, while revival is for one who has died.

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while you were looking on﴾, there are three opinions. The first: its meaning is that some of you look at others as they fall dead. The second: some of you look at the revival of others. The third: you look at the punishment as it descends upon you, and this is the saying of those who said: a fire descended and burned them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 55–56:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you said, "O Musa, we will never believe you until we see Allah openly," so the thunderbolt seized you while you were looking on.﴾ ﴿Then We revived you after your death that you might be grateful.﴾
