Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 57:

The Almighty said: ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds, and sent down upon you the manna and the quail. Eat of the good things which We have provided for you. And they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ (p-84) (Al-Ghamam): the clouds. It was called ghamam because it covers the sky (yaghummu al-sama'), that is, it veils it, and everything you cover, you have ghammamtahu (covered). This took place during the wandering in the wilderness (al-tih). Regarding the manna (al-mann) there are eight opinions. The first: it is that which falls upon the trees and the people eat it, said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi and al-Dahhak. The second: it is terengabin (tarnjabin, a sweet exudation), narrated from Ibn 'Abbas also, and it is the saying of Muqatil. The third: it is its gum (samgh), said by Mujahid. The fourth: it resembles thick syrup (al-rubb al-ghaliz), said by Ikrimah. The fifth: it is a drink, said by Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Rabi' ibn Anas. The sixth: it is thin bread (khubz al-ruqaq) like millet, or like pure flour (al-naqiyy), said by Wahb. The seventh: it is honey, said by Ibn Zayd. The eighth: it is ginger, said by al-Suddi.

Regarding the quail (al-salwa) there are two opinions. One: it is a bird; some said it resembles the quail (al-sumana), and some said it is the quail. The second: it is honey, mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari, who recited:

*And he swore to her by God, with all his effort, that you are sweeter than the salwa when its honey is extracted.*

The Almighty said: ﴿And they did not wrong Us﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: they did not diminish Us nor harm Us, rather they harmed themselves.

(p-85) Allah's words: ﴿And when We said, "Enter this town and eat from it wherever you wish, in abundance, and enter the gate prostrating, and say, 'Hittah' (a request for forgiveness), and We will forgive you your sins and increase [reward for] the good-doers."﴾

There are two opinions about who spoke to them. One is that it was Musa (Moses), after forty years had passed. The other is that it was Yusha' ibn Nun (Joshua), after the death of Musa.

The word qaryah (town) is derived from jam' (gathering), as in qaraytu al-ma' fi al-hawd, "I gathered the water in the basin." The miqra' is the basin in which water is collected.

As to what is meant by "this town," there are two opinions. One is that it is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and al-Suddi. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is Ariha (Jericho). Al-Suddi said: Ariha is a land between al-Maqdis. The second opinion is that it is a town among the nearest villages of al-Sham (Greater Syria), as said by Wahb.

Allah's words: ﴿and enter the gate prostrating﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: It is one of the gates of Bayt al-Maqdis, and it is called the Gate of Hittah. The words "prostrating" (sujjadan) mean "bowing" (rukka'an). Wahb said: They were commanded to prostrate in gratitude to Allah, the Exalted, when He returned them to it.

Allah's words: ﴿and say, Hittah﴾. Ibn al-Sammaify' and Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited (ḥiṭṭatan) in the accusative case (naṣb).

As to the meaning of hittah, there are three opinions. The first is that its meaning is "Seek forgiveness." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Wahb. Ibn Qutaybah said: It is a word that they were commanded to say with the meaning of seeking forgiveness, from hatatu, meaning: "Remove from us our sins."

The second is that its meaning is: "Say: this matter is true, as you were told." This was mentioned by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. The third is that its meaning is: "There is no god but Allah." This was said by Ikrimah. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: The meaning would then be: "Say that which removes your sins from you," and this is the statement: "There is no god but Allah."

As to why they were commanded to enter the town, there are two opinions. The first is that this was because of sins they had committed, so it was said: (Enter the town) and (enter the gate prostrating; We will forgive you your sins). This was said by Wahb. The second is that they grew weary of the manna and quails, so it was said: ﴿Go down to a city﴾, and the first place they encountered was Ariha, so they were commanded to enter it.

Allah's words: ﴿We will forgive you your sins﴾.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited (naghfir lakum) with the letter nun and a kasrah on the fa'. Nafi' and Aban (on the authority of 'Asim) recited (yaghfir) with a ya' that is damma and a fatha on the fa'. Ibn 'Amir recited with a ta' that is damma and a fatha on the fa'.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 59:**

The Exalted said: ﴿But those who did wrong substituted a word other than that which had been said to them, so We sent down upon those who did wrong a punishment from the sky for their defiance.﴾

Know that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded them when they entered (the town) with an action and a statement. The action was prostration (*sujud*), and the statement was *ḥiṭṭah* ("remission" or "forgiveness"). The people changed both the action and the statement.

(p. 86) As for the change in the action, there are five opinions on it.

The first is that they entered crawling on their buttocks (*mutazaḥḥifīn ʿalā awrākihim*). This was narrated by Abu Hurayra from the Prophet (ﷺ). The second is that they entered from their rear ends (*min qibali astāhim*), said by Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿIkrimah. The third is that they entered with their heads covered (*muqniʿī ruʾūsihim*), said by Ibn Masʿud. The fourth is that they entered on the edges of their eyes (*ʿalā ḥurūf ʿuyūnihim*), said by Mujahid. The fifth is that they entered lying on their backs (*mustalqīna*), said by Muqatil.

As for the change in the statement, there are also five opinions on it.

The first is that they said, in place of *ḥiṭṭah*, "a grain in a hair" (*ḥabbatun fī shaʿrah*). This was narrated by Abu Hurayra from the Prophet (ﷺ).

The second is that they said "wheat" (*ḥinṭah*), said by Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah, Mujahid, Wahb, and Ibn Zayd. The third is that they said "red wheat with a hair in it" (*ḥinṭatun ḥamrāʾu fīhā shaʿrah*), said by Ibn Masʿud. The fourth is that they said "a perforated grain of wheat in which there is a black barley grain" (*ḥabbatu ḥinṭatin mathqūbatun fīhā shuʿayratun sawdāʾ*), said by al-Suddi on the authority of his teachers. The fifth is that they said "sanbalāthā," said by Abu Salih.

As for *rijz*, it means punishment (*al-ʿadhāb*), said by al-Kisa'i, Abu ʿUbayda, and al-Zajjaj. They cited a verse of Ru'ba:

*Until we and he met his scheme with the rijz* (punishment).

Regarding the nature of this punishment, there are three opinions. The first is that it was darkness and death: there died of them in a single hour twenty-four thousand, and seventy thousand perished as a punishment. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second is that the plague (*ṭāʿūn*) struck them, and they were punished with it for forty nights, then they died. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih. The third is that it was snow, by which seventy thousand of them perished. This was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

(p-87) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when Moses prayed for water for his people, We said: "Strike the rock with your staff." And there gushed forth from it twelve springs. Every people knew its drinking-place. "Eat and drink of God's provision, and do not go about the earth spreading corruption."﴾

Istasqa (ask for water) here means: asked for that, like your saying istansara (asked for victory).

Regarding the rock there are two views.

One is that it was a well-known rock, a spring for Moses. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, 'Atiyyah, Ibn Zayd, and Muqatil. They differed about its description in three opinions. The first: it was a square rock, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: it was like the head of a bull, said by 'Atiyyah. The third: it was like the head of a sheep, said by Ibn Zayd. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is the one that carried off Moses' garments; then Jibril came to him and said: "Indeed God, exalted is He, says to you: Lift this rock, for I have power over it and for you it is a miracle." So whenever he needed water he would strike it.

The second view: he was commanded to strike any rock whatsoever, and the first is more established.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿there gushed forth from it﴾.

The estimated meaning is: he struck, and there gushed forth. Since "there gushed forth" indicated that he had struck, the mention of the striking was dispensed with. Similar to it is: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 63]. This was said by al-Farra'.

Since the people were twelve tribes, God brought forth for them twelve springs, and because there was rivalry among them, they were spared that (conflict) by this.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and do not go about spreading corruption﴾.

Al-'athw: the most severe corruption. It is said: 'athiya, 'atha, and 'a'a. Ibn al-Ri'qa' said:

Were it not for modesty, and that my head has been overtaken by white hair, I would have visited Umm al-Qasim.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 61:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you said, "O Moses, we will not be patient with one kind of food. So call upon your Lord to bring forth for us from what the earth grows – its green herbs, its cucumbers, its garlic, its lentils, and its onions." He said, "Would you exchange that which is inferior for that which is better? Go down to a city, for indeed you will have what you ask." And humiliation and poverty were stamped upon them, and they returned with anger from Allah. That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right. That is because they disobeyed and were transgressing.﴾

This was their statement during the wandering (al-tih). By "one kind of food" they meant the manna (al-mann) and the quails (al-salwa). Muhammad ibn al-Qasim said: The manna was eaten with the quails, and the quails with the manna, which is why they were one food.

Al-baql (green herbs) here is a generic noun (ism jins), and by it they meant herbs in general. I read to our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi, who said: The common people hold that al-baql is what humans alone eat, to the exclusion of animals, of the plants that sprout and need cooking to be eaten; but this is not so. Rather, al-baql is al-ushb (herbage), and what grows in spring that people and animals both eat. It is said: "baqalat al-ard" and "abqalat," both are eloquent dialect forms, meaning the land produced baql. And "ibtaqalat al-ibil" means the camels grazed on it. Abu al-Najm, describing camels, said:

They pastured at the first of the pasturing, between the spears of Malik and Nahshal.

Regarding "al-qithha'" (cucumbers) there are two dialects: kasr the qaf and damm it, and the kasr is better, and the majority recited with it. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Raja', Qatadah, Talhah ibn Musarrif, and al-A'mash recited with damm the qaf. Al-Farra' said: The kasr is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and the damm is the dialect of Tamim and some of Bani Asad.

Regarding "al-fum" there are three opinions.

The first: that it is wheat. This was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi (from his shaykhs), al-Hasan, and Abu Malik. Al-Farra' said: It is an ancient dialect; its people say: "fawwimu lana," meaning: bake bread for us.

The second: that it is garlic (al-thawm). This is the recitation of Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) and Ubayy: "wa-thawmiha," and al-Farra' preferred it, giving as reason that it was mentioned alongside what resembles it, and that the fa' is substituted for the tha', as the Arabs say: al-jadath and al-jadaf for the grave, and al-athafi and al-athathi for the stones placed beneath the cooking pot, and maghafir and maghathir for a kind of gum. This is the view of Mujahid, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Muqatil, al-Kisa'i, al-Nadr ibn Shumayl, and Ibn Qutaybah.

The third: that it is grains (al-hububat). Ibn Qutaybah and al-Zajjaj mentioned this.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Would you exchange that which is inferior﴾: meaning, He intended "that which is inferior" and ﴿that which is better﴾ meaning superior, i.e., the manna and quails are superior to what you requested.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Go down to a city﴾ has two views. The first: it is a noun for any city, not specified, said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd; they were commanded to go to a city because what they sought is found in cities. The second: that it intends the land named Egypt (Misr). In the recitation of Abd Allah, al-Hasan, Talhah ibn Musarrif, and al-A'mash it is "Misra" without tanwin. Abu Salih reported from Ibn Abbas that it means the Egypt of Pharaoh. This is the view of Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Dahhak, and al-Farra' preferred it, arguing from the recitation of Abd Allah. He said: al-A'mash was asked about it and said: It is the Egypt over which Salih ibn Ali was governor. Mufaddal al-Dabbi said: It was called Misr because it is the furthest limit of the East and the first limit of the West, so it is a boundary between them; and misr means a boundary. The people of Hajar used to write in their documents: "So-and-so bought the house with its misr," meaning with its boundaries. 'Adi said:

And the one who made the sun a misr, without any concealment, between day and night, has distinguished them.

Ibn Faris related that some people said it was called so because people aim for it (qasd al-nas iyyaha), like their saying: "masarat al-shah" when you milk it, since people aim for it and hardly turn away from it once they have settled there.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And humiliation was stamped upon them﴾: meaning, cling to it. Al-Farra' said: al-dhilla and al-dhull have the same meaning. Al-Hasan said: it is the jizyah (poll tax). Regarding al-maskana there are two views.

The first: that it is poverty and destitution, said by Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Suddi, and Abu 'Ubaydah; and it is narrated from al-Suddi that he said: it is poverty of the soul.

The second: submission, said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they returned﴾: meaning they came back (raja'u). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That﴾ refers to the anger. It was also said that it refers to everything they were obligated with of humiliation and poverty and other things.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they killed the prophets﴾.

Nafi' used to hamz "al-nabiyyin," "al-anbiya'," "al-nubuwwah," and whatever comes of that, except in two places in al-Ahzab: ﴿enter the houses of the Prophet﴾ (53) and ﴿if a woman gives herself to the Prophet﴾ (50). He left the hamz in these two places because two kasrah hamzahs of the same type would come together. The rest of the reciters do not hamz all the places. Al-Zajjaj said: The better is to leave the hamz. The derivation of al-nabi is from nabba' and anba', meaning he informed. It is also possible that it is from naba yanbu, meaning he rose, so that without hamz it is fa'il, from rif'ah (elevation). Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: The Children of Israel would kill three hundred prophets in a single day, then they would set up their vegetable market at the end of the day.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿without right﴾ has three views. The first: its meaning is "without crime," said by Ibn al-Anbari. The second: that it is an emphasis, like His saying: ﴿but it is hearts that go blind which are within the breasts﴾. The third: that it comes as a qualifier of their killing, that it was oppression, so it is like His saying: (p-91) ﴿My Lord, judge with truth﴾, where He described His judgment as true, without indicating that He judges other than with truth.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they used to transgress﴾: al-'udwan is the most severe injustice. Al-Zajjaj said: al-i'tida' is exceeding the measure in everything.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 62:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Christians, and the Sabians—whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous deeds—they will have their reward with their Lord, and no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾ — concerning them there are five opinions.

The first: they are a people who believed in ʿIsa (Jesus) before Muhammad ﷺ was sent. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: they are those who believed in Musa and acted by his law, until ʿIsa came, so they believed in him and acted by his law, until Muhammad came. This is the saying of al-Suddi, from his shaykhs. The third: they are the hypocrites; this was said by Sufyan al-Thawri. The fourth: they are those who were seeking Islam, such as Qass ibn Saʿida, Buhayra, Waraqa ibn Nawfal, and Salman. The fifth: they are the believers of this Ummah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who were Jews﴾ — al-Zajjaj said: the original meaning of hadu (هادوا) in the language is "they repented." It is narrated from Ibn Masʿud that the Jews were named thus due to the saying of Musa: ﴿We have turned back to You﴾ (hudna ilayka), and the Christians (al-Nasara) due to the saying of ʿIsa: ﴿Who are my helpers toward Allah?﴾ It is also said that the Christians were named after a village in which the Messiah dwelt, called Nasira, and it is said: due to their mutual aid (tanasur).

As for "al-Sabiʾun" (الصابئون), the majority of readers recited it with a hamza throughout the Qur'an, while Nafiʿ used to pronounce the hamza in all instances. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of al-Sabiʾin is those who leave one religion for another; it is said: "Sabaʾa fulan" when someone leaves his religion, and "sabaʾat al-nujum" when the stars rise [and "sabaʾa nabuhu" when his tooth emerges].

Regarding al-Sabiʾin there are seven opinions. The first: they are a sect of the Christians who are gentler in speech than them; they are the wanderers (al-saʾihun) whose heads are shaved in the middle; this was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: they are a people between the Christians and the Magians, having no religion of their own; this was said by Mujahid. The third: they are a people between the Jews and the Christians; this was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr. The fourth: they are a people like the Magians; this was said by al-Hasan and al-Hakam. The fifth: they are a group among the People of the Book who recite the Zabur (Psalms); this was said by Abu al-ʿAliya. The sixth: they are a people who pray toward the qibla, worship the angels, and recite the Zabur; this was said by Qatada. The seventh: they are a people who say only "There is no god but Allah," and have no deed, book, or prophet; this was said by Ibn Zayd.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿whoever﴾ (man amana) — regarding the repetition of the mention of belief, there are three opinions. One: when He mentioned with the believers groups of disbelievers, the phrase "whoever believes" returns to them. The second: the meaning is "whoever persists in his belief." The third: the first belief is the hypocrites' verbal profession of Islam, and the second is the belief of the hearts.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: he establishes the obligations.

Section

Is this verse muhkam (definitive) or mansukh (abrogated)? Concerning this there are two opinions.

One: it is muhkam; this was said by Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and others, and they estimated in it: "Indeed, those who believed, and whoever among those who were Jews believes." The second: it is mansukh by His saying: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾; this was mentioned by a group of exegetes.

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 63:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And [recall] when We took your covenant and raised above you the mount, [saying], "Take what We have given you with determination and remember what is in it that you might fear Allah."﴾

The address in this verse is to the Jews. The mithaq (covenant) is a mifal form from al-tawthuq (being bound firmly) by an oath, a pledge, or similar matters that confirm a statement.

Concerning this covenant there are three opinions. The first: He took their covenant that they would act upon what is in the Torah, but they disliked affirming what is in it, so He raised the mountain over them. This is related from Muqatil. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: They gave Allah a pledge that they would act upon what is in the Torah. When Musa brought it to them, they read what it contained of burdens, and they refused to accept it, so He raised the mount over them. The second: it is what Allah Exalted took from the messengers and their followers regarding belief in Muhammad (ﷺ). This is mentioned by al-Zajjaj. The third, also mentioned by al-Zajjaj, he said: It is possible that the covenant is the day He took the offspring from the loins of Adam.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We raised above you the mount﴾. Abu Ubayda said: al-tur (the mount) in the speech of the Arabs means the mountain. Ibn Qutayba said: al-tur means the mountain in Syriac. Ibn Abbas said: whatever of the mountains grows vegetation is a tur, and whatever does not grow is not a tur.

Which mountain was it? There are three opinions concerning this. One: a mountain from the mountains of Palestine, related from Ibn Abbas. The second: a mountain at the foot of which they had camped, related from Qatada. The third: the mountain upon which their Lord manifested Himself, related from Mujahid.

The majority of scholars hold that He raised the mountain over them only because of their refusal to accept the Torah. al-Suddi said: because of their refusal to enter the holy land.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Take what We have given you with determination﴾.

Concerning the meaning of al-quwwa (determination) there are four opinions. The first: diligence and striving, related from Ibn Abbas, Qatada and al-Suddi. The second: obedience, related from Abu al-Aliya. The third: acting upon what is in it, related from Mujahid. The fourth: sincerity, related from Ibn Zayd.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And remember what is in it﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions. One: remember what it contains of reward and punishment, related from Ibn Abbas. The second: its meaning is, study what is in it, related from al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That you might fear Allah﴾. Ibn Abbas said: that you might fear the punishment.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 64:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then you turned away after that, and were it not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have been among the losers﴾.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then you turned away﴾, meaning: you turned away from acting upon what is in it (the Torah), after giving the covenants that you would take it up earnestly. ﴿And were it not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have been among the losers﴾ through punishment.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 65–66:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you certainly knew those who transgressed among you regarding the Sabbath, so We said to them, "Be apes, despised and humiliated."﴾ As-Sabt: the well-known day. This is what Ibn al-Anbari said. The meaning of as-sabt in the speech of the Arabs is "cutting." It is said: "He sabata his head," when he shaved it and cut the hair from it. It is also said: "na'l sabtiyyah" (a sandal of sabt leather), when it was tanned with qaraz (a tanning plant) and its hair was shaved off. So the day was called sabt because Allah, exalted is He, began creation in it and ceased (the creation) in it, with some of the creation of the earth; or because Allah, exalted is He, commanded the Children of Israel in it to cut off work and leave it. He said: Some of them said: it was called sabt because Allah, exalted is He, commanded them to rest from work in it. This is an error, because it is known in the speech of the Arabs that "sabata" means "istarah" (he rested).

Regarding the manner of their transgression on the Sabbath there are two views. One: they took the fish on the day of the Sabbath; this was said by al-Hasan and Muqatil. The second: they held the fish back on the day of the Sabbath and took them on the day of Sunday. This is because a man would dig a pit and make a channel for it to the sea. When it was the day of the Sabbath, he opened the channel, although Allah had forbidden him work on the Sabbath. The waves would bring the fish until they cast them into the pit. The fish wished to leave but could not, so he took them on the day of Sunday. This was said by as-Suddi.

(p-95) The reference is to the story of their transformation.

Uthman ibn Ata narrated from his father, who said: Those who transgressed on the Sabbath were called with three calls. They were called, "O people of the town," and a group awoke, more than the first. Then they were called, "O people of the town," and men, women and children awoke. Allah said to them: ﴿Be apes, despised and humiliated.﴾ Those who had forbidden them would enter upon them and say, "O so-and-so, did we not forbid you?" And they would nod with their heads, "Yes." Qatadah said: So the people became apes that were chattering, with tails, after they had been men and women.

In a narration from Qatadah: The young men became apes and the elders became swine, and none were saved except those who had forbidden (the sin), while the rest perished. Others said: They were about seventy thousand, and the scholars hold this view, except for what is narrated from Mujahid, that he said: their hearts were transformed but their bodies were not transformed. This is a distant view. Ibn Abbas said: They did not live on the earth except three days, and no transformed creature lived on the earth beyond three days; they did not eat, drink, or breed. Muqatil claimed that they lived seven days and died on the eighth day, and this occurred in the time of Dawud, peace be upon him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿khasi'in﴾: al-khasi' in the language means "driven away," as it is said to the dog: "ikhsa'," i.e., "go far away."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We made it a deterrent for what was before it and what was after it, and an admonition for the God-fearing.﴾

Regarding the pronoun referring to it there are four views. One: it is the sin; narrated by Atiyyah from Ibn Abbas. The second: it is the punishment; narrated by ad-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas. al-Farra said: the pronoun is a reference to the transformation (the form) into which they were transformed. The third: it is the town, and what is meant is its people; said by Qatadah and Ibn Qutaybah. The fourth: it is the nation that was transformed; said by al-Kisa'i and az-Zajjaj.

Regarding "nakal" (deterrent) there are two views. One: it is the punishment; said by Muqatil. The second: it is a lesson; said by Ibn Qutaybah and az-Zajjaj.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for what was before it and what was after it﴾: there are three views. One: "for what was before it" of the towns, and "what was after it" (of the towns); narrated by Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas. The second: "for what was before it" of the sins, and "what was after it": what they did after it; narrated by Atiyyah from Ibn Abbas. The third: "for what was before it" of the years in which they committed acts of disobedience, and "what was after it": what came after them among the Children of Israel, so that they would not do the same deeds as theirs; said by Atiyyah.

Regarding "al-muttaqin" (the God-fearing) there are two views. One: it is general for every God-fearing person until the Day of Resurrection; said by Ibn Abbas. The second: what is meant by them is the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ); said by as-Suddi on the authority of his shaykhs, and mentioned by Atiyyah and Sufyan.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verses 67–68:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow." They said, "Do you take us in ridicule?" He said, "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant."﴾ ﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is." He said, "Indeed, He says it is a cow neither old nor virgin, median between that, so do what you are commanded."﴾

Mention of the cause of their being commanded to slaughter the cow.

Ibn Sirin narrated from Ubaydah, who said: There was a man among the Children of Israel who was sterile and had no offspring, and he had much wealth. His nephew was his heir. So the nephew killed him, carried him away at night, and brought him to another place, and placed him at the door of a man from among them. Then in the morning he claimed him, until they took up arms, and some of them rode against others. So they came to Moses and mentioned that to him, and he commanded them to slaughter the cow.

And al-Suddi narrated from his shaykhs that a man from the Children of Israel had a daughter and a poor nephew. The nephew proposed to his daughter, but he refused. So he became angry and said: "By Allah, I will kill my uncle, take his wealth, marry his daughter, and eat his blood-money." He went to him and said: "Some merchants have arrived in one of the tribes of the Children of Israel, so come with me and take for me from their trade, perhaps I will gain profit from it." So he went out with him, and when they reached that tribe, the youth killed him. Then he returned, and in the morning he came as if seeking his uncle, not knowing where he was. Then he found that the people of that tribe had gathered around him. So he restrained them and said: "You have killed my uncle," and he began weeping (p-97) and calling out: "O my uncle!"

Abu al-Aliyah said: The one who asked Moses to ask Allah for clarification was the killer. Others said: Rather, the people gathered and asked Moses, and when he commanded them to slaughter a cow, they said: "Do you take us in ridicule?"

Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, Ibn Amir and al-Kisa'i read هُزُؤًا (huzu’an) with a dammah on the ha', the zay and the hamzah. Hamzah, Isma'il, Khalaf in his choice, and al-Farra' from Abd al-Warith and al-Mufaddal read هُزْءًا (huz’an) with the zay sukun. Hafs narrated it with a dammah without hamzah. Abu Ali al-Farisi related that every noun of three letters whose first letter is dammah, among the Arabs some pronounce it heavy and some pronounce it light, such as al-'usr and al-yusr.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant."﴾

He disowned mockery because the mocker is ignorant and playful. So when it became clear to them that the matter was from Allah, they said: ﴿Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: They asked "what is it?" because they knew that a cow whose dead body is struck with part of it would be brought back to life.

As for al-fariḍ (old), it is the aged one; it is said: the cow became fāriḍ when she grew old. Al-bikr (virgin) is the young one who has not given birth, and al-ʿawān (median) is between the aged and the young. It is said: ḥarbun ʿawān when it is not the first war, but a second one.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verses 69–70:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what its color is." He said: "Indeed He says it is a yellow cow, bright in its color, pleasing to the beholders."﴾ ﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is, for indeed the cows have become confused to us. And indeed we, if Allah wills, will be guided."﴾

Regarding "yellow" (ṣafrāʾ) there are two opinions. The first: that it is from ṣufra (yellowness), which is the well-known color. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatada, Ibn Zayd, Ibn Qutayba, and al-Zajjaj. The second: that it means black. This was said by al-Hasan al-Basri, but a group rejected it. Ibn Qutayba said: "This is an error in describing cows; it is only used in describing camels. One says *baʿīr aṣfar*, meaning black, because a black camel has a yellowness mixed into its blackness." (p-98) What indicates this is His saying: ﴿bright in its color (fāqiʿun lawnuhā)﴾, and the Arabs do not say "black fāqiʿ," rather they say "intensely black (aswad ḥālik)" and "bright yellow (aṣfar fāqiʿ)."

Al-Zajjaj said: *Fāqiʿ* is a description of the intensely yellow, as one says *aṣfar fāqiʿ* (bright yellow), *aḥmar qānin* (deep red), *akhḍar nāḍir* (vivid green), *abyaḍ yaqaq* (pure white), and *aswad ḥālik* (jet black), *ḥulkūk* and *dajwajī*. These are the attributes of intensity in colors.

The meaning of ﴿pleasing to the beholders﴾ is that it pleases them. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The people were strict, so Allah was strict with them." Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Had the Children of Israel not made an exception (in saying *in shāʾa Allāh*), they would not have been given what they were given," meaning by that their saying.

﴿And indeed we, if Allah wills, will be guided.﴾

Regarding the intended meaning of their being guided there are two opinions. The first: they meant "guided to the cow," and this is the view of the majority. The second: guided to the killer; this was mentioned by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 2, verse 71:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He said: Indeed, He says it is a cow neither broken to labor, that plows the earth nor waters the tilth, sound with no blemish in it. They said: Now you have brought the truth. So they slaughtered it, though they nearly did not.﴾

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He said: Indeed, He says it is a cow neither broken to labor﴾. Qatadah said: "It has not been made submissive by work, so that it plows the earth." Ibn Qutaybah said: "It is said of animals, *dabbah dhalul* (ذَلُولٌ), meaning clearly tame, with the *dhal* kasra, and of people, *rajul dhalil* (ذَلِيلٌ), meaning clearly humbled, with the *dhal* damma."

﴿that plows the earth﴾: it turns it over for cultivation. The cow is called *al-muthirah* (the one that stirs up the earth). Al-Farra' said: "Stop at *dhalul* (ذَلُولٌ), because the meaning is: it is not tame so that it plows the earth." Ibn al-Qasim related that Abu Hatim al-Sijistani permitted stopping at *dhalul*, but then strongly denied it, giving as his reason that the one that plows the earth cannot be used to water the tilth; and whenever it plows the earth, it is tame. The meaning of ﹁nor waters the tilth﹂ is that water is not drawn with it to irrigate the crop.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿sound (*musallamah*)﴾. On this there are four opinions:
First: sound, free from defects. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Abu al-'Aliyah, Qatadah, and Muqatil.
Second: free from labor. This was said by al-Hasan and Ibn Qutaybah.
Third: free from a mark (*shiyah*, meaning a mark or patch of different color). This was said by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd.
Fourth: sound in its limbs and form. This was said by 'Ata al-Khurasani.

As for *shiyah* (شِيَةٌ, a mark of a different color), al-Zajjaj said: "*Al-washy* in the language means mixing one color with another. It is said: *washa al-thawb* (وَشَى الثَّوْبَ), I embroider the garment, *washyan*, as you say: *waddaytu fulanan adiyahu diyah*." The word *shiyah* is in the accusative because it follows a negation. The meaning of the sentence is: there is no color in it that differs from the rest of its color. 'Ata al-Khurasani said: "Its color is one uniform color."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Now you have brought the truth﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: "*Al-an* (الآنَ, now) is the present time in which you are; it is the boundary between the two times: the end of the past and the beginning of the future. The meaning of *you have brought the truth* is: you have made it clear to us."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿so they slaughtered it, though they nearly did not﴾. On this there are two opinions:
First: because of its high price. This was said by Ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi.
Second: out of fear of exposure regarding the identity of the killer among them. This was said by Wahb.

Ibn Abbas said: "They kept searching for the cow for forty years until they found it with a man, who refused to sell it except for its hide filled with gold." This is the view of Mujahid, Ikrimah, Ubaydah, Wahb, Ibn Zayd, al-Kalbi, and Muqatil regarding the amount of the price.

As for the cause for which its price rose, it may have two possibilities:
First: they were strict, so Allah was strict with them.
Second: as an honor from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to its owner, if he was dutiful to his parents. Some exegetes mentioned that there was a young man among the Children of Israel who was dutiful to his father. A man came seeking a commodity that was in his possession, so he went to sell it to him, but found the keys of his shop with his father, who was asleep. He did not wake him, and the buyer went away. The buyer then offered him a higher price; he went back to his father, found him still asleep, returned to the buyer and refused, and the buyer doubled the price again. This pattern continued between them until the buyer left. Allah rewarded him for his dutifulness to his father by making a cow from a cow, that cow.

[p. 100] It is related from Wahb ibn Munabbih in a lengthy report that a young man was dutiful to his parents, and he used to gather firewood on his back; when he sold it, he gave a third in charity, gave a third to his mother, and kept a third for himself. His mother said to him one day: "I inherited a cow from your father, and I left it among the cattle in the name of Allah. When you come to the cattle, call it by the name of the God of Abraham." He went and called it, and it came to him. Allah made it speak, and it said: "Ride me, young man." He said: "My mother did not order me to do this." It said: "O dutiful son to his mother! If you had ridden me, you would not have been able to control me. Go, for if she ordered the mountain to uproot itself from its base and go with you, it would uproot itself because of your dutifulness to your mother." When he brought it, his mother said: "Sell it for three dinars, with my consent." Allah sent an angel who said: "How much is this?" He said: "Three dinars, with my mother's consent." The angel said: "I will give you six, and do not consult her." He refused, returned to his mother, and told her. She said: "Sell it for six, with my consent." The angel came and said: "Take twelve and do not consult her." He refused, returned to his mother, and told her. She said: "My son, that is an angel. Say to him: How much do you order me to sell it for?" He came to him and said this to him. The angel said: "O young man, this cow of yours will be bought by Musa ibn 'Imran for a slain man who is to be killed among the Children of Israel."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 72:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when you killed a soul﴾. This verse is placed later in the recitation but earlier in meaning, because the reason for the command to slaughter the cow was the killing of the soul. The sense of the sentence is therefore: "And when you killed a soul and disputed concerning it, and asked Moses, and he said: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow.﴾" A parallel to this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He has not made for it any deviance﴾ ﴿[but made it] straight﴾ [al-Kahf: 1]. He intended: "He sent down the Book straight and did not make for it any deviance." So He placed the latter first and the former last, because this is a habit of the Arabs. Al-Farazdaq said:

Indeed, al-Farazdaq is a smooth, solid rock; the mountain goats have grown tall, yet they cannot reach it.

He intended: "the mountain goats have grown tall." And Jarir said:

The phantom visited, but where is it from you, a visit? So return to your visitor with a greeting, a greeting.

He intended: "The phantom visited for a visit, and where is it from you?" And another said:

The disobedient ones are better than the people, their leader; O people, spare the sitting women.

He intended: "The disobedient ones, the people's leader, are better than..." and "spare the women" [meaning the sense as to the women] — "so be shy of this."

As for His saying ﴿fa-idda'ratum﴾: it means "you disagreed." This is what Ibn Abbas and Mujahid said. Al-Zajjaj said: "Idda'ratum" means "tadara'tum" (you pushed against one another), i.e., you repelled one another and each cast blame upon the other. You say "daraʾtu fulanan" when you push him away, "dāraytuhu" when you are gentle with him, and "daraytuhu" when you deceive him. The "ta" was assimilated into the "dal" because they share the same point of articulation. As for what you concealed, it is the matter of the slain person.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 73:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We said, "Strike him with part of it." Thus Allah brings the dead to life and shows you His signs that you might reason.﴾

Whoever said, "They spent forty years searching for it," said: they struck his grave. Whoever did not say that said: they struck his body before burial. Regarding that with which he was struck, there are six sayings.

The first: that he was struck with the bone that adjoins the cartilage (ghudrūf). This was related by ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: that bone is the root of the ear. Some people claimed that this bone is not struck on anyone and then he lives. Al-Zajjaj said: the ghudrūf is in the ear; it is what resembles the thin bone above the earlobe, and it is all of the upper rim of the ear's shell, and it is the hanging place of earrings. As for the two bones behind the ear, the protruding ones at the back of the ear, they are called al-khashshawān, and one of them is khashshā' and khushshusha'.

The second: that he was struck with the thigh. This was also related from Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah, Mujahid, and Qatadah. ʿIkrimah and Mujahid mentioned that it was the right thigh.

The third: that it was the piece of flesh between the two shoulders. This was related by al-Suddi from his shaykhs.

The fourth: that it was the tail. This was related by Layth from Mujahid (p-102). The fifth: that it was the coccyx (ʿajb al-dhanab), which is a bone upon which the body is built; this was related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

The sixth: that it was the tongue. This was said by al-Dahhak.

In the speech there is an omission; its implied meaning is: So We said, "Strike him with part of it so that he may live," and they struck him, and he lived, rose up, and informed them of his killer.

Regarding his killer there are four sayings. The first: his nephews (banū akhīhi), related by ʿAtiyyah from Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: his paternal cousins (ibnā ʿammihi), related by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas; these two sayings indicate that his killer was more than one person. The third: his nephew (ibn akhīhi), said by al-Suddi from his shaykhs and ʿUbaydah. The fourth: his brother, said by ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Thus Allah brings the dead to life﴾: concerning this there are two sayings.

The first: that it is addressed to the people of Moses. The second: that it is addressed to the polytheists of Quraysh; He argued against them when they denied resurrection with what the People of the Book agree upon. Abu ʿUbaydah said: "His signs" means His wonders.

**The Qur'an, 2:74:** ﴿Then your hearts hardened﴾. Ibrahim ibn al-Sarri said: *qasat* (قَسَتْ) in the language means it became harsh, dried out, and *'asat* (عَسَتْ) likewise. So *qaswat al-qalb* (قَسْوَةُ القَلْبِ, hardness of the heart) is the loss of softness, mercy, and humility from it. *Al-qasi* (القاسِي) and *al-'asi* (العاسِي) mean one that is very firm and hard. Ibn Qutayba said: *qasat*, *'asat*, and *'attat* (عَتَتْ) have the same meaning, namely *yabisat* (يَبِسَتْ, became dry).

Scholars differ on who is meant by "them" (المُشارِ إلَيْهِمْ). The first view is that it refers to all of the Children of Israel. The second is that it refers to the killer. Ibn Abbas said: those who killed him, after he named his killer, said, "By God, we did not kill him."

As for the *kaf* in *dhalika* (ذَلِكَ, "that"), there are three views. The first is that it points to the reviving of the dead, so the address is to all the Children of Israel. The second is that it points to the words of the slain man, so the address is to the killer; the commentators mentioned both of these. The third is that it points to the signs that were explained earlier, such as the transformation of people into apes and swine, the lifting of the mountain, the gushing of water, and the reviving of the slain man; this was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

As for *aw* (أَوْ, "or"), there are views on it, the same ones that were mentioned in the verse ﴿or like a rain-cloud﴾, and they have already been discussed.

**The Qur'an:** ﴿And indeed among stones are those from which rivers gush forth﴾. Mujahid said: every stone from which water bursts forth, or which splits open and releases water, or which falls from the top of a mountain, does so out of the fear of God.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 75:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do you then hope that they will believe you, when a party of them used to hear the words of Allah and then distort them after they had understood them, while they knew?﴾

Regarding those addressed by this verse there are three opinions. The first: it is the Prophet (ﷺ) specifically, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Muqatil. The second: it is the believers, the implied meaning being: "Do you hope that you will make your Prophet believed?" as said by Abu al-ʿAliyah and Qatadah. The third: they are the Ansar, for when they embraced Islam they loved the Islam of the Jews because of the fosterage (rida ah, milk-kinship) that existed between them; this is mentioned by al-Naqqash. Al-Zajjaj said: the alif in "afa-tatmaʿūna" (afa-tatmaʿūna, "do you then hope") is the alif of interrogation, as if He had made them despair of hoping for their belief.

Regarding their hearing the words of Allah there are two opinions. The first: they read the Torah and distorted it; this is the saying of Mujahid and al-Suddi along with others. Thus their hearing the words of Allah is through the conveying of their Prophet, and their distortion (tahrif) is the changing of what is in it. The second: they are the seventy whom Musa chose, who heard the words of Allah directly (kifahan) at the mountain. When they came to their people they said: "He said to us such and such," and at the end of His speech He said: "If you are not able to abandon what I forbid you, then do what you are able to do." This is the saying of Muqatil, and the first is more sound. Some scholars, among them al-Tirmidhi, author of "al-Nawadir," rejected this second view with strong denial, and said: "Only Musa was singled out for speech; otherwise, what distinction would there be?" He counted this among the narrations transmitted by al-Kalbi, who was a liar.

The meaning of ﴿ʿaqalūhu﴾ (ʿaqalūhu, "they understood it") is: they heard it and retained it.

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿wa-hum yaʿlamūn﴾ (while they knew) there are two opinions. The first: while they knew that they had distorted it. The second: while they knew the punishment for distorting it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 76–77:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe." But when they are alone with one another, they say, "Do you speak to them of what Allah has disclosed to you, so that they may argue with you about it before your Lord? Do you not then use reason?" Do they not know that Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal?﴾

This verse was revealed concerning a group of the Jews. When they met the Prophet and the believers, they said, "We believe." But when they were alone with one another, they said, "Do you speak to them of what Allah has disclosed to you?" This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliyah, Mujahid, Qatadah, 'Ata' al-Khurasani, Ibn Zayd, and Muqatil.

Regarding the meaning of ﴿what Allah has disclosed to you﴾ there are two opinions. The first: it means what Allah has decreed upon you, for al-fath (disclosure, opening) means al-qada' (decree, judgment), as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord, judge between us and our people with truth﴾ [al-A'raf: 89]. Al-Suddi said, from his shaykhs: Some of the Jews had believed and then became hypocrites, and they used to tell the believers about what they had been punished with. So some of them said to others, "Do you speak to them of what Allah has disclosed to you?" [of the punishment, so that they would say: "We are more beloved to Allah than you, and more honored by Allah than you."] The second: its meaning is what Allah has taught you. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliyah, and Qatadah said: "What He disclosed to them" is what He revealed in the Torah concerning the description of Muhammad (ﷺ). Muqatil said: A Muslim would meet his ally or his foster-brother from among the Jews and ask him, "Do you find Muhammad in your Book?" They would say, "Yes, indeed he is true." Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and others heard this, and he said to the Jews in private, "Do you speak to the companions of Muhammad of what Allah has disclosed to you?" That is, of what He made clear to you in the Torah concerning the matter of Muhammad, so that they may dispute with you about it before your Lord by your acknowledgment that he is a Prophet. "Do you not then use reason?" Do you not understand that this is a proof against you?!

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿before your Lord﴾ has two opinions. The first: it means "in the judgment of your Lord," as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those are the liars in the sight of Allah﴾ [al-Nur: 13]. The second: he intended the Day of Resurrection.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe." Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 78:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among them are unlettered ones﴾ means: the Jews. The ummi (unlettered) is the one who neither writes nor reads; this is what Mujahid said. Regarding his being called ummi there are two views. One: because he is in the state of the ummah (nation) that has not learned the Book, so he is upon his natural disposition; this is what al-Zajjaj said. The second: that he is attributed to his mother (ummihi), because writing among men was rare compared with women. It was also said: because he is as his mother bore him.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They know not the Book﴾. Qatadah said: they do not understand what is in it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿except wishful fancies (amani)﴾. The majority of reciters read the ya' with shaddah (amaniyya). Al-Hasan and Abu Ja'far read it with the ya' lightened (takhfif). Likewise: ﴿Those are their wishful fancies﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111], and ﴿It is not by your wishful fancies, nor the wishful fancies of the People of the Book﴾ [al-Nisa': 123], and ﴿in his wish (umniyyatihi)﴾ [al-Hajj: 52], and ﴿and wishful fancies deceived you﴾ [al-Hadid: 14]; all of these, with the ya' lightened and the ha' of "amaniyyihim" kasra'd. There is no disagreement on the fathah of the ya' of "al-amani."

Regarding the meaning of the statement there are three views.

One: that they are falsehoods. Ibn 'Abbas said: "except amani" means: except a saying they utter with their mouths, a lie. This is the view of Mujahid and the preference of al-Farra'. al-Farra' mentioned that some of the Arabs said to Ibn Da'b while he was narrating: "Is this something you transmitted, or something you wished for?" meaning: "Did you fabricate it?"

The second: that amani means recitation (tilawah), so the meaning is: they know the understanding (fiqh) of the Book; they only confine themselves to what they hear being recited to them. The poet said:

"He wished for the Book of God on the first night, as Dawud wished for the Psalms at leisure."

This is the view of al-Kisa'i and al-Zajjaj.

The third: that amani are their wishes concerning God; this was said by Qatadah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they are only assuming (yazunnun)﴾. Muqatil said: they are not certain; so whether the leaders lied or told the truth, they followed them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 79:

Allah's statement: ﴿So woe to those who write the Scripture with their own hands, then say, "This is from Allah," to exchange it for a small price. So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they earn.﴾

This verse was revealed concerning the People of the Book [who] altered the Torah and changed the description of the Prophet (ﷺ) in it. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd and Sufyan. As for "woe" (al-waylu), Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Woe (wayl) is a valley in Hell, into which the disbeliever will plunge for forty autumns before reaching its bottom." Al-Zajjaj said: "Woe" is a word the Arabs say for anyone who has fallen into destruction, and they also use it for themselves. Its linguistic origin is punishment and ruin. Ibn al-Anbari said: It is also said that the meaning of "woe" is severe suffering from punishment. It is also said that its origin is "wayy li-fulan," meaning "grief for so-and-so." The usage of the two particles became frequent, so the lam was joined to "way" and they were made into a single particle; then "woe" was given a predicate with another lam. This is the view preferred by al-Farra'. The "Scripture" here means the Torah. The mention of "hands" is for emphasis, and "a small price" refers to whatever perishes of this worldly life.

Regarding "what they earn," there are two views: first, that it refers to the compensation for what they wrote; second, that it refers to the sin of what they did.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 80:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And they say: The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days.﴾ "They" refers to the Jews. Concerning what they meant by these days, there are two opinions.

(p-107) The first: they meant forty days. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Abu al-'Aliyah, Qatadah, and al-Suddi.

Why did they estimate them as forty? On this there are three opinions.

The first: they said, "The distance between the two edges of Jahannam is a forty-year journey, and we will cross the distance of each year in one day; then the punishment will end and the Fire will perish." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: they said, "Our Lord became displeased with us over a matter, so He swore to punish us for forty nights, then He will admit us into Paradise. So the Fire will not touch us except for forty days, the fulfilment of the oath (tahillat al-qasam)." This is the view of al-Hasan and Abu al-'Aliyah.

The third: that it is the number of days during which they worshipped the calf. This was said by Muqatil.

The second opinion: the numbered days are seven days, because according to them the world lasts seven thousand years, and people are punished one day for every thousand years of the days of the world, after which the punishment ends. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

**

﴿Say: Have you taken a covenant with God?﴾ That is: has a covenant been made with you that He will punish you only for this amount?!

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 81–82:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed﴾. "Bala" (balā, "yes indeed") is in the position of "na'am" (naʿam, "yes"), except that "bala" is the response to a negation, while "na'am" is the response to an affirmation. Al-Farra' said: If a man says to his companion, "You have nothing owed to me," and the other says, "Na'am," it is a confirmation that he owes him nothing. But if he says, "Bala," it is a rejection of his statement. Ibn al-Anbari said: "Bala" only connects with a denial because it is a return from denial to affirmation, so it is in the position of "bal" (bal, "rather, but"), and "bal" by its nature comes after a denial, as in their saying: "Your brother did not stand, rather your father (did)." And if a man says to another, "Will you not stand?" and he replies, "Bala," he means, "Bal, I will stand," so he added the alif to "bal" so that silence upon it would be fine, because if he had said "bal" alone, the listener would expect speech after "bal." So he added the alif so that this assumption would be removed from the addressee. (p-108)

The meaning of ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed﴾ is: "Bal man kasaba" (rather, whoever earns). Al-Zajjaj said: "Bala" is a rebuttal of their saying: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days, numbered﴾. The "evil deed" here is shirk (associating partners with God), according to the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah, Abu Wa'il, Abu al-ʿĀliyah, Mujahid, Qatadah, and Muqatil.

﴿And his sin has encompassed him﴾, that is: his wrongdoing has surrounded him on all sides. Nafi' read "khatī'atuhu" (his sin) in the plural, "khaṭī'ātuhu." ʿIkrimah said: he died without repenting from it. Abu Wa'il said: "al-khaṭī'ah" (khaṭī'ah, "sin, wrong") is an attribute of shirk. Abu ʿAli said: Either the meaning is that his sin has nullified his good deed (ahbatat), since the one who encompasses is greater than the one encompassed, so this is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed Hell is encompassing of the disbelievers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 49], and His saying ﴿Its enclosure surrounds them﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]; or the meaning of "ahāṭat bihi" is that it destroyed him, like His saying: ﴿Unless you are surrounded (by enemies)﴾ [Yusuf: 66].

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 83:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And [recall] when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾. This covenant is recorded as having been taken from them in the Torah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You worship﴾. ʿĀṣim, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir read it with the letter tāʾ, as direct address to them. Ibn Kathīr, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read it with the letter yāʾ, as a report about them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And to parents, good treatment﴾. That is: and We enjoined upon them, regarding their fathers and mothers, goodness. Al-Farrāʾ said: The Arabs say, "I enjoin you to it, good," and "I command you to it, good," meaning: "I command you to do it," and then "an" (that) is omitted, so that "good" is connected to the enjoining and the command. A poet said:

I marvelled at Dahmāʾ when they complained of us,
and at Abū Dahmāʾ when he enjoined us
good regarding them, as if we had been unkind to them.

As for good treatment of parents, it is their righteousness (birr). Ibn ʿAbbās said: Do not shake out your garment so that dust reaches them. ʿĀʾishah said: One who fixes his gaze upon his parent has not been dutiful to him. ʿUrwah said: Do not refrain from anything they both love.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And to the near of kin﴾. That is: and We enjoined upon them [good treatment] toward the near of kin, that they should keep up the ties of kinship. As for "orphans" (yatāmā), it is the plural of "yatīm". Al-Aṣmaʿī said: Orphanhood (yutm) among people is from the father's side, and among other than people it is from the mother's side. Ibn al-Anbārī said: Thaʿlab said: The meaning of yutm in the speech of the Arabs is isolation (infirād). So the meaning of "a yatīm child" is one isolated from his father. And we recited:

O Fāṭimah, indeed I am perishing, so be patient with me,
and do not grieve; every woman is a yatīm.

He said: It is narrated as "yatīm" and "yaʾīm". Whoever narrates "yatīm" with the tāʾ means: every woman is weak and alone. Whoever narrates it with the yāʾ means: every woman's husband dies leaving her. He said: Ibn al-Aʿrābī recited to us:

Three kinds of loves: a love of attachment,
and a love of flattery, and a love which is killing.

He said: We said to him, "Add more," and he said: "The line is yatīm," meaning: isolated. I read to our shaykh Abū Manṣūr the lexicographer, and he said: When the child reaches maturity, the name "yatm" departs from him. It is said: from it "yatama, yaytamu, yutman and yatman." The plural of yatīm is yatāmā and aytām. Every isolated thing among the Arabs is yatīm and yatīmah. He said: It is also said: the root of yutm is heedlessness, and the yatīm was named after it, because he is heedless of his dutifulness. A woman is called yatīmah as long as she is not married; when she marries, the name of yutm departs from her. It is said: the name of yutm never departs from her. Abū ʿAmr said: yutm is delay (ibṭāʾ), and from it the yatīm is derived, because kindness is delayed from him. "And the needy" (masākīn) is the plural of miskīn, and it is a name derived from sukūn (stillness), as if poverty has made the miskīn still.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And speak to people good [words]﴾. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir read ḥusnan with a ḍammah on the ḥāʾ and without shaddah. Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read ḥasanan with a fatḥah on the ḥāʾ and with shaddah. Abū ʿAlī said: As for whoever reads "ḥasanan", it is permissible that ḥasan is a dialectal form of ḥusn, like bukhl and bakhal, and rushd and rashad. This occurs in adjectives as it occurs in nouns; do you not see that they say "al-ʿarab" and "al-ʿurb"? It is also permissible that ḥasan is a verbal noun, like kufr, shukr and shughl, and the noun it modifies is omitted, as if he said: "Say a word that is good." And whoever reads "ḥasanan" makes it an adjective, and the estimate in his view is: "Say to people a good word," so the modified noun is omitted.

They differed regarding the addressees of this, on two views.

One: they are the Jews. This is said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Jurayj. Its meaning: be truthful and make clear the description of the Prophet.

The second: they are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). Abū al-ʿĀliyah said: Speak to people with what is known (maʿrūf). Muhammad ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn said: Speak to them with what you would love them to say to you. A group claimed that what is meant by this is leniency toward the disbelievers in calling them to Islam. On this view, it is abrogated by the verse of the sword.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then you turned away﴾. That is: you turned away, except for a few of you. Regarding them there are two views. One: they are those who did not alter. The second: they are those who believed in the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) during his time.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verses 84–85:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when We took your covenant: Do not shed your blood, nor expel yourselves from your homes⦆. That is: do not let some of you shed the blood of others, nor let some of you expel others from their homes. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Then you acknowledged the covenant on that day, and you today are witnesses to that. So the acknowledgment (iqrar) is directed to their predecessors, and the witnessing is directed to their successors. ﴿Then you are those who kill yourselves⦆. That is: some of you kill others. Al-Suddi related from his shaykhs, who said: The Qurayza were allies of the Aws, and the Nadir were allies of the Khazraj. They would fight in the war of Samir: the Qurayza would fight alongside their allies, the Nadir and their allies, while the Nadir would fight the Qurayza and their allies. They would defeat them, ruin their dwellings and expel them from them. When a man from either of the two parties was taken captive, they would gather for him until they ransomed him. The Arabs would reproach them for this, saying: How do you fight them and then ransom them? They would reply: We were commanded to ransom them, and killing them has been forbidden to us. The Arabs would say: Then why do you fight them? They would reply: We are ashamed that our allies should be humiliated. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, rebuked them, and said:

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verses 84–85:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when We took your covenant: Do not shed your blood, nor expel yourselves from your homes⦆. That is: do not let some of you shed the blood of others, nor let some of you expel others from their homes. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Then you acknowledged the covenant on that day, and you today are witnesses to that. So the acknowledgment (iqrar) is directed to their predecessors, and the witnessing is directed to their successors. ﴿Then you are those who kill yourselves⦆. That is: some of you kill others. Al-Suddi related from his shaykhs, who said: The Qurayza were allies of the Aws, and the Nadir were allies of the Khazraj. They would fight in the war of Samir: the Qurayza would fight alongside their allies, the Nadir and their allies, while the Nadir would fight the Qurayza and their allies. They would defeat them, ruin their dwellings and expel them from them. When a man from either of the two parties was taken captive, they would gather for him until they ransomed him. The Arabs would reproach them for this, saying: How do you fight them and then ransom them? They would reply: We were commanded to ransom them, and killing them has been forbidden to us. The Arabs would say: Then why do you fight them? They would reply: We are ashamed that our allies should be humiliated. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, rebuked them, and said:

The words of the Most High: ﴿You support one another [tazahirun]﴾. ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read (tuẓāhirūn), and in (al-Taḥrīm) they read (taẓāharā), with the ẓāʾ lightened. Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir read it with the ẓāʾ doubled and the alif retained. Abū ʿAlī said: whoever reads (tuẓāhirūn) with the ẓāʾ doubled has assimilated (idghām) the tāʾ into the ẓāʾ, because they are close in articulation, and so lightened it through assimilation. Whoever reads (tuẓāhirūn) lightened has deleted the tāʾ that the others assimilated, from the pronunciation, and so lightened it through deletion. The tāʾ that Ibn Kathīr assimilated is the same tāʾ that ʿĀṣim deleted. It is narrated from al-Ḥasan and Abū Jaʿfar (taẓẓahharūn), with the ẓāʾ doubled and no alif, so that the tazāhur means mutual aid. Ibn Qutaybah said: its root is from the back (ẓahr), as if tazāhur means that each of the two men, or of the other people, makes the other a back for himself, by which he strengthens himself and leans upon him. Muqātil said: "al-ithm" is disobedience, and "al-ʿudwān" is injustice.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them [tufādūhum]﴾. The root of "al-asr" is binding. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir read (asārā), and al-Aʿmash and Ḥamzah read (asrā). Al-Farrāʾ said: the people of the Ḥijāz pluralise asīr as "asārā", while the people of Najd mostly say "asrā", and this is the better of the two forms in Arabic, because it is like their saying jarīḥ and jarḥā, and ṣarīʿ and ṣarʿā. Al-Aṣmaʿī narrated from Abū ʿAmr that he said: "asārā" are those who were bound, while "asrā" are those who are in their hands, except that they were not bound. Al-Zajjāj said: "faʿlā" is the plural for everything with which people are afflicted in their bodies and minds. It is said: hālik and halkā, marīḍ and marḍā, aḥmaq and ḥamqā, and sakrān and sakrā. Whoever reads (asārā), then it is a plural of a plural: you say asīr, asrā, and asārā is the plural of asrā.

The words of the Most High: ﴿you ransom [tufādūhum]﴾. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿUmar and Ibn ʿĀmir read (tafdūhum). Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim and al-Kisāʾī read (tufādūhum) with an alif. Al-mufādāh is giving something and taking something in its place.

﴿Do you then believe in part of the Book﴾, which is: the ransoming of captives. ﴿and disbelieve in part﴾, which is: the expulsion and the killing. Mujāhid said: you ransom him in the hand of another, while you yourself kill him with your hand. ?!

Regarding the meaning of "al-khizy" there are two opinions. The first is that it is the poll-tax (jizyah), as said by Ibn ʿAbbās. The second is the killing of Qurayẓah and the banishment of al-Naḍīr, as said by Muqātil.

The words of the Most High: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought the worldly life at the price of the Hereafter﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: they are the Jews. Muqātil said: they sold the Hereafter for what they obtain of this world.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 87:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book﴾, meaning the Tawrah (the Torah). *Wa-qaffayna* means: We followed up (*atba'na*). Ibn Qutaybah said: it is derived from *al-qafa* (the back of the neck/nape). It is said: *qafawtu al-rajul*, when I walked in his footsteps. *Al-bayyinat* means the signs and the clear proofs, such as healing the blind-born and the leper, and bringing the dead back to life. *Wa-ayyadnahu* means: We strengthened him (*qawwaynahu*). *Al-ayd* means strength (*al-quwwah*).

Regarding *Ruh al-Qudus* (the Holy Spirit) there are three opinions.

The first: that it is Jibril (Gabriel). *Al-Quds* means purity (*al-taharah*). This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, and others. Ibn Kathir used to read *bi-Ruhi al-Qudsi* with the *dal* silent (*sakinat al-dal*). Abu Ali said: both the lightening and the heavy pronunciation of it are good, like *al-'unq* and *al-'unuq*, and *al-tunb* and *al-tunub*.

Regarding His strengthening him with it, there are three opinions, mentioned by al-Zajjaj. The first: that He strengthened by it the apparent evidence of his proof and the affair of his religion. (p-113) The second: to repel the Children of Israel from him when they intended to kill him. The third: that He strengthened him with it in all his circumstances.

The second opinion: that it is the Name by which he used to bring the dead to life. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas.

The third: that it is the Injil (the Gospel), said by Ibn Zayd.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 88:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they say, "Our hearts are wrapped."﴾ The majority (al-Jumhur) read the lam with sukun, while a group, among them al-Hasan and Ibn Muhaysin, read it with a damma. Al-Zajjaj said: One who reads (ghulfun) with sukun on the lam, its meaning is "possessors of wrappings" (dhawat ghulf), so it is as though they said: "Our hearts are in coverings." As for one who reads (ghulufun) with a damma on the lam, it is the plural of "ghilaf" (covering), so it is as though they said: "Our hearts are receptacles of knowledge; so why do they not understand, when they are receptacles of knowledge?!" According to the first reading, they mean his turning away from them, as though they were saying: "We understand nothing." According to the second, they are saying: "If your words were true, our hearts would have accepted them."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So little is it that they believe.﴾ On this there are five opinions.

The first: "So few of them are believed (yu'man)," said by Ibn Abbas and Qatada. The second: the meaning is "little is what they believe in." Mu'ammar said: They believe in a little of what is in their hands, and disbelieve in most of it. The third: the meaning is "they do not believe a little nor a lot." This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari, who said: "This is according to the dialect of a people of the Arabs, who say: 'Rarely have I seen the like of this man,' and they mean: 'I have not seen his like.'" The fourth: "they believe for a short time," like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Believe in what has been revealed to those who believed at the beginning of the day﴾; this too was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari. The fifth: the meaning is "their belief is little," mentioned by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari, who related two opinions regarding "ma" (what): the first is that it is superfluous (za'ida); the second is that "ma" encompasses all things and then particularizes some of what it generally covers by what is mentioned after it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 89–90:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Wretched is that for which they have sold themselves﴾. "Bi'sa" (wretched is): a word that comprehensively expresses all blame; its opposite is "ni'ma" (excellent is). "Ishtaraw" (they sold) means "baa'u" (they sold). What they sold it for is a little of this world.

His saying, the Exalted: "baghyan" (out of envy). Qatadah said: "Hasadan" (out of envy). The meaning of the statement is: they disbelieved out of envy, because God sent down His bounty upon the Prophet ﷺ.

Regarding His saying, the Exalted: "bi-ghadabin 'ala ghadab" (with wrath upon wrath), there are five opinions. The first: the first wrath was for their taking the calf, and the second was for their disbelief in Muhammad. This is related by al-Suddi from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas. The second: the first was for their denial of the Messenger of God, and the second was for their enmity toward Jibril. This was transmitted by Shahr from Ibn 'Abbas. The third: the first was when they said ﴿The hand of God is chained﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64], and the second was when they denied the Prophet of God. This was transmitted by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Farra' preferred it. The fourth: the first was for their denial of 'Isa and the Injil, and the second was for their denial of Muhammad and the Qur'an. This was said by al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Ikrimah, Abu al-'Aliyah, Qatadah, and Muqatil. The fifth: the first was for their altering the Torah, and the second was for their denial of Muhammad ﷺ. This was said by Mujahid.

"Muhin" (humiliating) means "mudhill" (degrading).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 91:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe in what Allah has sent down,"﴾ means: the Qur'an. ﴿They say, "We believe in what was sent down to us,"﴾ meaning: the Torah.

Regarding His saying ﴿and they disbelieve in what is beyond it﴾ there are two opinions. The first is that He meant what is other than it. Similar to this is His saying ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ [An-Nisa' 24]. This was said by al-Farra' and Muqatil. The second is: what comes after that which was sent down to them. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and it is the truth﴾ refers back to what is beyond it.

﴿Why then did you kill the prophets of Allah﴾ this is the answer to their saying, ﴿We believe in what was sent down to us,﴾ for the prophets came confirming the Torah. He attributed the killing to the later generations because they were following the opinion of the earlier ones. (p-115) And "taqtuluna" (you kill) is used in the sense of "qataltum" (you killed), so the present tense is placed in the position of the past, because the mind does not go to anything else. They recited in support of this:

*He witnessed against al-Hutay'ah when he meets his Lord, that al-Walid has more right to the excuse.*

He meant: "yashhadu" (he witnesses).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 92–93:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Moses certainly came to you with clear proofs﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: it refers to what was in the Tablets of the lawful and the unlawful; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. The second: it refers to the nine signs; this is the view of Muqatil.

Regarding the pronoun in "ba'dahu" (after him) there are two opinions. The first: it refers to Moses, so its meaning is: after his departure to the mountain; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil. The second: it refers to the coming, because "ja'akum" (came to you) indicates the coming. Mentioning their worship of the calf is a refutation of their saying: ﴿We believe in what was sent down to us﴾.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They said, "We hear and we disobey"﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: Whenever they looked at the mountain, they would say, "We hear and we obey," and whenever they looked at the Book, they would say, "We hear and we disobey."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they were made to drink into their hearts the calf﴾, meaning: they were made to drink the love of the calf. He omitted the genitive noun, which is "love," and placed the genitive-dependent noun in its position. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197] [meaning: the time of Hajj]; and His saying: ﴿Have you made the providing of water for the pilgrims...﴾ [al-Tawbah: 19] [meaning: have you made the one in charge of providing water for the pilgrims...]; and His saying: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82] [meaning: its people]; and His saying: ﴿Then We would have made you taste double [the punishment] of life﴾ [al-Isra': 75], meaning: double the punishment of life. And His saying: ﴿Had it not been for... monasteries, churches, and prayer-places [synagogues] would have been demolished﴾ [al-Hajj: 40], meaning: houses of prayer. And His saying: ﴿Rather, it was your scheming by night and day﴾ [Saba': 30], meaning: your scheming in them. And His saying: ﴿Then let him call his council﴾ [al-'Alaq: 17], meaning: his people. (p-116) From this is the saying of the poet:

"I was informed that fire was kindled after you, and the assembly was abused after you, O Kulayb."

Meaning: the people of the assembly. Another said:

"The worst of deaths is a dead man among his people,"

meaning: the worst of deaths is the death of a dead man among his people.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Wretched is what your faith commands you"﴾, meaning: that you deny the messengers, kill the prophets without right, and conceal the guidance.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If you are believers﴾. Regarding "in" (if) there are two opinions. The first: it is in the sense of negation, so the meaning is: you were not believers when you disobeyed Allah and worshipped the calf. The second: "in" is a conditional particle linked to what precedes it, so the meaning is: if you are believers, then wretched is the faith that commands you to worship the calf and kill the prophets; this was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.
