Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 94–96:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: If the Last Abode with Allah is yours exclusively, then wish for death, if you are truthful﴾. The Jews used to claim that Allah, Exalted is He, had created Paradise only for Israel (Ya'qub) and his offspring, so this verse was revealed. Among the proofs that they knew the Prophet ﷺ was truthful is that they did not wish for death. The greatest proof of his truthfulness is that he informed that they would not wish for it, by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾, and none of them wished for it. As for ﴿what their hands have sent ahead﴾, it refers to the killing of the prophets, their denial of them, and their alteration of the Torah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you will surely find them﴾. The lam is the lam of oath, and the nun is for emphasis. The meaning: you will surely find the Jews, when they are called to wish for death, the most eager of people for life, and more eager than those who associated partners (with Allah). Regarding "those who associated partners," there are two views. One: they are the Magians (Majus), said by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Qutaybah (Ibn Qutayba) and al-Zajjaj. The second: they are the polytheists of the Arabs, said by Muqatil.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Each one of them wishes he could be given a life of a thousand years﴾. Regarding the pronoun in "ahadihim" (of them), there are two views. One: it returns to those who associated partners, said by al-Farra'. The second: it returns to the Jews, said by Muqatil. Al-Zajjaj said: He mentioned "a thousand years" because it is the upper limit of what the Magians used to invoke for their kings; a king would be told, "Live a thousand Nawruz and a thousand Mihrajan."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verses 97–99:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Jibril...﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'Who comes to you of the angels?' He said: 'Jibril.' They said: 'That one descends with war and fighting; he is our enemy.' So this verse and the one following it were revealed."

Regarding Jibril there are eleven dialects (lughat).

The first: Jibril, with a kasra on the jim and the ra, without a hamza. This is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and Ibn ʿAmir and Abu ʿAmr recited with it. Waraqa ibn Nawfal said:

"And Jibril comes to him, and Mikal with them both, from Allah, a revelation that expands the breast, sent down."

ʿImran ibn Hattan said:

"And the Spirit, Jibril, is among them, with no equal to him, and Jibril was trusted by Allah."

Hassan said:

"And Jibril, the messenger of Allah, is among us, and the Holy Spirit has no equal."

The second dialect: Jabril, with a fatha on the jim and a kasra on the ra, followed by a silent ya, without a hamza, on the pattern fa'lil. Al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin recited with it. Al-Farra' said: "I do not favor it, because there is no fa'lil in speech. Yet I do not see that al-Hasan recited it except that it is correct, because it is a foreign (a'jami) name."

The third: Jabra'il, with a fatha on the jim and the ra, followed by a kasra hamza, on the pattern jabra'il. Al-A'mash, Hamza and al-Kisai recited with it. Al-Farra' said: "This is the dialect of Tamim and Qays and many of the people of Najd." Al-Zajjaj said: "It is the finest of the dialects." Jarir said:

"They worshipped the cross and denied Muhammad, and denied Jabra'il and denied Mikal."

The fourth: Jabra'il, with a fatha on the jim and the ra, and a hamza between the ra and the lam, with a kasra, without elongation, on the pattern jabra'il. Abu Bakr related it from ʿAsim.

The fifth: Jabra'illu, with a fatha on the jim, a kasra on the hamza and a shadda on the lam. This is the recitation of Aban from ʿAsim and Yahya ibn Yaʿmur.

The sixth: Jibra'il, with a kasra hamza followed by a ya with the alif.

The seventh: Jibra'iyil, with two ya's after the alif, the first of which is kasra.

The eighth: Jabrin, with a fatha on the jim and a nun in place of the lam.

The ninth: Jibrin, with a kasra on the jim and a nun. Al-Farra' said: "This is the dialect of Banu Asad." I read to our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi, from Ibn al-Anbari, who said: "There are nine dialects for Jibril," and he mentioned them.

Ibn al-Anbari mentioned in his book "The Refutation of One Who Opposes the Mushaf of ʿUthman" Jibra'il, with a fatha on the jim, the alif affirmed, and a kasra hamza with no ya after it. And Jabra'in, with a fatha on the jim, a kasra hamza followed by a ya and a nun.

As for Mikail, there are five dialects.

The first of them: Mikal, on the pattern mif'al, without a hamza. This is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and Abu ʿAmr and Hafs from ʿAsim recited with it.

The second: Mika'il, with a silent ya after the hamza, on the pattern Mika'il. This is the dialect of Tamim and Qays and many of the people of Najd. Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza, al-Kisai and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim recited with it.

The third: Mika'il, with a kasra hamza after the alif without a ya, on the pattern Mika'il. Nafi', Ibn Shanabudh and Ibn al-Sabbah all recited with it, from Qunbul.

The fourth: Mika'il, on the pattern Mika'il, with which Ibn Muhaysin recited.

The fifth: Mika'in, with a hamza followed by a ya and a nun after the alif. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned it.

Al-Kisai said: "Jibril and Mikail are names the Arabs did not know; when they came, the Arabs arabicized them." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Jibril and Mikail are like your saying ʿAbd Allah and ʿAbd al-Rahman. Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verses 100–101:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿A party of those who were given the Scripture cast away﴾ — he means the Jews. And "the Scripture" is the Torah.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 102:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they followed what the devils recited﴾.

There are two reports concerning the occasion of its revelation.

The first: "The Jews would not ask the Prophet about anything from the Torah without him answering them. So they asked him about sorcery (sihr) and disputed with him about it, and this verse was revealed." This was said by Abu al-'Aliyah.

The second: "When Sulayman (Solomon) was mentioned in the Qur'an, the Jews of Madinah said: 'Do you not marvel at Muhammad? He claims that the son of Dawud was a prophet! By God, he was nothing but a sorcerer.' So this verse was revealed." This was said by Ibn Ishaq.

"Tatlu" (تَتْلُو) means "talat" (تَلَتْ, it recited/followed), and "'ala" (عَلَى) means "fi" (في, "during"). This was said by al-Mubarrad. Al-Zajjaj said: His saying ﴿over the kingdom of Sulayman﴾ means "during the reign of Sulayman."

Concerning how the devils "recited" over the kingdom of Sulayman, there are six opinions.

(p-121) The first: When Sulayman lost his kingdom, the devils wrote down sorcery and buried it beneath his prayer place. When he died, they extracted it and said: "With this he used to rule the kingdom." This meaning was mentioned by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the view of Muqatil.

The second: Asif used to write down what Sulayman commanded and bury it beneath his throne. When Sulayman died, the devils extracted it and wrote between every two lines sorcery and falsehood, and attributed it to Sulayman. Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: The devils wrote sorcery after the death of Sulayman, and then attributed it to him. This was said by Ikrimah.

The fourth: The devils invented sorcery, and Sulayman took it and buried it beneath his throne so that people would not learn it. When he died, they extracted it and taught it to the people, saying: "This is the knowledge of Sulayman." This was said by Qatadah.

The fifth: Sulayman took covenants from the beasts. Whenever a beast harmed a person, he would appeal to it by that covenant, and it would desist. Then the sorcerers added rhymed prose and sorcery. This was said by Abu Mijlaz.

The sixth: In the time of Sulayman, the devils used to eavesdrop (istiraq al-sam') and would hear from the speech of the angels what would happen on earth of death, rain, or events. They would come to the soothsayers (kahanah) and inform them, and the soothsayers would tell the people, and the people would find it as they had said. Then, when the soothsayers felt secure from them, they lied to them [and inserted other things into it], adding seventy words with every word. The people wrote that narration in books, and it spread among the Children of Israel that the jinn know the unseen. So Sulayman sent out to the people, gathered those books into a chest, and buried them beneath his throne. No devil could approach the throne without being burned [and he said: "I will not hear anyone claiming that the devils know the unseen except that I will strike off his neck"]. When Sulayman died, a devil came to a group of the Children of Israel and guided them to those books, saying: "Sulayman only governed the affairs of creation by this." So it spread among the people that Sulayman was a sorcerer, and the Children of Israel took those books. When Muhammad (ﷺ) came, they disputed with him by them. This is the view of al-Suddi.

"Sulayman" is a Hebrew name, and the Arabs spoke it in the pre-Islamic era. Al-Nabighah made it "Sulaym" out of necessity, saying:

"And Sulaym wove every fleeting judgment"

And al-Hutay'ah was compelled to make it "Salam," saying:

"In it are the spears, and in it every full coat of mail, / tightly woven, firm, from the weaving of Salam."

Both of them intended Dawud, the father of Sulayman, but the meter was not sound for them, so they made it "Sulayman" and changed it.

Thus I read it to our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi. And in His saying ﴿but Sulayman did not disbelieve﴾ there is evidence for the disbelief of the sorcerer, because they were attributed to sorcery and not to disbelief.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿but the devils disbelieved﴾.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and 'Asim read "wa-lakinna" (وَلَكِنَّ) with a shaddah on the nun and the nun of "al-shayatin" (الشَّيَاطِينَ) in the accusative. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "lakin" (لَكِنْ) with the nun lightened and the nun of "al-shayatin" in the nominative.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and what was sent down to the two angels﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and al-Zuhri read "al-malakayn" (الْمَلِكَيْنِ) with a kasrah on the lam. The reading of the majority is more sound.

Concerning "ma" (what) there are two opinions. The first: it is conjoined to the first "ma," so the construction is: "and they followed what the devils recited and what was sent down to the two angels." The second: it is conjoined to "sihr" (sorcery), so the construction is: "they taught people sorcery and taught them what was sent down to the two angels." If it is asked: if sorcery was sent down to the two angels, why were they disliked? The answer has two aspects, mentioned by Ibn al-Sarri. The first: they used to teach people what sorcery is and command them to avoid it, and in that there is wisdom, since if a questioner asked "what is fornication?" it would be obligatory to inform him of it and let him know that it is forbidden. The second: it is possible that God tested the people through the two angels, so whoever accepted learning it became a disbeliever, and whoever did not accept it was a believer, just as they were tested by the river of Talut.

Concerning what was sent down to the two angels there are two opinions. The first: it is sorcery, narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, and Ibn Zayd. The second: it is the separation between a man and his wife, not sorcery, narrated from Mujahid, Qatadah, and from Ibn 'Abbas in two versions. Al-Zajjaj said: This is also a category of sorcery.

The reference to the story of the two angels.

The scholars mentioned that the two angels were only sent down to earth for a reason: when the sins of the children of Adam increased, the angels invoked curses upon them. God, may He be exalted, said: "If desire and the devils were sent down among you in the same position as they are among the children of Adam, you would do the same as they did." So they spoke to themselves that if they were tested, they would hold fast. So God revealed to them (p-124) [that] they should choose two angels from the best of you. They chose Harut and Marut. This is related from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas.

The scholars differed over what the two did of disobedience, in three opinions. The first: they committed fornication, murder, and drank wine. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: they acted unjustly in judgment. This was said by 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Utbah. The third: they only intended disobedience and nothing more. It is related from 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, that Zuhrah was a beautiful woman, and that she came before the two angels Harut and Marut to dispute. Each of them solicited her for herself without knowing of his companion. They used to ascend to heaven at the end of the day. She said to them: "By what do you descend and ascend?" They said: "By the Greatest Name of God." She said: "I will not comply with what you want until you teach it to me." So they taught it to her, and she flew to heaven, and God transformed her into a star.

In a hadith: "The Prophet (ﷺ) cursed Zuhrah and said: 'She tempted two angels.'" However, these matters are far from authentic. Some have interpreted this, saying: when he saw the star, he mentioned that woman (p-125), not that the woman was transformed into a star.

The scholars differed over the manner of their punishment. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud that they are suspended by their hair until the Day of Resurrection. Mujahid said: they are placed in a well filled with fire.

As for Babil (Babylon), it is related from al-Khalil that the tongues of the people were confused (tabalbalat) there. They differed over its boundaries in three opinions. The first: it is Kufah and its surroundings, said by Ibn Mas'ud. The second: it is from Nasibayn to Ra's al-'Ayn, said by Qatadah. The third: it is a mountain in a depression of the earth, said by al-Suddi.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We are only a trial﴾, that is: a test and a tribulation.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿except by the permission of God﴾, meaning: by His decree. ﴿And they certainly knew﴾: a reference to the Jews. ﴿that whoever purchases it﴾, meaning: chooses it, meaning: sorcery. The lam is the lam of oath. As for "khalaq" (الخَلاقُ), al-Zajjaj said: it is the portion and the abundant share of good.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And how wretched is that for which they sold their souls﴾, that is: they sold them for it. ﴿If only they knew﴾ the punishment for it.

(p-126) * Section

The jurists differed over the ruling on the sorcerer. The school of our Imam Ahmad, may God be pleased with him, holds that he becomes a disbeliever by his sorcery, whether or not he killed by it. Is his repentance accepted? There are two narrations. Al-Shafi'i said: he does not become a disbeliever by his sorcery. If he kills by his sorcery and says: "My sorcery kills the like of him, and you intended that," he is killed in retaliation (qawd). If he says: "It may kill, it may err," he is not killed, and blood money (diyah) is due. As for the sorcerer of the People of the Book, he is not killed according to Ahmad unless he harms the Muslims, in which case he is killed for breaking the covenant. In this the man and the woman are equal. Abu Hanifah said: the ruling on the sorcerer of the People of the Book is the same as the ruling on the sorcerer among Muslims regarding the obligation of execution. As for the female sorcerer, he said: she is imprisoned and not killed.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 103–104:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if only they had believed﴾ — meaning: the Jews. And "al-mathuba" (reward) means: the recompense. ﴿If only they knew﴾ — al-Zajjaj said: that is, they would teach by their knowledge.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O you who believe, do not say "raina"﴾ — The majority of readers recited it without tanwin, while al-Hasan, al-A'mash and Ibn Muhaysin recited it with tanwin, "wa-ra'ina" without tanwin (from ra'aytu, "to watch over/attend to") and with tanwin (from al-ru'una, "foolishness/rudeness"). Ibn Qutayba said: "Raina" with tanwin is a noun derived from al-ra'n and al-ru'una; he meant: do not say it out of ignorance or stupidity. Others said: when a man wanted his companion to listen attentively, he would say, "Ri'ni sam'aka" (give me your attention), so the hypocrites would say "raina," meaning, "you are a fool." As for His saying "unzurna" (look upon us), it has the meaning of "intazirna" (wait for us). Mujahid said: "unzurna" means: listen to us. Ibn Zayd said: do not hasten against us.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 105:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book do not wish﴾

Ibn 'Abbas said: They are the Jews of Madinah and the Christians of Najran, and the polytheists are the polytheists of the people of Makkah.

﴿that there should be sent down to you﴾, i.e., upon your Messenger. ﴿any good from your Lord﴾: he meant prophethood and Islam.

(p-127) Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: By "good" he meant knowledge, jurisprudence (fiqh) and wisdom (hikmah).

﴿But Allah specifies for His mercy whom He wills﴾

Regarding this mercy there are two opinions. The first: that it is prophethood, said by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, Mujahid and al-Zajjaj. The second: that it is Islam, said by Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verses 106–107:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whatever sign We abrogate﴾.

The occasion of its revelation: the Jews said, when the qibla was abrogated: "Muhammad permits his companions whatever he wishes, and forbids them whatever he wishes." So this verse was revealed.

Al-Zajjaj said: Naskh (abrogation) in the language is: the annulling of a thing and the setting up of another in its place. The Arabs say: "The sun abrogated (nasakhat) the shade," when it removes it and takes its place. Regarding the meaning intended by this naskh there are three opinions. The first: the removal of both the wording and the ruling. The second: the replacing of a verse with another; both of these are narrated from Ibn Abbas, and the first is the view of al-Suddi. The second is the view of Muqatil. The third: the removal of the ruling while the wording remains; this was narrated by Mujahid from the companions of Ibn Mas'ud, and Abu al-'Aliyah also said this. Ibn Amir recited (مَا نَنْسَخُ) with a damma on the nun and a kasra on the sin. Abu Ali said: meaning, "what we find to be abrogated," like your saying: "I praised (ahmadtu) so-and-so," meaning: I found him praiseworthy; and he finds it abrogated only by His abrogating it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or cause it to be forgotten﴾. Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr recited (نَنْسَأها) with a fatha on the nun and with the hamza, and the meaning is "we delay it." Abu Zayd said: "The camels delayed (nasa'at) from the watering-place," and if he causes them to delay (anse'ahā) it means he postponed them; and from this comes al-nasi'a (deferred payment) in sale. Regarding the meaning of "we delay it" there are three opinions. The first: we delay it from abrogation, so we do not abrogate it; this was said by al-Farra'. The second: we delay its sending down, so we never send it down at all. The third: we delay it from being acted upon by our abrogating it; Abu Ali al-Farisi related these two. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas recited (تَنْسَها) with an open ta' and a nun. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and al-Dahhak recited (تُنْسَها) with a damma on the ta'. Nafi' recited (أَوَنُنْسُها) with two nuns, the first vowelled with a damma and the second sukun. He intended: "or We cause you to forget it" (nunsikaha), from forgetting.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We bring a better than it﴾. Ibn Abbas said: "with greater ease than it, and more facilitating for the people."

His saying: ﴿or its like﴾, that is, in reward and benefit; so the wisdom in replacing it with its like is testing.

﴿Do you not know﴾: its wording is the wording of a question, but its meaning is affirmation and establishing. Sovereignty (al-mulk) in the language is the completeness of power and its firmness; so Allah, mighty and majestic, judges over His servants as He wills, and with rulings other than what He wills.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 108:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger⦆ [the verse as cited begins: "Or do you wish to question your Messenger"].

Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are five reports.

The first: "Rafi' ibn Huraymila and Wahb ibn Zayd said to the Messenger of Allah: 'Bring us a Book that we may read, sent down to us from the heaven, and cause rivers to gush forth for us, so that we may follow you.' Then this verse was revealed." This is related from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: "The Quraysh asked the Prophet ﷺ to make Safa into gold for them. He said: 'It shall be yours, like the table [of food] for the Children of Israel, [if you disbelieve]'; but they refused." This is related from Mujahid.

(p-129) The third: "A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if only our expiation were like the expiations of the Children of Israel!' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'O Allah, we do not desire it. What Allah has given you is better than what He gave the Children of Israel. When one of them committed a sin, he would find it written on his door along with its expiation. If he expiated it, it would be a disgrace for him in this world; and if he did not expiate it, it would be a disgrace for him in the Hereafter. Allah has given you better than what He gave the Children of Israel.'" Then He said: ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself [then seeks forgiveness of Allah will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful]﴾ [al-Nisa', 110]. And he said: "The five daily prayers, and Friday to Friday, are an expiation for what is between them." Then this verse was revealed. This is related by Abu al-'Aliya.

The fourth: "'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya al-Makhzumi came to the Prophet ﷺ with a group of Quraysh and said: 'O Muhammad, by Allah, I will not believe in you until you bring Allah and the angels before me as a tribe.' Then this verse was revealed." This is mentioned by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The fifth: "A group of the polytheists came to the Prophet ﷺ. Some of them said: 'We will not believe you until you make a spring gush forth for us from the earth.' Another said: 'I will not believe you until the mountains of Makkah are moved away for us.' 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya said: 'I will not believe you until you bring a Book from the heaven, containing: From Allah, Lord of the worlds, to Ibn Abi Umayya: Know that I have sent Muhammad to the people.' Another said: 'Why did you not bring your Book all at once, as Musa brought the Torah?' Then this verse was revealed." This is mentioned by Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Anbari.

Regarding those addressed in this verse there are three views.

One: they are the Quraysh, related from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. Two: the Jews, related from Muqatil. Three: all the Arabs, related from Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. (p-130)

Regarding "am" (أم) there are two views.

One: it means "bal" (بل, "rather"). The Arabs say: "Is there a right of mine upon you, or (am) are you known for injustice?" They mean: "Rather, you are." And they recited:

"She appeared like the horn of the sun in the brightness of the forenoon, and her form— or (am) are you more beautiful in the eye?"

This is mentioned by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj.

Two: it is interrogative. If an objector says: "It is only interrogative when it follows an interrogative before it; where is the interrogative that preceded it?" then there are two answers. The first: an interrogative did precede it, namely His saying: ﴿Do you not know that Allah is over all things competent?﴾. This is mentioned by al-Farra'. Likewise Ibn al-Anbari said: it is linked back to the alif in "Do you not know." If it is objected to this answer, that the phrase "Do you not know" refers to a single person while "you wish" refers to a group, the answer is: the address shifted from the singular to the plural, because what was addressed to the Prophet ﷺ was addressed to his community too; so he was satisfied with the first address for his community, then made the meaning explicit in the second address. A similar case is His saying: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them for their waiting period﴾ [al-Talaq, 1]. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned this answer. The second answer concerning "am" is that it is interrogative and not linked to anything. Al-Farra' said: when the interrogative occurs in the middle of speech, it begins with the alif and with "am"; and when no speech precedes it, it is only with the alif or with "hal." Ibn al-Anbari said: "am" functions like "hal," except that the difference between them is that "hal" is an initial interrogative, which does not occur in the middle or at the end, while "am" is a medial interrogative, which occurs only after speech.

As for "the Messenger" here, it is Muhammad ﷺ. And what was asked of Musa before, in their saying: ﴿Show us Allah openly﴾ [al-Nisa', 153]. Did they ask this of a prophet or not? There are two views on this. One: they did ask it, saying: ﴿We will not believe you until you bring Allah and the angels as a group before us﴾ [al-Isra', 92], related from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: they pressed their questions excessively, so it was said to them through this verse: "Perhaps you wish to ask Muhammad that Allah show you openly," related from Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. (p-131)

Kufr (الكفر) means denial (الجحود), and iman (الإيمان) means affirmation (التصديق). Abu al-'Aliya said the meaning of ﴿whoever substitutes hardship for ease﴾ is: whoever exchanges hardship for ease. And sawa' al-sabil (سواء السبيل) means its middle (وسطه).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 109:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Many of the People of the Scripture wish⦅ ... ⦆﴾

Regarding its occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) there are three opinions. The first: Huyayy ibn Akhtab and Abu Yasir were zealously striving to turn people away from Islam, so this verse was revealed. This was said by Ibn Abbas. The second: Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf used to satirize the Prophet and incite the disbelievers of Quraysh against him in his poetry, and the polytheists and the Jews of Madinah used to harm the Messenger of Allah when he arrived there; so the Prophet was commanded to pardon them, and this verse was revealed. This was said by Abd Allah ibn Ka'b ibn Malik. The third: a group of Jews invited Hudhayfah and Ammar to their religion, but they refused, so this verse was revealed. This was said by Muqatil.

The meaning of "wadda" is "loved and wished." "People of the Scripture" means the Jews. Al-Zajjaj said: "min 'indi anfusihim" is connected to "wadda kathir" and not to "hasadan," because a person's envy arises only from within himself, and the meaning is that their wish for your disbelief comes from within themselves, not that the truth is with them. As for envy (hasad), it is wishing for the removal of a blessing from the one envied, even if it does not pass to the envier; ghibta (wholesome desire to match) differs from it, for it is wishing for a similar blessing without wishing for its removal from the one envied. Some of them defined envy, saying: it is a harm that befalls a person through knowledge of the good condition of the righteous. It is not permissible for the virtuous person to be envious, because the virtuous person follows what is beautiful. (p-132) Some of the wise said: everyone can be satisfied except the envious, for he is satisfied only by the removal of your blessing. Al-Asma'i said: I heard a Bedouin say: "I have not seen a wrongdoer more like a wronged person than the envious: constant sorrow, perpetual breath, a bewildered mind, and a regret that never ends."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿until Allah brings His command⦅ ... ⦆﴾ Ibn Abbas said: Allah brought His command regarding the Banu al-Nadir through exile and banishment, and regarding Quraydhah through killing and taking captives.

Section

It has been narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Abu al-Aliyah, and Qatadah, may Allah be pleased with them, that the pardon and forgiveness were abrogated (mansukh) by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah or the Last Day and do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden⦅ ... ⦆﴾ [al-Tawbah: 29]. A group of exegetes and jurists rejected this view, arguing that Allah did not command pardon and forgiveness absolutely, but commanded it up to a limit (ghayah), and what comes after the limit differs in ruling from what came before it. Something of this nature is not a case of abrogation; rather, the first ruling's period has ended with its limit, and the latter requires a different ruling.

Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary on 2:110:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You will find it﴾, meaning: you will find its reward.

(p-133) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they say: None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians.﴾

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The Jews of Medina and the Christians of Najran disputed in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ. The Jews said: 'The Christians are not upon anything, and none will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew,' and they disbelieved in the Injil and in ʿIsa. The Christians said: 'The Jews are not upon anything,' and they disbelieved in the Torah and in Musa. So God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those are their wishful fancies.﴾"

Know that the speech in this verse is concise (mujmal), and its meaning is: the Jews said, "None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew (hud)," and the Christians said, "None will enter Paradise except one who is a Christian (nasrani)." The word "Yahud" is the plural of "ha'id." ﴿Those are their wishful fancies⦆ means: that is something they wish for, and an assumption they assume. This is the meaning of the statement of Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid.

﴿Say: Produce your proof⦆ means: your argument, if you are truthful that Paradise is entered only by one who is a Jew or a Christian. Then God, exalted is He, made clear that it is not as they claimed, and said: ﴿Yes, whoever submits his face⦆ — "aslama" here means: sincerely devoted. Regarding "the face" there are two views. One: that it is the religion. The second: that it is the deed.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and he is a doer of good⦆ means: in his deed. ﴿Then for him is his reward⦆. Al-Zajjaj said: he means, "so he will enter Paradise."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they recite the Book⦆ means: each of them recites his own Book while affirming what he disbelieved in. This was said by al-Suddi and Qatada. ﴿Thus said those who do not know⦆ — regarding them there are two views. One: they are the polytheist Arabs, who said to Muhammad and his companions, "You are not upon anything," as related by al-Suddi from his shaykhs. The second: they are nations that existed before the Jews and Christians, such as the people of Nuh, Hud, and Salih, as said by ʿAta'.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection⦆. Al-Zajjaj said: he means the judgment that separates them, so He will show them, plainly, who enters Paradise and who enters the Fire. As for the judgment between them regarding the creed, He has already made it clear to them in this world by establishing the correct proofs.

﴿Say: Produce your proof⦆ means: your argument, if you are truthful that Paradise is entered only by one who is a Jew or a Christian. Then God, exalted is He, made clear that it is not as they claimed, and said: ﴿Yes, whoever submits his face⦆ — "aslama" here means: sincerely devoted. Regarding "the face" there are two views. One: that it is the religion. The second: that it is the deed.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and he is a doer of good⦆ means: in his deed. ﴿Then for him is his reward⦆. Al-Zajjaj said: he means, "so he will enter Paradise."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they recite the Book⦆ means: each of them recites his own Book while affirming what he disbelieved in. This was said by al-Suddi and Qatada. ﴿Thus said those who do not know⦆ — regarding them there are two views. One: they are the polytheist Arabs, who said to Muhammad and his companions, "You are not upon anything," as related by al-Suddi from his shaykhs. The second: they are nations that existed before the Jews and Christians, such as the people of Nuh, Hud, and Salih, as said by ʿAta'.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection⦆. Al-Zajjaj said: he means the judgment that separates them, so He will show them, plainly, who enters Paradise and who enters the Fire. As for the judgment between them regarding the creed, He has already made it clear to them in this world by establishing the correct proofs.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 114:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And who is more unjust than those who prevent the mosques of Allah﴾ — the scholars differed concerning who this was revealed about, into two opinions.

(p-134) One of them: that it was revealed concerning the Romans, who had backed Bukhtansar (Nebuchadnezzar) in the ruin of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), because the Children of Israel had killed Yahya ibn Zakariyya (John the Baptist). So he ruined it, and carcasses were thrown into it. This was said by Ibn Abbas, along with others. The second: that it was revealed concerning the polytheists who stood between the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and Makkah on the day of al-Hudaybiyya. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Concerning what is meant by its ruin there are two opinions. One: that it means he demolished it. The second: that it means he prevented the mention of Allah in it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those – it was not for them to enter it except in fear﴾ — concerning this there are two opinions. One: that it is a report about their condition after that. As-Suddi said: no Roman would enter Bayt al-Maqdis except while fearing that his neck would be struck, or he has been made fearful by paying the jizya. The second: that it is a report in the sense of a command, its meaning being: you must strive earnestly in fighting them so that no one enters it except while in fear.

﴿For them in this world is disgrace﴾ — concerning this there are three opinions. One: that their disgrace is the jizya; this was said by Ibn Abbas. The second: that it is the conquest of Constantinople; this was said by as-Suddi. The third: that it is their expulsion from the Masjid al-Haram, so that no polytheist ever enters it openly; this was said by Ibn Zayd.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 115:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west﴾.

Regarding its revelation there are four opinions. The first: "The Companions were with the Messenger of Allah on a campaign on a pitch-dark night, and they did not know the qiblah. So each one of them made a marker (masjid) in front of himself and prayed. When they awoke in the morning, they found themselves facing other than the qiblah, so they mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah, and Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse." Narrated by ʿĀmir ibn Rabīʿah. The second: that it was revealed concerning voluntary supererogatory prayer (tatawwuʿ bi-l-nafilah), related from Ibn ʿUmar. The third: that when His saying was revealed, ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir: 60], they said, "Where?" and this verse was revealed, related from Mujahid. The fourth: that when the Negus (al-Najashi) died, and the Prophet ﷺ commanded them to pray over him, they said, "He did not pray towards the qiblah," so this verse was revealed, related from Qatadah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then there is the Face of Allah﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions. One: "Then Allah is there," meaning His knowledge is with you wherever you are; this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and Muqatil. The second: "Then there is the qiblah of Allah," related from ʿIkrimah and Mujahid. Al-Wasiʿ (the All-Encompassing) is He whose richness encompasses the poverty of His servants and who provides for all His creation. Al-wisʿah (abundance) in the speech of the Arabs means richness (al-ghina).

Section

This verse has an operative ruling for the mujtahid who prays towards other than the qiblah, and for the voluntary prayer of one riding a mount, and for one in fear. Some people have held that it was abrogated, saying: when it was revealed, the Messenger of Allah turned towards Bayt al-Maqdis, and then this was abrogated by His saying: ﴿And wherever you are, turn your faces towards it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144].

This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas. Our shaykh ʿAli ibn ʿUbaydullah said: There is no text in the Qur'an specifically commanding prayer towards Bayt al-Maqdis, and His saying ﴿Wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾ is not an explicit command to face Bayt al-Maqdis; rather it contains what indicates that all directions are equal in the permissibility of facing them. Given this, it is established that facing Bayt al-Maqdis was obligatory by the Sunnah, and then it was abrogated by the Qur'an.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 116:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "Allah has taken a son."﴾

Scholars differed about who this verse was revealed concerning, giving four opinions.

The first: it was revealed concerning the Jews, when they made ʿUzayr the son of Allah. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: it was revealed concerning the Christians of Najran, when they said, "ʿIsa is the son of Allah." This was said by Muqatil.

The third: it refers to the Christians and the polytheists of the Arabs, because the Christians said, "ʿIsa is the son of Allah," and the polytheists said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah." This was mentioned by Ibrahim ibn al-Sarri.

The fourth: it refers to the Jews, the Christians and the polytheists of the Arabs. This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi.

As for qunut (devout obedience, standing in worship), al-Zajjaj said: "In the language it has two meanings. One of them is standing. The second is obedience. The well-known meaning in the language and usage is that qunut is supplication while standing, so the qanit is one who stands before the command of Allah. It may also apply to all acts of obedience, because if there is no standing on two feet, then it is standing in intention." Ibn Qutayba said: "I do not see the root meaning of qunut except obedience, because all the characteristics of prayer, standing in it, supplication and other things arise from it."

Regarding the meaning of qunut here, the exegetes have three opinions. The first: it is obedience. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and Qatada. The second: it is acknowledgment of worship. This was said by ʿIkrima and al-Suddi. The third: it is standing. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Rabi'.

Regarding the meaning of standing, there are two sayings. The first: it is standing before Him by bearing witness to servitude. The second: it is standing before Him on the Day of Resurrection. If it is asked: how is this statement general when many of creation are not obedient to Him? There are three answers to this. The first: its outward form is general, but its meaning is specific; the meaning is that all the people of obedience are devoutly obedient to Him. The second: the shadows of the disbelievers prostrate to Allah in the mornings and evenings, so qunut is attributed to them in this sense. The third: every created thing is devoutly obedient in that the effect of His creation is upon it and His rulings flow over it, and this is a sign of its submission to the Lord. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned these.

**The words of the Most High: ﴿Originator of the heavens﴾**

*Al-Badi'* means *al-Mubdi'* (the Originator). Whoever brings something into existence that has no precedent is said to have *abda'ta* (you originated). Al-Khattabi said: *al-Badi'* is on the pattern *fa'il* (in the sense of *maf'il*, the active-participle form), and its meaning is that He created creation by bringing it into being without a model that preceded it.

**The words of the Most High: ﴿And when He decrees a matter﴾**

Ibn Abbas said: the meaning of *al-qada'* (decree) is *al-iradah* (will). Muqatil said: when He decrees a matter in His knowledge, then to it He says: "Be," and it is. The majority read the *nun* of *fayakun* with a *damma*, in the *raf'* (nominative) on the basis of *al-qat'* (a new independent sentence, not a conditional response). The meaning is: "so it is." Ibn Amir read it with a *fatha* on the *nun* (*fayakuna*). Makki ibn Abi Talib said: the *nasb* (accusative) is on the basis of *al-jawab* (response to the conditional), but there is remoteness in it.

**Section**

Our companions used the word "Be" (*kun*) as evidence for the eternity of the Qur'an. They said: if "Be" were created, it would need to be brought into existence by another "Be," and that would continue infinitely, and an infinite regress is impossible. If it is objected that this is address to something non-existent, the answer is that it is an address of *takwin* (bringing into being) that manifests the effect of power; and it is impossible that the one addressed should already exist, because by the address it came to be, so its existence before it or with it is impossible. What confirms this is that what will be is conceived in knowledge, so it resembles the existent thing, and therefore its address is permissible.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 118:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who do not know said, "Why does Allah not speak to us?"﴾ Concerning them there are three opinions. The first: they are the Jews; this is related from Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: they are the Christians; this is related from Mujahid. The third: they are the polytheists of the Arabs; this is related from Qatada, and al-Suddi, on the authority of his shaykhs. "Lawla" here carries the meaning of "halla" (why not / would that).

Concerning ﴿those before them﴾ there are three opinions. The first: they are the Jews; this is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid. The second: they are the Jews and the Christians; this is related from al-Suddi, on the authority of his shaykhs. The third: the Jews, the Christians and others among the disbelievers; this is related from Qatada.

﴿Their hearts have become similar﴾, that is, in disbelief.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 119:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth﴾.

Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are two accounts. The first: "The Prophet (ﷺ) once said: 'I wish I knew what my parents did!' So this verse was revealed." This was related by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'If Allah sent down His punishment upon the Jews, they would have believed.' So this verse was revealed." This was related by Muqatil.

Regarding the meaning of "the truth" (al-ḥaqq) here, there are three opinions. The first: it is the Qur'an, related by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: it is Islam, related by Ibn Kaysan. The third: it is truthfulness (al-ṣidq).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you will not be questioned about﴾. The majority read the taʾ with a ḍammah, as a statement of fact, and the meaning is: you are not responsible for their deeds. Nafiʿ and Yaʿqub read it with a fatḥah on the taʾ and a sukun on the lam, as a prohibition against asking about them.

(p-138) Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash permitted that the meaning of this reading is: "Do not ask about them, for they are in a grave matter," so that this is by way of magnifying what they are in. As for al-Jahim: al-Farra' said: al-Jahim is the fire, and blazing fire upon blazing fire. Abu ʿUbayda said: al-Jahim is the fierce, raging fire. Al-Zajjaj said: al-Jahim is the fire of intense fuel; one says "jahama fulan al-nar" when he intensifies its fuel. It is also said of the eye of a lion: juḥmah, because of its intense blazing. It is also said of the fuel of war, meaning the intensity of fighting in it: jahim (jāḥim). Ibn Faris said: al-jāḥim is a place of intense heat. Al-Aʿsha said:

"They prepare for battle before its meeting, on the morning of the grip of might, while death is a jāḥim (blazing ember)."

For this reason al-Jahim was so named. Ibn al-Anbari said: Ahmad ibn ʿUbayd said: the fire was only named jahim because its fuel is abundant, from the Arabs' saying: "jahamtu al-nar ajhamuha," when you increase its fuel for it.

ʿImran ibn Hittan said:

"He sees obedience to Allah as guidance, and its opposite as error, which the blazing ember of coals burns its people in."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 120:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians﴾.

Regarding the occasion of its revelation, there are three reports.

The first: The Jews of Madinah and the Christians of Najran had been hoping that the Prophet ﷺ would pray facing their qibla. When he was turned toward the Ka'bah, they despaired of him, and this verse was revealed. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: They invited him to their religion, and so it was revealed. This was said by Muqatil.

The third: They used to ask him for a truce (hudnah) and would tempt him into thinking that if he made a truce with them, they would agree with him. So it was revealed. Its meaning was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

Al-Zajjaj said: The millah (religion, community of faith) in the language means the sunnah (way, path) and the tariqah (method, course). Ibn 'Abbas said: "Guidance of Allah" (huda Allah) here means Islam. Regarding what came to him of knowledge (al-'ilm), there are four views. The first: it is the turning toward the Ka'bah, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: it is the clarification that the religion of Allah is Islam. The third: it is the Qur'an. The fourth: (p-١٣٩) knowledge of the misguidance of the people.

﴿You have from Allah no protector﴾ who would benefit you, ﴿nor any helper﴾ who would prevent you from His punishment.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 121–124:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾.

The scholars differed about who this verse was revealed concerning, on two views. One: it was revealed concerning those Jews who believed; this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: it concerns the believers among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ; this is the view of ʿIkrimah and Qatadah. As for "the Book," there are two views. One: it is the Qur'an; this is the view of Qatadah. The second: it is the Torah; this is the view of Muqatil.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿who recite it as it should be recited﴾, meaning: who act upon it as it should be acted upon; this is the view of Mujahid.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They believe in it﴾. Regarding the pronoun in "bihi" (in it) there are two views. One: it refers to the Book. The second: it refers to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. What follows this has already been explained, up to His saying: ﴿And when Abraham was tried by his Lord with certain words﴾. Al-ibtila' (trial) means testing. As for Ibrahim, there are six dialects. The first: Ibrahim, which is the common dialect (al-lughah al-fashiyyah). The second: Ibraham. The third: Ibraham. The fourth: Ibrahim; these were mentioned by al-Farra'. The fifth: Ibraham. The sixth: Ibaraham. ʿAbd al-Muttalib said:

"I have sought refuge with what Ibaraham sought refuge with, facing the Ka'bah, while he was standing."

And he also said:

"We are the people of God in His Ka'bah; that has not ceased to be so since the time of Ibarahim."

As for "the words" (al-kalimat), there are five views.

One: they are five in the head and five in the body. The ones in the head: the parting of the hair (al-farq), rinsing the mouth (al-madmadah), inhaling water into the nose (al-istinshaq), trimming the moustache (qass al-shārib), and the siwak. In the body: paring the nails, shaving the pubic area (halq al-'anah), plucking the armpit hair (natf al-ibt), cleansing with water after relieving oneself (al-istitabah), and circumcision. This was narrated by Tawus from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: they are ten, six in a person and four in the rites (al-mashaʿir). Those in a person: shaving the pubic area, plucking the armpit hair, paring the nails, trimming the moustache, the siwak, and ritual washing from major impurity (al-ghusl min al-janabah), and washing on Friday. Those in the rites: circumambulating the House, the sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwah, stoning the pillars (ramy al-jimar), and the ifadah. This was narrated by Hanash ibn ʿAbd Allah from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: they are the rites (al-manasik); this was narrated by Qatadah from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The fourth: He tried him with the star, the sun, the moon, the emigration, the fire, the sacrifice of his son, and circumcision; this is the view of al-Hasan.

The fifth: they are every request in the Qur'an, like His saying: ﴿My Lord, make this city secure﴾ [Ibrahim: 35] and the like; this is the view of Muqatil. Whoever said they are actions he performed said: the meaning of "fa-atammahunna" (and he fulfilled them) is that he acted upon them. Whoever said they are supplications and requests said: the meaning of "fa-atammahunna" is that Allah granted him what he asked for in them. It has been related from Abu Hanifah that he read "Ibrahimu" with a damma on the mim and "rabbahu" with a fatha on the ba', meaning: he tested his Lord to see whether He would answer his supplication and take him as a friend or not.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And from my offspring﴾. Regarding "dhurriyyah" (offspring) there are two views. One: it is of the form fi'liyyah from the root dharr, because Allah brought forth creation from the loins of Adam like dhurr (tiny particles). The second: its original form is dharrurah, on the pattern fa'lulah; but since the doubling occurred frequently, the final ra' was replaced by a ya', so it became dhuriyyah, then the waw was assimilated into the ya', so it became dhurriyyah. Al-Zajjaj mentioned both, and preferred the first.

As for "the covenant" (al-ʿahd) here, there are seven views. One: it is leadership (al-imamah); this was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said so. The second: it is obedience (al-ta'ah); this was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas. The third: mercy (al-rahmah); this is the view of ʿAta' and ʿIkrimah. The fourth: religion (al-din); this is the view of Abu al-ʿAliyah. The fifth: prophethood (al-nubuwwah); this is the view of al-Suddi from his shaykhs. The sixth: security (al-aman); this is the view of Abu ʿUbaydah. The seventh: the pact (al-mithaq); this is the view of Ibn Qutaybah. The first is the most sound.

As for the intended meaning of "the wrongdoers" (al-zalimin) here, there are two views. One: they are the disbelievers; this is the view of Ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi. The second: they are the sinners; this is the view of ʿAta'.

The ones in the head: the parting of the hair (al-farq), rinsing the mouth (al-madmadah), inhaling water into the nose (al-istinshaq), trimming the moustache (qass al-shārib), and the siwak. In the body: paring the nails, shaving the pubic area (halq al-'anah), plucking the armpit hair (natf al-ibt), cleansing with water after relieving oneself (al-istitabah), and circumcision. This was narrated by Tawus from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: they are ten, six in a person and four in the rites (al-mashaʿir). Those in a person: shaving the pubic area, plucking the armpit hair, paring the nails, trimming the moustache, the siwak, and ritual washing from major impurity (al-ghusl min al-janabah), and washing on Friday. Those in the rites: circumambulating the House, the sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwah, stoning the pillars (ramy al-jimar), and the ifadah. This was narrated by Hanash ibn ʿAbd Allah from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: they are the rites (al-manasik); this was narrated by Qatadah from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The fourth: He tried him with the star, the sun, the moon, the emigration, the fire, the sacrifice of his son, and circumcision; this is the view of al-Hasan.

The fifth: they are every request in the Qur'an, like His saying: ﴿My Lord, make this city secure﴾ [Ibrahim: 35] and the like; this is the view of Muqatil. Whoever said they are actions he performed said: the meaning of "fa-atammahunna" (and he fulfilled them) is that he acted upon them. Whoever said they are supplications and requests said: the meaning of "fa-atammahunna" is that Allah granted him what he asked for in them. It has been related from Abu Hanifah that he read "Ibrahimu" with a damma on the mim and "rabbahu" with a fatha on the ba', meaning: he tested his Lord to see whether He would answer his supplication and take him as a friend or not.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And from my offspring﴾. Regarding "dhurriyyah" (offspring) there are two views. One: it is of the form fi'liyyah from the root dharr, because Allah brought forth creation from the loins of Adam like dhurr (tiny particles). The second: its original form is dharrurah, on the pattern fa'lulah; but since the doubling occurred frequently, the final ra' was replaced by a ya', so it became dhuriyyah, then the waw was assimilated into the ya', so it became dhurriyyah. Al-Zajjaj mentioned both, and preferred the first.

As for "the covenant" (al-ʿahd) here, there are seven views. One: it is leadership (al-imamah); this was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said so. The second: it is obedience (al-ta'ah); this was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas. The third: mercy (al-rahmah); this is the view of ʿAta' and ʿIkrimah. The fourth: religion (al-din); this is the view of Abu al-ʿAliyah. The fifth: prophethood (al-nubuwwah); this is the view of al-Suddi from his shaykhs. The sixth: security (al-aman); this is the view of Abu ʿUbaydah. The seventh: the pact (al-mithaq); this is the view of Ibn Qutaybah. The first is the most sound.

As for the intended meaning of "the wrongdoers" (al-zalimin) here, there are two views. One: they are the disbelievers; this is the view of Ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi. The second: they are the sinners; this is the view of ʿAta'.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 121–124:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾.

The scholars differed about who this verse was revealed concerning, on two views. One: it was revealed concerning those Jews who believed; this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: it concerns the believers among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ; this is the view of ʿIkrimah and Qatadah. As for "the Book," there are two views. One: it is the Qur'an; this is the view of Qatadah. The second: it is the Torah; this is the view of Muqatil.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿who recite it as it should be recited﴾, meaning: who act upon it as it should be acted upon; this is the view of Mujahid.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They believe in it﴾. Regarding the pronoun in "bihi" (in it) there are two views. One: it refers to the Book. The second: it refers to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. What follows this has already been explained, up to His saying: ﴿And when Abraham was tried by his Lord with certain words﴾. Al-ibtila' (trial) means testing. As for Ibrahim, there are six dialects. The first: Ibrahim, which is the common dialect (al-lughah al-fashiyyah). The second: Ibraham. The third: Ibraham. The fourth: Ibrahim; these were mentioned by al-Farra'. The fifth: Ibraham. The sixth: Ibaraham. ʿAbd al-Muttalib said:

"I have sought refuge with what Ibaraham sought refuge with, facing the Ka'bah, while he was standing."

And he also said:

"We are the people of God in His Ka'bah; that has not ceased to be so since the time of Ibarahim."

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 125:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when We made the House a place of return for the people﴾. "The House" here is the Kaʿba. The definite article (al-) may be used for a known referent (al-maʿhud) or for the genus (al-jins). When the addressees knew that He did not mean the genus, it was taken to refer to the known thing. Al-Zajjaj said: "al-mathab and al-mathaba are the same, like al-maqam and al-maqama." Ibn Qutayba said: "al-mathaba is the place of return, from your saying 'thubtu ila kadha', meaning 'I returned to it'. And 'thaba ilayhi jismuhu ba'da al-ʿilla' means his body returned after illness, when it recovered." He meant that people return to it time and again.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And a sanctuary﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "He means that whoever commits a crime elsewhere and then takes refuge in it is safe. However, the people of Makka should not trade with him, give him food or drink, shelter him, or speak to him until he leaves. When he leaves, the legal punishment is carried out on him." Qadi Abu Yaʿla said: "He described the House as safe, but what is meant is the entire sacred precinct (al-Haram), as in His saying ﴿an offering reaching the Kaʿba﴾, where what is meant is the whole Haram, because one does not slaughter in the Kaʿba or in the Masjid al-Haram. This is a ruling, not merely a statement of fact."

Regarding ﴿the station of Ibrahim﴾ there are three opinions. The first: it is the whole Haram, said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: it is ʿArafa, Muzdalifa and the jamarat (stoning pillars), said by ʿAta'. It is also narrated from Mujahid as two opinions. It has been reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAta' and Mujahid that they said: "The whole Hajj is the station of Ibrahim." The third: it is the stone, said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr, and this is the most sound view. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah! If only we took the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer!" Then this was revealed.

(p-142) Regarding the cause of Ibrahim standing on the stone, there are two accounts. The first: he came seeking his son Ismaʿil and did not find him. His wife said to him: "Get down." He refused. She said: "Let me wash your head." She brought him a stone, and he placed his foot on it while he was riding. She washed one side of his head, then lifted the stone, and his foot had sunk into it. She placed it under the other side and washed it, and his foot sank into it again. So Allah made it a sign of him. This was mentioned by al-Suddi from Ibn Masʿud and Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: he stood on the stone to build the House while Ismaʿil handed him the stones. This was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

The majority of reciters, including Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, ʿAsim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i, read (wa-ittakhidhu) with a kasra on the kha', as a command. Nafiʿ and Ibn ʿAmir read it with a fatha on the kha', as a statement. Ibn Zayd said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Where do you see that we should pray?' ʿUmar said: 'At the station.' Then this was revealed: ﴿And take from the station of Ibrahim a place of prayer﴾." Abu ʿAli said: the reason for the fatha on the kha' is that it is coordinated (maʿtuf) with what precedes it, as if he said: "and when they took". The fatha on the kha' is confirmed by the fact that what follows is a statement, namely His saying: "and We commanded".

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We charged Ibrahim and Ismaʿil﴾, meaning: We ordered them and enjoined them. Ismaʿil is a non-Arabic name, and it has two forms: Ismaʿil and Ismaʿin. They recited:

"The neighbours of the tribe said when we arrived: 'This, by the Lord of the House, is Ismaʿin.'"

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That you purify My House﴾. Qatada said: "He means from the worship of idols, polytheism, and false speech." If it is said: there was no house there, so what is the meaning of ordering them to purify it? There are two answers. The first: there were idols there, and they were ordered to remove them. This was said by ʿIkrima. The second: its meaning is "build it purified." This was said by al-Suddi.

Al-ʿakifun means those who remain (al-muqimun). It is said: ʿakafa, yaʿkifu and yaʿkufu, ʿukufan, meaning he stayed, and from this comes i'tikaf (seclusion in worship). Ibn ʿAbbas narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah, may He be exalted, sends down on every night and on the day of one hundred and twenty mercies, which descend upon this House: sixty for those who circumambulate, forty for those who pray, and twenty for those who look on."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 126:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Abraham said, "My Lord, make this a secure city"﴾. Al-balad (city): the foremost of the towns. Al-balid: one who dwells in a city. Al-balda: the foremost part. And the she-camel "placed her balda" (her chest) when she knelt down. What is meant by al-balad here is Makkah. The meaning of ﴿secure﴾ is: possessing security. The security of the city is a metaphor, and what is meant is that those in it are secure. Regarding what is meant by this security, there are three opinions. The first: he asked Him for security from killing. The second: from being swallowed up by the earth and from being struck by stones (from the sky). The third: from famine and drought. Mujahid said: Abraham said, "for those who believe," and Allah, mighty and majestic, said: "And whoever disbelieves, I will provide for him [too] for a little while."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then I will grant him enjoyment﴾. Ibn Amir recited (fa-umatti'uhu) with the lightened form, from amta'a (to grant enjoyment). The rest recited it with the doubled form, from matta'a (to give enjoyment). Al-imta' (granting enjoyment): giving that by which enjoyment is attained. Al-mut'ah (enjoyment): taking one's share of the pleasure of what one desires. With what does He grant him enjoyment? There are two opinions. The first: with security. The second: with provision.

Al-idtirar (compulsion): being driven to something. Al-masir (the final destination): that to which the matter ends.

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 2, verses 127–129:

*Al-qawa'id* (the foundations) are the foundations of the House, and its singular is *qa'idah*. As for *qawa'id al-nisa'* (women past childbearing), its singular is *qa'id*, meaning an old woman.

﴿Our Lord, accept from us﴾: meaning, "they both say, 'Our Lord,'" so this is omitted, as in His saying: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate, [saying], "Peace be upon you"﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 25]. He intended: "they say."

*Al-Sami'* (the All-Hearing) means *al-sami'* (the hearer), but it is more intensive, because the pattern *fa'il* conveys emphasis. Al-Khattabi said: *al-sama'* may also mean acceptance and response, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I seek refuge in You from a supplication that is not heard," meaning, that is not answered. And the words of the one praying, "Allah hears the one who praises Him" (*sami'a Allahu liman hamidah*), mean that Allah accepts the praise of the one who praises Him. They recited:

*I called upon Allah until I feared that Allah would not hear what I say.*

The reference is to the building of the House.

Anas narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The angels used to make pilgrimage to the House before Adam."

Ibn 'Abbas said: When Adam was sent down, Allah the Exalted said: "O Adam, go and build Me a House, circumambulate it, and remember Me around it, just as you saw My angels doing around My Throne." So he set off running until he reached the Sacred House, and he built it from five mountains: from Lebanon, Tur Sinai, Tur Zita, al-Judi, and Hira'. Adam was the first to lay its foundations and to circumambulate it. He continued to do so until Allah sent the Flood, which obliterated the site of the House. Then Allah raised up Ibrahim and Isma'il.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: When Allah commanded Ibrahim to build the House, he was distressed by it and did not know how to proceed. So Allah sent down to him something like a cloud, in which there was a head that spoke. It said: "O Ibrahim, build upon my shadow." When he had built upon it, it rose. In another narration, it used to rise for him each day as he built upon it. He said: Ibrahim dug beneath the *sakinah* (tranquility), and it revealed foundations which thirty men could not move. When he reached the place of the Black Stone, he said to Isma'il: "(p-145) Find me a stone." So he went seeking a stone, and Jibril came with the Black Stone and placed it. When Isma'il came back, he said: "Who brought you this stone?" He replied: "One who did not rely on your building or mine."

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Musayyib, and Abu al-'Aliyah said: They raised the foundations which had existed before that time.

Al-Suddi said: When Allah commanded him to build the House, he did not know where to build it. So Allah sent a wind which swept clean the area around the Ka'bah, revealing the original foundation upon which the House had stood before the Flood.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord, and make us Muslims [in submission] to You﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: *Muslim* in the language means one who has surrendered to the command of Allah and submitted. *Al-manasik* means the acts of worship. Every act of worship is a *mansak* and a *mansik*, and from this the worshipper is called *nasik*. The sacrificial animal offered to draw near to Allah, mighty and majestic, is called *al-nasikah*. It seems that the original meaning of *nusuk* is indeed the sacrifice offered to Allah the Exalted.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿And show us our rites﴾: meaning, our places of sacrifice. This was said by Mujahid. Others said: they are all the acts of the Hajj.

Ibn Kathir read *wa-arina* with the *ra'* vowelless (*wa-arna*). Also ﴿Rabbi arini﴾ [Al-A'raf: 143] and ﴿arina allazayni adallana﴾ [Fussilat: 29]. Nafi', Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read *arina* with a kasrah on the *ra'* in all of these. Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir read likewise, except that they made the *ra'* vowelless in *arina allazayni* alone. Al-Farra' said: The people of the Hijaz say *arina*, while many Arabs make the *ra'* vowelless, saying *arna manasikana*, and some trustworthy reciters read it so. Some of them recited:

*Sulaymá said, "Buy us flour, and buy quickly a skilled servant."*

Al-Kisa'i recited to me:

*Whoever fears Allah, Allah is with him, and the provision of Allah comes morning and evening.*

Qatadah said: Allah showed them their rites: the standing at 'Arafat, the departure from Muzdalifah (Jam'), the throwing of the pebbles (*ramy al-jimar*), the circumambulation, and the running between Safa and Marwah (*sa'y*).

Abu Mijlaz said: When Ibrahim finished the House, Jibril came to him and showed him the circumambulation. Then he brought him to the Jamrat al-'Aqabah, where Satan confronted him. Jibril took seven pebbles and gave Ibrahim seven, and said to him: "Throw and say Allahu akbar." They threw and said Allahu akbar with each throw until Satan disappeared. Then he brought him to the middle Jamrah, where Satan confronted them both. Jibril took seven pebbles and gave Ibrahim seven pebbles, and said: "Throw and say Allahu akbar." They threw and said Allahu akbar with each throw until Satan disappeared. Then he brought him to the farthest Jamrah, where Satan confronted them both. Jibril took seven pebbles and gave Ibrahim seven pebbles. He said to him: "Throw and say Allahu akbar." They threw and said Allahu akbar with each throw until Satan disappeared. Then he brought him to Mina and said: "Here people shave their heads." Then he brought him to Jam'; he said: "Here people gather." Then he brought him to 'Arafah and said: "Have you recognized it?" He said: "Yes." He said: "For this reason it was named 'Arafat."

His saying the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves﴾. Regarding the *ha'* and the *mim* in *fihim* (among them), there are two views. The first: they refer to the descendants, as said by Muqatil and al-Farra'. The second: they refer to the people of Makkah, in His saying: ﴿and provide for its people﴾. The messenger here is Muhammad (ﷺ). Abu Umamah narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that it was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what was the beginning of your affair?" He said: "The supplication of my father Ibrahim, the glad tidings of 'Isa, and my mother saw that a light had emerged from her, by which the palaces of Syria were illuminated." *Al-Kitab* is the Qur'an. *Al-Hikmah* (wisdom) is the Sunnah, as said by Ibn 'Abbas. It is also reported from him that *al-hikmah* means jurisprudence (*fiqh*), what is lawful and unlawful, and the admonitions of the Qur'an. Wisdom (*hikmah*) was so named because it prevents ignorance (*jahl*).

Regarding His saying the Exalted: ﴿and purify them﴾, there are three views. The first: its meaning is that He takes zakat from them and purifies them by it, as said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Farra'. The second: He purifies them from shirk and disbelief, as said by Muqatil. The third: He calls them to that by which they become pure (*azkiya'*).

(p-147) His saying the Exalted: ﴿Indeed You, You are the Exalted in Might﴾. Al-Khattabi said: *al-'izz* in the speech of the Arabs has three meanings. The first: domination, as they say, "Whoever is mighty plunders," meaning whoever overpowers, despoils. From it one says *'azza ya'uzzu* (with a damma on the 'ayn in the present), as in His saying: ﴿and he overpowered me in speech﴾ [Sad: 23]. The second: strength and power, from which one says *'azza ya'azzu* (with a fatha on the 'ayn in the present). The third: that it means preciousness and rarity, from which one says *'azza ya'izzu* (with a kasrah on the 'ayn in the present). The meaning of *al-'Aziz* encompasses that He is the one to whom nothing is equal and for whom there is no like.

Al-Khattabi said: *al-sama'* may also mean acceptance and response, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I seek refuge in You from a supplication that is not heard," meaning, that is not answered. The reference is to the building of the House.

Anas narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The angels used to make pilgrimage to the House before Adam."

So Allah sent down to him something like a cloud, in which there was a head that spoke. It said: "O Ibrahim, build upon my shadow." When he had built upon it, it rose. Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 130–132:

Allah's words: ﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Ibrahim﴾

The occasion of its revelation: Abdullah ibn Salam invited his two nephews, Muhajir and Salama, to Islam. Salama embraced Islam, while Muhajir turned away from Islam, so this verse was revealed. This is reported by Muqatil. Al-Zajjaj said: The "min" in its wording has the form of an interrogative, and its meaning is affirmation and reproach. The meaning is: None turns away from the religion of Ibrahim except one who has made a fool of himself. It is said: "raghibtu fi al-shay'" (I desired the thing) when I wanted it, and "raghibtu 'anhu" (I turned away from it) when I abandoned it. The millah (religion) of Ibrahim is his din (religion).

Allah's words: ﴿except one who has made a fool of his soul﴾ On this there are four opinions. The first: its meaning is "except one who has made a fool of himself," said by al-Akhfash and Yunus. Yunus said: For this reason it transitive to the soul and put it in the accusative (nasb). Al-Akhfash said: The soul is in the accusative because the preposition has been dropped, since the meaning is "except one who has been foolish in his soul."

The poet said:

"We make meat dear to the guests raw, and we cheapen it when the cooking pots have ripened it."

The second: "except one who has destroyed his soul," said by Abu 'Ubayda. The third: "except one whose soul has become foolish," as one says: "ghabana fulan ra'yahu" (so-and-so was deceived in his opinion). This is the view of al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba. Al-Farra' said: The verb was transferred from the soul to the pronoun of "man," and the soul was put in the accusative as a specification (tashbih bi al-tafsir), as one says: "diqtu bi al-amr dhar'an" (I was constricted by the matter in my capacity), meaning: "my capacity was constricted by it." Similar to it is: ﴿and the head has flamed with grey hair﴾ [Maryam: 4]. The fourth: "except one who has been ignorant of his soul, not reflecting upon it," and this is the choice of al-Zajjaj.

Allah's words: ﴿And indeed he, in the Hereafter, is among the righteous﴾ Ibn al-Anbari said: among those righteous in standing with Allah, the Exalted. Al-Zajjaj said: The righteous (al-salih) in the Hereafter is the successful one.

Allah's words: ﴿When his Lord said to him: Submit﴾ This was at the time of the choosing. Ibn 'Abbas said: When he saw the star, the moon and the sun, his Lord said to him: Submit, i.e., devote yourself sincerely.

Allah's words: ﴿And ordained﴾ Ibn 'Abbas and the people of Madina read (wa-awsa) with an alif and a light sad, while the rest read without an alif with a doubled sad. This is due to the difference of the codices (al-masahif). Ibn Nasir informed us, saying: Thabit informed us, saying: Ibn Qushaysh informed us, saying: Ibn Hayawayh informed us, saying: Ibn al-Anbari narrated to us, saying: Tha'lab informed us, saying: Khalaf ibn Hisham al-Bazzar dictated to me, saying: The codices of the people of Madina and the people of Iraq differed in twelve letters: The people of Madina wrote (wa-awsa) and the people of Iraq wrote (wa-wassa). The people of Madina wrote: "sari'u ila maghfiratin min rabbikum" [Al 'Imran: 133] without a waw, and the people of Iraq: (wa-sari'u). The people of Madina wrote: "yaqulu alladhina amanu" [al-Ma'ida: 56], and the people of Iraq: (wa-yaqulu). The people of Madina wrote: "man yartadid" [al-Ma'ida: 57], and the people of Iraq: (man yartadd). The people of Madina wrote: "alladhina attakhadhu masjidan" [al-Tawba: 108], and the people of Iraq: (wa-alladhina). The people of Madina wrote: "khayran minhuma munqalaban" [al-Kahf: 37], and the people of Iraq: (minha). The people of Madina wrote: "fa-tawakkal 'ala al-'Aziz al-Rahim" [al-Shu'ara: 217], and the people of Iraq: (wa-tawakkal). The people of Madina wrote: "wa-an yazhara fi al-ard al-fasad" [Ghafir: 26], and the people of Iraq: (aw an yuzhira). The people of Madina wrote in "Ha Mim 'Ayn Sin Qaf": (bima kasabat aydikum) without a fa', and the people of Iraq: (fa-bima). The people of Madina wrote "ma tashtahihi al-anf" [al-Zukhruf: 71] with a ha', and the people of Iraq: (ma tashtahi). The people of Madina wrote: "fa-inna Allaha al-Ghaniyy al-Hamid" [al-Hadid: 26], and the people of Iraq: (inna Allaha huwa al-Ghaniyy al-Hamid). The people of Madina wrote: "fa-lam yakhafu 'uqbaha" [al-Shams: 15] and the people of Iraq: (wa-la yakhafu).

Wa-awsa is more emphatic than awsa, because it denotes many repetitions, and the ha' in "biha" refers to the question. This is said by 'Ikrima and al-Zajjaj. Muqatil said: His sons were four: Isma'il, Ishaq, Madyan, and Madda'in. Others besides Muqatil mentioned that they were eight.

Allah's words: ﴿So do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ He means: hold fast to Islam, so that when death overtakes you, it finds you upon it.

The people of Madina wrote: "fa-inna Allaha al-Ghaniyy al-Hamid" [al-Hadid: 26], and the people of Iraq: (inna Allaha huwa al-Ghaniyy al-Hamid). The people of Madina wrote: "fa-lam yakhafu 'uqbaha" [al-Shams: 15] and the people of Iraq: (wa-la yakhafu).

Wa-awsa is more emphatic than awsa, because it denotes many repetitions, and the ha' in "biha" refers to the question. This is said by 'Ikrima and al-Zajjaj. Muqatil said: His sons were four: Isma'il, Ishaq, Madyan, and Madda'in. Others besides Muqatil mentioned that they were eight.

Allah's words: ﴿So do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ He means: hold fast to Islam, so that when death overtakes you, it finds you upon it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verses 133–134:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub?﴾

The occasion of its revelation: "The Jews said to the Prophet (ﷺ): Do you not know that Ya'qub (Jacob) enjoined his sons on the day he died in Judaism? So this verse was revealed." This was related by Muqatil.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is a community that has passed away.﴾ That is, it has gone by. It refers to Ibrahim and his sons, and Ya'qub and his sons.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verses 133–134:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub?﴾

The occasion of its revelation: "The Jews said to the Prophet (ﷺ): Do you not know that Ya'qub (Jacob) enjoined his sons on the day he died in Judaism? So this verse was revealed." This was related by Muqatil.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is a community that has passed away.﴾ That is, it has gone by. It refers to Ibrahim and his sons, and Ya'qub and his sons.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verses 135–136:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say: Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided.﴾

Its meaning: The Jews said, "Be Jews," and the Christians said, "Be Christians, and you will be guided."

﴿Rather, [follow] the religion of Ibrahim, a ḥanīf (upright in devotion).﴾ The meaning is: Rather, we follow the religion of Ibrahim in his state of ḥanīfiyya (uprightness). Regarding the term ḥanīf (upright in devotion) there are two opinions. The first is that it means one who inclines toward worship. Al-Zajjaj said: "The ḥanīf in the language is one who inclines toward a thing. It is derived from their saying, 'a man who is aḥnaf (knock-kneed),' which is one whose two feet both incline toward each other with their toes." Umm al-Ahnaf was lulling him with her verse:

Yes, by God, were it not for the bend in his leg,
And the slenderness of his shin from his thinness,
There would not be among your youths one like him.

The second is that it means one who is straight, and from this the lame man was called ḥanīf, looking to his soundness. This is the view of Ibn Qutayba. The exegetes have described the ḥanīf with various attributes. ʿAṭāʾ said: he is the sincere one (al-mukhlis). Ibn al-Sāʾib said: he is the one who performs ḥajj. Others said: he is the one who affirms God's oneness, performs ḥajj, sacrifices, is circumcised, and faces the Kaʿba.

As for the Asbāṭ (the tribes): they are the sons of Yaʿqūb, and they were twelve men. Al-Zajjaj said: the sibṭ in the language is the group of people who trace back to one father. And the sibṭ in the language is a tree that has branches (qabāʾil), so the sibṭ are those who come from one tree.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verses 135–136:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say: Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided.﴾

Its meaning: The Jews said, "Be Jews," and the Christians said, "Be Christians, and you will be guided."

﴿Rather, [follow] the religion of Ibrahim, a ḥanīf (upright in devotion).﴾ The meaning is: Rather, we follow the religion of Ibrahim in his state of ḥanīfiyya (uprightness). Regarding the term ḥanīf (upright in devotion) there are two opinions. The first is that it means one who inclines toward worship.
