**The Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 2, Verse 137**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Then if they believe﴾. He means: the People of the Book.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿in the like of what you believe in﴾. There are three opinions on this.

The first is that its meaning is: "like your faith." The preposition *bā'* (the letter *ba*, "in") has been added for emphasis (*ta'kid*). It is added in the same way in His words: ﴿And shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree﴾ [Maryam: 24]. This is the view of Ibn al-Anbari.

The second is that what is meant here is the Book, and the sense is: "If they believe in your Book as you believed in their Book." This is the view of Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi.

The third is that *mithl* (the word "like") here is extraneous (*silah*, a word that adds no meaning of its own), and the sense is: "If they believe in what you believe in." A parallel is His words: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11]. That is, "there is nothing like Him." They also recited:

*O you who blame me, leave me from your blame;*
*my kind does not accept from your kind.*

That is, "I do not accept from you."

As for *al-shiqaq* (the word "opposition" in the verse), it means hostility and enmity. From it comes the saying: "So-and-so has split the staff of the Muslims," meaning that he has separated himself from what they were united upon, following their Imam. It is as if he has come to be in a split (*shaqq*) other than their split.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So Allah will suffice you against them﴾. This is a guarantee of victory for the Prophet (ﷺ).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 138:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The baptism of Allah﴾. The occasion of its revelation: the Christians, when a child was born to one of them and seven days passed over him, would dip him in water they had, called al-Ma'muudiyya (the baptismal font), in order to purify him by it, and they would say: "This is the purification of the place of circumcision." When they did this, they would say: "He has become a true Christian." So this verse was revealed. This was related by Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliya, Mujahid, al-Nakha'i, and Ibn Zayd said: "The baptism of Allah" means His religion.

Al-Farra' said: ﴿baptism of Allah﴾ [in the accusative] is governed by being a repetition of "the religion" (al-milla).

Ibn 'Abla read "Sibghatu Allah" in the nominative, meaning: "This is the baptism of Allah." Likewise he read "Millatu Ibrahim" in the nominative, meaning: "This is the religion of Ibrahim."

Ibn Qutayba said: The intended meaning of "the baptism of Allah" is circumcision. He called it "baptism" because the Christians used to dye (baptize) their children in water, and they would say: "This is a purification for them, like circumcision for the ḥanīfs." Then Allah, exalted is He, said: "The baptism of Allah," i.e., hold fast to the baptism of Allah, not the baptism of the Christians to their children. By it He intended the religion of Ibrahim.

Others said: The religion was only called "baptism" to show its effect on the person, like the appearance of dye on cloth.

(p-152) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do you dispute with us concerning God?﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: He means the Jews of Medina and the Christians of Najran. Al-muhajjah (disputation) is contention over religion. The Jews said, "We are the People of the First Book." It was also said: the Jews backed the idol-worshippers, so it was said to them: "You claim that you are monotheists, and we are monotheists too; why then do you side with those who do not affirm the oneness of God?"

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿To us our deeds, and to you your deeds﴾. Most of the exegetes said: this statement implied a kind of leniency, and then it was abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verses 140–141:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do you say that Abraham and Ishmael﴾ — the verse.

The occasion of its revelation: the Jews of Medina and the Christians of Najran said to the believers: "The prophets of God were from us, from the Children of Israel, and they were upon our religion." So this verse was revealed. This is related by Muqatil. The meaning of the verse: God has informed us of the religion of the prophets, and no one knows it better than He does.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr, and Abu 'Amr recited (ʾam yaqūlūna), with the yā' (ya), as a report about the Jews. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim recited (taqūlūna), with the tā' (ta), because preceding it is a direct address, namely "Do you argue with us" (ʾatuḥājjūnanā), and after it is (qul ʾa-antum ʾa'lamu), "Say: Are you more knowing?"

Regarding the testimony that they concealed, there are two opinions. The first: God, exalted is He, had given them a testimony concerning Abraham and those mentioned with him, that they were Muslims, and they concealed it. This is said by al-Hasan and Zayd ibn Aslam. The second: they concealed Islam and the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), while they knew that he was a prophet whose religion is Islam. This is said by Abu al-'Aliyah and Qatadah.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verses 140–141:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do you say that Abraham and Ishmael﴾ — the verse.

The occasion of its revelation: the Jews of Medina and the Christians of Najran said to the believers: "The prophets of God were from us, from the Children of Israel, and they were upon our religion." So this verse was revealed. This is related by Muqatil. The meaning of the verse: God has informed us of the religion of the prophets, and no one knows it better than He does.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr, and Abu 'Amr recited (ʾam yaqūlūna), with the yā' (ya), as a report about the Jews. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim recited (taqūlūna), with the tā' (ta), because preceding it is a direct address, namely "Do you argue with us" (ʾatuḥājjūnanā), and after it is (qul ʾa-antum ʾa'lamu), "Say: Are you more knowing?"

Regarding the testimony that they concealed, there are two opinions. The first: God, exalted is He, had given them a testimony concerning Abraham and those mentioned with him, that they were Muslims, and they concealed it. This is said by al-Hasan and Zayd ibn Aslam. The second: they concealed Islam and the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), while they knew that he was a prophet whose religion is Islam. This is said by Abu al-'Aliyah and Qatadah.

(p-153) His words, exalted is He: ﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾.

There are three views concerning them. The first: they are the Jews, related by al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, Mujahid, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The second: they are the people of Makkah, related by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. The third: they are the hypocrites, mentioned by al-Suddi from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas. It is possible that all of them said this, and the verse was revealed after the change of the qibla. "Al-sufaha'" means: the ignorant. "What turned them away" means: what diverted them from their qibla, that is, the qibla of al-Muqaddas (Jerusalem).

The scholars differed over the length of the Prophet's ﷺ prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis after his arrival in Madinah, with six views. The first: it was sixteen months, or seventeen, related by al-Bara' ibn 'Azib. The second: seventeen months, related by Ibn 'Abbas. The third: thirteen months, related by Mu'adh ibn Jabal. The fourth: nine months, or ten months, related by Anas ibn Malik. The fifth: sixteen months. The sixth: eighteen months; both of these last two views are related from Qatadah.

As for whether his facing Bayt al-Maqdis was by his own judgment or by revelation, there are two views. The first: it was by the command of Allah, the Exalted, and His revelation, related by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj. The second: it was by his own effort and judgment, related by al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliyah, 'Ikrimah, and al-Rabi'. Qatadah said: the people would face whichever direction they wished, based on His saying: ﴿And to Allah belong the east and the west﴾ [al-Baqarah: 115]. Then He commanded them to face Bayt al-Maqdis. Regarding the reason for His choosing Bayt al-Maqdis, there are two views. The first: to win over the People of the Book, mentioned by some of the exegetes. The second: to test the Arabs with something other than what they were accustomed to, related by al-Zajjaj.

(p-154) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Thus We have made you a middle nation﴾.

The occasion of its revelation: the Jews said, "Our qibla is the qibla of the prophets, and we are the just ones among the people." So this verse was revealed. This was related by Muqatil. The ummah (community) means the group, and the wasat (middle) means the just, as related from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Sa'id, Mujahid, and Qatadah. Ibn Qutaybah said: wasat means just and best, and from it is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The best of them said﴾ [al-Qalam: 28], meaning the most just and the best of them. The poet said:

They are a middle people, whose judgment the people are content with, when one of the great calamities befalls you.

The root of this is that the best of things are their middle parts, while excess and deficiency are both blameworthy. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari mentioned that it is from moderation in action: the Muslims did not fall short in their religion as the Jews did, for they killed the prophets and altered the Book of God, nor did they exaggerate as the Christians did, for they claimed that 'Isa is the son of God. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: there is an omission in this statement, and its meaning is: I made your qibla a middle between the two qiblas, for the Jews pray toward the west and the Christians toward the east, and you are between them.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾. Concerning this there are two views. One: its meaning is that you may bear witness for the prophets against their nations. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "On the Day of Resurrection a prophet will come with one man with him, and a prophet will come with two men with him, and a prophet will come with more than that. It will be said to them: Did this one convey to you? They will say: No. It will be said to the prophet: Did you convey to them? He will say: Yes. It will be said: Who will bear witness for you? He will say: Muhammad and his community. They will bear witness that the messengers had conveyed. It will be said: What is your knowledge? They will say: (p-155) Our Prophet informed us that the messengers had conveyed, so we believed him. That is His saying: ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾." This is the view of 'Ikrimah and Qatadah. The second: its meaning is that you may be witnesses for Muhammad (ﷺ) over the nations: the Jews, the Christians, and the Magians. This was said by Mujahid.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ). Against what does he bear witness over them? There are three views. One: their deeds, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, and Ibn Zayd. Two: their conveying of the message, as said by Qatadah and Muqatil. Three: their faith, as said by Abu al-'Aliyah. According to this, "over you" means "for you." 'Ikrimah said: no one from this community will be questioned except its own prophet.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We did not make the qibla which you were upon﴾, meaning the qibla of Bayt al-Maqdis. ﴿except that We might know﴾. Concerning this there are four views. One: that We might see. Two: that We might distinguish; both related from Ibn 'Abbas. Three: that We might make it known as an actual occurrence, since His knowledge is eternal; this was said by a group of the people of tafsir, and it returns to Ibn 'Abbas's view "that We might see." Four: that the knowledge refers to the addressees, and the meaning is: that you yourselves may know; this was said by al-Farra'.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿from him who turns back on his heels﴾, meaning he who returns to disbelief. This was said by Ibn Zayd and Muqatil.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed it was a great thing﴾. Concerning what is referred to there are two views. One: that it is the turning toward the Ka'bah. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, and Muqatil. Two: that it is the qibla of Bayt al-Maqdis before the change from it. This was said by Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Zajjaj.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And God would not let your faith go to waste﴾. It was revealed upon an occasion: that the Muslims said, "O Messenger of God! What about our brothers who died while praying toward Bayt al-Maqdis?" So God revealed: ﴿And God would not let your faith go to waste﴾. The faith mentioned here is meant as the prayer, according to the consensus of the scholars. It was said that prayer was called faith because it comprises speech, intention, and action. Al-Farra' said: He attributed faith to the living believers, and the meaning includes those among the Muslims who died before the qibla was changed, because they are included with them in the religion.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Surely He is Compassionate (ra'uf)﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs from 'Asim read "la-ra'uuf" (لَرَؤُوفٌ) on the pattern of la-ra'uuf... in all of the Qur'an, and the reason for this is that fa'ul is more common in their speech than fa'il, so the pattern of daruub and shakuur is more widespread than the pattern of hadhir and yaqizh. Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "la-ra'uf" (لَرَؤُفٌ) on the pattern of ra'uf. It is said that this is the prevalent reading among the people of the Hijaz. Jarir said:

You see for the Muslims a right upon you, like the action of the kind and compassionate parent.

Ra'uf in the sense of raheem (merciful); this is the view of al-Zajjaj. Al-Khattabi mentioned from some scholars that ra'fah is a more intense and tender mercy. He said: It is said that ra'fah is more specific, and rahmah is more general.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 144:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven﴾

The occasion of its revelation: the Prophet ﷺ loved to be turned toward the Ka'bah. This was said by al-Bara', Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Musayyib, Abu al-'Aliyah, and Qatadah. Some exegetes (mufassirun) mentioned that this verse was revealed before His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾. They differed concerning the reason the Prophet chose the Ka'bah over Bayt al-Maqdis, on two views. One: it was the qiblah of Ibrahim; this is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: to oppose the Jews; this was said by Mujahid. The meaning of "the turning of his face" is his looking toward it to the right and to the left. "Fi" here means "ila" (toward), and "tarduha" means "tuhibbuha" (you love it). "Al-shatr" means "the direction" without any disagreement. Ibn 'Umar said: "A caller came to the people while they were in the Dawn prayer at Quba', and said: 'Indeed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ has had a Qur'an revealed to him tonight, and he has been commanded to face the Ka'bah; so face it.' [Their faces had been toward Syria], so they turned around while they were in their prayer."

Section

The scholars differed as to what time the qiblah was changed, on three views. One: it was changed during the Zuhr prayer on Monday, the middle of Rajab, seventeen months after the Messenger of Allah's arrival in Madinah; this was said by al-Bara' ibn 'Azib and Ma'qil ibn Yasar. The second: it was changed on Tuesday, the middle of Sha'ban, eighteen months after his arrival in Madinah; this was said by Qatadah. The third: it was changed in Jumada al-Akhirah; this was related by Ibn Salamah the exegete from Ibrahim al-Harbi.

Concerning ﴿those who were given the Scripture﴾ there are two views. One: the Jews; this was said by Muqatil. The second: the Jews and the Christians; this was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿that it is the truth﴾ refers to what He commanded of facing the Ka'bah. Then He threatened them in the rest of the verse for concealing what they knew. From where did they know that it is the truth? On this there are four views. One: that in their Scripture is the command to face it; this was said by Abu al-'Aliyah. The second: they know that the Masjid al-Haram is the qiblah of Ibrahim. The third: that in their Scripture it is stated that Muhammad is a truthful messenger, so he does not command except with truth. The fourth: that they know the permissibility of abrogation (naskh).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 145:

The occasion of its revelation: the Jews of Madina and the Christians of Najran said to the Prophet: "Bring us a sign just as the prophets before you brought." So this verse was revealed. Related by Muqatil.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They do not follow your qibla﴾ — he means: the Ka'ba. ﴿Nor is any of them a follower of the qibla of another﴾ — because the Jews pray facing Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) to the west, and the Christians face the east. ﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾ — by praying toward their qibla ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾. Muqatil said: he means by "knowledge": clarification (al-bayan).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 146:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those whom We have given the Book recognize it﴾. Regarding the pronoun in "yaʿrifūnahu" (they recognize it) there are two opinions. The first: it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ); this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: it refers to the changing of the qiblah toward the Kaaba; this was said by Abu al-ʿAliyah, Qatadah, al-Suddi, and Muqatil. It is also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas as well. Regarding "the truth which they conceal" there are two opinions. The first: it is the Prophet (ﷺ); this was said by Mujahid. The second: it is the turning toward the Kaaba; this was said by al-Suddi, and Muqatil along with others.

Regarding His saying: ﴿while they know﴾ there are two opinions. The first: while they know that it is true. The second: while they know the punishment that is upon the one who opposes it.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾.

Al-Zajjaj (Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj, a grammarian and exegete) said: That is, this truth is from your Lord. And "those who doubt" (al-mumtarun) are those who are in doubt, and the address is general.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 148:

That is: for every people there is a religion and a direction (jihah). What is meant by al-wijhah is the qibla (the direction of prayer), as said by Ibn 'Abbas and others. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said jihah and wijhah. Regarding "huwa" there are three opinions. The first: it refers back to God, Exalted, so the meaning is: God is the one who turns them toward it, that is, He commanded them to face it. The second: it refers back to the one who turns (al-mutawalli), so the meaning is: he himself turns toward it, and "huwa" is then a pronoun for kull (each). The third: it refers back to the House, as said by Mujahid: He commanded every people to reach the Ka'bah. The majority read ﴿muwalliha﴾, while Ibn 'Amir, and al-Walid from Ya'qub, read "huwa mawlaha" with an alif after the lam, so the pronoun "huwa" refers to kull, and the meanings of the two readings are close.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿So race to the good works﴾, that is: hasten to them. Qatadah said: do not be defeated concerning your qibla. ﴿Wherever you may be, Allah will bring you all together﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: this refers to the Day of Resurrection. As for the repetition of His saying:

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 149–150:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾. It is a repetition for emphasis, to cut off the hope of the People of the Book that the Muslims would ever return to their qibla.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So that people will have no argument against you﴾. Regarding "the people" there are two opinions. The first: they are the People of the Book; this is the view of Ibn Abbas, Abu al-Aliyah, Qatadah, and Muqatil. The second: they are the polytheists of the Arabs; this was related by al-Suddi from his shaykhs. Whoever holds the first view says: the argument of the People of the Book was that they said to the Prophet (ﷺ), "What is wrong with you that you have abandoned the qibla of Bayt al-Maqdis? If it was misguidance, then you were worshipping God by it; and if it was guidance, then you have departed from it." Qatadah said: they said, "The man has longed for his father's house and his people's religion." Whoever holds the second view says: the argument of the polytheists (p-160) was that they said, "He has returned to your qibla, and he will soon return to your religion."

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: except one who wrongs by his argument regarding what has become clear to him, just as you say, "You have no argument against me except injustice," meaning: "You have no claim against me at all, but you are unjust to me." Ibn Abbas said: ﴿So do not fear them﴾ regarding your turning toward the Ka'bah, ﴿but fear Me﴾ regarding abandoning it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 149–150:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾. It is a repetition for emphasis, to cut off the hope of the People of the Book that the Muslims would ever return to their qibla.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So that people will have no argument against you﴾. Regarding "the people" there are two opinions. The first: they are the People of the Book; this is the view of Ibn Abbas, Abu al-Aliyah, Qatadah, and Muqatil. The second: they are the polytheists of the Arabs; this was related by al-Suddi from his shaykhs. Whoever holds the first view says: the argument of the People of the Book was that they said to the Prophet (ﷺ), "What is wrong with you that you have abandoned the qibla of Bayt al-Maqdis? If it was misguidance, then you were worshipping God by it; and if it was guidance, then you have departed from it." Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 151:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿As We have sent among you a messenger from among yourselves﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "Kama" (as) cannot serve as a response (jawab) to what precedes it, and the better view is that it is linked to His saying: ﴿So remember Me﴾. Its meaning has also been related from ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujahid, and Muqatil. The verse is addressed to the polytheists of the Arabs. As for His saying, ﴿and purify them﴾, there are three opinions, which have already been mentioned in the story of Ibrahim. "The Book" is the Qur'an. "The Wisdom" is the Sunnah.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 152:

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿فاذْكُرُونِي﴾

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So remember Me﴾

Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jubayr said: "Remember Me through obedience to Me, and I will remember you through My forgiveness."

Ibrahim ibn al-Sarri said: "Just as I have bestowed upon you the Message, so remember Me through My Oneness and through affirming My Prophet." He said: If it is asked, "How can the response to ﴿As We have sent﴾ be ﴿So remember Me﴾, when His saying ﴿So remember Me﴾ is a command and His saying ﴿I will remember you﴾ is its consequence?" The answer is that the meaning is: "If you remember Me, I will remember you."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And be grateful to Me﴾. Gratitude (al-shukr) is acknowledging the right of the benefactor together with praising him.

(p-161) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, seek help through patience and prayer﴾.

The occasion of its revelation: the polytheists said, "Muhammad will return to our religion, just as he returned to our qibla." So this verse was revealed. This is related from Qatadah. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Seek help in pursuing the Hereafter through patience in performing the obligations, and through prayer." The discussion of patience, and the explanation of seeking help through it and through prayer, has already passed.

Occasion of revelation: they used to say of those slain at Badr and Uhud, "So-and-so died at Badr, so-and-so died at Uhud." So this verse was revealed. Ibn 'Abbas said this.

He put "al-amwat" (the dead) in the nominative by supposing a pronoun referring to their names, meaning: "Do not say: they are dead." Al-Farra' mentioned something similar.

If it is said: "We see them as dead, so what is the point of the prohibition?" The answer: the meaning is, "Do not say: they are dead, whose souls do not reach the Gardens and who do not obtain the gifts of God that the living obtain. Rather, they are alive: their souls are in the crops of green birds that roam in Paradise. So they are alive in this respect, even though they are dead in respect of the departure of the souls." Ibn al-Anbari mentioned this.

If it is said: "Are not all the believers blessed after their death? Why did you single out the martyrs?" The answer: the martyrs were preferred over others in that they are provided with the food and dishes of Paradise, while others are blessed with less than that. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari mentioned this.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verses 155–156:

Al-Farra' said: "Min" (مَن) indicates that for each category of these there is an implied thing, so its estimate is: with something of fear, and something of hunger, and something of loss of wealth.

Regarding those intended in this verse there are four opinions. The first: they are specifically the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), as reported by 'Ata'. The second: they are the people of Makkah. The third: that this will occur at the end of time. Ka'b said: "A time will come upon people when a palm tree will bear nothing but one date." The fourth: that the verse is general in its application.

As for fear, Ibn 'Abbas said: it is panic in battle. Hunger: the famine that afflicted the people of Makkah for seven years. Loss of wealth: the loss of their property; and of lives, by death and killing that befell them; and the fruits did not yield as they used to yield. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi related from some scholars: that fear is in jihad, hunger is in the obligation of fasting, and loss of wealth is what is obligated in it of zakat and hajj and the like. And lives: what is martyred from them in battle; and fruits: what is obligated in them of charities. ﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾ of these trials, of Paradise.

Know that He only informed them of what would afflict them so that they would prepare their souls for patience, for that would be further for them from despair. ﴿They say, "Indeed we belong to Allah"﴾, meaning: we are His servants, He does with us what He wills, ﴿and indeed to Him we will return﴾, meaning: we affirm the resurrection and the recompense for our deeds, and the reward for our patience. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: This nation has been given, at the time of calamity, something that the prophets before them were not given: ﴿Those who, when a disaster strikes them, say, "Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return." Those upon them are blessings from their Lord and mercy﴾. Had the prophets been given it, Ya'qub would have been given it. Did you not hear His saying: ﴿"Oh, my grief over Joseph"﴾? Al-Farra' said: The Arabs have three forms for calamity: musība, muṣāba, and muṣwiba. Al-Kisa'i claimed that he heard a Bedouin say: "May Allah mend your calamity (muṣwibatak)."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 157:

(p-163) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Upon them are blessings from their Lord﴾

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "The blessings from Allah are forgiveness. ﴿And those are the guided ones﴾ by the istirja' (the saying, "Indeed, we belong to Allah and to Him we shall return")."

'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "What a fine pair of portions, and what a fine bonus!" ﴿Upon them are blessings from their Lord and mercy, and those are the guided ones﴾.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verses 158–159:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwa are among the symbols (sha'a'ir) of Allah.﴾

There are three reports concerning the occasion of its revelation.

The first: "Some men from the Ansar, who used to pronounce the talbiyah for Manat in the Jahiliyyah (Manat was an idol between Mecca and Medina), said: 'O Messenger of Allah! In the past we did not circumambulate between al-Safa and al-Marwa, out of reverence for Manat. Is there any blame upon us if we circumambulate between them?' So this verse was revealed." Narrated by Urwa from A'isha.

The second: The Muslims did not circumambulate between al-Safa and al-Marwa, because there were statues and idols upon al-Safa. So this verse was revealed. Narrated by Ikrima from Ibn Abbas. Al-Sha'bi said: "There was an idol upon al-Safa called Isaf, and an idol upon al-Marwa called Na'ila. The people of the Jahiliyyah used to run between them and rub them. When Islam came, they refrained from running between them, so this verse was revealed."

The third: "The Companions said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'In the Jahiliyyah we used to circumambulate between al-Safa and al-Marwa, and Allah, may He be exalted, mentioned the circumambulation of the House but did not mention it between al-Safa and al-Marwa. Is there any blame upon us if we do not circumambulate between them?' So this verse was revealed." Narrated by al-Zuhri from Abu Bakr ibn Abd al-Rahman from a group of the people of knowledge.

Ibrahim ibn al-Sarri said: In the language, al-Safa means hard, solid stones that produce nothing. It is a plural, its singular being safah and saffa, like hasah and hasa. Al-Marwa means soft stones. These two places are among the symbols of Allah, that is, among the markers of His acts of worship. The singular of sha'a'ir is sha'irah. The sha'a'ir are everything connected with a standing place (at 'Arafat), running (sa'y), or sacrifice. Also, sha'a'ir derives from "sha'arat bi-l-shay'" (she perceived the thing) when she knew of it; so the markers which are acts of worship of Allah were called sha'a'ir Allah. Al-Hajj in the language means intention (al-qasd), and likewise every person who intends something is called one who has "i'tamara" it. Al-janah means sin, taken from "janaha" when one inclines and deviates; its origin is the wing of a bird (janah al-ta'ir). The Muslims avoided circumambulating between them only because of the presence of idols there, so it was said to them: the placing of idols between them before Islam does not require avoiding them. Therefore Allah, mighty and majestic, informed them that there is no blame (janah) in circumambulating between them, and that whoever volunteers to do so, indeed Allah is Appreciative (shakir), Knowing (alim). Thanks from Allah (al-shukr) means reward and good praise.

The majority read (wa-man tatawwa'a) with the ta' and a fatha on the 'ayn: among them Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ibn Amir. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (yatawwa') with the ya' and a jazm on the 'ayn. Their difference is similar concerning the word after it, in verses after this one.

**Section**

The narration from our Imam Ahmad concerning running between al-Safa and al-Marwa differs. Al-Athram transmitted that whoever abandons the running has not had his Hajj validated. Abu Talib transmitted that there is nothing upon one who abandons it, whether intentionally or forgetfully, though one should not abandon it. Al-Maymuni transmitted that it is a voluntary act (tatawwu').

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We sent down of clear proofs and guidance﴾. Abu Salih reported from Ibn Abbas: it was revealed concerning the leaders of the Jews, who concealed what Allah had sent down in the Torah of clear proofs and guidance. The clear proofs are the lawful and the unlawful, the prescribed punishments and the obligations. The guidance is the description and attributes of the Prophet. ﴿After We have made it clear to the people﴾: Muqatil said, "to the Children of Israel." Regarding "the Book" there are two opinions. The first: it is the Torah, which is the saying of Ibn Abbas. The second: it is the Torah and the Gospel, said by Qatada. ﴿Those﴾ refers to the two words. ﴿Allah curses them﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: The root of la'n (curse) in the language is expulsion; "Allah cursed Iblis" means He expelled him. Then this meaning shifted to become a statement. Al-Shammakh said, describing water:

*I startled the sandgrouse by it, and drove away from it the place of the wolf, like a cursed man (al-la'in).*

That is, the expelled one. Regarding the ones who curse (al-la'inun) there are four opinions. The first: they are the beasts of the earth, narrated by al-Bara' from the Prophet ﷺ, and it is the saying of Mujahid and Ikrima. Mujahid said: they say, "We were only denied rain because of your sins," so they curse them. The second: they are the believers, said by Abdullah ibn Mas'ud. The third: they are the angels and the believers, said by Abu al-Aliya and Qatada. The fourth: they are the jinn, humankind, and every creature, said by Ata'.

**Section**

This verse requires the manifesting of the sciences of the religion, whether explicitly stated or derived by inference. It indicates the impermissibility of taking a wage for that, since it is not permissible to claim payment for what is obligatory to perform. Al-A'raj narrated from Abu Hurayra that he said: "You say that Abu Hurayra narrates too much from the Prophet ﷺ, but Allah is the one to whom we return. By Allah, were it not for a verse in the Book of Allah, I would never have narrated anything to anyone," and then he recited ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We sent down﴾ to its end.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 160:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Except those who repent﴾.

Ibn Mas'ud said: "Except those of the Jews who repented, amended their deeds, and made clear the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in their scripture."

Section

Some scholars have held that the verse before this one is abrogated (mansukh) by the exception in this one. This is not abrogation (naskh), because the exception (istithna') is the removal of part of what the wording encompasses, and that calls for specification (takhsis) rather than abrogation. What confirms this is that an abrogating text and an abrogated text cannot both be acted upon; acting on one requires abandoning the other. Here, however, it is possible to act upon both the excepted and the excepting clauses.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 161:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers﴾.

He made dying upon disbelief a condition only because its ruling becomes settled by dying upon it. If it is said: how does He say ﴿and the people all together﴾ when the people of his own religion do not curse him? There are three answers to this. The first: they will curse him in the Hereafter. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection some of you will disown others and some of you will curse others﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 25]. And He said: ﴿Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister﴾ [al-A'raf: 38]. The second: the intended meaning of "the people" here is the believers; this was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Qatadah, and Muqatil. On this view it is of the general (al-'amm) that is intended as the specific (al-khass). The third: the curse of the majority is attributed to all, by giving the ruling of the majority precedence over the minority.

"His saying, ﴿abiding therein﴾: regarding the pronoun (hā' al-kināya, the pronoun of reference "-hā" in "fīhā"), there are two opinions. The first: it refers back to the curse (al-la'na), as said by Ibn Mas'ud and Muqatil. The second: it refers to the Fire (al-nār), even though it has not been previously mentioned, since it is known."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 163:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And your God is one God﴾.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The disbelievers of Quraysh said: 'O Muhammad, describe your Lord for us and trace His lineage (unsubhu).' So this verse was revealed, and Surat al-Ikhlas." And *ilah* (deity) means: the one worshipped (*al-maʿbud*).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾.

Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are three views. The first: the polytheists said to the Prophet, "Make Safa gold for us, if you are truthful," so this verse was revealed. Al-Suddi related it from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas. The second: "When they said, 'Describe your Lord for us and give us His lineage,' the verse ﴿And your God is One God﴾ was revealed. They said, 'Show us a sign of that,' so ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ was revealed, up to His saying ﴿who reason﴾." Abu Salih related it from Ibn 'Abbas. The third: when ﴿And your God is One God﴾ was revealed, the disbelievers of Quraysh said, "How can one God suffice for the people?" So this verse was revealed. 'Ata' said this.

As for "the heavens" (al-samawat): they point to their Maker, since they stand without pillars, and in them are manifest signs, the least of which indicates their Originator. Likewise the earth, in the appearance of its fruits, the spreading out of its plains, and the setting of its mountains, and other things. ﴿And the alternation of night and day﴾: each of them came into being after it had not been, and passes away after it had been. ﴿And the ship (al-fulk)﴾: the ships. Ibn Qutayba said: the singular and plural are expressed with one form. Al-Yazidi said: its singular is fulka, and it may be masculine or feminine. Al-Zajjaj said: al-fulk means ships, and it may be singular or plural, because the pattern fa'al and fu'ul have the same plural, and they often come with one meaning, as in al-'ajam and al-'ujum, al-'urub and al-'arab, al-fulk and al-falak. It is also said that al-fulk applies to anything round or having roundness. ﴿The sea﴾ (al-bahr): the abundant water. ﴿With what benefits people﴾ of livelihoods. ﴿And what Allah sends down from the sky of water﴾ means the rain. Rain falls with one meaning, and the parts of the earth and the air are of one meaning, yet the kinds differ in plants, in tastes, in colours and in the varied shapes. In this there is a refutation of those who say it is the act of Nature, for if it were so, its effect would have to be uniform, since what is uniform does not produce what is diverse. He, glorified is He, pointed to this meaning in His saying: ﴿Watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in produce﴾ [al-Ra'd: 4].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He scattered (wa batha)﴾, that is, He dispersed.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the turning of the winds (wa tasrif al-riyah)﴾. Ibn Kathir read al-riyah in the plural in five places: here; in [al-Hijr: 22] ﴿And We send the winds fertilising﴾; in [al-Kahf: 46] ﴿which the winds scatter﴾; in [al-Rum: 46] the first letter, al-riyah; and in [al-Jathiyah: 4] ﴿and the turning of the winds﴾. The rest of the Qur'an he read as al-rih in the singular. Abu Ja'far read al-riyah in the plural in fifteen places in al-Baqarah, and in [al-A'raf: 56] ﴿He sends the winds﴾, in [Ibrahim: 18] ﴿the wind blew violently upon it﴾, in [al-Hijr: 22] ﴿the winds fertilising﴾, in [al-Isra: 69], in [al-Kahf: 45] ﴿which the winds scatter﴾, in [al-Anbiya': 81], (p-169) in [al-Furqan: 48] ﴿He sends the winds﴾, and in al-Naml. The second group: from [al-Rum: 48], in [Saba': 12], in [Sad: 36], in [al-Shura: 33] ﴿He stills the winds﴾, and in [al-Jathiyah: 5] ﴿and the turning of the winds﴾. Nafi' agreed with him except in al-Isra, and the winds of Sulayman [al-Anbiya': 81]. Abu 'Amr agreed with Nafi' except in two letters: al-rih in Ibrahim and in al-Shura, and he agreed with Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir. Hamza read al-riyah in the plural in two places: in al-Furqan, and the first letter of al-Rum; the rest in the singular. Al-Kisa'i was like Hamza, except that he added to it in [al-Hijr: 22] ﴿the winds fertilising﴾. They did not differ regarding what has no alif and lam. Whoever read the plural, then each wind equals its fellow in indicating the Oneness (of God) and in benefit; and whoever read the singular intended the genus.

The meaning of the turning of the winds is their changing: at one time north, at another south, at another the dabur (west wind), at another the sabā (east wind), and at another as a punishment or as mercy. ﴿And the subjected cloud (al-sahab al-musakhkhar)﴾: the made submissive. The sign in it is from four aspects: the beginning of its existence, the end of its dissolving, its standing without a support or a tie, and its being sent to wherever Allah, the Exalted, wills. ﴿Are signs (la-ayat)﴾. The ayah is the sign.

ʿAbd al-Wahhab al-Hafiz informed us, saying: 'Asim informed us, saying: Ibn Bishran informed us, saying: Ibn Safwan informed us, saying: Ibn Abi al-Dunya narrated to us, saying: Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Affan narrated to me, from Mubarak ibn Fudala, who said: I heard al-Hasan say: They (meaning the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ) used to say: "Praise be to Allah the Gentle, who, if He had made this creation a perpetual creation that does not change, the doubter concerning Allah would have said: 'If this creation had a Lord, He would have made it new.' Allah, the Exalted, has indeed made it new by what you see of the signs: He brought a light that spread between the two horizons, and placed in it livelihood and a blazing lamp; then, when He wills, He takes that creation away and brings a darkness that spreads between the two horizons, and places in it rest, stars and a shining moon; and when He wills, He builds a structure and places in it rain, lightning, thunder and thunderbolts as He wills; and when He wills, He turns that away; and when He wills, He brings a cold that makes people shiver, and when He wills, He takes that away and brings a heat that takes the breath of people, so that people may know that this creation has a Lord who makes it new by what you see of the signs. Likewise, when He wills, He takes away this world and brings the Hereafter."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 165:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And among the people are those who take, besides Allah, equals (andad)﴾.

Regarding "andad" (equals) there are two views, which have already been mentioned at the beginning of the surah. As for His words: ﴿They love them as they love Allah﴾, there are two views.

The first: its meaning is, "They love them as the believers love Allah." This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, Abu al-Aliyah, Ibn Zayd, Muqatil, and al-Farra'.

The second: "They love them as they love Allah," that is, they make the idols equal to Allah the Exalted in love. This is the choice of al-Zajjaj, who said: "The first view is worthless, and the proof that refutes it is His words: ﴿But those who believe are stronger in love for Allah﴾." The exegetes said: "Stronger in love for Allah" than the idolaters are for their idols.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And if only those who did wrong could see﴾. Abu Amr, Ibn Kathir, Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read (yaraa) with the letter ya', and its meaning is: if only they could see the punishment of the Hereafter, they would know that all power belongs to Allah. Nafi', Ibn Amir, and Ya'qub read (walaw taraa) with the letter ta', addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and what is meant is all people. Its response (jawab) is omitted; its estimated form is: "you would see a tremendous matter," just as you say: "If only you had seen so-and-so while the whips were striking him." The response was omitted because the meaning is clear without it. Abu Ali said: He said "idh" and did not say "idha," although "idh" refers to the past, in order to bring the matter near, so he used the example of the past tense. The response of "law" was omitted because it is more majestic, since the one issuing the warning goes to every kind of threat. Abu Ja'far read (inna al-quwwata lillahi) and (inna Allaha) with a kasra on the hamzah in both, as a new independent statement, as if he were saying: (p-171) "Do not let grieve you what you see of their love for their idols. (Indeed, all power belongs to Allah.)" Ibn Abbas said: "al-quwwah" means power and protection.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 166–167:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿from those who were followed﴾. There are two opinions regarding them. The first: they are the leaders and chieftains. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu al-ʿAliyah, Qatadah, Muqatil, and al-Zajjaj. The second: they are the devils. This was said by al-Suddi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and they see the punishment﴾ includes all of them. ﴿and their means of connection are cut off from them﴾, i.e., from them, like His saying: ﴿so ask about it one well-informed (khabiran)﴾ [al-Furqan: 59]. Regarding the asbab (means, ties) there are four opinions. The first: they are the mutual affections (al-mawaddat). Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, and Qatadah went to something similar. The second: they are the deeds (al-aʿmal). This was narrated by al-Suddi from Ibn Masʿud and Ibn ʿAbbas, and it is the view of Abu Salih and Ibn Zayd. The third: they are the ties of kinship (al-arham). This was narrated by Ibn Jurayj from Ibn ʿAbbas. The fourth: they include all of that. Ibn Qutaybah said: They are the ties by which they used to connect with one another in this world. As for calling them asbab, the sabab (cause, means) in the language is the rope; then it was said of anything by which one reaches the desired goal: sabab. The karrah (return) is the return to the world. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah, among others.

﴿So we would disown them﴾, meaning: the leaders, ﴿as they have disowned us﴾ in the Hereafter.

﴿Thus Allah will show them their deeds﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, like the disowning of some of them by others, Allah will show them their deeds as regrets (hasarat) upon them, because the deeds of the disbeliever will not benefit him. Ibn al-Anbari said: Allah will show them their ugly deeds as regrets upon them when they see the best recompense given to the believers for their deeds. He said: It is also permissible that the meaning is: Thus Allah will show them the reward of their good deeds and its recompense, so he omitted the recompense (al-jaza’) and placed the deeds in its position. Ibn Faris said: The hasrah is the grief (taleuhhuf) over a thing that has passed. Others said: The hasrah is the most intense remorse.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 168:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O mankind, eat of what is lawful and good in the earth﴾. It was revealed concerning Thaqif, Khuza'ah, and the Banu 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah, regarding what they forbade for themselves of the tilth and livestock, and they forbade the baheerah (a she-camel whose ears were slit and released), the saa'ibah (a beast released freely), and the haam (a stallion camel released after a set number of services). This was related by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read (khutuwat) with the taa' pronounced heavy (khuṭuwāt). Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and Hamzah read (khutwat) with the taa' sukun and light (khuṭwāt). Al-Hasan and Abu al-Jawza' read (khatwat) with a fatha on the kha' and a sukun on the taa', without hamz. Abu 'Imran al-Jawni read with a damma on the kha' and the taa', with hamz. Ibn Qutaybah said: "Khutuwatuhu: his path and his way. It is the plural of khutwah, and the khutwah with a damma on the kha' is the distance between the two feet, while with a fatha it is a single act of stepping." Their following his footsteps means that they forbade things that God had made lawful, and made lawful things that God had forbidden.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾. That is, manifest. It was said: he made his enmity manifest through what happened between him and Adam.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 169:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He only commands you to evil﴾. As-su' (evil) is every sin and ugliness. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was named "su'" because its consequences are bad (tasu'u 'awaqibuhu). It was also said: it is so named because its manifestation is displeasing (yasu'u izharuhu). ﴿And immorality (al-fahsha')﴾ comes from fahusha ash-shay', meaning the thing exceeded its proper measure (idha jaza qadrahu). Regarding what is meant by it here, there are five opinions. The first: it is every act of disobedience for which there is a prescribed punishment (hadd) in this world.

(p-173) The second: it is that which is not recognized in the Sharia (shari'a) or the Sunna (sunna). The third: it is stinginess (bukhl). These three opinions are transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas. The fourth: it is fornication (zina), said by as-Suddi. The fifth: it is acts of disobedience (ma'asi), said by Muqatil.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that you say about Allah what you do not know﴾, meaning: that He has forbidden you what He has not forbidden.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 170:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down,"﴾.

The scholars differed regarding who this verse was revealed about, in three opinions. The first: it was revealed about those to whom it was said, ﴿Eat of what is on the earth, lawful and good﴾. According to this, the pronoun (al-ha' wal-mim, i.e., the "them" in "lahum") refers back to them. This is the view of Muqatil. The second: it was revealed about the Jews, and it is a separate narrative, so the pronoun (al-ha' wal-mim) is a reference to something not previously mentioned. Ibn Ishaq narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas. The third: it was revealed about the polytheists of the Arabs and the disbelievers of Quraysh, so the pronoun refers back to His saying: ﴿And among the people are those who take, besides Allah, equals (andad)﴾.

According to the first opinion, what is meant by "that which Allah has sent down" is the making lawful of what is lawful and the making unlawful of what is unlawful. According to the second, it is Islam. According to the third, it is monotheism (tawhid) and Islam. And (alfayna) means "we found" (wajadna).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Even though their fathers did not understand anything﴾ of the religion, and were not guided to it, would you still follow them even in their error and their fabrication?!

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 171–172:

Allah's statement: ﴿And the example of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts to that which does not hear except a call and cry﴾

(p-174) Regarding the meaning of this verse there are three opinions.

The first: its meaning is, "And the example of those who disbelieve is like the example of the cattle which the shepherd calls to." This is the view of al-Farra' (al-Farra') and Tha'lab (Tha'lab), who both said: "He attributed the example (mathal) to those who disbelieved, then likened them to the shepherd, and did not say 'like the sheep.' The meaning is: 'And the example of those who disbelieve is like the example of the cattle which do not understand what the shepherd says beyond the sound. If the shepherd says to them, "Graze," or "Drink," they do not know what he is saying to them. Likewise are those who disbelieve regarding what comes to them of the Qur'an and the warning of the Messenger.'" So the comparison is attributed to the shepherd, while the meaning lies in the one being herded. This is evident in the speech of the Arabs, who say: "So-and-so fears you like the fear of the lion," meaning: "like his fear of the lion [because the lion is well known as the one who causes fear]." The poet said:

"It was an obligation, what you say, as the fornication was an obligation for stoning."

The meaning: "As stoning was the obligation for fornication."

The second: its meaning is, "And the example of those who disbelieve, and our example in admonishing them, is like the example of the one who calls out and the one called out to." So "we have given the example" is omitted for brevity, since the speech contains what indicates it. This is the view of Ibn Qutaybah and al-Zajjaj.

The third: "And the example of those who disbelieve in their calling upon their gods whom they worship is like the example of the one who shouts (yan'iq)." This is the view of Ibn Zayd. The one who shouts (alladhi yan'iq) is the shepherd. It is said: "He shouted (na'aqa) at the sheep, (yan'iqu) na'aqan, na'iqan, nu'aqan, nu'qanan." Ibn al-Anbari said: "What is widespread in the speech of the Arabs is that na'aqa is said only of calling out to sheep alone, for the sheep hear the sound but do not grasp the meaning."

﴿Deaf, dumb﴾: He described them as deaf and dumb only because, in their refusal to accept what they hear, they are in the position of one who does not hear; likewise in speech and sight. The explanation of this meaning has already preceded.

Allah's statement: ﴿And the example of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts to that which does not hear except a call and cry﴾

(p-174) Regarding the meaning of this verse there are three opinions.

The first: its meaning is, "And the example of those who disbelieve is like the example of the cattle which the shepherd calls to."
