(p-175) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He has only forbidden you carrion﴾.

Abu Ja'far read "al-maytatah" here, and in al-Ma'idah and an-Nahl, and "baldatan maytan" [Qaf: 11] with the doubled ya (tashdid), wherever it occurs. In the usage of the Shari'ah (ʿurf al-sharʿ), "maytah" (carrion) is the term for every animal whose soul has departed without zakah (ritual slaughter). It has been said that the wisdom behind the prohibition of carrion is that the blood coagulates in it upon death, which causes harm to the one who eats it. Sometimes the slaughtered animal is also called "maytah" by ruling (hukman), because its ruling is the ruling of carrion, as with the sacrifice of an apostate. As for blood, what is forbidden of it is that which is poured forth (masfuh), based on His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or blood poured forth﴾ [al-An'am: 145]. Qadi Abu Ya'la said: As for the blood that remains in the crevices of the meat after slaughter, and what remains in the veins, it is permissible.

As for the flesh of swine, what is meant is its whole body, and he specified the flesh because it is the main object of consumption. Al-Zajjaj said: "Khinzir" (swine) includes both the male and the female. The meaning of ﴿and that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾ [al-Baqarah: 173] is that over which the voice has been raised by naming other than Allah. Similar to this is "al-ihlal" for Hajj, which is merely raising the voice with the talbiyah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So whoever is compelled﴾, meaning: forced by necessity. Abu Ja'far read "fa-mani adturra" (with a kasrah on the ta') wherever it occurs. Ibn Muhaysin assimilated the dad into the ta'.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿neither desiring nor transgressing﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "al-baghy" is the intention of corruption; it is said: "baghā al-jurh" when the wound progresses toward corruption. Regarding His saying: ﴿neither desiring nor transgressing﴾, there are four opinions. The first: its meaning is not rebelling against the rulers, nor transgressing by cutting the road; this is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid. The second: not desiring in eating beyond his need, nor transgressing by eating it while he finds other food; this is the view of al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Qatadah and al-Rabi'. The third: "not desiring" means one who considers it lawful (mustahill), and "nor transgressing" means one who is not compelled; this is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Muqatil. The fourth: not desiring it for the sake of his appetite, nor transgressing by eating to satiety; this was said by al-Suddi.

Section

The meaning of necessity in the permissibility of carrion is that one fears for his own self or some of his limbs. Ahmad, (p-176) may Allah be pleased with him, was asked about the one under compulsion who does not eat carrion, and he mentioned from Masruq that he said: whoever is compelled and does not eat, then dies, enters the Fire. As for the amount he may eat, Hanbal transmitted: he eats the amount that keeps him from dying. And Ibn Mansur transmitted: he eats the amount by which he becomes sufficient. The apparent meaning of the first is that it is not permissible for him to eat to satiety, and this is the view of Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i; the apparent meaning of the second is the permissibility of eating to satiety, and this is the view of Malik.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 174:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has revealed of the Book﴾.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: It was revealed concerning the Jews, who concealed the name of the Prophet (ﷺ) and altered it in their book. "The little price" is what they obtain from their followers of worldly gain. ﴿Those eat nothing into their bellies except the Fire﴾. Al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH; a grammarian and Qur'an scholar) said: its meaning is that those who consume it are punished by it, so it is as if they are eating the Fire.

﴿And Allah will not speak to them﴾. This is evidence that Allah does not speak to the disbelievers, nor does He call them to account.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And will not purify them﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions. The first: He does not purify their deeds; this was said by Muqatil. The second: He does not praise them; this was said by al-Zajjaj. The third: He does not cleanse them from the filth of their disbelief and their sins; this was said by Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 175:

Allah's words: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error﴾ means: they chose it over guidance.

Allah's words: ﴿So how patient they are for the Fire!﴾ There are four opinions concerning this. The first: its meaning is, "How patient they are at a deed that leads them to the Fire!" This was said by ʿIkrimah and al-Rabiʿ. The second: "How bold they are toward the Fire!" This was said by al-Hasan and Mujahid. al-Kisa'i mentioned that a Bedouin was sworn to falsely by a man, and the Bedouin said, "How patient you are regarding Allah," meaning, "How bold you are." The third: "How long they will remain in the Fire!" as you say, "How patient so-and-so is with imprisonment," meaning, "How long he remains in it." This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj. (p-177) The fourth: the meaning is, "What has made them patient with the Fire?!" This was said by Ibn al-Anbari. Regarding "mā" there are two views. One: it is interrogative, its implied sense being, "What is it that has made them patient?" This was said by ʿAta', al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, and Abu Bakr ibn ʿAyyash. The second: it is exclamatory of wonder, like your saying, "How good Zayd is!" and "How knowledgeable ʿAmr is!" Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning of the verse is amazement, and Allah causes the created beings to be amazed, but He does not experience amazement as they do.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 176:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, those who differ concerning the Book﴾, there are two opinions regarding it.

One of them: it is the Torah (al-Tawrah). Then, concerning their disagreement about it, there are three opinions. The first: that the Jews and the Christians differed about it; the Christians claimed in it the description of ʿĪsā (Jesus), and the Jews denied that. The second: that they opposed what is in the Torah concerning the description of Muhammad (ﷺ). The third: that they opposed their predecessors in adhering to it.

The second: it is the Qur'an. Among them were those who said: it is poetry, and among them were those who said: it is only taught to him by a human being.

Al-shiqaq (al-shiqaq, "dissension") is the hostility of some of them toward others. Concerning the meaning of "baʿid" (far) there are two opinions. One: that some of them are far removed in opposing others; this was said by al-Zajjaj. The second: that it is far from guidance.

The verbal noun of the phrase: "His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces﴾."

Qatadah said: "It was related to us that a man asked about 'righteousness' (al-birr), so this verse was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called him and recited it to him."

There are two views on who was addressed by it. The first is that they are the Muslims. The second is that they are the People of the Two Books (Jews and Christians). According to the first view, its meaning is: righteousness does not consist entirely in prayer, but true righteousness is what is in this verse. This meaning is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ata', al-Dahhak, and Sufyan. According to the second view, its meaning is: righteousness is not the Jews' prayer toward the west, nor the Christians' prayer toward the east, but true righteousness is what is in this verse. This is the view of Qatadah, al-Rabi', 'Awf al-A'rabi, and Muqatil.

Hamzah and Hafs, from 'Asim, read (لَيْسَ البِرَّ) with the *ra'* in the accusative (*naṣb*). The rest read it in the nominative (*raf'*). Abu 'Ali said: both are good, because each of the two nouns, the subject of *laysa* (ism *laysa*) and its predicate (khabar), is definite. When both are definite, they are equivalent in that either may serve as the subject and the other as the predicate, just as two indefinite nouns are interchangeable.

There are three views on the meaning of *al-birr*. The first is faith (*al-Iman*). The second is piety (*al-taqwa*). The third is the deed that brings one closer to Allah.

Regarding His saying, ﴿But righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah﴾, there are two views. The first is that its meaning is: "But righteousness is the righteousness of one who believes in Allah." The second is: "But the possessor of righteousness is one who believes in Allah." Both are related by al-Zajjaj. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read (وَلَكِنَّ البِرَّ) with the *nun* of *lakinna* lightened and the *birr* in the nominative. He mentioned the Last Day because the idol-worshippers did not believe in the Resurrection.

Regarding the meaning of "the Book" here, there are two views. The first is that it is the Qur'an. The second is that it means the books in general, and thus the Jews are included, because they denied some of the prophets and rejected the Qur'an.

Regarding His saying, ﴿and gives wealth, despite love for it﴾, there are two views concerning the pronoun in "*ḥubbihi*" (its love). The first is that it refers to the wealth. The second is that it refers to the giving. Al-Hasan, when he recited it, would say: "[This refers to giving] apart from the obligatory zakat."

His saying, ﴿to relatives﴾, means the relatives of the giver. We have explained the meaning of "the orphans and the needy" at the verse eighty-three of this surah. As for "the wayfarer" (ibn al-sabil), there are three views. The first is that it is the guest; this was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, Muqatil, al-Farra', Ibn Qutaybah, and al-Zajjaj. The second is that it is one who passes by you while traveling; this was said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas, and it is related from Mujahid and Qatadah as in both of the first two views. It has been related from Imam Ahmad that he said: it is the one who is cut off from his means, wishing to reach another land. This is the choice of Ibn Jarir al-Tabari, Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi, and al-Qadi Abu Ya'la. What confirms it is that *al-sabil* is the path, and *ibn al-sabil* is its companion, the one who travels upon it, so he has a right upon whoever passes by him if he is in need. Perhaps the proponents of the first view pointed to this, since if he is a traveler, he is a guest who has not yet settled. The third view is that he is one who intends a journey but does not find the means for it; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi and others, from al-Shafi'i.

His saying, ﴿and for the captives﴾, means: for the freeing of captives. Then there are two views. The first is that they are the *mukatabun* (slaves who have contracted to buy their freedom), who are assisted in their contract with what they need to gain their freedom. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd, and al-Shafi'i. The second is that they are slaves who are purchased with this portion and then freed; this was narrated by Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas, and Malik ibn Anas, Abu 'Ubayd, and Abu Thawr said likewise. From Ahmad there are views like both.

As for *al-ba's'a* (hardship), it is poverty. *Al-darra'* (adversity) is sickness. *Ḥina al-ba's* (the time of battle) is fighting, as al-Dahhak said.

﴿Those are the ones who are true﴾. Abu al-'Aliyah said: they spoke of faith and verified it through action.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 178:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the murdered﴾. Shaybан narrated from Qatadah that the people of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam) had among them transgression and obedience to Satan. If a tribe (ḥayy) among them had numbers and protection, and its slave killed the slave of another people, they would say: "We will not kill for him except a free man," out of pride in their superiority over others. And if a woman from among them killed a woman from another people, they would say: "We will not kill for her except a man." So this verse was revealed. The meaning of "prescribed" (kutiba) is "obligated," as said by Ibn ʿAbbas and others. Al-qiṣāṣ (retaliation, in the sense of requiting an act with its like) is derived from: qaṣṣ al-athar (tracing the footprints). If it is said: how can it be an obligation when the guardian (walī) is given the choice between it and forgiveness? The answer: it was obligated upon the killer toward the guardian, not upon the guardian.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But whoever is pardoned by his brother in anything﴾, that is: regarding the blood of his brother, meaning he leaves off killing for him and accepts the blood-money (diyah) from him. His saying "from his brother" indicates that the killer has not left Islam. ﴿Then there should be a suitable follow-up﴾, that is: a demand for it made in a fitting manner, by the one receiving the blood-money instructing the demander to make the demand in a gracious way that does not oppress him. ﴿And payment to him with good conduct﴾: he commands the one making the demand not to diminish (the payment) or to procrastinate. ﴿That is an alleviation from your Lord﴾. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: the ruling of Allah upon the People of the Torah was that the killer of deliberate murder be killed, not pardoned, and no blood-money be taken from him. So Allah granted the Ummah of Muhammad a concession: if the guardian of the one killed deliberately wishes, he may kill, if he wishes he may pardon, and if he wishes, he may take the blood-money.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So whoever transgresses﴾, that is: wrongs, by killing the killer of his companion after taking the blood-money; ﴿for him is a painful punishment﴾. Qatadah said: he is killed, and blood-money is not accepted from him.

Section

A group of the exegetes held that the implication (dalil al-khitab) of this verse is abrogated, because when He said: ﴿the free for the free﴾, it implied that a slave is not to be killed for a free person, and likewise when He said: ﴿and the female for the female﴾, it implied, by way of the implication of the discourse, that a male is not to be killed for a female; and that is abrogated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the soul is for the soul﴾. Our shaykh ʿAli ibn ʿAbd Allah said: this, according to the jurists, is not abrogation, because the jurists say: the implication of the discourse is a proof so long as it is not opposed by a stronger proof.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 179:

(p-181) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And in retribution (qisas) there is life for you﴾.

Al-Zajjaj said: When a man knows that if he kills, he will be killed, he refrains from killing. Thus there is life in that for the one who intended to kill him, and for himself, because he refrained on account of retribution. The poet took up this meaning and said:

"Convey to Abu Malik from me a message,
and in reproach there is life among people."

He means that when they reproach one another, reproach reconciles between them. Al-albab (the minds) are the intellects. He addressed them specifically with this address, although the address is general, because they are the ones who benefit from the address, since they comply with His command and refrain by His prohibition.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So that you may be God-conscious (la'allakum tattaqun)﴾. Ibn Abbas said: "So that you may be God-conscious regarding blood." Ibn Zayd said: "So that you may be wary lest he kill him and you be killed for him."

Section

Ibn Mansur related from Ahmad: If a man kills a man with a stick, or strangles him, or smashes his head with a stone, he is to be killed in the same manner in which he killed. The apparent meaning of this is that retribution may be carried out by other than the sword, and that it may be carried out with an instrument like the one with which he killed, and this is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i. Harb related from him: If he killed him with a piece of wood, retribution is accepted by the sword. Abu Talib related: If he strangled him, he is killed by the sword. The apparent meaning of this is that retribution is only by the sword, and this is the view of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 180:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿It has been prescribed for you, when death approaches any of you﴾.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is "and He prescribed for you," except that when the speech is long it dispenses with the conjunction "wa" (and), and it is understood that its meaning is the meaning of "wa." The intended meaning is not "He prescribed for you that one of you should make a bequest at the time of death," because at that time he is preoccupied. Rather, the meaning is: "He prescribed for you that you should make bequests while you are able to do so," so that a man says: "If I die, then such-and-such is for so-and-so." As for "the good" (khayr) here, it is wealth, according to the consensus of the scholars.

On the amount of wealth in which this bequest applies, there are six opinions. The first: it is one thousand dirhams or more, narrated from Ali and Qatadah. The second: it is seven hundred dirhams or more, narrated by Tawus from Ibn Abbas. The third: sixty dinars or more, narrated by Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas. The fourth: it is a large amount of wealth beyond the maintenance of one's dependants. Aishah said to a man who asked her: "I want to make a bequest." She said: "How much wealth do you have?" He said: "Three thousand." She said: "How many dependants do you have?" He said: "Four." She said: "This is a small amount, so leave it for your dependants." The fifth: it is from one thousand dirhams down to five hundred, said by Ibrahim al-Nakha'i. The sixth: it is the little and the much, narrated by Ma'mar from al-Zuhri. As for "the reasonable" (al-ma'ruf), it is that in which there is no injustice (haif).

Section

Was the bequest recommended (nadb) or obligatory? There are two opinions. The first: it was recommended. The second: it was obligatory, and this is the more sound, because of His saying ﴿prescribed﴾, meaning: obligated. Ibn Umar said: This verse was abrogated (nusikhat) by the verse of inheritance. Ibn Abbas said: It was abrogated by: ﴿For men there is a share of what the parents and the relatives leave﴾ [An-Nisa: 7]. The scholars agree on the abrogation of the bequest to parents and to the relatives who inherit. They differ regarding the relatives who do not inherit: is a bequest obligatory for them? There are two opinions, the more sound of which is that it is not obligatory for anyone.

Allah's words: ﴿Then whoever alters it﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever alters the matter of the bequest after hearing it, its sin rests only upon the one who alters it, not upon the testator, nor upon the beneficiary. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing﴾ of what the testator has said, ﴿Knowing﴾ of what the executor does with it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 182:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then whoever fears from a testator﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim read (mūṣin) with a sukun on the waw. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim read "mūṣin" with a fatha on the waw and a shaddah on the sad. Regarding the meaning of "fear" here there are two opinions. One: it means knowledge. The other: it means fear itself. On the first view, the wrong (jawr) has already occurred; on the second, he fears its occurrence. "Janaf" (deviation, from al-Jana f) is inclination away from the truth. Al-Zajjaj said: janafan means inclination, or ithman means he intended sin. Ibn 'Abbas said: janaf is error, and ithm is deliberate intent. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: janaf is departure from the truth, and it may be used of both the one who errs and the one who acts deliberately, except that the exegetes understood janaf as applying to the one who errs and ithm as applying to the one who acts deliberately.

Regarding the interpretation of this verse there are two opinions. One: its meaning is that whoever attends a man who is dying, and he is excessive in his bequest or falls short of a right, then he should instruct him to act justly; this is the view of Mujahid. The second: its meaning is that whoever bequeaths with injustice, and his guardian (wali) rejects his bequest, or a leader among the leaders of the Muslims returns it to the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Prophet, then there is no sin upon him; this is the view of Qatadah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and makes reconciliation among them﴾, that is, among those to whom he bequeathed, though no mention of them has preceded; but when he mentioned the testator, the implicit meaning of the discourse indicated that there is a beneficiary. al-Farra' recited:

"And I do not know, when I aim for a land desiring good, which of the two will come upon me:
Is it the good that I seek,
or the evil that seeks me?"

In the first line he referred to evil by way of allusion after mentioning only good, because of the indication contained in the implied meaning of the wording.

(p. 184) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who believe, fasting has been prescribed for you﴾.

Linguistically, *al-siyam* (fasting, *sawm*) means abstention in general. One says *samat al-khayl* ("the horses fasted") when they stop running, and *samat al-rih* ("the wind fasted") when it stops blowing. In the sacred law, *al-sawm* is abstention from food, drink, and sexual intercourse, combined with the intention (*niyyah*) to do so.

As for "those before you," there are three opinions. The first is that they were the People of the Book, related by 'Ata al-Khurasani from Ibn 'Abbas, and this is the view of Mujahid. The second is that they were the Christians, said by al-Sha'bi and al-Rabi'. The third is that they were all the religious communities (*milal*), mentioned by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

Regarding the point of comparison in the particle *ka* (as) in ﴿as it was prescribed﴾, there are two views.

The first is that the comparison concerns the ruling and manner of fasting, not its number. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "It was prescribed for them that if one of them slept before eating, it was not lawful for him to eat until the next night, and wives were forbidden to them during the night of fasting, and this remained binding on them. But you have been granted a concession." On this view, this verse is abrogated (*mansukhah*, i.e., its ruling has been superseded) by His saying: ﴿It has been made lawful for you, on the night of fasting, to go to your wives﴾ [al-Baqara: 187], because that verse distinguished the fasting of the People of the Book from the fasting of the Muslims.

The second is that the comparison concerns the number of days. Then there are two views on this. The first is that fasting three days of every month was obligatory on this community, and that it had also been obligatory on those before them. 'Atiyya related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿as it was prescribed for those before you﴾ that he said: "It was three days of every month, and then it was abrogated by Ramadan." Ma'mar related from Qatada: "God had prescribed on people before Ramadan three days of every month." On this view, the verse is abrogated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾.

The second is that He prescribed for those before us the fasting of Ramadan itself. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The Christians moved it forward a day and then a day, and postponed a day, then they said: 'We will move forward ten and postpone ten.'" al-Suddi related from his shaykhs: "The fasting of Ramadan became hard for the Christians, so it kept shifting for them through winter and summer. When they saw this, they gathered (p. 185) and made a fast in the interval between winter and summer, and they said: 'We will add twenty days, to expiate what we did.'" On this view, the verse is definite (*muhkamah*, i.e., not abrogated).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿so that you may become righteous﴾. Because fasting is a means to piety (*taqwa*), since it restrains the soul from much of what it craves of sins. It was also said: "so that you may guard against what is forbidden during fasting."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 184:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Days numbered﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "Ayyaman" is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf), as if He said: fasting was prescribed for you in these days. The governing element (al-'amil) in it is "al-siyam" (fasting), as if the meaning is: He prescribed for you that you fast numbered days. Regarding "these days" there are three opinions. The first: they are three days of every month. The second: they are three days of every month plus the day of ʿAshura'. The third: they are the month of Ramadan, and this is the most sound (al-asahh). On this view the verse is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated), while on the two views before it, it is mansukh (abrogated). ﴿So whoever among you is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾: in it there is an implied element (idmar): "so he breaks the fast."

Section

Illness and travel are not absolute. The sick person for whom fasting does not cause harm is not permitted to break the fast; the concession is conditional upon fasting increasing the illness. The scholars agreed that travel has a defined measure, but they differed about its determination. Ahmad, Malik and al-Shafiʿi said: its minimum is a journey of sixteen farsakh, two days. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: its minimum is a journey of three days, a journey of twenty-four farsakh. Al-Awzaʿi said: its minimum is one day's stage (marhala), a journey of eight farsakh. It was also said: the word "safar" (journey) is derived from "safar," which means uncovering, as one says: "the woman uncovered (safarat) her face," and "the morning brightened (asfara)" when it shone; so going out to a distant place was called "safar" because it uncovers the character of the traveller.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And for those who are able to fast [but with difficulty], there is a ransom: feeding a poor person﴾. It was reported from Ibn Masʿud, Muʿadh ibn Jabal, Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas, Salama ibn al-Akwaʿ, ʿAlqama, al-Zuhri and others regarding this verse that they said: whoever wished fasted, and whoever wished broke the fast and paid the ransom, feeding one poor person for each day, until the verse was revealed: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾. On this view, the meaning of the speech is: "And for those who are able to fast but do not fast, there is a ransom," and then it was abrogated. It was narrated from ʿIkrima that he said: it was revealed concerning the pregnant woman and the nursing woman. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and Ibn ʿAbbas read: "wa-ʿala alladhina yuṭawwiqunahu" with a damma on the yaʾ, a fatha on the ṭaʾ, and a shadda on the waw. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it refers to the old man and the old woman.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿ransom: feeding a poor person﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, ʿAsim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "fidyatun" with tanwin, and "ṭaʿamu al-miskin" in the singular. Nafi' and Ibn ʿAmir read "fidyatu" without tanwin, "ṭaʿamu" in the genitive (bi-l-khafd), and "masakin" in the plural. Abu ʿAli said: the meaning of the first reading is: for each one, the food of one poor person. Similar to it is: ﴿lash them eighty [lashes]﴾ [al-Nur: 4], i.e., lash each one of them eighty. Abu Zayd said: "We came to the amir, and he clothed each one of us with a robe, and gave each one of us a hundred," meaning he did that to each one of us. He said: as for the one who attributes the ransom to the food, it is like the attribution of a part to that of which it is a part; that is, he called the food by which the ransom is paid "fidya," then attributed the fidya to the food which encompasses the fidya and other things; so on this view it is of the type of: "a ring of iron."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever volunteers good﴾. In it there are three opinions. The first: its meaning is: whoever feeds two poor persons; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid. The second: that volunteering is feeding poor persons; this was said by Tawus. The third: that it is adding to what the poor person needs for his sustenance; this is narrated from Mujahid, and Anas ibn Malik did it when he became old. ﴿And that you fast is better for you﴾ refers to those previously mentioned, the healthy residents who were given the choice between fasting and feeding, as we related at the beginning of the verse from the early generations (al-salaf). It does not refer to the sick, the travellers, the pregnant and the nursing, since breaking the fast is better for them than fasting, and they have been forbidden to expose themselves to destruction; and this strengthens the view of those who say the verse was abrogated.

(p-187) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The month of Ramadan﴾

Al-Akhfash said: "Shahru Ramadan" is in the nominative (marfu') as an explanation (tafsir) of "days" (al-ayyam), as if, when He said ﴿numbered days﴾, He explained them by saying: they are the month of Ramadan. Abu 'Ubayd said: Mujahid recited it in the accusative, "shahra Ramadan," and I think he put it in the accusative in the sense of incitement (al-igra'), i.e., "Upon you is the month of Ramadan, so fast it," like His saying: ﴿the religion of your father﴾ and His saying: ﴿the dye of Allah﴾. I say: Among those who recited it in the accusative were Mu'awiyah, al-Hasan, Zayd ibn 'Ali, 'Ikrimah, and Yahya ibn Ya'mur.

Ibn Faris said: al-ramd is the heat of stones from the intensity of the sun's heat. It is said: "Shahru Ramadan" is named from the intensity of heat, because when they transferred the names of the months from the earlier language, they named them after the times in which they fell. This month coincided with the days of ramad (scorching heat). It is pluralized as ramadanat, armida', and armidah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions. The first: that the Qur'an was sent down in it all at once, on the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr), to the House of Honor (bayt al-'izzah) from the lowest heaven. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: that its meaning is that He sent down the Qur'an with the obligation of its fasting; this was narrated from Mujahid and al-Dahhak. The third: that its meaning is that the Qur'an began to be revealed in it upon the Prophet ﷺ; this was said by Ibn Ishaq and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. Muqatil said: al-Furqan is the way out in religion from doubt and error.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾, i.e., whoever is present and not traveling. If it is asked: what is the benefit of repeating the mention of illness and travel in this verse, when it has already been mentioned? It is answered: because in the preceding verse there is an abrogated ruling, so He repeated it lest it be linked with the abrogated ruling.

(p-188) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah desires ease for you﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, and al-Dahhak said: ease is breaking the fast during travel, and hardship is fasting during it. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: i.e., that was easier for you, so do: fasting or breaking the fast during travel.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and that you complete the period﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i recited (wa-li-tukmilu) with a light kaf (sukun on the kaf). Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, recited it with a doubled mim, like "wassa" and "awsa." Ibn 'Abbas said: "and that you complete the number of what you broke." Some said: the intended meaning is: do not add to what was obligated, as the Christians did, and do not shift it from its time as they shifted it. ﴿and that you magnify Allah for having guided you﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is incumbent on the Muslims, when they see the crescent of Shawwal, to glorify Allah until they finish their festival. If it is asked: what is the reason for the waw entering in His saying: ﴿and that you complete the period and that you magnify Allah﴾, when there is nothing for it to be conjoined to? The answer: this waw conjoins the lam that follows it to a deleted lam, and the meaning is: "and He does not desire hardship for you, so that He may make you happy, and so that you complete the period." The first lam was deleted because its meaning is clear. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

Section

From the Sunnah is the public proclamation of takbir on the night of Fitr, the night of Nahr, and when they go out to the musalla (prayer ground). The reports from Ahmad, may Allah be pleased with him, differed as to when one stops on the Fitr festival. Harb transmitted from him: one stops after the imam finishes the khutbah. al-Athram transmitted: when one reaches the musalla, one stops. Qadi Abu Ya'la said: he means: when one reaches the musalla and the imam has come out.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 186:

There are five reports concerning the occasion of its revelation.

The first: "A bedouin Arab came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'Is our Lord near, so that we may address Him privately, or is He far, so that we must call out to Him?' Then this verse was revealed." It was related by al-Saltt ibn Hakim, from his father, from his grandfather.

The second: "The Jews of Medina said: 'O Muhammad! How does our Lord hear our supplication, when you claim that between us and the heaven is a distance of five hundred years' journey?!' Then this verse was revealed." It was related by Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas.

The third: "They said: 'O Messenger of Allah! If we knew which hour is most beloved to Allah for us to make our supplication in, [we would do so].' Then this verse was revealed." This was stated by Ata'.

The fourth: The Companions of the Prophet said to him: "Where is Allah?" Then this verse was revealed. This was stated by al-Hasan.

The fifth: When eating and intercourse became forbidden to the Muslims after sleep during the first fast, a man among them ate after he had slept, and a man had intercourse after he had slept. They asked: "How is repentance for what they did?" Then this verse was revealed. This was stated by Muqatil. The meaning of the speech is: "If they ask you about Me, then inform them that I am near."

Concerning the meaning of "ujib" (I answer), there are two views. The first: it means "I hear" (asma'), stated by al-Farra' and Ibn al-Qasim. The second: that it is from ijaba (answering), as in ﴿So let them respond to Me﴾, meaning: let them answer Me. The poet said:

A caller who called out, "O you who answers to generosity," but no one answered him at that time.

He meant: no one answered him. This is the view of Abu Ubayda, Ibn Qutayba, and al-Zajjaj. ﴿That perhaps they may be rightly guided﴾. Abu al-Aliyah said: meaning, "that they may be guided."

Section

If someone says: This verse indicates that Allah, exalted is He, answers the supplications of those who supplicate, yet we see many supplicants whose supplications are not granted!

The answer: Abu Sa'id related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "No Muslim makes a supplication to Allah, Exalted is He, containing no severing of kinship and no sin, except that Allah gives him through it one of three things: either He hastens his supplication for him, or He stores it up for him in the Hereafter, or He averts from him an equivalent evil."

Another answer: The answering of supplication depends on conditions, the root of which is obedience to Allah, and among them is eating what is lawful, for eating what is unlawful prevents the answering of supplication. Among them is presence of the heart; in some hadith: "Allah accepts the supplication of a heart that is heedless and distracted."

Another answer: The supplicant may believe that the benefit lies in granting what he asked, while the benefit may not lie in that, so he is granted his original aim, which is seeking benefit; and the benefit may lie in delay or in refusal.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 187:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of the fast to go in unto your wives (al-rafath)﴾.

The occasion of revelation of this verse was that the Companions, if a man slept before eating and having intercourse, became forbidden to him (p-191) until he broke his fast. An old man from the Ansar came to his household while he was fasting, and said, "Serve me food." They said, "Wait until we warm some food for you." He lay his head down and slept, and when they brought the food he said, "I had already slept." He spent the night turning from his back to his side. When morning came, he went to the Prophet (ﷺ) and told him. Then 'Umar ibn al-Khattab stood up and said, "O Messenger of Allah! Last night I desired my wife, and she said, 'I have already slept.' I supposed she was pretending, so I lay with her, and then she told me she had been asleep." Allah the Exalted then revealed concerning 'Umar ibn al-Khattab: ﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of the fast to go in unto your wives﴾, and He revealed concerning the Ansari: ﴿And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread of dawn﴾. This is the view of a group of exegetes (mufassirun).

They differed about the name of this Ansari, with four opinions. The first: Qays ibn Sirmah, related by al-Bara'. The second: Sirmah ibn Anas, related by al-Qasim ibn Muhammad. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla said: Sirmah ibn Malik. The third: Damrah ibn Anas. The fourth: Abu Qays ibn 'Umar. Abu Bakr al-Khatib mentioned two of these views.

As for "al-rafath," Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ata', al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, and others said: it is intercourse.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them﴾. Concerning this there are two views. One: that the garment (libas) means rest and tranquility. Similar is ﴿He made the night a garment (libas)﴾ [al-Furqan: 47], meaning a rest. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and Qatadah. The second: that they are like a garment, because each one joins their skin to the skin of the other, so He referred metaphorically to their coming together unclothed by the term "garment." Al-Zajjaj said: The Arabs call a woman "libas" and "izar" (wrapper). Al-Nabigha al-Ja'di said:

"When a bedfellow bends her neck, she bends and becomes a garment over him."

(p-192) And another said:

"Let me convey to Abu Hafs a message: may my trusted brother be ransomed for you by my izar."

He meant by "izar" his wife.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: He means you were betraying them by committing what is forbidden to you. Ibn 'Abbas said: By this He meant the act of 'Umar, for he went to his wife, and when he had bathed he began to blame himself and weep. ﴿So now, associate with them (ba-shiruhunna)﴾: the origin of mubashara is the joining of skin to skin. Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning of mubashara here is intercourse. ﴿And seek what Allah has prescribed for you﴾. Concerning this there are four views. One: that it is offspring, related by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, and others. Some scholars said: since mubashara may occur for things less than intercourse, He permitted them the intercourse which from such a union produces offspring, so He said: ﴿seek what Allah has prescribed for you﴾, meaning offspring. The second: that what He prescribed for them is the concession (rukhsa), the view of Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. The third: that it is the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr), related by Abu al-Jawza' from Ibn 'Abbas. The fourth: that it is the Qur'an, so the meaning of the speech is: follow the Qur'an. Whatever is made lawful for you and you are commanded to do, that is what is sought. This is the choice of al-Zajjaj.

«His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you﴾. 'Adi ibn Hatim said: When this verse was revealed, I took two cords, one white and one black, and placed them under my pillow. I kept getting up during the night and could not distinguish the black from the white. When morning came, I went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and told him. He laughed and said: "If your pillow is then wide! That is only the whiteness of day from the blackness of night."» Sahl ibn Sa'd said: This verse was revealed: ﴿until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread﴾, and "from the dawn" had not yet been revealed. So when men wished to fast, one of them would tie a black thread and a white thread to his feet, and would continue eating and drinking until their difference became clear to him. Then Allah revealed afterwards "from the dawn," and they understood that what was meant was the night and the day.

Section

If one doubts whether dawn has come, should he abandon the pre-dawn meal (suhur) or not? The apparent meaning of Ahmad's words indicates that he should not abandon suhur, but should keep eating until he is certain that dawn has risen. Malik said: I dislike that he eat if he doubts the rising of dawn, and if he eats, then he must make up the fast. Al-Shafi'i said: there is nothing upon him.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not associate with them while you are devoting yourselves to worship in the mosques (ʿakifun)﴾. Concerning this mubashara there are two views. One: that it is intercourse, which is the view of most scholars. The second: that it is what is less than intercourse, such as touching and kissing, related by Ibn Zayd. Qatadah said: a man in retreat, when he left the mosque and met his wife, would have intercourse with her if he wished, so Allah admonished them concerning this.

Section

I'tikaf (retreat in the mosque for worship) linguistically means staying put. It is said: So-and-so is "mu'takif" upon such-and-such, or "'akif." It is a recommended act, but if a person makes a vow to do it, it becomes obligatory. It is not valid except in a mosque in which congregational prayers are held. For a woman, a mosque in which congregational prayer is held is not a condition, since congregational prayer is not obligatory for her. Is it valid without fasting? Concerning this there are two narrations from Ahmad.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: He means the mubashara. ﴿So do not approach them﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The limits (hudud) are what Allah has forbidden from violating, so it is not permissible to exceed them. The root of hadd in language is prevention, and from it comes "hadd al-dar" (the boundary of a house), which is that which prevents others from entering it. Al-hidad in language means the chamberlain and the gatekeeper, and everyone who prevents something is a "hidad." Al-A'sha said:

"We stood up, and our rooster had not yet crowed, toward a large jar beside its guardian."

(p-194) That is, beside its lord, who prevents it except by what he wishes. A woman "ahaddat" (mourned) over her husband and "haddat" when she gave up adornment and refrained from it. "Ahaddat al-nazar ila fulan" means you prevent your gaze from others. Iron was called "hadid" because enemies are prevented by it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus Allah makes clear﴾, meaning: like this clarification which He mentioned.

**The words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not consume one another's wealth unjustly﴾.**

**Occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul, the historical circumstances in which a verse was revealed):** "Imru al-Qays ibn Abis and Abdan al-Hadrami disputed over a piece of land. Abdan was the claimant and had no evidence. Imru al-Qays wanted to swear an oath, so the Prophet ﷺ recited to him: ﴿Indeed, those who sell the covenant of God and their oaths for a small price﴾ [Al 'Imran: 77]. He disliked swearing the oath and did not pursue the dispute over the land, so this verse was revealed." This is the view of a group of scholars, among them Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The meaning of the verse is: do not let some of you consume the wealth of others, as in His words: ﴿So kill yourselves﴾.

Qadi Abu Ya'la said: "Falsehood (al-batil) takes two forms. The first is to take someone's property without the owner's consent, such as theft, usurpation and embezzlement. The second is to take it with the owner's consent, such as gambling, singing for pay, and the price of wine." Al-Zajjaj said: "Al-batil means injustice (al-zulm)."

As for ﴿وَتُدْلُوا﴾ (*wa-tudlu*, "and send down"), its root in the language is from *adlaytu al-dalw*, meaning when you lower the bucket to fill it, and *dalawtuha*, meaning when you draw it up. The phrase *adla fulanun bihujjatihi* means he put forward his argument and presented it as sound. So the meaning of the sentence is: you act upon what the presenting of an argument requires, while you betray the trust, although you know that the proof is against you in reality.

Regarding the word *bihā* ("with it" / "by them"), there are two views. The first is that it refers to the wealth, as if He said: do not bribe the rulers' unjust judgments with part of it. The second is that it refers to the dispute (al-khusumah). If it is asked: why did He repeat the mention of eating, saying ﴿wa-la ta'kulu﴾ and then ﴿li-ta'kulu﴾? The answer is that He connected the first term with *bil-batil* ("unjustly") and the second with *bil-ithm* ("sinfully"), and repeated it to add to the meaning. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 189:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the new moons﴾.

This verse, from its beginning up to His saying ﴿and the Hajj﴾, was revealed on account of a occasion, which is that two men among the Companions said: "O Messenger of Allah! What is the matter with the crescent, that it appears thin, then increases and fills out until it becomes round and complete, and then keeps decreasing and thinning until it returns as it was?" So this was revealed: ﴿They ask you about the new moons. Say: They are timings for the people and for the Hajj﴾. This is the saying of Ibn Abbas.

And from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is not righteousness that you enter the houses from their backs﴾ to its end, it indicates another occasion, which is that when they performed Hajj and then came to Madinah, they would not enter from a door, but would come to the houses from their backs. A man forgot and entered from a door, so this was revealed: ﴿It is not righteousness that you enter the houses from their backs﴾. This is the saying of al-Bara' ibn Azib.

As for the reason why they would not enter the houses through their doors, there are four opinions. The first: they did this because of the state of ihram (ihram: the sacred state of pilgrimage), said by Ibn Abbas, Abu al-Aliyah, al-Nakha'i, Qatadah, and Qays al-Nahshali. The second: because of the entering of the sacred month, said by al-Bara' ibn Azib. The third: that the people of the Jahiliyyah, when one of them intended something and was prevented from it, would not enter his house through its door until he had accomplished what he had intended, said by al-Hasan. The fourth: that the people of Madinah, when they returned from their festival, did this, narrated by Uthman ibn Ata' from his father.

As for the interpretation: they asked him about the wisdom behind the increase and decrease of the new moons, so he informed them that they are measures for what people need in their fasting, their Hajj, and other matters. Al-Ahilla (ahilla: the new moons) is the plural of hilal (hilal: the crescent). How long does the hilal remain under this name? Regarding this, the Arabs have four opinions. The first: that it is called hilal for two nights of the month. The second: for three nights, after which it is called qamar (qamar: the moon). The third: until it becomes hajr (tahjir: when it moves in a thin line), which is the saying of al-Asma'i. The fourth: until its light overcomes the darkness of the night. Ibn al-Sarri related these opinions and preferred the first, saying: the derivation of hilal is from their saying "istahalla al-sabiyy" (the child cried out) when he is born, and "ahl al-qawm bil-hajj" (the people raised their voices) when they raised their voices with the talbiyah; so it was named hilal because, when it is seen, people raise their voices with its mention.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But righteousness is in one who fears Allah﴾ is similar to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But righteousness is in one who believes in Allah﴾, and its explanation has already passed. The readers differed concerning "al-buyut" (the houses) and similar words. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir and al-Kisa'i read with a kasra on the ba' of "al-biyut", the ayn of "al-'iyun" (the springs), and the ghayn of "al-ghiyub" (the unseen). It is related from Nafi' that he read with a damma on the ba' of "al-buyut", the ayn of "al-'uyun", the ghayn of "al-ghuyub", the jim of "al-judub" (the collars), and the shin of "al-shuyukh" (the elders). Qalun related from him that he read the ba' of "al-buyut" with a kasra. Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read all five letters with a damma, while Hamzah read all of them with a kasra, and there is difference of narration from Asim. Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads "al-buyut" with a damma does so according to the original plural form: bayt and buyut, like qalb and qulub, and fals and fulus. As for the one who reads with a kasra, he has kasra for the ya' that follows the ba'; and this is considered weak by the Basrans, because there is no fa'ul pattern with a kasra on the fa' in the language. I heard our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi say: when the plural is on the pattern fa'ul and its second letter is a ya', it is permissible to use both damma and kasra; one says buyut and biyut, shuyukh and shiyukh, and qiyud and qiyud.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 190:

(p-197) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you﴾.

The occasion of its revelation: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was prevented from the House, and slaughtered his sacrificial animal at al-Hudaybiyah, and the polytheists made a treaty with him that he would return in the coming year, he returned. When he prepared for the coming year, his companions feared that Quraysh would not keep their word to them in this matter, and that they would bar them and fight them, and his companions disliked fighting in the sacred month. So this verse was revealed." This was related by Ibn ʿAbbas.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But do not transgress﴾, that is: do not wrong. Concerning the meaning of this transgression there are four opinions. The first: that it is killing women and children; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid. The second: that its meaning is: do not fight those who have not fought you; this was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Abu al-ʿAliyah, and Ibn Zayd. The third: that it is committing what they were forbidden from; this was said by al-Hasan. The fourth: that it is their initiating the fighting within the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) in the sacred month; this was said by Muqatil.

Section

The scholars differed: is this verse abrogated (mansukhah) or not? There are two opinions.

One of them: it is abrogated (mansukhah). Those who held this view differed concerning what in it was abrogated, into two opinions.

One of them: that what was abrogated is its beginning, which is his saying: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you﴾. They said: this implies that fighting is permitted against those of the disbelievers who fight, and not permitted against those who do not fight; and this is abrogated by his saying: ﴿And kill them wherever you overtake them﴾. The second: that what was abrogated from it is ﴿but do not transgress﴾, and for those holding this view there are two opinions concerning this transgression. One: that it is killing those who do not fight. The second: that it is the polytheists initiating fighting; and this is abrogated by the verse of the sword.

The second opinion: that it is muhkamah (not abrogated), and its meaning according to those holding this view is: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you﴾, namely those who have prepared themselves for fighting. As for one who has not prepared himself for fighting, such as monks, aged elders, the chronically ill, the blind, and the insane, these do not fight; and this is a ruling that remains and is not abrogated.

Section

The scholars differed concerning the first verse revealed permitting fighting, into two opinions. One: it is his saying, exalted is He: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought, because they have been wronged﴾ [al-Hajj: 39]. This was said by Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, and al-Zuhri. The second: it is this verse: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾. This was said by Abu al-ʿAliyah and Ibn Zayd.

**Allah's saying: ﴿And kill them wherever you find them﴾.**

That is: find them. It is said: "thaqiftuhu athqafuhu" means "when you find him."

Qadi Abu Ya'la said: Allah's saying ﴿And kill them wherever you find them﴾ is general, covering all the polytheists, except those in Makkah. They were ordered to be expelled from it, except for those who fight them, and they were ordered to be fought. This is shown by His saying in the same passage: ﴿And do not fight them at al-Masjid al-Haram until they fight you there﴾. The polytheists had harmed the Muslims in Makkah until they forced them out, so it is as though they had expelled them. As for "fitnah" (trial, persecution, or disbelief), there are two views. The first is that it means shirk (polytheism), as said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Qatadah, and others. The second is that it means a believer's apostasy to the worship of idols, as said by Mujahid. On the first view, the meaning is: the polytheism of these people is greater (p-199) than your killing them in the sacred precinct. On the second view, the apostasy of a believer to idols is more severe for him than killing someone wrongfully.

**Allah's saying: ﴿And do not fight them﴾.** Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and 'Asim read: ﴿And do not fight them at al-Masjid al-Haram until they fight you there. But if they fight you, then kill them﴾ (using the verb "qatala" with the alif, "yuqatilukum" and "qatilu-hum"). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read: "wa la taqtulu-hum hatta yaqtulukum, fa in qataluku-m," with the alif omitted in these words, "taqtulu" and "yaqtulukum" (without the alif in "qatala"-forms). All agree on His saying ﴿kill them﴾. Those who read with the alif argued from His saying: ﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah﴾. Those who omitted the alif argued from His saying: "kill them."

**Section**

The scholars differed concerning His saying:

﴿And do not fight them at al-Masjid al-Haram until they fight you there﴾

Is it abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later one) or not? Mujahid, with a group of jurists, held that it is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated), and that one fights there only if one is fought. This is shown by the authentic hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he delivered a sermon on the day of the Conquest of Makkah, saying: "O people! Allah made Makkah sacred on the day He created the heavens and the earth. It was not lawful for anyone before me, nor will it be lawful for anyone after me. It was made lawful for me only for an hour of the day, and then it returned to being sacred until the Day of Resurrection." So the Prophet (ﷺ) made clear that in that hour he was specially permitted, by way of takhsis (specification), not by way of naskh. Thus the sanctity of fighting in the Haram is established, except when they fight, in which case they are repelled. This ruling is continuous and not abrogated.

Qatadah held that it is abrogated by His saying: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [at-Tawbah: 5]. This orders fighting them in the non-sacred area and in the sacred area and in every circumstance. Ar-Rabi' ibn Anas and Ibn Zayd held that it is abrogated by His saying: ﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah﴾. Muqatil claimed that it is abrogated by His saying: ﴿And kill them wherever you find them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191]. The first view is the most sound.

**Allah's saying: ﴿But if they fight you, then kill them﴾.** Muqatil said: that is, "then fight them."

"Allah's words: ﴿And if they cease﴾

There are three opinions on this. The first: its meaning is, "If they cease from their polytheism and from fighting you." The second: from their disbelief. The third: from fighting you, but not from their disbelief. According to the first two opinions, the verse is muhkam (firm, not abrogated), and the meaning of ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is: He forgives their polytheism and their transgression. According to the last opinion, there are two views on the meaning of His words ﴿Forgiving and Merciful﴾. The first: He forgives you, since He has lifted from you the obligation of fighting them. The second: its meaning is that He commands you to forgive and show mercy to them. According to this view, the verse is mansukh (abrogated) by the verse of the sword."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 193:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah﴾.

Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, and others said: the fitnah here is shirk (associating partners with God).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And religion is for God﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: that is, [the religion becomes] sincerely devoted to Him in tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness). Al-ʿUdwan (transgression) means injustice (zulm), but it is meant here as recompense. The recompense is called "transgression" by way of responding to something with its like, as in His saying: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same way﴾. The wrongdoers (al-zalimun) here are the polytheists (al-mushrikun), as stated by ʿIkrimah, Qatadah, and others.

(p-201) Section

It has been related from a group of the exegetes, among them Qatadah, that His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But if they cease, then there is no hostility except against the wrongdoers﴾ is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword. This holds only if we say that the meaning of the speech is: "If they cease fighting you while remaining upon their religion." But if we say that its meaning is: "If they cease from their religion," then the verse is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 194:

His saying, Most High: ﴿The sacred month is for the sacred month, and for sacred things there is retribution﴾.

This verse was revealed on account of a specific occasion (sabab), and the scholars differed concerning it on two views (qawlan).

The first: "The Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions set out as pilgrims (mu'tamirin) in Dhu al-Qa'dah, with the sacrificial animals (al-hady) with them, and the polytheists (al-mushrikun) blocked them. The Prophet of Allah made a treaty with them that he would turn back from them and return the following year, so that he could stay in Makkah for three nights, and not enter it with weapons, and not take out anyone from the people of Makkah. When the following year came, he and his companions set out and entered it. The polytheists boasted over him, since they had turned him back at Hudaybiyyah, so Allah requited them (fa-aqassahu Allah minhum) and brought him into Makkah in the month in which they had turned him back. Then He said: ﴿The sacred month is for the sacred month, and for sacred things there is retribution﴾." Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ata', Abu al-'Aliyah, Qatadah, and others held this meaning.

The second: "The polytheists of the Arabs said to the Prophet, peace be upon him: Have you forbidden us to fight in the sacred month? He said: 'Yes.' They intended to take advantage of the sacred month and fight him in it, so this verse was revealed," meaning: if they make lawful (istahallu) anything of yours in the sacred month, then make lawful from them the like of it. This is the saying of al-Hasan, and Ibrahim ibn al-Sarri and al-Zajjaj chose it.

As for the proponents of the first view, they say the meaning of the verse is: the sacred month in which you entered the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) is [matched] with the sacred month in which they blocked you, the previous year. ﴿And for sacred things there is retribution﴾: I have exacted retribution for you from them in Dhu al-Qa'dah, just as they blocked you in Dhu al-Qa'dah.

Al-Zajjaj said: "The sacred month" means the fighting of the sacred month with the sacred month. Allah, Most High, informed that the matter of these sacred things is not permissible for the Muslims except as retribution. Then this was abrogated (nasakha) by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf). It was also said: He used the plural "sacred things" (al-hurumat) because He intended the sacred month together with the sacred city and the sanctity of the state of ihram (hurmat al-ihram).

His saying, Most High: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: whoever fights you in the Sacred Precinct, then fight him. The response to transgression is called transgression (i'tida') only because the form of the two acts is one, even though one of them is obedience and the other disobedience. Al-Zajjaj said: The Arabs say: "So-and-so wronged me, so I wronged him," meaning: I requited him for his wrong. "So-and-so acted ignorantly toward me, so I acted ignorantly toward him." The explanation of this meaning has already preceded at the beginning of the surah.

His saying, Most High: ﴿And fear Allah﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "And fear Allah," and do not begin them with fighting in the Sacred Precinct.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verses 195–196:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And spend in the way of Allah﴾

This verse was revealed on account of a specific occasion, and concerning it there are two reports.

(p. 203) The first: "When the Prophet ﷺ ordered preparation for Makkah, some of the Bedouins said: 'O Messenger of Allah! With what should we prepare? By Allah, we have neither provisions nor wealth!' So this was revealed." This was narrated by Ibn Abbas.

The second: The Ansar used to spend and give charity, but then a year of drought struck them, so they withheld. So this was revealed. This was narrated by Abu Jubayra ibn al-Dahhak.

The word *sabil* (way, path) linguistically means "the road." This term was used for jihad because it is the path on which one fights to uphold the religion. *Al-tahlukah* (destruction) means ruin. Our shaykh, Ali ibn Ubayd Allah, said: His saying, ﴿And do not shave your heads until the sacrificial animal reaches its place of sacrifice﴾ required the prohibition of shaving the hair, whether one had an injury or not, until the revelation of: ﴿So whoever among you is ill or has an injury of the head, then a ransom﴾. This therefore indicates the permissibility of shaving the hair when there is injury, together with a ransom, and so it became an abrogation (*naskh*) of its earlier prohibition.

The meaning of the verse is: "So whoever among you (that is, among those in the state of ihram, whether confined or not confined) is ill and needs to wear clothing or something else forbidden by ihram, and does it, or has an injury of the head and shaves, then a ransom of fasting." (p. 206) Regarding the fasting there are two sayings:
First: It is three days. This was narrated in the hadith of Ka'b ibn Ujrah, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ, and this is the view of the majority.
Second: It is fasting ten days. This was narrated from al-Hasan, Ikrimah, and Nafi'.

Regarding the charity there are two sayings:
First: It is feeding six needy persons. This was narrated in the hadith of Ka'b, and it is the view of those who said the fast is three days.
Second: It is feeding ten needy persons. This is the view of those who made the fast of ten days obligatory.

The *nusuk* (sacrificial act) is the slaughter of a sheep. It is said: "I performed *nasak* for Allah," meaning: "I slaughtered for Him." Regarding *nusuk* there are two dialects: with a damma on the nun and the sin, and this is how the majority read it; and with a damma on the nun with the sin sukun, which is the reading of al-Hasan.

The discussion of what is feasible of the sacrificial animal has already passed. ﴿But whoever does not find [an animal], then fasting three days during Hajj﴾. Al-Hasan said: They are the day before the Tarwiyah (the eighth of Dhu al-Hijjah), and [the day of] the Tarwiyah, and [the day of] Arafah. This is the view of Ata', al-Sha'bi, Abu al-Aliyah, Ibn Jubayr, Tawus, and Ibrahim, and it has been transmitted from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him. It has also been narrated from al-Hasan and Ata' that they both said: "On whichever days of the ten he wishes, he may fast them." It was transmitted from Tawus, Mujahid, and Ata' that they said: "In whichever months of Hajj he wishes, let him fast them." It was transmitted from Ibn Umar that he said: "From the time he enters the state of ihram until the day of Arafah." (p. 207)

If he does not find the sacrificial animal and does not fast the three days before the day of sacrifice (*yawm al-nahr*), what does he do? Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Tawus, and Ibrahim said: He is only obligated to the animal and does not fast. Ibn Umar and Aisha said: He fasts the days of Mina. **Section**

If he finds the sacrificial animal after having begun the three-day fast, he is not obligated to break it. This is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifah said: He must break it, and upon him is the animal. Ata' said: If he fasted two days and then became well-off, then upon him is the animal. If he fasted three days and then became well-off, then let him fast the seven, and there is no animal upon him.

Regarding the meaning of His saying, ﴿during Hajj﴾, there are two sayings: The first: its meaning is "during the months of Hajj." The second: "during the time of entering the state of ihram for Hajj."

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and seven when you return﴾, there are two sayings:
The first: "when you return to your cities." This was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Abu al-Aliyah, al-Sha'bi, and Qatadah.
The second: "when you return from your Hajj." This is the view of Ata', Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Hanifah, and Malik.

Al-Athram said: I said to Abu Ubayd Allah, meaning Ahmad ibn Hanbal: "The fasting of the seven days when he returns, when does he fast them? On the road, or in his household?" He said: "All of that has been interpreted by the people." It was said to Abu Abd Allah: "So he separated between them, and permitted that."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is ten complete﴾. Concerning it there are five sayings.

First: Its meaning is: complete in standing in place of the sacrificial animal. This was the view of Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan. Qadi Abu Ya'la said: It could have been that one would suppose that the three days stand in place of the animal in the matter of completing the reward, so Allah, exalted is He, informed us that the ten in their entirety are what stand in its place.

Second: The conjunction *waw* (and) may stand in place of *aw* (or) in some contexts, among them His saying: ﴿So marry what seems good to you of women, two and three and four﴾. So Allah, mighty and majestic, removed the possibility of choice in this verse by His saying: ﴿That is ten complete﴾. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

Third: That this is for emphasis, and they recited for al-Farazdaq:

"Three and two, so they are five, and a sixth that leans toward my flank."

And another said:

"Would that you had asked the hosts of Kindah, on the day they turned back, where is which of us?"

And another said:

"How many a blessing was his, how many, how many."

The Qur'an was revealed in the language of the Arabs, and they repeat a thing for its emphasis.

Fourth: Its meaning is: "That is ten complete in the distinction (*fasl*), even though the three are during Hajj and the seven are after it, so that it does not come to anyone's mind that the seven are less than the three." This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Fifth: It is a statement in the form of a report, but its meaning is an imperative. Its implied meaning is: "That is ten, so complete them."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is for whoever's family is not present at the Sacred Mosque﴾. Regarding what is referred to by "this," there are two sayings: The first: it is the enjoyment (*tamattu'*) by Umrah until Hajj. The second: it is the recompense by the sacrifice and the fasting. The *lam* in "for whoever" in this view carries the meaning of "upon." As for "those present at the Sacred Mosque": Ibn Abbas, Tawus, and Mujahid said: They are the people of the Sacred Precinct (*al-haram*). Ata' said: They are whoever's dwelling is within the *mawaqit* (the stations of ihram). Ibn al-Anbari said: The meaning of the verse is that this obligation is for those who are from outside, and He only mentioned "his family" (*ahluh*), which is what is meant by "presence," because the usual thing for a man is that he resides where his family resides.
