The first: that it is what exceeds the need of a person and his dependents; related by Miqsam from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: what their souls are content to give, of little or much; related by 'Atiyyah from Ibn 'Abbas. The third: that it is the moderate course between extravagance and stinginess; said by al-Hasan, 'Ata', and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The fourth: that it is the obligatory charity; said by Mujahid. The fifth: that it is what its amount is not clearly defined for them, from their saying "'afa al-athar" when it becomes faint and effaced; our shaykh related this from a group of exegetes.

* Section

The scholars of abrogation (naskh) and abrogated (mansukh) have discussed this verse. al-Suddi related from his shaykhs that it was abrogated by zakat, while others refused to say it was abrogated. The decisive resolution of this is: whenever we say that by this verse the giving of surplus wealth in charity was obligated upon them, or that this verse obligated a charity before zakat, then the verse is abrogated by the verse of zakat. And whenever we say that it is applied to the obligatory zakat, as Mujahid said, or to the recommended charity, then it is muhkam (not abrogated).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus Allah makes clear.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: He said "thus" while addressing a group, because the group's meaning is the tribe, as if He said, "Thus, O tribe." It is also permissible that the kaf refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), as if He said, "Thus, O Prophet," because the address to him includes the address to his community. Ibn al-Anbari said: The kaf in "kadhalika" is a reference to what has been explained about spending, as if He said, "Like that which He has explained to you concerning spending, Allah makes the verses clear." It is also permissible that "kadhalika" does not refer to what precedes it, so its meaning is "thus," said by Ibn 'Abbas. ﴿So that you may reflect﴾ ﴿upon this world and the Hereafter﴾, so that you may know the superiority of the one over the other, and so you may work for what remains of the two.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 220:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They ask you about orphans﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are two accounts. The first: when Allah, may He be exalted, revealed ﴿And do not approach the property of an orphan except in the best manner﴾ [al-Isra' 34] and ﴿Indeed, those who consume the properties of orphans unjustly﴾ [al-Nisa' 9], those who had an orphan's property set out, separating the orphan's food from their own food and his drink from their drink. They would set aside some of the food, keeping it for him until he ate it or it spoiled. This weighed heavily on them, so they mentioned it to the Prophet (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, and Muqatil. The second: "The Arabs used to be very harsh regarding the matter of the orphan, to the point that they would not eat with him from his dish, nor would they employ a servant for him. So they asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about mixing with them, and this verse was revealed." This was related by al-Suddi from his shaykhs, and it is the saying of al-Dahhak.

Concerning those who asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about this, there are two accounts. The first: the one who asked him was Thabit ibn Rifa'ah al-Ansari; this was said by Muqatil. The second: 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah; this was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Setting things right for them is best﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: its meaning is: increasing their wealth, and abstaining from consuming it is better for whoever is in charge of it. ﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾, that is: they are your brothers, and the ruling concerning your brothers applies to them. Ibn 'Abbas said: mixing means that you drink from their milk and they drink from yours, and you eat from their dish and they eat from yours. ﴿And Allah knows the corrupter from the one who sets things right﴾, meaning: the one who deliberately consumes an orphan's property, from the one who is scrupulous and strives only for setting things right. ﴿And had Allah willed, He would have put you in difficulty﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, He would have made you fall into hardship and constrained you. Ibn al-Anbari said: the root of 'anat is hardship. The Arabs say: "So-and-so 'tanattata' so-and-so and 'u'annitu-hu," meaning: he presses hard upon him and obliges him to do what is difficult for him to perform. [He said: then it was transferred to the meaning of ruin.] The derivation of the word is from the Arabs' saying: "akamah 'anut," when it is hard and difficult to ascend (al-masʻad); so this term came to be used for every hardship.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 221:**

The first report: "A man called Mirthad ibn Abi Mirthad was sent by the Prophet (ﷺ) to Makkah to bring out some Muslims there who were prisoners. When he arrived there, a woman called Inaq heard of him. She had been his lover in the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam). When he became Muslim, he turned away from her. She came to him and said: 'Woe to you, O Mirthad! Will you not be alone with me?' He said: 'Islam has come between me and you. But if you wish, I will marry you, once I return to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and ask his permission for that.' She said to him: 'Do you find me a burden?!' and she called for help against him. They beat him severely, then they let him go. When he had finished his business in Makkah, he returned to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him: 'Is it permissible for me to marry her?' Then this verse was revealed." This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas. Muqatil ibn Sulayman mentioned that the man was Abu Mirthad al-Ghanawi.

The second report: "Abdullah ibn Rawahah had a black slave-woman. He became angry with her and slapped her. Then he regretted it and came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and told him about the matter. [The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'What is she, O Abdullah?'] He said: '(p-246) O Messenger of Allah, she fasts, prays, performs the ablution well, and bears witness that there is no god but Allah and that you are the Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'O Abdullah, she is a believer.' He said: 'By Him who sent you with the truth, I will certainly free her and marry her.' So he did that. Some Muslims criticized him and said: 'He married a slave-woman!' They used to prefer marrying polytheist women for the sake of their lineage. So this verse was revealed." This was narrated by al-Suddi from his shaykhs.

Some exegetes (mufassirun) have mentioned that the story of Inaq and Abu Mirthad was the reason for the revelation of the words of the Most High: ﴿And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe﴾, and that the story of Ibn Rawahah was the reason for the revelation of His words: ﴿And a believing slave-woman is better than a polytheist woman﴾.

As for the tafsir (explanation), al-Mufaddal said: The original meaning of nikah (marriage) is intercourse, and then this usage became widespread until the contract itself was called nikah. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has forbidden marriage to polytheist women, both as a contract and as intercourse.

Regarding "polytheistic women" here there are two opinions. The first is that it includes the women of the People of the Book and others, and this is the view of most scholars. The second is that it is specific to idolatresses, and this is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Nakha'i, and Qatadah.

Regarding the meaning of "slave-woman" there are two opinions. The first is that it means a female slave, and this is the view of most scholars, so the meaning would be: marrying a believing slave-woman is better than marrying a free polytheist woman. The second is that it means a woman, even if she is not a slave, as one says: "This is the maidservant of Allah." This is the view of al-Dahhak. The first opinion is more sound.

Regarding His words: ﴿Even if she pleases you﴾ there are two opinions. The first: by her beauty and attractiveness. The second: by her lineage and descent.

**Section**

The scholars of naskh (abrogation) differed concerning this verse. Those who said that "polytheistic women" refers to idolatresses held that the verse is muhkam (clear, not abrogated). Some who supported this view claimed that the Jews and Christians are not polytheists with respect to Allah, even if they deny the prophethood of our Prophet. Our shaykh said: This is a corrupt view for two reasons. First, the true reality of shirk (associating partners with Allah) is established regarding them, since they said: "Uzayr is the son of Allah," and "the Messiah is the son of Allah." Second, their disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ) necessitates that they say what he brought is not from Allah, and attributing that to someone other than Allah is shirk (p-247).

As for those who said that the verse is general over all polytheist women, they have two opinions. The first is that part of its ruling was abrogated by His words: ﴿And chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:6], and the ruling remained clear regarding non-People of the Book. The second is that it is neither abrogated nor abrogating, but rather it is general over all polytheist women, and what is excluded from its generality, namely the permission to marry a disbelieving woman, is excluded by a specific proof, which is His words: ﴿And chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:6]. This verse specified the generality of the former verse without abrogation, and this is the view of the majority of jurists (fuqaha'). Its meaning has been transmitted from a group of the Companions, among them Uthman, Talhah, Hudhayfah, Jabir, and Ibn 'Abbas.

His words: ﴿And do not marry polytheistic men﴾ mean: do not marry your women to them until they believe. The discussion of His words ﴿And a believing slave is better﴾ and of His words ﴿Even if he pleases you﴾ is similar to the discussion at the beginning of the verse.

His words: ﴿And Allah calls to Paradise and forgiveness by His permission﴾. The majority read "al-maghfirah" (forgiveness) in the genitive case, but al-Hasan and al-Qazzaz, from Abu 'Amr, read it in the nominative case.

He said, Exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about menstruation.﴾ Thabit narrated from Anas, who said: "When a woman among the Jews menstruated, they would not eat with her, drink with her, or cohabit with her in the houses. The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about that, and this verse was revealed. The Prophet (ﷺ) then commanded them to eat with them, drink with them, and be with them in the houses, and to do everything except intercourse."

Ibn Abbas said: "A man called Ibn al-Dahdah, from the Ansar, came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'How should we deal with women when they menstruate?' So this verse was revealed."

Regarding al-mahid (menstruation, ḥayḍ), there are two views. The first is that it is a noun for menstruation (ḥayḍ). Al-Zajjaj said: "It is said: the woman menstruated (ḥāḍat), tahīdu ḥayḍan, maḥāḍan, and maḥīḍan." Ibn Qutaybah said: "al-Maḥīḍ is al-ḥayḍ." The second is that it is a noun for the place of menstruation, like al-maqīl (the place of qaylūlah, the midday rest) and al-mabīt (the place of spending the night). Qadi Abu Ya'la mentioned that this is the apparent meaning of Ahmad's words. As for the proponents of the first view, they reinforced it by saying that the wording itself supports their position, since He described it as "an injury" (adhan), and that is a description of the menstrual blood, not of the place. As for the proponents of the second view, they said: "It is not impossible that al-maḥīḍ is a description of the place, and then it was described by what is near it and adjacent to it, as with al-'aqīqah, which is a name for a child's hair, and the sheep slaughtered at the shaving of the child's head was also called by it, figuratively. Likewise al-rāwiyah is a name for a camel, and a water-skin was called rāwiyah figuratively." The injury (adhan) befalls the one who has intercourse through the impurity and the stench of the smell. It was also said: intercourse with a menstruating woman causes a severe ailment with pain.

﴿So keep away from women during menstruation.﴾ What is meant is abstaining from intercourse in the vagina, because al-maḥīḍ is either the blood itself or the vagina itself.

﴿And do not approach them﴾, meaning do not approach their intercourse. This is an emphasis on His words: ﴿keep away from women﴾.

He said, Exalted is He: ﴿until they are purified﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs from 'Asim recited it as (ḥattā yaṭhurna) with a light pronunciation. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim recited it as (yaṭṭahharna), with the ṭā' and hā' doubled and vowelled with fatḥah. Ibn Qutaybah said: yaṭhurna means the blood stops from them. It is said: "The woman became pure (ṭahurat) and became pure (ṭahurat)," when she sees purity, even if she does not wash with water. Whoever recited (yaṭṭahharna) with doubling intends: they perform ghusl with water. The original is yataṭahharna, and the tā' was assimilated into the ṭā'. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid said: "until they are pure from the blood. Then, when they become pure, they perform ghusl with water."

He said, Exalted is He: ﴿then go to them﴾, a permission after a prohibition, not an obligation.

He said, Exalted is He: ﴿from where Allah has commanded you﴾. In this there are four views.

The first: its meaning is: from before purity, not from before menstruation. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Abu Razin, Qatadah, al-Suddi, and others.

The second: its meaning is: go to them from where Allah has commanded you not to approach them, which is the place of menstruation. This was said by Mujahid. Those who supported this view said: He only said "Allah has commanded you," while the meaning is "He has forbidden you," because a prohibition is a command to leave what is forbidden, and "min" here has the meaning of "fi" (in), like His words: ﴿when it is called for prayer on the day of Friday﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 9].

The third: go to them from before lawful marriage, not from before immorality. This was said by Ibn al-Hanafiyyah.

The fourth: its meaning is: go to them from the directions in which it is lawful to approach a woman, and do not approach them from where it is not appropriate, such as when they are fasting, observing i'tikaf, or in ihram. This is the view of al-Zajjaj and Ibn Kaysan.

Regarding His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who are constantly repentant﴾, there are two views. The first: those who repent (al-tawwabin) from sins. This was said by 'Ata' and Mujahid, among others. The second: those who repent from coming to menstruating women. This was mentioned by some of the exegetes.

Regarding His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and loves those who purify themselves﴾, there are three views. The first: those who purify themselves from sins. This was said by Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Abu al-'Aliyah. The second: those who purify themselves with water. This was said by 'Ata'. The third: those who abstain from anal intercourse with women. This was narrated from Mujahid.

* Section

The minimum period of menstruation is one day and one night according to one of the two narrations from Ahmad. The second narration says: one day. Abu Hanifah said: its minimum is three days. Malik and Dawud said: there is no minimum limit for it. As for its maximum, there are two narrations from Ahmad. One of them is fifteen days, which is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i. The second is seventeen days. Abu Hanifah said: its maximum is ten days.

Menstruation prevents ten things: performing prayer, the obligation of prayer, performing fasting (but not its obligation), sitting in the mosque, i'tikaf (seclusion in the mosque), tawaf (circumambulation), reciting the Qur'an, carrying the mushaf, sexual enjoyment in the vagina, and the occurrence of the intention to divorce.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 223:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you﴾ — concerning the occasion of its revelation there are three opinions.

The first: The Jews denied the permissibility of approaching a woman except from in front of her, and they found fault with whoever approached her in other than that manner, so this verse was revealed. It is narrated from Jabir, al-Hasan, and Qatadah.

The second: "A tribe from Quraysh used to marry women in Makkah and enjoy them facing forward and from behind. When they came to Madinah and married from among the Ansar, they went to do the same, but the women refused it. The matter reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed." It was related by Mujahid from Ibn Abbas.

The third: "Umar ibn al-Khattab came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'I am ruined! I turned my saddle last night.' Then this verse was revealed." It was related by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn Abbas.

Al-harth (tilth) means cultivated land. Here it is used as a metaphor for intercourse, so He called them a tilth because they are the field of children, just as land is for crops. If it is said: "Nisa'" (women) is plural, so why did He not say: "harut" (a plural form of harth)? There are three answers to this, mentioned by Ibn al-Qasim al-Anbari the grammarian:

The first: that al-harth is a verbal noun (masdar) in the place of the plural, so it takes the singular form, just as the Arabs say: "ikhwatuka sawm" (your brothers are fasting) and "awladuka fitr" (your children are breaking the fast), meaning: fasting and breaking the fast, so the verbal noun by its singular form conveys the sense of the plural.

The second: that He intended "haruth lakum" (tillages for you), and He suffices with the singular of the plural, as the poet said:

"Eat in half of your bellies, you will live"

meaning: in the halves of your bellies.

The third: that He used the singular "harth" only because the women are likened to it, and they are not of its kind; the meaning is: your women are like tillages for you.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Come to them however you wish﴾ — concerning this there are three opinions.

The first: that it means "how you wish," and then there are two views. One is that the meaning is: how you wish, facing forward or from behind, in any state, so long as the approach is in the vagina. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Atiyyah, al-Suddi, and Ibn Qutaybah, among others. The second is that the verse was revealed concerning coitus interruptus (al-'azl). This was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, so the meaning would be: if you wish, withdraw, and if you wish, do not withdraw.

The second opinion: that it means "if you wish" and "whenever you wish." This is the view of Ibn al-Hanafiyyah and al-Dahhak, and it is also related from Ibn Abbas.

The third: that it means "where you wish." This is reported from Ibn Umar and Malik ibn Anas, and it is corrupt for several reasons. The first: when Salim ibn Abdullah learned that Nafi' had related this from Ibn Umar, he said: "The slave lied. Abdullah only said: 'They approach their wives in their posteriors.'" As for the companions of Malik, they deny its authenticity from Malik. The second: Abu Hurayrah related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Cursed is whoever approaches women in their posteriors," which indicates that the verse does not mean this. The third: the verse alerted to the place of the child by His saying: ﴿so come to your tilth﴾, and the place of sowing is the place of the child. Ibn al-Anbari said: Since Allah explicitly mentioned the tilth, and by the tilth plants grow, and the child is likened to a plant, it is not permissible for intercourse to occur in a place from which there is no child.

The fourth: that the prohibition of approaching a menstruating woman was for the reason of harm, and harm is inherent in this place and does not leave it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And send forward for yourselves﴾ — concerning this there are four opinions.

The first: that its meaning is: send forward for yourselves righteous deeds. It was related by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

The second: send forward the mention of Allah's name at intercourse. It was related by Ata' from Ibn Abbas.

The third: send forward for yourselves in seeking a child. This was said by Muqatil.

The fourth: send forward obedience to Allah and following His command. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 224:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle for your oaths﴾. There are four reports concerning the occasion of its revelation.

The first: it was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Rawahah, who had a dispute with his brother-in-law (khitn). Abdullah swore that he would not enter upon him nor speak to him, and he began saying: "I have sworn by Allah, so it is not lawful for me [to break it], unless you fulfil my oath (tabarr yamini)." Then this verse was revealed. This was reported by Ibn Abbas.

The second: a man used to swear by Allah that he would not uphold his kinship ties, nor reconcile between people. So this verse was revealed. This was reported by al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

The third: it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr when he swore that he would not spend on Mistah. This was reported by Ibn Juraij.

The fourth: it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, who swore that he would not support his son Abd al-Rahman until he embraced Islam. This was reported by the two named Muqatil, Ibn Hayyan and Ibn Sulayman.

Al-Farra' said: the meaning is, "And do not make Allah an obstacle (mu'taridan) for your oaths." Abu Ubayd said: "a target (nasban) for your oaths," as if he meant: you set Him up as an obstacle in every matter, so you swear by Him.

Concerning the meaning of the verse there are three opinions.

The first: its meaning is, "Do not swear by Allah that you will not act righteously, nor be God-fearing, nor reconcile between people." This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ata, Ibn Jubayr, Ibrahim, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, al-Suddi, Muqatil, al-Farra', Ibn Qutaybah, al-Zajjaj, and others.

The second: its meaning is, "Do not swear by Allah falsely in order to protect the creatures, act kindly toward them, and reconcile between them through falsehood." This meaning was related by Atiyyah from Ibn Abbas.

The third: its meaning is, "Do not swear by Allah excessively, even if you are righteous and reconciling, for excessive swearing by Allah is a form of audacity toward Him." This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 225:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for what is unintentional in your oaths﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: In the speech of the Arabs, al-laghw (idle, unintended utterance) is that which is discarded and upon which no matter is bound, and whatever is not taken into account is called laghw. Ibn Faris said: The derivation of this is from the saying of people about the young camels that are not counted in the blood-money and other matters, that they are laghw. It is said of them: laghā yalghū. And you say: laghiya bi-l-amr, when he became attached to it (lahija bihi). It was also said: the derivation of the word lughah (language) is from this, [meaning that its speaker is attached to it]. Regarding the meaning of laghw here, there are five opinions.

The first: that one swears to something he thinks is as he swore, then it becomes clear to him that it is other than that. This is the view of Abu Hurayrah, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Ata, al-Sha'bi, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi (from his shaykhs), Malik, and Muqatil.

The second: that it is saying "No, by Allah" and "Yes, by Allah" without intending to bind oneself by an oath. This is the view of Aishah, Tawus, Urwah, al-Nakha'i, and al-Shafi'i. The proponents of this view cite the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿But He holds you accountable for what your hearts have earned﴾, and the earning of the heart is its binding and intention. These two opinions are transmitted from Imam Ahmad. His son Abd Allah narrated from him that he said: "Laghw, in my view, is that one swears an oath while thinking it is so, and there is no expiation. And a man swears but does not bind his heart to anything, so there is no expiation."

The third: that it is the oath of a man while he is angry, narrated by Tawus from Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: that it is a man's oath to commit a sin, so let him break it, make expiation, and there is no sin upon him. This was said by Said ibn Jubayr.

The fifth: that a man swears to something and then forgets it. This was said by al-Nakha'i.

The saying of Aishah is the most correct of all. Hanbal said: Ahmad was asked about laghw, and he said: "A man swears, saying, 'No, by Allah,' and 'Yes, by Allah,' not intending to bind the oath. But when he binds himself by an oath, expiation becomes obligatory for him."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But He holds you accountable for what your hearts have earned. And Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing﴾. Mujahid said: That is, what your hearts have bound themselves to. "Al-Halim" is the one of forgiveness who is not provoked by anger so as to hasten, nor is he made light by the ignorance of the ignorant while being able to punish. Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi said: Whoever overlooks while unable to retaliate does not deserve the name al-Halim; rather, al-Halim is the forgiving one while able, the deliberate one who does not hasten to punishment. Some poets have excelled in verses on this meaning, saying:

Peoples do not attain glory, even if they are noble, until they abase themselves, even if they are mighty, to other peoples.

And they insult them, and you see the faces flushed, not the forgiveness of abasement but the forgiveness of forbearance.

He said: It is said: halama al-rajul yahlumu hulman, with the lam pronounced with a damma in the past and the future. And halama fi al-nawm, with the lam pronounced with a fatha, yahlumu hulman, with the lam in the future and the ha in the verbal noun both pronounced with a damma.

Section

Oaths are of two kinds: those concerning the past and those concerning the future. The oath concerning the past is of two kinds: a forbidden oath, which is the false oath, namely that one says, "By Allah, I did not do it," when he did, or, "I did do it," when he did not. And a permissible oath, which is that he is truthful in his saying, "I did not do it," or, "I did do it." The oath concerning the future has five divisions. The first: an oath whose binding is an act of obedience, whose persistence in it is obedience, and whose undoing is disobedience, such as swearing, "I will surely pray the five prayers, and I will surely fast Ramadan," or "I will drink wine." The second: its binding is disobedience, its persistence in it is disobedience, and its undoing is obedience; it is the reverse of the first. The third: an oath whose binding is obedience, whose persistence in it is obedience, and whose undoing is disliked, such as swearing, "I will surely perform the voluntary acts of worship." The fourth: an oath whose binding is disliked, whose persistence in it is disliked, and whose undoing is obedience; it is the reverse of the one before it. The fifth: an oath whose binding is permissible, whose persistence in it is permissible, and whose undoing is permissible, such as swearing, "I will not enter a town in which there is someone who wrongs people, nor travel a frightening road," and the like.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 226:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For those who swear off their wives﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: In the Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance), when a man asked his wife for something and she refused to give it to him, he would swear that he would not approach her for a year, or two years, or three, and so he would leave her neither a widow nor a married woman. When Islam came, Allah made that period four months, and Allah revealed this verse.

Sa῾id ibn al-Musayyab said: The ila᾽ (oath of abstention from wives) was a harm inflicted by the people of the Jahiliyyah. A man did not desire a woman, nor did he want anyone else to marry her, so he would swear that he would never approach her. Allah, Exalted is He, made the term by which one knows what a man truly feels toward a woman four months, and revealed this verse.

Ibn Qutaybah said: Yu᾽lun (﴿yu'lūna﴾) means yahlifun (they swear). It is said: "ʾalaytu min imra᾽ati, ʾūlī ʾīlāʾan," when a man swears that he will not have intercourse with his wife. The noun is al-ʾalyah (the oath).

Al-Zajjaj said: From ila᾽ one says: ʾalaytu, ʾūlī, ʾīlāʾan, wa-ʾalīyatan, wa-ʾulwatan, wa-ʾalwatan, wa-ʾilwatan. The form with kasrah (ʾilwah) is the least common of the dialects. Kathir said:

"It was said: the swearers—one who keeps his oath is guarded, and if the oath escapes him, he is still righteous."

Ibn al-Anbari related from some of the lexicographers that he said: "min" (﴿min﴾) is in the sense of "fi" (in) or "ʿala" (upon), and the implied meaning is: they swear regarding the intercourse with their wives. So the word for intercourse was omitted and "the women" was put in its place, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿what You promised us upon Your messengers﴾ (Al ʿImran: 194), meaning: upon the tongues of Your messengers. It was also said that there is an omission in the speech, its estimate being: they swear, they withdraw from their wives. Al-tarabbus means waiting. A man is not a muʾli (one who has made an ila᾽) unless he swears by Allah that he will not have intercourse with his wife for more than four months. If he swears for four months or less, he is not a muʾli. This is the view of Malik, Ahmad, and al-Shafiʿi. Fa᾽u (﴿fāʾū﴾) means they returned, and its meaning is: they returned to intercourse, as said by ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jubayr, Masruq, and al-Shaʿbi. If the muʾli has an excuse which prevents him from being able to have intercourse, then he says: "Whenever you are able, you will have intercourse with her," and this is the sense of his saying fayʾah (return). If he is able and does not do it, he is commanded to divorce; if he does not divorce, the judge divorces her on his behalf.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then indeed Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾. ʿAli and Ibn ʿAbbas said: Forgiving of the sin of the oath.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if they are resolved upon divorce﴾, meaning: they carry it out.

Regarding the resolve to divorce there are two views.

The first: once the four months have passed, the husband becomes obligated either to return (to his wife) or to divorce. This is related from ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, Ibn ʿUmar, Sahl ibn Saʿd, ʿĀʾishah, Ṭāwūs, Mujāhid, al-Ḥakam, and Abū Ṣāliḥ. Abū Ṣāliḥ reported it from twelve men among the Companions. It is also the view of Mālik, Aḥmad, and al-Shāfiʿī.

The second: he does not return (to his wife) until four months have passed, and she is then divorced by that alone, without his pronouncing a divorce. The proponents of this view differed about what kind of divorce falls upon her, on two views. The first: a single irrevocable (bāʾin) divorce. This is related from ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, Ibn ʿUmar, Zayd ibn Thābit, and Qabīṣah ibn Dhuʾayb. The second: a single revocable (rajʿī) divorce. This is related from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, and Ibn Shubrumah.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾. Concerning this there are two views. The first: He is Hearing of his divorce and Knowing of his intention. The second: He is Hearing of his oath and Knowing of it.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 228:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The divorced women shall wait by themselves for three menstrual cycles (quru')﴾. The occasion of its revelation: a woman, when she was divorced while still desiring her husband, would say, "I am pregnant," though she was not pregnant, so that he would take her back. And if she was pregnant but disliked him, she would say, "I am not pregnant," so that he could not take her back. When Islam came, they persisted in this, so there was revealed His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them at their waiting period (iddah) and count the waiting period﴾ [al-Talaq: 1]. Then there was revealed: ﴿The divorced women shall wait by themselves for three menstrual cycles﴾. Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn Abbas.

As for the explanation (tafsir): *talaq* (divorce) means release. Ibn al-Anbari said: it comes from the Arabs' saying, "I released the she-camel (atlaqtu al-naqah), and she was released (talaqat)," when she had been tied, and I loosened the tie from her and let her go. So the situation that befalls the woman was likened to this, because she had been connected to the man by ties, and these ties were like a binding on her; when he divorced her, he severed the ties. It is also said: "the woman was divorced (tullliqat)" and "she was divorced (taliqat)." Others said: *talaq* derives from "I released a thing from my hand," except that, because they used the two expressions so often, they distinguished between them, so that *tatliq* would be specific to wives.

As for *quru'*: it is used to mean purity (tuhr), and it is also used to mean menstruation (hayd). It is said: "the woman menstruated (aqra'at)" when she menstruated, and "she became pure (aqra'at)" when she became pure. The Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning the woman with istihada: "She shall sit out the days of her *iqra'*," meaning the days of her menstruation. Al-A'sha said:

> Every year you are a raider on a raid, your resolve (azimah) of striving (azaiyak) pulls it taut to its farthest point,
>
> Leaving wealth to inherit, and in the tribe there is elevation, for what was lost of your women's *quru'* therein.

He meant by *quru'* the periods of purity, because when he went away from his women, he lost their periods of purity. The philologists differed about the original meaning of *quru'* on two views. The first: its original meaning is "time"; it is said, "So-and-so returned to his *qur'*," meaning to his time at which he used to return. [And it was said he returned to his *qari'* as well.] Al-Hudhali said:

> I disliked the barrenness, the barrenness of the Banu Shalil, when the winds blow at its *qari'*.

So menstruation comes at a time, and purity comes at a time. This is the view of Ibn Qutaybah. The second: its original meaning is "gathering." The Arabs' saying "I read the Qur'an (qara'tu al-Qur'an)" means "I pronounced it gathered." And *qur'* is the gathering of blood in the body, which occurs only in purity, though it may also be that its gathering is in the womb; both are good. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

The jurists differed about *al-aqra'* on two views. The first: they are menstruations. This is related from Umar, Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Musa, Ubadah ibn al-Samit, Abu al-Darda, Ikrimah, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Sufyan al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, al-Hasan ibn Salih, Abu Hanifah and his companions, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal, may Allah be pleased with him, for he said: "I used to say the *quru'* are the periods of purity, but today I go to the view that they are menstruations." The second: they are periods of purity. This is related from Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn Umar, (p-260) Aisha, al-Zuhri, Aban ibn Uthman, Malik ibn Anas, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad alluded to it.

The wording of His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿The divorced women shall wait﴾ is in the form of a report, but its meaning is a command, like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The mothers shall breastfeed their children for two full years﴾. The form of a command may also come with the meaning of a report, like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Let the Most Merciful extend for him an extension﴾ [Maryam: 75]. And what is meant by "the divorced women" in this verse are the adult women who have been consummated with, who are not pregnant.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs﴾. On this there are three views. The first: it is pregnancy; this was said by Umar, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, Muqatil, Ibn Qutaybah, and al-Zajjaj. The second: it is menstruation; this was said by Ikrimah, Ata', al-Nakha'i, and al-Zuhri. The third: pregnancy and menstruation; this was said by Ibn Umar and Ibn Zayd.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If they believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ came in the form of a warning to them and an emphasis. Al-Zajjaj said: it is like when you say to a man, "If you are a believer, do not oppress." Concerning the reason for this warning there are two views. The first: it is because of what the husband is entitled to of return (rij'ah), said by Ibn Abbas. The second: because of attributing the child to other than its father, said by Qatadah. It was also said: when the woman desired her husband, she would say, "I am menstruating," though she had become pure; and when she was averse to him, she would conceal her menstruation until she bathed, so that he would miss her.

*Al-bu'ulah* means husbands. "That" (dhalika) refers to the waiting period; this was said by Mujahid, al-Nakha'i, Qatadah, and others. In the verse there is evidence that the particularity of the final part of an expression does not prevent the generality of its beginning, nor does it necessitate restricting it, because His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The divorced women shall wait﴾ is general, covering both the irrevocably divorced (mabtutat) and the revocably divorced (raj'iyyat), while His saying, may He be exalted: (p-261) ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back﴾ is specific to the revocably divorced.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If they intend reconciliation﴾. It was said: a man, when he wished to harm his wife, would divorce her once and leave her; then when her waiting period was nearly over, he would take her back, then leave her for a period, then divorce her again; so they were forbidden from that. The apparent meaning of the verse requires that he only owns the right of return in a way other than harming her by prolonging the waiting period on her. However, His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not retain them to harm them, that you may transgress﴾ indicates the validity of the return even if he intends harm, because if the return were not valid when done with harmful intent, he would not be a wrongdoer by doing it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they have rights similar to those upon them, according to what is reasonable﴾, which is: good companionship and beautiful association. It was related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he was asked about the woman's right over the husband, and he said: "That he feeds her when he eats, clothes her when he clothes himself, does not strike the face, does not revile, and does not shun her except within the house." Ibn Abbas said: "I love to adorn myself for the woman, just as I love that she adorn herself for me, due to this verse."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the men have a degree over them﴾. Ibn Abbas said: by the dowry he gave her and the wealth he spent on her. Mujahid said: by striving (jihad) and inheritance. Abu Malik said: he divorces her, and she has no say in the matter at all. Al-Zajjaj said: he derives pleasure from her as she derives pleasure from him, and he has the superiority by his spending. Abu Hurayrah narrated (p-262) from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "If I were to command anyone to prostrate to anyone, I would command the woman to prostrate to her husband." And the daughter of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: "We would not speak to our husbands except as you speak to your commanders."

**Section**

The scholars differed about this verse: does it fall under the abrogated verses (al-mansukhat) or not? On two views. The first: it falls under that. Those who held this differed about what in it was abrogated. A group said: what is abrogated of it is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The divorced women shall wait by themselves for three menstrual cycles﴾. They said: it was obligatory for every divorced woman to observe a waiting period of three *quru'*, then the ruling for the pregnant woman was abrogated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And for those with children, their term is until they give birth﴾ [al-Talaq: 4], and the ruling for the woman divorced before consummation by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them, you have no waiting period for them to count﴾ [al-Ahzab: 49]. This is related from Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak, among others. Another group said: its first part is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated), and what is abrogated is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back﴾. They said: when a man divorced his wife, he had more right to her return, whether the divorce was three or less, then this was abrogated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him after that until she marries another husband﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230]. The second view: the whole verse is muhkam, its first part is general, and the verses concerning the number (of waiting periods) specified that general rule, and this is not abrogation. As for what was said about the return (irtija'), we have mentioned that the meaning of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back in that case﴾ is: within the waiting period before the completion of the three *quru'*. This view is the sound one.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 229:

As for the interpretation, regarding His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿Divorce is twice﴾, there are two opinions. The first: it is an explanation of the sunnah (the prescribed way) of divorce, and that one pronounces one revocable divorce in each menstrual cycle (qur') – this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. The second: it is an explanation of the divorce after which the husband has the right of return (raj'ah), said by 'Urwah, Qatadah, Ibn Qutaybah, al-Zajjaj and others.

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿then retention in kindness﴾ means: then it is obligatory upon you to retain [her] in kindness, which is what is recognized as upholding the right in retaining the woman. 'Ata', Mujahid, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: what is meant by His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿then retention in kindness﴾ is the return (raj'ah) after the second [divorce].

Regarding His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿or release with good treatment﴾, there are two opinions. The first: what is meant by it is the third divorce, said by 'Ata', Mujahid and Muqatil. The second: it is refraining from returning to her until her waiting period ('iddah) ends, said by al-Dahhak and al-Suddi. Qadi Abu Ya'la Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn al-Farra' said: this is the correct view, because He said right after the verse: ﴿And if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him afterward until she marries another husband﴾, and what is meant by this divorce is undoubtedly the third. It is therefore necessary that His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿or release with good treatment﴾ be understood as leaving her until her waiting period ends, because if it were understood as the third, then His statement ﴿And if he divorces her﴾ would have to be understood as a fourth, and this is not permissible.

(p-264) * Section

Divorce is of four kinds:

Obligatory, recommended, forbidden, and disliked. The obligatory: the divorce of the one who makes an oath of abstention (mu'li) after the waiting period, if he does not return; and the divorce by the two arbiters in a dispute between spouses, if they see separation as necessary. The recommended: when they do not agree and the dispute between them intensifies, so that they may both be freed from sin. The forbidden: during menstruation, if she is one with whom he has consummated the marriage, and in a purity period in which he has had intercourse with her before she has become clean. The disliked: when their situation is upright and each of them is fulfilling the right of the other.

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿And it is not lawful for you to take anything of what you have given them﴾ was revealed concerning "Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas. His wife came to the Prophet, ﷺ, and said: By God, I do not blame Thabit regarding religion or character, but I [dislike disbelief in Islam] and cannot endure him out of hatred." The Prophet ﷺ said to her: "Will you return his garden to him?" She said: Yes. So the Prophet ﷺ commanded him to take it and not to increase [his claim]." Narrated by 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas.

They differed over the name of his wife. Ibn 'Abbas said: Jamilah. Yahya ibn Abi Kathir traced her lineage, saying: Jamilah daughter of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, and Muqatil gave her a kunyah, saying: Umm Habibah daughter of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy. Others said: she was only Jamilah, the sister of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy. Yahya ibn Sa'id narrated from 'Amrah two reports: one of them is that she was Habibah daughter of Sahl, and the second is Sahlah daughter of Habib.

(p-265) This was the first khul' (divorce by compensation) in Islam. The word "fear" (khawf) in the verse means knowledge: Abu 'Ubayd said: the meaning of His statement (alla yakhafa): they be certain (yuqinā). The limits (hudud) have already been explained in meaning.

The meaning of the verse is: if the woman fears that she will disobey God regarding her husband's rights because of her hatred of him, and the husband fears that he will transgress against her because of her refusal to obey him, then it is permissible for him to take from her a ransom (fidyah), if she requests that. This is according to the reading of the majority, with a fatha on the "ya'" of (yakhafa). Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Abu Ja'far, Hamzah and al-A'mash read (yukhafa) with a damma on the ya'.

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿But if you fear﴾ – Qatadah said: it is addressed to the rulers (wulat). ﴿then there is no blame upon either of them﴾ – upon the woman ﴿concerning what she ransoms herself with﴾ and upon the husband concerning what he takes, because it is the price of his right. Al-Farra' said: it is permissible that the husband alone is meant, even though both have been mentioned, as in His statement: ﴿From them emerge the pearl and the coral﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 22], whereas it emerges from only one of them; and His statement: ﴿they forgot their fish﴾ [Al-Kahf: 61], whereas only one of them forgot.

Section

Is it permissible for him to take from her more than what he gave her? There are two opinions. The first: it is permissible, and this was said by 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Uthman, 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Nakha'i, al-Dahhak, Malik and al-Shafi'i. The second: it is not permissible, and this was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, 'Ata', al-Sha'bi, Tawus, Ibn Jubayr, al-Zuhri and Ahmad ibn Hanbal; and it has also been reported from 'Ali and al-Hasan. Is khul' permissible without the authority (sultan)? 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Ali, Ibn 'Umar, Tawus, Shurayh and al-Zuhri said: it is permissible, and this is the view of the majority of scholars. Al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin and Qatadah said: it is not permissible except before the authority.

(p-266) His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him after that until she marries another husband﴾. Muqatil mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning Tamima bint Wahb ibn Atik al-Nadiri, whose husband was Rifa'a ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Qurazi. But other than Muqatil said: "She was Aisha bint Abd al-Rahman ibn Atik. She was married to Rifa'a ibn Wahb ibn Atik, who was her paternal cousin, and he divorced her three times. After him she married Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Zubayr. Then he divorced her, and she came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'I was married to Rifa'a, and he divorced me, and he finalised my divorce. Then I married after him Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Zubayr, and he divorced me before he had touched me. Shall I return to my paternal cousin?' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ smiled and said: 'Do you want to return to Rifa'a? No, not until you taste his honey and he tastes yours.'"

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then if he divorces her﴾ means the husband who divorces her twice. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada said: it is the third divorce. Know that Allah, exalted is He, after the discussion of the ruling on khul' (divorce by compensation), returned with this verse to completing the discussion of divorce.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then if he divorces her﴾ means the second husband. ﴿There is no blame upon them both﴾ means the woman and the first husband. ﴿If they think that they will keep within the limits of Allah﴾. Tawus said: this refers to what Allah has obligated on each of them of good companionship and good association.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And these are the limits of Allah; He makes them clear﴾. The reading of the majority is (yubayyinuha) with the letter ya'. Al-Hasan, Mujahid and al-Mufaddal from Asim read it with the letter nun (nubayyinuha). For ﴿a people who know﴾, al-Zajjaj said: they know that the command of Allah is true.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 231:**

(p-267) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when you divorce women and they reach their term﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: A man would divorce his wife, then take her back (*raj'ah*, revocation of divorce) before the end of her *'iddah* (the waiting period), then divorce her again [doing that], harming her and [making it difficult for her] (*'udhl*) by this means, so this verse was revealed. Here *al-ajal* (the term) means the time of the *'iddah*. The meaning of "reaching" here is approaching the term, not actually arriving at its end, as one says, "I reached the city" when you approached it, and "I reached the city" when you entered it. The scholars interpreted this "reaching" as approaching because after the *'iddah* has ended there is no return (*raj'ah*).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿then retain them honourably﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatadah said: It means taking her back before the end of the *'iddah*.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or release them honourably﴾. This means leaving her until her *'iddah* ends. The honourable manner in retention is to fulfil the rights that are due to her. The honourable manner in release is not to intend to harm her, such as by prolonging her *'iddah* through revocation. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And do not retain them to harm them, so that you transgress﴾. This was said by al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah and others. Al-Dahhak said: They only harmed the woman so that she would ransom herself (*yaftadi*). ﴿And whoever does that﴾, namely the transgression, ﴿has certainly wronged his soul﴾ by committing sin.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not take the signs of Allah in mockery﴾. There are two views on this. The first is that it refers to a man who divorces, or takes back, or frees a slave, and then says, "I was only joking." This was narrated from 'Umar, Abu al-Darda' and al-Hasan. The second is that it refers to one who harms his wife by prolonging her *'iddah* through revocation and divorce. This was said by Masruq and Muqatil.

**

(p-268) ﴿And remember the favour of Allah upon you and what He has sent down to you of the Book and wisdom, by which He admonishes you﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: Guard His favour upon you through Islam. He said: The Book is the Qur'an, and the wisdom is *fiqh* (understanding of the law). ﴿And fear Allah﴾ regarding harm, ﴿and know that Allah is, of all things, ﴾ concerning Him and other than Him, ﴿Knowing﴾.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 232:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you divorce women and they have reached their term, do not prevent them﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are two accounts.

The first: al-Hasan narrated that Ma'qil ibn Yasar had given his sister in marriage to a man from among the Muslims. She remained with him for a while, then he divorced her with one pronouncement [and then left her alone], and her waiting period (iddah) elapsed, so she became more entitled to herself. Then he proposed to her along with the other suitors, and she agreed to return to him. He then proposed to Ma'qil (for her hand), but Ma'qil became angry and said: "I honoured you by giving her to you, and you divorced her! No, by God! She will never return to you, ever, for as long as you live." Al-Hasan said: God, mighty and majestic, knew the man's need for his wife and the woman's need for her husband, so this verse was revealed. Ma'qil heard it and said: "I hear and obey my Lord." He summoned her husband and said: "I will marry her to you and honour you." Abd al-Ghani al-Hafiz reported from al-Kalbi that he named this woman, saying: Jamilah daughter of Yasar.

The second: Jabir ibn Abd Allah al-Ansari had a paternal cousin (daughter) whose husband divorced her with one pronouncement. Her waiting period ended, then he came back wanting to take her back, but Jabir refused and said: "You divorced our cousin, and now you want to marry her a second time?" The woman wanted her husband and had persuaded him, so this verse was revealed. al-Suddi said: As for the reaching of the term in this verse, it means the completion of the waiting period, unlike the term in the previous verse. Al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, said: The difference between the two statements indicates that the two "reaching of the term" are distinct.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿do not prevent them﴾. This is addressed to the guardians (awliya', sing. wali, i.e. marriage guardians). Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Qutaybah and others said: its meaning is: do not confine them. The Arabs call difficulties "mu'dilat" (intractable matters), and a disease that has defied treatment is "da'un 'udal" (an incurable disease). Aws ibn Hajar said:

"Your brother who keeps the covenant is not the one who blames you if you turn away, and pleases you when you come near;
But rather it is the distant one who, when you are safe, and the close friend, when matters become grave (a'dala)."

And Layla al-Akhyaliyyah said:

"When al-Hajjaj alights in a sick land, he traces its disease to its furthest root and cures it.
He cures it of the incurable disease that is in it: a youth who, when he shakes the spear, gives it drink."

Al-Zajjaj said: The root of "'adl" (prevention) comes from the saying of the Arabs: "'adalat al-dajajah," so it is "mu'dil," when its egg is held back and stuck and does not come out; and "'adalat al-naqah" also, when her offspring is held back in her womb.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿when they agree among themselves in a reasonable manner﴾. Al-Suddi and Ibn Qutaybah said: its meaning is: when the spouses agree to a valid marriage. Al-Shafi'i said: This verse is the clearest proof that a woman may not marry except through a guardian.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is admonished to him who among you believes in God and the Last Day﴾. Muqatil said: the reference is to the prohibition upon the guardian against preventing. Al-Zajjaj said: He said "dhalika" and not "dhalikum," though He is addressing a group, because the word for a group is singular in form, and the meaning is: "that, O group."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is purer for you﴾, meaning: returning the women to their husbands is better than separating them, ﴿and purer﴾, i.e., more cleansing for your hearts from doubt, so that there is no kind of affection between them that would bring them together in a way that is not for good.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God knows and you do not know﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: its meaning is: He knows the affection each of them has for the other, as said by Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak. The second: He knows your interests, immediate and deferred, as said by al-Zajjaj and others.

**Ibn al-Jawzi, *Zad al-Masir*, on Surah 2, verse 233:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The mothers shall suckle their children﴾. Its wording is that of a report (khabar), but its meaning is a command (amr), as in His saying: ﴿And the divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228].

Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la said: This command is directed at the fathers, because the obligation of nursing (al-istirda', having the child suckled) rests upon them, and not upon the mothers. The evidence is His saying: ﴿and upon the one to whom the child belongs is their provision and their clothing﴾, and His saying: ﴿So give them their payment﴾ [al-Nisa': 24]. Had it been obligatory upon the mother, she would not deserve a wage.

Is this general to all mothers? There are two opinions on this.

The first: It is specific to divorced women. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Muqatil, and others.

The second: It is general to wives and divorced women. Accordingly, we say: she may hire herself out to suckle her child, whether she is with the husband or divorced. This was said by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi, among others.

Al-hawl (the full year) means the year. As for His saying ﴿complete﴾ (kamilayn), there are two opinions.

The first: It has entered for emphasis (li-l-ta'kid), as in His saying: ﴿That is ten complete﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196].

The second: Since it is permissible to say "two years" (hawlayn) while meaning less than them, just as He said: ﴿And whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 203]—and it is known that one hastens in a day and part of another—and the Arabs say, "I have not seen so-and-so since two days," while they mean a day and part of another, then "complete" was stated to clarify that it is not permissible to reduce from them. This is the view of al-Zajjaj and al-Farra'.

**Section**

The scholars of al-naskh wa'l-mansukh (abrogation) differed regarding this portion of the verse. Some said: It is muhkam (not abrogated), and its purpose is to specify the period of nursing, and rulings are connected to it. Among them: that it is the complete nursing period; that the father is obligated to bear the cost of nursing for the period of two years, and the judge compels him to do so; and that the prohibition by nursing (tahrim al-radd', prohibition of marriage through suckling) is established within the period of two years and is not established beyond it.

It is reported from Qatadah, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, and others that it is mansukh (abrogated) by His saying: ﴿But if they both desire weaning by mutual consent﴾.

Our shaykh 'Ali ibn 'Ubayd Allah said: This view is far-fetched, because God, exalted is He, said at the beginning: ﴿for whoever wishes to complete the nursing﴾. Then, when He said in the second part: ﴿But if they both desire weaning by mutual consent﴾, the choice was given between the two desires, and that does not contradict the period fixed for completion.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for whoever wishes to complete the nursing﴾, meaning: this determination by the two years is for those who wish to complete the nursing. Mujahid recited "an yutimma" with two taws and with raf' (nominative), and it is the narration of al-Halabi from 'Abd al-Warith. The mention of completion alerts to the negation of the ruling of nursing after the two years. Most of the readers recite the ra' of "al-ridaah" (nursing) with a fatha. Talhah ibn Musarrif, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, and Abu Raja' recited it with a kasra. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said al-ridaah with fatha and kasra of the ra', and the fatha is more common. It is also said: "What led him to that was only baseness." The "ridaah" with fatha here, and no other.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and upon the one to whom the child belongs is their provision and their clothing﴾. He means: the father. ﴿their provision and their clothing﴾: He means: the nursing women.

His saying: ﴿according to what is reasonable (bi'l-ma'ruf)﴾ indicates that what is obligatory is according to the man's circumstance, in his poverty and his wealth, since it is not reasonable to oblige the poor man with what he cannot bear, nor the wealthy man with a trifling amount. The verse also contains evidence for the permissibility of ijtihad (independent reasoning) in the rulings of new events, since the determination of maintenance "according to what is reasonable" can only be reached through dominant opinion (ghalib al-zann), as it is measured by custom.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿No soul is burdened except according to its capacity﴾, meaning: except what it can bear. ﴿No mother shall be harmed through her child﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Aban from 'Asim recited "la tudarru" with raf' of the ra'. Nafi', 'Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i recited it with nasb (fatha) of it. Abu 'Ali said: Whoever recites with raf', does so because of the preceding nominative word, which is "la tukallifu," so he made it follow what precedes it, so that the wording would be similar. Whoever recites with nasb makes it a command, and makes the ra' vowelled with fatha so that its vowel agrees with what precedes it, which is the alif. Ibn Qutaybah said: Its meaning is "la tudarrir," so the first ra' was assimilated into the second. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Let not the harm of the husband lead the divorced woman to abandon her child to him. Mujahid said: She should not refuse to nurse him out of harm to his father, nor should the father harm his child by preventing his mother from nursing him, in order to grieve her thereby. 'Ata', Qatadah, al-Zuhri, Sufyan, al-Suddi, and others said: If she is content with what others would accept, she has more right to him. Abu Ja'far recited "la tudarru" with its lightening and sukun (lightening and sukun).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And upon the heir﴾. There are four opinions concerning it.

The first: that it is the heir of the child. This is the view of 'Ata', Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn Abi Layla, Qatadah, al-Suddi, al-Hasan ibn Salih, and Muqatil, among others. The proponents of this view differed. Some said: It is the child's heir from among his 'asabah (male agnatic relatives), whoever he may be. This is reported from 'Umar, 'Ata', al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ibrahim, and Sufyan. Others said: It is the child's heir in general, male or female. This is reported from Ibn Abi Layla, Qatadah, al-Hasan ibn Salih, Ishaq, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Others said: (p-273) It is whoever is a mahram (unmarriageable) relative among the heirs of the child. This is reported from Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad.

The second opinion: that what is meant by the heir here is the heir of the father. This is reported from al-Hasan and al-Suddi.

The third: that what is meant by the heir is the surviving one of the child's two parents after the death of the other. This is reported from Sufyan.

The fourth: that by the heir is meant the child himself, and the maintenance is upon him; if he owns nothing, then it falls upon his 'asabah. This was said by al-Dahhak and Qubaysah ibn Dhu'ayb.

Our shaykh 'Ali ibn 'Ubayd Allah said: This opinion does not contradict the view of the one who said: what is meant by the heir is the child's heir, because maintenance is owed to the one who is inherited from by the heir when the poverty of the one spending upon him is established.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The like of that﴾. There are three opinions concerning it.

The first: that it refers to the wage of nursing and the maintenance. This is reported from 'Umar, Zayd ibn Thabit, al-Hasan, 'Ata', Mujahid, Ibrahim, Qatadah, Qubaysah ibn Dhu'ayb, and al-Suddi, and it was chosen by Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: that the reference by "that" is to the prohibition of harm. This is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi, and al-Zuhri, and it was chosen by al-Zajjaj.

The third: that it refers to all of that. This is reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Muqatil, Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi, and it was chosen by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la. What supports this is that it is conjoined (ma'tuf) to what precedes it, and it has been established that upon the one to whom the child belongs is the maintenance and the clothing, and that he must not cause harm. Therefore His saying ﴿the like of that﴾ must refer to all that is upon the one to whom the child belongs.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if they both desire weaning by mutual consent﴾. Al-fisal means weaning (al-fitam). Ibn Qutaybah said: It is said: "The mother weaned the child (fasalat al-sabiyy)" when she weaned him. From this is said of a young camel when it is separated from nursing: fasil, because it is separated (fasl) from its mother, and the root of fasl is separation. Mujahid said: Consultation regarding what is less than two years: if the mother wishes to wean and the father refuses, it is not for her to do so; and if he wishes it and she does not, it is not for him to do so, until it occurs by mutual consent and consultation between them. He means: not harming themselves or their child.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you wish to have your children nursed by others﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, for your children. Muqatil said: If the mother is not content with what others would accept, there is no blame upon the father if he has the child nursed by another for his child.

And regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿when you hand over what you have given according to what is reasonable﴾, there are two opinions. The first: when you hand over, O fathers, to the mothers of the children the wages for what they nursed before they refused, this was said by Mujahid and al-Suddi. The second: when you hand over to the wet-nurse (al-zi'r) her wage according to what is reasonable, this was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Muqatil.

Ibn Kathir recited "ma ataytum" with qasr (short vowel). Abu 'Ali said: Its explanation is to supply within it: "what you have given" (ma ataytum), its payment or its driving, so he deleted the mudaf (the governed noun) and placed the mudaf ilayh (the governing noun) in its place, [so the supposed meaning is "what you have given it," then the pronoun was deleted from the relative clause], as you say: "I came to Jamil," meaning: "I did it."

**The Word of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And those of you who die﴾**, i.e., who receive death (*yaqbidun bil-mawt*, "are taken by death").

Al-Mufaddal related from 'Asim that he read *yatawaffawna* with an open *ya'* (*bi-fath al-ya'*) in both places.

Ibn Qutayba said: It is from *istifa' al-'adad* (the complete counting of a number), and *istifa' al-shay'* (taking a thing in full), meaning that we account for it entirely. One says *tawaffaytuhu* and *istawfaytuhu*, just as one says *tayaqqantu al-khayr* and *istayqantuhu* (I was certain of the good, and I was certain of it). This is the root meaning. Then death was called *wafat* and *tawf*.

*(Yatarabbasna)*: they should wait, i.e., they should await.

Al-Farra' said: He said *ʿashra* (ten) and not *ʿashratan* (the feminine form), because when the Arabs leave the number of nights and days unspecified, they give precedence to the nights. To the point that they say, "We fasted ten days of Ramadan," because of their frequent giving precedence to the nights over the days. When they state the number together with its specification (*tafsir*), the feminine (*ināth*) appears without *ha'* and the masculine (*dhukur*) with *ha'*, as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿He subjected them against them for seven nights and eight days, in succession﴾ [al-Haqqah: 7]. (p-275)

If it is asked: What is the wisdom in adding these ten? The answer: It shows the soundness of the pregnancy (*haml*) with the breathing of the spirit into the fetus. This was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and Abu al-'Aliyah, and the authentic hadith from the Prophet ﷺ supports it: "Indeed, the creation of one of you is gathered in his mother's womb for forty days [as a drop], then it becomes a clot like that, then a lump like that, then the angel is sent to it and the spirit is breathed into it."

**Section**

This verse abrogates (*nasikhah*, i.e., it is an instance of *naskh*, abrogation) the verse similar to it, which comes after verses, and it is the words of Allah: ﴿And those of you who die and leave wives behind, let them make a bequest for their wives, provision until the end of a year﴾ [al-Baqarah: 240]. That is because that [verse] required the 'iddah (waiting period) to be one year. We will mention what relates to it there, if Allah wills. As for the verse we are explaining: it has been related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said it was abrogated by the words of Allah: ﴿And for those with children, their term is that they deliver their burden﴾ [al-Talaq: 4]. The sound view is that it is general (*'amm*) and has been entered by specification (*takhsis*), because its apparent meaning requires that the widow's 'iddah be four months and ten days, whether she is pregnant or not pregnant. However, the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿And for those with children, their term is that they deliver their burden﴾ specified the pregnant women. This is also specific to free women, for the 'iddah of a slave woman is two months and five days. Thus it becomes clear that this verse is among the general text which has been entered by specification.

**The Word of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Then when they have reached their term﴾**, meaning: the completion of the 'iddah.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 235:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿There is no blame upon you﴾. On this there are two views. The first is that its meaning is: there is no blame upon men for marrying them after this. The second is that its meaning is: there is no blame upon men for not objecting to them when they adorn themselves and marry. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: "It is addressed to their guardians."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿concerning what they do with themselves in an honourable manner﴾. On this there are two views. The first is that it refers to adorning oneself and making oneself attractive for marriage, as said by al-Dahhak and Muqatil. The second is that it refers to marriage itself, as said by al-Zuhri and al-Suddi. "Al-Khabir" (the All-Aware) is among the names of Allah the Exalted, and its meaning is: the One who knows the reality of a thing, who is acquainted with its essence. "Khabir" as an attribute of created beings is used only for a kind of knowledge, namely that which is reached through effort (ijtihad), not the kind of knowledge known by the evident intellect. The knowledge of Allah the Exalted is equal in what is obscure and subtle and in what is manifest and apparent.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you allude to of a proposal to women﴾. This is addressed to one who wishes to marry a woman who is in her waiting period (iddah). Ta'rid (allusion) means hinting and suggesting without disclosure; it is an indication through speech to what is not explicitly mentioned in the speech. Al-khitbah, with a kasra on the kha', is the request for marriage; al-khutbah, with a damma on the kha', is like a message which has a beginning and an end. Ibn Abbas said: "Allusion is that he says: 'I wish to marry.'" Mujahid said: "That he says: 'Indeed you are beautiful, indeed you are good, and indeed you are for good.'"

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿or you conceal within yourselves﴾. Al-Farra' said: "In it there are two dialects: kanantu al-shay' and akmantuhu." Thalab said: "Akmantu al-shay' means: when I conceal it within myself; kanantuhu means: when I cover it with something." Ibn Qutaybah said: "Akmantu al-shay' means: when I conceal it, and this verse is an example of it; kanantuhu means: when I protect it, and from it is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿as if they were preserved eggs﴾ [al-Saffat: 49]." Some of them make kananta and akmanta to have the same meaning.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Allah knows that you will remember them﴾. Mujahid said: "Its meaning is your remembering them in yourselves."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿but do not promise them in secret﴾. On this there are four views. The first is that the intended meaning of "secret" here is marriage, as said by Ibn Abbas, who recited the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

Did not Basbasah claim today that I have grown old, and that those like me should not witness the secret?

In another narration: "witness the frivolity." Al-Farra' said: "We see that it is among the things Allah has referred to by euphemism, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself﴾ [al-Nisa': 43]." Al-Zajjaj reported from Abu Ubaydah that the secret is engaging in intercourse through forbidden marriage [al-muharram], and he recited:

And he forbids the secret of his neighbour to them, while their neighbour eats the nose of the dishes.

Ibn Qutaybah said: "The secret is borrowed for marriage, because marriage happens in secret. So the meaning is: do not promise them with marriage [while they are in the waiting period] explicitly ﴿except that you say a known saying﴾, in which you do not mention indecency or marriage." The second view is that promising in secret is saying to her: "I love you, and pledge to me that you will not marry anyone other than me," which is also narrated from Ibn Abbas. The third is that the intended meaning of "secret" is fornication, as said by al-Hasan, Jabir ibn Zayd, Abu Mijlaz, Ibrahim, Qatadah, and al-Dahhak. The fourth is that the meaning is: do not marry them secretly during their waiting period; when it ends, make that public, as said by Ibn Zayd.

Concerning "the known saying" there are two views. The first is that it is allusion to her, which is the view of Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ata', al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, al-Sha'bi, Mujahid, Ibrahim, Qatadah, and al-Suddi. The second is that it is informing her guardian of his desire for her, which is the view of Ubaydah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and do not resolve upon the tie of marriage﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "Its meaning is: do not resolve upon the tie of marriage, and 'upon' ('ala') is omitted for lightness, as they say: 'Zayd struck the back and the belly,' meaning: upon the back and the belly." ﴿until the decreed term reaches its end﴾, that is: until the prescribed obligation of the Book reaches its term. He said: "It is also possible that 'the Book' means 'the obligation', like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183]. So the meaning is: until the obligation reaches its term." Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, Qatadah, and al-Suddi said: "The reaching of the Book to its term is the completion of the waiting period."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And know that Allah knows what is in your souls﴾. Ibn Abbas said: "[He knows] of your fulfilment (of the covenant), so beware lest you oppose Him in His command." As for "al-Halim" (the Forbearing), its explanation has already passed.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 236:

(p-279) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women as long as you have not touched them﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read "tamassuhunna" (have touched them) without an alif wherever it occurs, with a fatha on the ta'. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "tamasshunna" with an alif and a damma on the ta', in both places here and in al-Ahzab, where it is the third occurrence. Abu 'Ali said: each of fa'ala and fa'ala (the two verb patterns) may be used to mean what the other means; we say "tarraqtu al-na'l" (I beat/hammered the sandal) and "'aqabtu al-lis" (I retaliated against the thief). Muqatil ibn Sulayman said: this verse was revealed concerning "a man of the Ansar who married a woman from Banu Hanifa, and did not name a dowry for her, then divorced her before he had touched her. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Have you given her any provision?' He said: No. He said: 'Give her provision, even if it is with your cap.'" The meaning of the verse: as long as you have not touched them, and have not set a obligatory dowry for them. "Aw" may sometimes mean "wa" (and), as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not obey from among them a sinner or a disbeliever﴾ [al-Insan: 24].

Al-mass (touching) means marriage (intercourse), and al-faridah (the obligation) means the dowry. The verse indicates the permissibility of concluding a marriage contract without naming a dowry. ﴿And provide for them﴾, that is, give them what they may enjoy from your wealth according to your circumstances of wealth and poverty. Al-mata' (provision) is the name of what is benefited from, and this is the meaning of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The wealthy according to his means, and the straitened according to his means﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "qaddarahu" with a sukun on the dal in both places; Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a vowel on both letters; and from 'Asim, both readings are reported. They are two dialects.

(p-280) * Section

Is this provision obligatory or recommended? On this there are two opinions. The first: it is obligatory. Those who hold this view differ as to which divorced women it is owed to, in three opinions. The first: it is owed to every divorced woman; this is reported from 'Ali, al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Zuhri. The second: it is owed to every divorced woman except the one for whom a dowry was fixed and who was not touched; for her is owed half of what was fixed. This is reported from Ibn 'Umar, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, Shurayh and Ibrahim. The third: it is owed to a divorced woman before consummation when no dowry was named for her; if he has consummated with her, there is no provision, and she has the mahr al-mithl (the customary dowry). This is reported from al-Awza'i, al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa and Ahmad ibn Hanbal. The second opinion: the provision is recommended and is not obligatory on anyone, whether a dowry was named for the woman or not, whether he consummated with her or not. This is the view of Malik, al-Layth ibn Sa'd, al-Hakam and Ibn Abi Layla.

The scholars differed on the amount of the provision. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib that its highest level is a servant, and its lowest is a garment in which she may pray. It is reported from Hammad and Abu Hanifa that he assessed it as half the dowry of her equivalent. From al-Shafi'i and Ahmad: it is according to his means of wealth and poverty, so it is determined by the judgment of the judge (ijtihad al-hakim). It is reported from Ahmad: the provision is in the amount of the clothing with which prayer is valid, which is a shirt and a head-covering (khimar). His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿a provision in accordance with what is reasonable﴾, that is, according to what is possible; and al-haqq (the duty) means what is obligatory. Mentioning "the good-doers" and "the God-fearing" is a form of emphasis.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 237:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them﴾, meaning: before intercourse (al-jima'), ﴿and you have already specified for them an obligation﴾, meaning: you have made obligatory for them something you have committed yourselves to, which is the dower (al-mahr). ﴿Unless they forgo﴾, meaning: the women. The forgoing of the woman is her abandonment of her right to the dowry.

Regarding the one in whose hand is the marriage tie (al-ʿuqdat al-nikah), there are three opinions. The first: that it is the husband. This is the view of ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, Jubayr ibn Mut'im, Ibn al-Musayyab, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Shurayh, Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Dahhak, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi, al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas, Ibn Shubrumah, al-Shafiʿi, and Ahmad, may Allah be pleased with them, along with others.
