The second: that it is the guardian (al-wali). This is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, ʿAlqamah, Tawus, al-Shaʿbi, and Ibrahim, along with others. The third: that it is the father of the virgin (abu al-bikr). This is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Zuhri, and al-Suddi, along with others.

According to the first opinion, the forgoing of the husband is that he completes the dowry for her. According to the second, the forgoing of the guardian is the abandonment of her right if she refuses; this is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu al-Shaʿtha'. According to the third, His saying ﴿unless they forgo﴾ applies specifically to previously married women (al-thayyibat), and His saying ﴿or he forgoes﴾ applies specifically to the father of the virgin; this is what al-Zuhri said. The first opinion is the most sound, because the marriage tie has left the hand of the guardian and passed into the hand of the husband, and forgoing is properly applied to what a person owns, whereas the guardian's forgoing would be a forgoing of what he does not own. Moreover, He said: ﴿And do not forget graciousness among yourselves﴾, and graciousness in this context is a person giving up his own property, not the property of another.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that you forgo is nearer to righteousness﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: that it is addressed to both spouses together; this is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and Muqatil. The second: that it is addressed to the husband alone; this is said by al-Shaʿbi, and he used to recite it as "wa-an yaʿfuwa" with the letter ya'.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not forget graciousness among yourselves﴾ is addressed to both spouses. Mujahid said: it is the man completing the dowry and the woman giving up her half of it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 238:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Guard strictly over the prayers﴾. *Al-muhafaza* means persistence and constancy. *Al-salawat* (the prayers), with the definite article, refers to what is already known, and what is meant is the five daily prayers.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and the middle prayer﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: When this waw comes in a specifying sense, it indicates the superiority of what it specifies, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [al-Baqarah: 97]. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were in the middle prayer like this, and he interlaced his fingers.

Then there are five opinions about it.

The first is that it is the 'Asr prayer. Muslim related in his *Afrad*, from the hadith of 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said on the day of the Confederates: "They kept us busy from the middle prayer, the 'Asr prayer. May Allah fill their graves and their houses with fire." Ibn Mas'ud, Samura and 'A'isha related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that it is the 'Asr prayer. Muslim related in his *Afrad*, from the hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, who said: This verse was revealed: "Guard strictly over the prayers [and the middle prayer and the 'Asr prayer]," and we recited it as long as Allah willed. Then Allah abrogated it (naskh), and it was revealed: ﴿Guard strictly over the prayers and the middle prayer﴾. This is the view of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy, Abu Ayyub, Ibn 'Umar in one report, Samura ibn Jundub, Abu Hurayra, Ibn 'Abbas in the report of 'Atiyya, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, 'A'isha in one report, Hafsa, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ata' in one report, Tawus, al-Dahhak, al-Nakha'i, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Zirr ibn Hubaysh, Qatada, Abu Hanifa, Muqatil, and others. It is also the position of our companions (the Hanbalis).

The second is that it is the Fajr prayer. This was reported from 'Umar, 'Ali in one report, Abu Musa, Mu'adh, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, Abu Umama, Ibn 'Umar in the report of Mujahid, Zayd ibn Aslam, Ibn 'Abbas in the report of Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi, 'Ikrima, Jabir ibn Zayd, Anas ibn Malik, 'Ata', 'Ikrima, Tawus in the report of his son, 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad, Mujahid, Malik, and al-Shafi'i. Abu al-'Aliya related that he said: I prayed the dawn prayer (al-ghadah) with the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and I asked them: "Which is the middle prayer?" They said: "The one you prayed just before."

The third is that it is the Zuhr prayer. This was reported from Ibn 'Umar, Zayd ibn Thabit, Usama ibn Zayd, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, and 'A'isha in one report. Dumayra related from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: It is the Friday prayer, and on the other days it is the Zuhr prayer.

The fourth is that it is the Maghrib prayer. This was reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Qabisa ibn Dhu'ayb.

The fifth is that it is the final 'Isha prayer. Ali ibn Ahmad al-Naysaburi mentioned it in his *Tafsir*.

Regarding the meaning of "al-wusta" (the middle), there are three opinions. The first is that it is the middlemost of the prayers in position (in the day). The second is that it is the middlemost in duration. The third is that it is the best of them. The middle of a thing is its best and most balanced part, and from this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143].

If we say that *al-wusta* means *al-fudla* (the most excellent), then anyone who holds a view about it may claim it. If we say it is the middlemost in duration, then it is the Maghrib prayer, because the least of the obligatory prayers is two rak'ahs and the most is four. If we say it is the middlemost in position, then those who say it is the 'Asr prayer can argue: before it there are two prayers in the daytime, and after it there are two prayers at night, so it is the middle one. As for those who say it is the Fajr prayer, 'Ikrima said: It is a middle point between night and day. Likewise Ibn al-Anbari said: It is a middle point between night and day. He said: I heard Abu al-'Abbas, meaning Tha'lab, say: For the Arabs, the beginning of the day is the rising of the sun. Ibn al-Anbari said: On this basis, the dawn prayer is part of the night prayers. He said: Others said: Rather, it is part of the day prayers, because the beginning of its time is the beginning of the time of fasting. He said: The correct view in our opinion is that pure night ends with the break of dawn, and pure day begins with the rising of the sun, and what lies between the break of dawn and the rising of the sun may be called day, and may be called night, because of the darkness and light found in it. So this is a view by which both positions can be upheld. Ibn al-Anbari said: As for those who say it is the Zuhr prayer, they say it is the middle of the day. As for those who say it is the Maghrib prayer, they argue that the first prayer to be made obligatory was the Zuhr, so the Maghrib became the middle one. As for those who say it is the 'Isha prayer, they say it lies between two prayers that are shortened (in travel).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And stand before Allah in devout obedience﴾. What is meant by standing here is standing in the prayer. As for *qunut*, we have explained it earlier. Regarding its meaning here there are three opinions. The first is that it means obedience; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, al-Sha'bi, Tawus, al-Dahhak, Qatada, and others. The second is that it means prolonging the standing in the prayer; this was reported from Ibn 'Umar and al-Rabi' ibn Anas, and from 'Ata' as in both views. The third is that it means refraining from speech in the prayer. Zayd ibn Arqam said: We used to speak during the prayer until this verse was revealed: ﴿And stand before Allah in devout obedience﴾, and we were commanded to be silent and forbidden to speak.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 239:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you fear, then [pray] on foot or riding﴾. That is, if you fear an enemy, then pray on foot (rijalan). Rijal is the plural of rajil (one on foot), and rukban is the plural of rakib (one riding). This indicates the emphasis on the prayer, because He commanded its performance in every state. It has been said that this verse was revealed after the one in Surah an-Nisa', because Allah, exalted is He, described for them the prayer of fear in His saying: ﴿And when you are among them and you establish prayer for them﴾ [an-Nisa': 102]. Then this verse was revealed: ﴿And if you fear﴾, that is, a fear greater than that, so pray at the time of close fighting however you are able. If it is asked: how is this verse reconciled with what Ibn Abbas narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "he prayed on the day of the Trench the Dhuhr and the 'Asr, and the Maghrib and the 'Isha' after the twilight had disappeared"? The answer: Abu Sa'id narrated that this was before the revelation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you fear, then [pray] on foot or riding﴾. Abu Bakr al-Athram said: Allah has indeed made clear that this action which was on the day of the Trench is abrogated (mansukh).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you are secure, then remember Allah﴾. Regarding this remembrance there are two opinions. The first: that it is the prayer, so its meaning is: pray as you used to pray while secure. The second: that it is praise of Allah and glorifying Him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 240:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those of you who die and leave wives behind﴾. Ibn Hayyan narrated: "This verse was revealed concerning a man from the people of al-Ta'if, called Hakim ibn al-Harith. He emigrated to Madinah, and with him were his parents and his wife, and he had children. He died, and that was brought to the Prophet (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed. The Prophet (ﷺ) gave his parents and his children from his inheritance, and he did not give his wife anything, except that he commanded them to spend on her from the estate of her husband for a year."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a bequest for their wives﴾. Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and Ibn 'Amir read "wasiyyatan" (a bequest) with the accusative (naṣb), while Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read "wasiyyatun" with the nominative (raf'). And from 'Asim there are both readings. Abu 'Ali said: whoever reads it with the accusative takes it as governed by a verb, meaning: let them make a bequest (liyuwsu wasiyyatan). Whoever reads it with the nominative has two options:

(p-286) One: that he makes "al-wasiyyah" (the bequest) the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is "li-azwajihim" (for their wives). The second: that he supposes a predicate for it, its estimate being: "so upon them is a bequest." What is meant is one who is approaching death, so let him make a bequest, because the one who has already died is not commanded or forbidden.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿provision until the year﴾. That is: provide for them until the year is over, and do not expel them. What is meant by this is the year's maintenance, its clothing and its housing. ﴿But if they leave﴾, that is, of their own accord, ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾, meaning: the guardians of the deceased, ﴿for what they do with themselves of what is reasonable﴾, meaning adorning themselves to seek marriage. And concerning what it is that the blame is lifted from the men regarding this, there are two opinions. One: that it concerns cutting off the maintenance from them if they leave before the year is over. The second: concerning not preventing them from leaving, because remaining for the year was not obligatory for them; rather they were free in that matter.

Section

The scholars of tafsir mention that the people of the Jahiliyyah, when one of them died, his wife would remain in his house for a year, being maintained from his inheritance. When the year was complete, she would come out to the door of her house, carrying a piece of camel dung, and she would throw it at a dog, and by that she would exit her waiting period (iddah). The meaning of throwing the dung was that she would say: "My remaining after the death of my husband is less significant to me than this dung." Then Islam came, and it confirmed them in what they had been upon, of remaining the year, by this verse. Then that was abrogated by the verse preceding it in the arrangement of the Qur'an, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those of you who die and leave wives behind, they shall wait by themselves for four months and ten days﴾, and the command to bequeath to her was abrogated by what was prescribed for her of the inheritance.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for divorced women is a provision according to what is customary﴾. The discussion of *mut'ah* (the provision or gift given to a divorced woman) has already preceded, with what suffices in it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 242:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus does Allah make clear to you His signs﴾, meaning: just as He made clear the rulings mentioned earlier. ﴿Thus does Allah make clear to you His signs so that you may understand (la'allakum ta'qilun)﴾, meaning: He establishes for you the attribute of the intelligent by your putting into practice what He has made clear to you. The fruit of intellect (ʿaql) is the practice of upright things. Do you not see His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Repentance is only incumbent upon Allah for those who do evil in ignorance﴾ [An-Nisa: 17]? They were only called ignorant (juhhal, plural of jahil) because they preferred their desires over what they knew to be the truth.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 243:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes⦌ — its meaning: "Have you not known?" Ibn Qutayba said: This is in the manner of wonder, as you say: "Do you not see what so-and-so is doing?"

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿while they were thousands﴾ — concerning this there are two views. The first: its meaning is "while they were in agreement" (mu'talifun); this was said by Ibn Zayd. The second: that it refers to number, and this is the view of the scholars, who differed regarding their number, in seven sayings. The first: they were four thousand. The second: forty thousand, both reported from Ibn Abbas. The third: ninety thousand, said by Ata' ibn Abi Rabah. The fourth: seven thousand, said by Abu Salih. The fifth: thirty thousand, said by Abu Malik. The sixth: "a few over thirty thousand" (bid'a wa-thalathina alfan), said by al-Suddi. The seventh: eight thousand, said by Muqatil. Regarding the meaning of "He said to them: Die," there are two views. The first: they fled from the plague (ta'un), which had descended upon them; this was said by al-Hasan and al-Suddi. The second: they were commanded to engage in jihad, and they fled from it; this was said by Ikrima and al-Dahhak, and from Ibn Abbas, like the two views above.

The reference to their story.

Husayn ibn Abd al-Rahman narrated from Hilal ibn Yasaf, who said: There was a community of the Children of Israel such that when the plague struck among them, their wealthy would leave and their poor would remain. Those who remained died, and those who left were saved. The nobles said: "If we remained as these did, we would perish." And the poor said: "If we departed as these did, we would be safe." So in one of the years their opinion united that they should all depart together, and they departed and died, and became bones glistening, so the people of the houses and the roads swept them from their houses and roads. A prophet of the prophets passed by them and said: "O my Lord, if You willed, You would have revived them, and they would have worshipped You, and begotten children who would worship You, and populated Your lands." [He said: "Would You love it if I did so?" He said: "Yes."] It was said to him: "Speak with such-and-such," and he spoke with it, and he looked at the bones coming forth from the bones that were not part of them to those that were part of them. Then it was said to him: "Speak with such-and-such," and he spoke with it, and he looked at the bones being clothed with flesh and sinews. Then it was said to him: "Speak with such-and-such," and he looked, and behold, they were sitting, glorifying God and sanctifying Him. And God revealed this verse concerning them. This narration indicates the long duration in which they remained dead. In some reports: they remained dead for seven days; and it was said: eight days.

Concerning the prophet who supplicated for them, there are two views. The first: he was Hizqil (Ezekiel). The second: he was Shim'un (Simeon). If it is said: how were these made to die twice, when God, the Exalted, has said: ﴿except the first death⦌ [al-Dukhan: 56]? The answer: their death by punishment did not finish their lifespans, so it was like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and the one who has not died in her sleep⦌ [al-Zumar: 42]. It was also said: their revival was a sign from the signs of their prophet, and the signs of the prophets are rare and are not to be measured against; so the meaning of His saying, the Exalted, ﴿except the first death⦌ is the death that is not among the signs of the prophets, nor for a rare matter. In this story there is an argument against the Jews, since the Prophet ﷺ informed them of a matter they had not witnessed while they knew its truth; and an argument against those who deny the Resurrection, for He showed them by the revival of the dead in this world. Ibn al-Anbari related all of this.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, God is bountiful to mankind⦌ — the Mighty and Majestic drew attention, by mentioning His favour upon these, to His favour upon all of His creation, despite the scarcity of their gratitude.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 244:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾. Regarding those addressed by this, there are two opinions. The first: they are the ones whom Allah caused to die and then brought back to life; this was said by al-Dahhak. The second: it is an address to the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ). Its meaning is: do not flee from death as these people fled, for fleeing does not benefit you. ﴿And know that Allah is Hearing﴾ of your statements, ﴿Knowing﴾ of what your inner thoughts conceal.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 245:**

Allah's words: ﴿Who is it that will lend to Allah?﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: The origin of *qard* (loan) is what a person gives or does in order to be repaid for it. Linguistically, its root meaning is "cutting," and from it comes *al-miqrad* (scissors). So the meaning of "aqradtuhu" (I lent him) is: I cut for him a portion for which he will repay me. If it is asked, "What is the reason for calling charity a loan?" the answer has three aspects.

(p-290) The first is that this loan is repaid with a reward. The second is that its repayment is deferred until the Day of Resurrection. The third is to affirm the entitlement to reward through it, since there is no loan without a return that is owed because of it. As for the Jews, they were ignorant of this, so they said: "Does Allah borrow from us?" As for the Muslims, they trusted in Allah's promise and hastened to deal with Him.

Ibn Mas'ud said: "When this verse was revealed, Abu al-Dahdah said: 'Does Allah really want a loan from us?' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Show me your hand.' He said: 'I have lent my garden to my Lord.' His garden had six hundred palm trees. Then he came to the garden and said: 'O Umm al-Dahdah, come out of the garden, for I have lent it to my Lord.'" In some wordings: "She went to her children, taking out what was in their mouths and shaking out what was in their sleeves. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'How many a luxuriant date cluster in Paradise belongs to Abu al-Dahdah!'"

There are six opinions on the meaning of *qard hasan* (the good loan). The first: it is purely for Allah, as said by al-Dahhak. The second: it is given with a willing heart, as said by Muqatil. The third: it is lawful (*halal*), as said by Ibn al-Mubarak. The fourth: one seeks its reward from Allah. The fifth: one does not follow it with reminders or harm. The sixth: it is of the best of one's wealth.

Allah's words: ﴿and He will multiply it for him﴾. Abu Amr recited *fayudā'ifuhu* with an *alif* and a *raf'* (nominative *damma*) on the *fa'*, and so throughout the Qur'an, except in Surat al-Ahzab, where the verse "its punishment will be doubled for her" (*yudā'afu lahā al-'adhābu di'fayn*) is recited with the *alif*. Nafi', Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited all of these with the *alif* and *raf'* on the *fa'*. Ibn Kathir recited *fayuḍa'ifuhu* with *raf'* on the *fa'*, without an *alif*, throughout the Qur'an. Ibn Amir recited *fayuḍa''ifuhu* with a shaddah on the *'ayn* and no *alif*, throughout the Qur'an. Asim agreed with him on the *nasb* (accusative *fatha*) of the *fa'* in *fayuḍā'ifahu*, but he placed the *alif* throughout the Qur'an.

Abu Ali (al-Farisi) said: For the *raf'* there are two possibilities. The first is that it is coordinated with what is in the relative clause, namely *yuqriḍu* (lends). The second is that it begins a new clause. Whoever reads it in the accusative (*nasb*) treats the sentence according to its meaning, since the meaning is: "Would it be that he lends?" So he construes *fayuḍā'ifahu* accordingly. He said: The meanings of *ḍā'afa* and *ḍa'afa* are the same, and *al-muḍā'afah* (multiplication) is adding to a thing until it becomes double or more.

(p-291) Regarding the great multiplication there are two opinions. The first is that its number cannot be counted, as said by Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi. Abu Uthman al-Nahdi narrated from Abu Hurayrah that he said: "Allah writes for the believer, for one good deed, two thousand thousand good deeds." Then he recited this verse and said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'Allah multiplies a good deed two thousand thousand times.'" The second is that its measure is known: a dirham is seven hundred, as mentioned in the verse that follows it, as said by Ibn Zayd.

Allah's words: ﴿And Allah withholds and extends﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited *yabsuṭu* and *basṭatan* with the letter *sin*. Nafi' recited both with the letter *sad*. Regarding the meaning of the statement there are two opinions. The first is that it means: He restricts provision for whomever He wills and extends it to whomever He wills, as said by Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd. The second is: He withholds the hand of whomever He wills from spending in His way, and extends the hand of whomever He wills to spend, as said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi and others.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 246:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not considered the eminent men (al-mala', the notables) of the Children of Israel﴾. Al-Farra' said: "Al-mala' means men in every (p-٢٩٢) Qur'an; women are never among them, and likewise the qawm (people), the nafar (group), and the rahT (company)." Al-Zajjaj said: "Al-mala' are the dignitaries and the people of judgment. They were called mala' because they are capable (malee'un) of what is needed from them."

Regarding their prophet, there are three opinions. The first is that he was Shamwil (Samuel), as said by Ibn 'Abbas and Wahb. The second is that he was Yusha' ibn Nun (Joshua son of Nun), as said by Qatada. The third is that he was a prophet called Sam'un with the unpointed sin, named by his mother for this reason: she supplicated God to grant her a boy, her supplication was heard concerning him, so she named him accordingly. This is the saying of al-Suddi.

The reason for their asking for a king was that their enemy had overcome them.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Let us fight﴾. The recitation (qira'a) of the majority (al-Jumhur) is with the nun and the jussive (jazm). Ibn Abi 'Ablah read it with the ya' and the nominative (raf'), as a reference to the king.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Would you perhaps...﴾ The recitation of the majority is with a fatha on the sin (ʿasaytum). Nafi' read it with a kasra here and in the surah of Muhammad, and both are dialects (lughatan).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If fighting is prescribed for you﴾, meaning obligated (furiḍa). ﴿That you will not fight﴾, meaning: perhaps you will turn cowardly (tajbununa).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And we have been expelled from our homes﴾. They mean that some of us were expelled, namely those among them who were taken captive and subdued. Its apparent meaning is general, but its intended meaning is specific (khusus).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They turned away﴾, meaning they turned away from jihad. ﴿Except a few﴾, and they are those who crossed the river, whose mention will come later.

Al-Zajjaj said: Talut, Jalut, and Dawud are not declined (la tanṣarif), because they are foreign (ʿajamiyya) names and they are definite (maʿarif), so definiteness and foreignness are combined in them.

The meaning of His, the Exalted's, words: "How can he have kingship over us?" means: from what direction would kingship be his over us? Ibn ʿAbbas said: They only said this because among the Children of Israel there were two tribes (sibṭān): in one of them was prophethood, and in the other was kingship, and he was not from either of the two tribes. Qatada said: Prophethood was in the tribe of Levi, and kingship was in the tribe of Judah.

His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿"And he has not been given abundance of wealth."﴾ That is: he has not been given what a king uses to hold dominion. ﴿He said: "Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you."﴾ That is: He preferred him. It is "iftaʿala" from al-ṣafwa (the choice part). And al-basta (expansiveness): it is abundance (al-siʿa). Ibn Qutayba said: it comes from your saying "basaṭtu al-shayʾ," when it was gathered and I opened it and widened it. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Talut was the most knowledgeable of the Children of Israel in war, and he would surpass people by his shoulders, his neck, and his head.

(p-294) Was this increase in size before the kingship, or was it added to him after the kingship? In this there are two opinions. One of them: it was before the kingship, said by Wahb and al-Suddi. The second: it was after the kingship, said by Ibn Zayd. What is meant by enlargement of the body is the excellence of strength, since the custom is that whoever is greater in body is greater in strength. Al-wasiʿ: the wealthy one.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 248:

Allah's words: ﴿And their Prophet said to them: Indeed the sign (āyah) of his kingship﴾. The word āyah means "sign" (ʿalāmah), so the meaning is: the sign of Allah's granting him kingship. ﴿That there will come to you the chest (tābūt)﴾. This is a figurative usage (majāz) of speech, because the chest is brought, not that it "comes" by itself. A similar example is ﴿Then when the matter is resolved (ʿazama al-amr)﴾. Such usage is permissible because there is no confusion in it, as we explained in His words: ﴿so their commerce did not profit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16].

It is reported from Ibn Masʿud and Ibn ʿAbbas that they said to their Prophet: "If you are truthful, bring us a sign that indicates he is a king," and so he said this to them. Wahb said: He gave them the choice of whatever sign they wished, and they said: that the chest be returned to us.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: The chest was made of shimshar wood, with plates of gold upon it, and it used to be with the prophets when they attended a battle; they would send it before them, seeking victory through it, and in it was the sakinah (tranquility).

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: It was about three cubits by two cubits. Muqatil said: When the Children of Israel scattered and disobeyed the prophets, Allah gave their enemy power over them, and they overcame them and took it.

Regarding the sakinah there are seven opinions:
First: that it is a gentle wind with a face like a human face; narrated by Abu al-Ahwas from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him.
Second: that it is a creature the size of a cat, with two eyes that have rays; when the two hosts met, it would extend its paw and look at them, and the army would be routed from terror. Narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas. Mujahid said: the sakinah has a head like a cat's head and two wings.
Third: that it is a basin of gold [from Paradise] in which the hearts of the prophets were washed; narrated by Abu Malik from Ibn ʿAbbas.
Fourth: that it is a spirit from Allah that speaks; whenever they disagreed about something, it spoke to them and informed them of the clarification of what they sought; narrated by ʿAbd al-Samad ibn Maʿqil from Wahb ibn Munabbih.
Fifth: that the sakinah is the signs they recognize, by which they become tranquil; narrated by Ibn Jurayj from ʿAta ibn Abi Rabah. al-Zajjaj took a similar view, saying: sakinah is from sukun (stillness), so its meaning is: in it is that which you find tranquility in when it comes to you.
Sixth: that sakinah here means dignity (waqar); narrated by Maʿmar from Qatadah.
Seventh: that sakinah means mercy; said by al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas.

As for the remainder (baqiyyah), there are nine opinions:
First: that it is the shattered fragments of the tablets which broke when Musa threw them down along with his staff; said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah, and al-Suddi.
Second: that it is the fragments of the tablets; said by ʿIkrimah, who did not mention the staff. It was also said: Musa only made the chest in order to gather the fragments of the tablets within it.
Third: that it is the staff of Musa and the sakinah; said by Wahb.
Fourth: the staff of Musa, the staff of Harun, their garments, two tablets of the Torah, and the manna; said by Abu Salih.
Fifth: that the baqiyyah is knowledge and the Torah; said by Mujahid and ʿAta ibn Abi Rabah.
Sixth: that it is the fragments of the tablets, a qafiz of manna in a basin of gold, the staff of Musa and his turban; said by Muqatil.
Seventh: that it is a qafiz of manna and the fragments of the tablets; related by Sufyan al-Thawri from some scholars.
Eighth: that it is the staff of Musa and the two sandals; also mentioned by al-Thawri from some people of knowledge.
Ninth: that the intended meaning of the baqiyyah is jihad in the way of Allah, and they were commanded with that; said by al-Dahhak.

The intended meaning of "the family of Musa and the family of Harun" is Musa and Harun themselves. Abu ʿUbaydah recited:

"Do not weep for one dead after another: ʿAli and ʿAbbas and the family of Abu Bakr, beloved ones."

He means Abu Bakr himself.

Allah's words: ﴿carried by the angels﴾. The majority read "tahmiluhu" with a ta'; al-Hasan, Mujahid and al-Aʿmash read it with a ya'. Regarding the place from which the angels carried it to them, there are two opinions:
One: that it was lifted up with the angels between heaven and earth from the time it left the Children of Israel; said by al-Hasan.
Two: that it was on the earth.

Regarding which place it was in, there are two opinions:
One: that it was in the hands of the Amalekites, who had buried it. Ibn ʿAbbas said: The people of Jalut took the chest and buried it in a place where they relieved themselves; then hemorrhoids (al-basur) seized them and they perished. Then the people of another city took it, and calamity befell them and they perished, and so on, until five cities were destroyed. So they brought it out on two cows and directed them toward the Children of Israel, and the angels drove the two of them.
Two: that it was in the wilderness of al-Tih, where Yusha left it, and they did not know its place until the angels brought it; said by Qatadah.

Regarding how the angels brought it, there are two opinions:
One: that they brought it themselves. Wahb said: They said to their Prophet: "Set for us a time when it will come to us." He said: "The morning." So they did not sleep that night, and the angels arrived with it at dawn, and they heard the rustling of the angels carrying it between heaven and earth.
Two: that the angels brought it on a cart and two bulls; also reported from Wahb. According to the first view, the meaning of "tahmiluhu" is "carrying it" (tuqilluhu); according to the second, the meaning of "hamalaha iyyahu" is that they caused its carrying. al-Zajjaj said: In the language it is permissible to say "I carried the thing" when I was the cause of its being carried.

Allah's words: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for you﴾, i.e., a sign indicating the granting of kingship to Talut. The exegetes said: When the chest came to them and they acknowledged his kingship, he prepared to set out, and they hastened in obedience to him and went out with him. That is His words: ﴿...﴾.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When Talut set out with the troops﴾ means he went out and departed. There are three opinions on the number of those who went out with him. The first is seventy thousand, related from Ibn 'Abbas. The second is eighty thousand, said by 'Ikrimah and al-Suddi. The third is one hundred thousand, said by Muqatil. He said: They marched in intense heat, so Allah tested them with the river. *Al-ibtila'* (trial) means testing. For the word *al-nahr* (river) there are two dialectal forms. One is with a vowelled *ha'* (*nahr*), which is the recitation (*qira'ah*) of the majority. The other is with the *ha'* made silent (*nahr*), and al-Hasan and Mujahid recited it this way. Regarding this river there are two opinions. The first is that it is the river of Palestine, said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi. The second is that it is a river between the Jordan and Palestine, said by 'Ikrimah, Qatadah and al-Rabi' ibn Anas. The wisdom in testing them with it was that Talut would know who among them had the intention to fight and who did not.

His saying: ﴿So he is not of me﴾ means: he is not of my companions.

His saying: ﴿except one who takes a handful﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read *ghurfatan* with a fatha on the *ghayn*. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma on the *ghayn*. Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads it with a fatha intends one scoop with the hand, and whoever reads it with a damma intends a full handful. Muqatil claimed that the *ghurfah* was what a man would drink from, along with his animal and his servants, and with which he would fill his waterskin. Some exegetes said: he did not mean a cupped handful, but rather one drink from a waterskin, a jar, or something similar. Regarding the number of the few who drank only one handful, there are two opinions. The first is that they were four thousand, said by 'Ikrimah and al-Suddi. The second is three hundred and thirteen men, and this is the sound view, based on what is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said to his companions on the day of Badr: "You are in the number of the companions of Talut on the day of meeting Jalut." On the day of Badr they were three hundred and thirteen men.

His saying: ﴿We have no strength﴾ means we have no power. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said *ataqtu al-shay'a ito'aqatan wa taqatan wa taw'an* (أطَقْتُ الشَّيْءَ إطاقَةً وطاقَةً، وطَوْقًا), like your saying *ata'tuhu ita'atan wa ta'atan wa taw'an* (أطَعْتُهُ إطاعَةً وطاعَةً وطَوْعًا), meaning "I had the ability for the thing."

They differed about those who said this, on three opinions. The first is that they were those who drank more than one handful; they turned back and did not witness the battle, and they were people of doubt and hypocrisy, said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi. The second is that they were those among the believers whose insight was weak, said by al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. The third is that it was the statement of those who crossed with him, and some of them said it to one another because of how few they saw themselves to be. This is the choice of al-Zajjaj.

His saying: ﴿Those who think﴾. Regarding this *zann* (thinking/assumption) there are two opinions. The first is that it means certainty (*yaqin*), said by al-Suddi and others. The second is that it is the *zann* meaning uncertainty and doubt, for the people imagined, because of their small number, that they would be killed and would meet Allah, said by al-Zajjaj and others. Regarding those who held this assumption there are two opinions. The first is that they were the three hundred and thirteen, who said to those who turned back: "How many a small group has overcome a large group," said by al-Suddi. The second is that they were the people of firm resolve and merit among the three hundred and thirteen. *Al-fi'ah* means a group. Al-Zajjaj said: they were called *fi'ah* from the saying *fa'awtu ra'sahu bil-'asa* (فَأوْتُ رَأْسَهُ بِالعَصا) and *fa'aytuhu* (فَأيْتُهُ), meaning when I split it open.

His saying: ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾. Al-Hasan said: by the help of Allah.

His saying: ﴿And Allah is with the patient﴾, meaning with victory and assistance.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 250:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When they went forth to face Goliath and his armies﴾ means: they came out into the open (al-buraz) from the land, and al-buraz is what is apparent and level. ﴿Pour upon us patience﴾ (afrigh) is in the sense of "pour" (usubb). ﴿And make firm our feet﴾ means: strengthen our hearts so that our feet may be made firm, for feet only stand firm when hearts are strong. Muqatil said: Jalut (Goliath) and his soldiers used to worship idols.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 251:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So they routed them﴾ means: they broke them and drove them back. Al-Zajjaj said: The root of hazm (routing, breaking) in the language is breaking a thing and folding part of it over another. It is said: a waterskin is munhazim [and muhazzam] when part of it has been folded over another while dry, and a reed is munhazim when it has been broken and split. The Arabs say: hazamtu 'ala Zayd, meaning: I inclined toward him (ʿaṭaftu ʿalayhi).

The poet said:

I have turned toward you today, daughter of Malik, so be generous to us with gifts and bestow your favor.

It is also said: I heard the hazmat al-ra'd (the crash of thunder). Al-Asma'i said: It is as though it were a sound in which there is a cracking.

Dawud: he was the Prophet of Allah, Abu Sulayman, and his name is a non-Arabic name. It is said that the brothers of Dawud were with Talut, and Dawud went to look at them. Stones called out to him: "Take me!" So he took them and came to Talut, who said: "What will I have if I kill Jalut?" He said: "A third of my kingdom, and I will marry you to my daughter." So Jalut was killed.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah gave him the kingdom﴾ means: He gave Dawud the kingdom of Talut. Concerning what is meant by "wisdom" here there are two views. The first: it is prophethood, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: it is the Zabur (Psalms), said by Muqatil. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and taught him of what He willed﴾ has three views. The first: it is the craft of making armour. The second: the Zabur. The third: the speech of the birds (mantiq al-tayr).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And had Allah not repelled some people by means of others﴾ — the majority read (daf'a Allahu) here without an alif, and in al-Hajj; Nafi', Ya'qub and Aban read (wa-law-la difa') with an alif in both places. Abu 'Ali said: the two meanings are close. The poet said:

I was eager to defend them, but when death came, it could not be repelled.

Concerning the meaning of the statement there are two views. The first: its meaning is that Allah repels, through those who obey Him, those who disobey Him, just as He repelled from those who stayed behind from Talut through those who obeyed Him; otherwise the sinners would have been destroyed by swift punishment. This was said by Mujahid. The second: its meaning is that, had Allah not repelled the polytheists by means of the Muslims, the polytheists would have overcome the earth, killed the Muslims, and destroyed the mosques. This was said by Muqatil. The meaning of ﴿the earth would have been corrupted﴾ is that its inhabitants would have been destroyed.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 252:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿These are the verses of Allah, which We recite to you in truth﴾. That is: We relate to you some of the reports of the earlier nations.

(p-301) ﴿And indeed, you are among the messengers﴾. Your ruling is their ruling: whoever believes you, his path is the path of those who believed them, and whoever disobeys you, his path is the path of those who disobeyed them.

Part Three

The Qur'an quotations are in ﴿ ﴾, following the instructions.

**"Among them are those to whom Allah spoke"** (﴿مِنهم مَن كَلَّمَ اللَّهُ﴾). He means Musa (Moses), peace be upon him.

Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu Nahik, and Ibn al-Sami'fa' read it as "مِنهم مَن كالَمَ اللَّهَ" (*kālama*, with a long alif and a light *lām*), with the word *Allāh* in the accusative (*naṣb*). In this reading the verb is from *mukālama* (speaking with), and *Allāh* is the object, so the sense is that Musa spoke with Allah, rather than that Allah spoke to him.

Regarding His saying, **"and He raised some of them by degrees"** (﴿وَرَفَعَ بَعْضَهم دَرَجاتٍ﴾), there are two opinions.

The first is that by "those raised by degrees" he means Muhammad (ﷺ), because he was sent to all people, whereas the others were sent only to their own communities. This is the view of Mujahid.

The second is that it refers to the preference of some of them over others in what Allah gave them. This is the view of Muqatil.

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: *darajāt* is the plural of *daraja* (degree, rank), which means a level or station. Its original meaning is the rungs and steps of a ladder, and then it is used for the elevation of positions and ranks.

The explanation of "*al-bayyināt*" (the clear proofs) and "*Rūḥ al-Qudus*" (the Holy Spirit) has already been given earlier.

His saying, **"Had Allah willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another"** (﴿وَلَوْ شاءَ اللَّهُ ما اقْتَتَلَ الَّذِينَ مِن بَعْدِهِمْ﴾), means: after the prophets. Qatadah said: after Musa and Isa (Jesus), peace be upon them both. Muqatil said: there were a thousand prophets between the two of them.

His saying, **"but they differed"** (﴿وَلَكِنِ اخْتَلَفُوا﴾), means: the nations.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 254:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, spend from what We have provided for you﴾. This verse urges charity and spending in the various ways of obedience. Al-Hasan said: it means the obligatory zakah (obligatory almsgiving).

(p-302) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿before there comes a Day﴾, meaning the Day of Resurrection, ﴿in which there is no trade﴾. Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr recited "لا بَيْعَ فِيهِ وَلا خُلَّةَ وَلا شَفَاعَةَ" with the accusative (naṣb) and without tanwin (nunation). The same applies to "لا بَيْعَ فِيهِ" in Surah Ibrahim, and to "لا لَغْوَ فِيها وَلا تَأْثِيمَ" in Surah al-Tur. Nafi', Asim, Ibn Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited all of these with the nominative (raf') and tanwin. Ibn Abbas said: there is no ransom (fidyah) in it. It was said: the word "bay'" (trade) is mentioned because it involves exchange and taking a substitute. Khullah means friendship. It was also said: these things are negated because it refers to the disbelievers, and these things do not benefit them. For this reason He said: ﴿And the disbelievers, they are the wrongdoers﴾.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 255:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah! There is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of existence.﴾ Muslim related in his Sahih from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that the Prophet ﷺ said to him: "O Abu al-Mundhir! Do you know which verse in the Book of Allah is the greatest?" He said: I said: ﴿Allah! There is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of existence.﴾ He said: So he struck me on the chest and said: "May knowledge be pleasant for you, O Abu al-Mundhir!"

Abu 'Ubayda said: al-Qayyum (the Sustainer) is the One who does not cease, because His attribute of existence is constant, such that change is not possible for Him in any way whatsoever. Al-Zajjaj said: al-Qayyum is the one who maintains the management of the affairs of creation. Al-Khattabi said: al-Qayyum is the One who stands, persisting without cessation. Its form is fa'yul from al-qiyam (standing), and it is an intensive adjective denoting standing over a thing. It is also said: He is the one who stands over everything in preservation. One says: "I stood over the matter" when I took charge of it with care and welfare.

In al-Qayyum there are three dialectal forms: al-Qayyum, which is how the majority recited it; al-Qiyam, which is how 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abi 'Abla and al-A'mash recited it; and al-Qayyim, which is how Abu Razin and 'Alqama recited it. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned that it is likewise in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud. He said: The original form of al-Qayyum is al-Qayyuwm. When the yā' and the wāw came together, with the preceding letter being silent, both were made into a doubled yā'. The original form of al-Qiyam is al-Qawwam. Al-Farra' said: The people of the Hijaz change the pattern fi'al to fay'al, so they say for the goldsmith: sayyagh.

As for al-sinah (drowsiness), it is slumber without sleep, and from it comes wasnan (drowsy). Ibn al-Riqa' said:

"As if she, among the women, was given by him two eyes, black-and-white, of a gazelle of the sands, having a stout bulk."

"A drowsy one whom slumber overcame, so it made a veil over his eye, a drowsiness, though he is not asleep."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾ Some scholars said: He did not say "wal-ardīn" (and the earths) because the plural had already been mentioned for the heavens, so this sufficed, and similarly ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾, where He did not say "al-anwar" (the lights).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Who is it that intercedes with Him except by His permission?﴾ In this there is a refutation of those who said: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to Allah in nearness﴾ [az-Zumar: 3].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them.﴾ The apparent meaning of the speech requires that it refers to all creation. Muqatil said: The intended referents are the angels. Regarding what is meant by ﴿what is before them and what is behind them﴾ there are three opinions. The first: what is before them is the matter of the Hereafter, and what is behind them is the matter of this world; this is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada. The second: what is before them is this world, and what is behind them is the Hereafter; this was said by al-Suddi, from his shaykhs, and by Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj and al-Hakam ibn 'Utayba. The third: what is before them is what preceded their creation, and what is behind them is what follows their creation; this was said by Muqatil.

(p-304) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they do not encompass anything﴾. Al-Layth said: It is said of anyone who has secured something, or whose knowledge reaches its furthest extent: "He has encompassed it." The intended meaning of knowledge here is what is known. ﴿His Kursi has encompassed the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: it contained and was sufficient for them. Regarding what is meant by al-Kursi there are three opinions. The first: it is a Kursi above the seventh heaven, beneath the Throne. The Prophet ﷺ said: "The seven heavens in comparison to the Kursi are nothing but like a ring thrown down in a desert land." This is the opinion of Ibn 'Abbas in the narration of 'Ata'. The second: the intended meaning of the Kursi is the knowledge of Allah the Exalted; this was related by Ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas. The third: the Kursi is the Throne; this was said by al-Hasan.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it does not tire Him﴾, meaning: it does not burden Him. It is said: "The thing ya'uduh a'dan wa iyadan" (burdened him). Al-Awd means heaviness. This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, and the majority.

Al-'Aliyy: the Exalted, the Dominant; it is fa'il in the sense of fa'il. Al-Khattabi said: It may also derive from al-'uluww, which is the verbal noun of 'alā ya'lu, so he is 'ali, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Most Merciful, established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5]. It may also be from 'ala' al-majd wa'l-sharaf (the loftiness of glory and nobility); it is said from it: 'ala ya'la 'ala'an. The meaning of al-'Azim: possessor of greatness and majesty. Greatness with regard to Him, exalted is He, refers to the magnitude of His station and the sublimity of His rank, not the size that is a attribute of bodies.

**Section**

Scholars of the abrogating and the abrogated (*al-nāsikh wa-l-mansūkh*, the study of which verses abrogate others) differed regarding this part of the verse. One group held that it is *muḥkam* (not abrogated), and that it is among the general (*ʿāmm*) rulings that have been specified (*makhṣūṣ*). It was specified for the People of the Book, who are not compelled to accept Islam but are given the choice between it and paying the *jizya* (poll tax). This is the meaning reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and Qatāda.

(p-306) Ibn al-Anbārī said: The meaning of the verse is: "Religion is not what one professes outwardly under compulsion, while the heart does not bear witness to it and the inner consciences do not hold it. Rather, religion is that which is firmly established in the heart." Another group held that it is abrogated, saying: "This verse was revealed before the command to fight." According to their view, it is abrogated by the "verse of the sword." This is the position of al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Suddī, and Ibn Zayd.

Here, "religion" (*al-dīn*) is intended to mean Islam. *Al-rushd* (right guidance) is truth, and *al-ghayy* (error) is falsehood. It was also said that they refer to faith and disbelief.

As for *al-ṭāghūt* (the transgressor, false object of worship), it is a noun derived from *al-ṭughyān*, which means exceeding the limit. Ibn Qutayba said: *al-ṭāghūt* can be singular or plural, masculine or feminine. God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Their protectors are the *ṭāghūt*﴾ and He said: ﴿And those who avoid the *ṭāghūt* from worshipping it﴾ [Az-Zumar: 17]. There are five opinions regarding what is meant by *al-ṭāghūt* here:

1. It is Satan. This was said by ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Shaʿbī, al-Suddī, Muqātil, and others.
2. It is the soothsayer (*kāhin*). This was said by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Abū al-ʿĀliya.
3. It is the sorcerer. This was said by Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn.
4. It is the idols. This was said by al-Yazīdī and al-Zajjāj.
5. It is the rebellious leaders of the People of the Book. This too was mentioned by al-Zajjāj.

God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Then he has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾. This is a parable for faith, likening adherence to it to holding fast to a firm handle. Al-Zajjāj said: The meaning of the statement is: "He has tied for himself a firm knot." *Al-infiṣām* (breaking) is the breaking of a thing without separating it completely.

﴿اللَّهُ وَلِيُّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾: that is, the one who manages their affairs, guides them, helps them, and assists them. "Al-zulumāt" (the darknesses) means misguidance, and "al-nūr" (the light) means guidance. "Al-ṭāghūt" (the rebellious powers) means the devils. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, and others. Muqātil said: "Those who disbelieve" are the Jews, and "al-ṭāghūt" is Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf. [p-307] Al-Zajjāj said: "Al-ṭāghūt" here is singular in form but has the meaning of a plural, and this is permissible in the language when the context contains an indication of the plural. The poet said:

*Therein are the carcasses of the worn-out (camels); as for their bones, they are white, and as for their hides, they are tough.*

He meant "their hides" (julūdahā). If it is asked: When were the believers in darkness, and when were the disbelievers in light? There are three answers to this:

The first: God's protection of the believers from falling into misguidance is a bringing them out of the darkness of disbelief. The embellishment by the disbelievers' companions of falsehood for them, through which they deviate from guidance, is a bringing them out of the light of guidance. The word "bringing out" (al-ikhrāj) is used here figuratively. It may be said of one who abstains from something: "He came out of it," even if he had not entered into it. God said: ﴿Indeed, I have left the religion of a people who do not believe in God﴾ [Yūsuf: 37], and He said: ﴿And among you is one who is returned to the most abject old age﴾ [al-Naḥl: 70]. Evidence for this has already preceded in His saying: ﴿And to God are all matters returned﴾ [al-Baqara: 210].

The second: the faith of the People of the Book in the Prophet before a light had appeared to them, and their disbelief in him after it had appeared, is an exit into darkness.

The third: when the miracles of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) became manifest, the one who opposed him was departing from a light that he already knew, and the one who agreed with him was departing from the darknesses of ignorance into the light of knowledge.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 258:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord?﴾ The meaning of "Have you not considered" has already been discussed. "Hajja" means "disputed" (khasama), and he was Nimrod according to the consensus of the scholars (al-jama'a). Ibn 'Abbas said: he ruled the earth, its east and its west. Two believers and two disbelievers ruled the earth: the believers were Sulayman ibn Dawud and Dhu al-Qarnayn, and the disbelievers were Nimrod and Bukhtnassar.

Ibn Qutayba said: the meaning of the verse is that he argued with Abraham because God had given him kingship, so he became conceited about himself and his kingdom.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When Abraham said, "My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death."﴾ Some of them said: this is an answer to an earlier question that is not mentioned, its implied form being: he said to him, "Who is your Lord?" and he said, "My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death." Nimrod said, "I give life and cause death." Ibn 'Abbas said: he meant, "I leave alive whomever I wish and kill whomever I wish." If it is asked: why did Abraham move to a different argument and turn away from supporting the first one? The answer is that Abraham saw, from the corruption of his opponent's objection, something that showed the weakness of his understanding, for he countered the wording with its like and forgot the difference between the two actions. So he moved to another argument, intending to cut off the debate, not out of inability to support the first one.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So the one who disbelieved was confounded.﴾ That is: his argument was cut off, so he was bewildered. Abu Razin al-'Uqayli and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read "fabuhita" with a fatha on the ba' and the ha'. Abu al-Jawza', Yahya ibn Ya'mur and Abu Haywa read "fabuhita" with a fatha on the ba' and a damma on the ha'. Al-Kisa'i said: among the Arabs there are those who say "bahita" and "bahuta," with a kasra or damma on the ha'. ﴿And God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾: meaning the disbelievers. Muqatil said: He does not guide them to the proof, and by this he meant Nimrod.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 259:

Allah's words: ﴿Or like the one who passed by a town﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: This is joined (ma'tuf) to the meaning of the statement before it. Its meaning is: "Have you not considered the one who argued with Ibrahim, or the one who passed by a town?" Regarding what is meant by "the town," there are two views. The first: it is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) when Bukhtanassar (Nebuchadnezzar) destroyed it; this was said by Wahb, Qatadah, and al-Rabi' ibn Anas. The second: it is the town from which thousands went out fearing death; this was said by Ibn Zayd. As for the one who passed by it, there are three views. The first: he was 'Uzayr; this was said by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu al-'Aliyah, 'Ikrimah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Naji'ah ibn Ka'b, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, and Muqatil. The second: he was Irmiya; this was said by Wahb, Mujahid, and 'Abdullah ibn 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr. The third: he was a disbelieving man who doubted the Resurrection; this was also reported from Mujahid. "Khawiyah" means "empty" (al-khaliyah), said al-Zajjaj. Ibn Qutaybah said: "Khawiyah" means ruin, and "'urush" means roofs; the origin of this is that the roofs fall, and then the walls fall upon them. ﴿He said, "How will Allah bring this to life?"﴾, i.e., how will He revive it. If we say this man was a prophet, then it is the statement of one who wishes to see how resurrection occurs, or seeks to be reassured, so he glorifies Allah's power. If we say he was a disbelieving man, then it is the statement of a doubter. The first view is more sound.

Allah's words: ﴿So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him﴾.

This refers to his story.

Naji'ah ibn Ka'b narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: 'Uzayr, the Prophet of Allah, left his city, and he was a young man. He passed by a town which was empty upon its roofs, and he said: "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?" So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him. The first thing Allah created in him was his eyes; he began to look at his bones joining one to another, then they were clothed with flesh, and the spirit was breathed into them. Al-Hasan said: Allah took him at the beginning of the day and raised him at the end of the day after a hundred years. Muqatil said: It was called out from the sky: "How long have you remained?" Qatadah said: He said: "I remained a day," then he looked and saw a remnant of the sun, and said: "Or part of a day." This indicates that he was 'Uzayr. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Irmiya stayed in the land of Egypt, and Allah revealed to him that he should go to the land of Iliya'. He mounted his donkey, took with him a basket of grapes and figs, and with him a new waterskin, containing water. When he came in sight of Bayt al-Maqdis and what surrounded it of villages [and mosques], he saw a ruin that cannot be described. [When he saw the demolition of Bayt al-Maqdis like a great mountain] he said: "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?" Then he dismounted at a place, tied up his donkey, [and hung up his waterskin], and Allah cast sleep upon him, and took his soul for a hundred years. When seventy years had passed, Allah sent an angel to a king of the kings of Persia, a great one, and said: "Allah commands you to march with your people and rebuild Bayt al-Maqdis, Iliya' and its land until it returns to being more populous than it was." [The king said: "Give me three days to prepare for this work and the tools that will fix it," so he gave him three days.] He appointed three hundred overseers, and to each overseer he gave a thousand workers, and the tools needed [so his overseers set out there with three hundred thousand workers]. When they began the work, Allah returned the spirit of life to the eyes of Irmiya, while the rest of his body was dead, and he looked at it being rebuilt. When it was completed after thirty years, Allah returned the spirit to him, and he looked at his food and drink, and they had not changed. [He looked at his donkey standing as it was the day he tied it, having neither eaten nor drunk; he looked at the rope on the donkey's neck, and it had not changed, new, though the wind of a hundred years, the cold of a hundred years, and the heat of a hundred years had passed over it, and it had not changed nor diminished at all. His body had been wasted by decay, so Allah caused new flesh to grow on him, and his bones rose up while he watched. Allah said to him: "Look at your food and drink, they have not changed; look at your donkey; and We will make you a sign for the people; and look at the bones, how We raise them, then clothe them with flesh." When it became clear to him, he said: "I know that Allah is over all things capable."] Muqatil claimed that this story took place after the raising of 'Isa, peace be upon him.

Allah's words: ﴿How long have you remained?﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and 'Asim recited "labithtu" and "labithtum" everywhere in the Qur'an with the ta' made clear. Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i recited with idgham (assimilation): "labittu." Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: Whoever makes "labithtu" clear does so because the points of articulation differ, since the zay, dhal, and tha' are from one region (hayyiz), and the ta', ta', and dal are from another region; when the points of articulation differ and the regions differ, it is not assimilated. Whoever assimilates treats them as two identical letters, because the two letters agree in that both are from the tip of the tongue and the roots of the front teeth, and they agree in being voiceless (hams); he saw the difference between them as slight, so he treated them as identical. As for his food and drink, Wahb said: He had with him a basket containing grapes and figs, and a jug containing water. al-Suddi said: He had figs and grapes, and his drink was from pressed juice; the figs and grapes had not turned sour, and the juice had not fermented.

Allah's words: ﴿It has not changed﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir recited "yatasanna" and "iqtadih" and "ma aghna 'anni maliyah" and "sultaniyah" and "mahiyah" with the ha' maintained in connected speech (wasl). Hamzah omitted them in connected speech, and al-Kisa'i agreed with him in omitting two places ("yatasannah" and "iqtadih"); all of them pause on the ha'. They did not differ regarding "kitabiyah" and "hisabiyah," which have the ha' both in connection and in pause. As for the meaning of "lam yatasanna," Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and others said: it has not changed. Ibn Qutaybah said: it has not changed by the passing of years over it, and the word is derived from "sanah" (year); it is said: "sana'hat al-nakhlah" when the palm tree bore fruit for a year and skipped a year.

Allah's words: ﴿Look at your donkey﴾. Muqatil said: Look at it, its bones having become white and its joints scattered, and Allah restored it.

Allah's words: ﴿And that We may make you a sign for the people﴾. The lam is connected to a hidden verb whose implied meaning is: "We did that to you so that We might show you Our power, and that We might make you a sign for the people," i.e., a marker of Our power; the verb was omitted to clarify its meaning. Ibn 'Abbas said: He died at the age of forty, and his son was twenty; then he was raised at the age of forty, and his son was a hundred and twenty; then he came until he reached his people in Bayt al-Maqdis and said to them: "I am 'Uzayr." They said: "Our fathers told us that 'Uzayr died in the land of Babylon." He said to them: "I am he; Allah sent me to you to renew your Torah for you, which had been lost, and none of them was reading it, so he dictated it to them."

Allah's words: ﴿And look at the bones﴾. It was said: he meant the bones of himself; it was said: the bones of his donkey; and it was said: both of them together.

Allah's words: ﴿How We raise them﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu 'Amr recited "nunshiruha" with the first nun dammah, the shin kasrah, and the ra' dammah. Its meaning is: We revive them; it is said: "Allah raised the dead" (anshara) and "nashara" them. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i recited "nunshizuha" with a dammah on the nun and the zay, from "nashaz," which means elevation. The meaning is: We raise some of them to others for the sake of life. al-A'mash recited "nanshuzuha" with a fathah on the nun and a dammah on the shin with the zay. al-Hasan and Aban from 'Asim recited "nanshuruha" with a fathah on the nun and the ra', as if it were from "nashr" (unfolding) after folding (tayy); so death had folded them, and revival unfolded them.

Allah's words: ﴿When it became clear to him﴾, i.e., the revival of the dead became clear to him. ﴿He said, "I know"﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir recited "a'lamu" with the alif cut off and the mim dammah. The meaning is: I have now known what I used to know unseen through direct witnessing. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited with the alif joined and the mim sukun, in the sense of a command, and beginning with a kasrah on the hamzah according to their recitation; the apparent meaning of the speech is that it is a command from Allah to him. Abu 'Ali said: he made himself like another, and commanded and addressed himself. al-Ja'fi, from Abu Bakr, recited "i'lam" with a kasrah on the lam, in the sense of a command to make another know.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 260:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not believed?﴾ That is: Have you not indeed believed that I give life to the dead? Ibn Jubayr said: Have you not been certain of the intimate friendship (khullah)?

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Yes, but that my heart may be at rest.﴾ The "lam" (of purpose, al-lam) is connected to a hidden verb; its estimated form is: "Rather, I asked you so that my heart may be at rest," or "Show me, so that my heart may be at rest." Then, regarding its meaning, there are four sayings. The first: "So that I may know that You answer me when I call upon You," related by Ibn Abbas. The second: "So that my heart may increase in certainty," related by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Al-Hasan said: Ibrahim was certain, but the report is not like direct witnessing (mu'ayanah). The third: "So that my heart may be at rest through the intimate friendship," also related from Ibn Jubayr. The fourth: that his heart was attached to seeing the giving of life to the dead, so he intended: "So that his heart may be at rest through sight," related by Ibn Qutaybah. Others said: His soul yearned to see that, and one who seeks a thing is restless until he attains his desire. What indicates that he did not ask out of doubt is that he said: ﴿Show me how You give life to the dead﴾ and he did not say: "Do You give life to the dead?"

(p-314) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Take four of the birds﴾ Regarding the birds he took, there are seven sayings. The first: they are the dove, the rooster, the crane, and the peacock, related by Abdullah ibn Hubayrah from Ibn Abbas. The second: they are the peacock, the rooster, the Sindhi hen, and the goose, related by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas. In another wording, related by al-Dahhak, in place of the Sindhi hen is the ra'l, which is the young ostrich. The third: they are the shi'anin (a kind of bird), which were their offerings on that day, related by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. The fourth: they are the peacock, the vulture, the raven, and the rooster, also related from Ibn Abbas. The fifth: they are the rooster, the peacock, the raven, and the pigeon, said by Ikrimah, Mujahid, Ata, Ibn Jurayj, and Ibn Zayd. The sixth: they are a rooster, a raven, a duck, and a peacock, related by Layth from Mujahid. The seventh: they are the rooster, the duck, the raven, and the dove, said by Muqatil. Ata al-Khurasani said: Allah revealed to him that he should take a duck, a black raven, a white dove, and a red rooster.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then make them incline toward you﴾ The majority read it with a ḍammah on the ṣād (ṣurhunna), and the meaning is: incline them toward you. It is said: "I inclined the thing and it leaned (infaana)," that is, I inclined it so it tilted. They cited the verse:

"Allah knows that we, in our glancing at our neighbors on the day of parting, are inclined (ṣūr)."

So the meaning of the statement is: gather them to you. ﴿Then place upon every mountain a portion of them﴾ This implies their cutting up. Ibn Qutaybah said: "their cutting" is omitted, and what is stated, ﴿then place upon every mountain a portion of them﴾, suffices in place of "cut them up," because it indicates it. This is like your saying: "Take this garment and place on every spear you have a flag from it," meaning: cut it, and do that. Abu Ja'far, Hamzah, Khalaf, and al-Mufaddal, on the authority of Asim, read (fa-ṣurhunna ilayk) with a kasrah on the ṣād. Al-Yazidi said: both are one. Ibn Qutaybah said: the kasrah and the ḍammah are two dialects. Al-Farra' said: most of the Arabs use the ḍammah on the ṣād, and al-Kisa'i related to me that he heard some of Banu Sulaym say: "ṣirtuhu, fa-ana aṣīruhu." It is related from Ibn Abbas, Wahb, Abu Malik, Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali, and al-Suddi that the meaning of the form with a kasrah on the ṣād is: cut them up. It is related from Abu Ubaydah that he said: its meaning with the ḍammah is: gather them, and with the kasrah: cut them up.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then place upon every mountain a portion of them﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: place upon every mountain from each one of them a portion. It is related from Awf, on the authority of al-Hasan, who said: Slaughter them and pluck them, then cut them into pieces, then mix them all together, then divide them into four portions, and place on every mountain a portion. Then he withdrew from them and called them, and each limb began to run to its companion until they stood up as they were, and then they came to him running. Qatadah said: He held their heads in his hand, and the bone went to the bone, the feather to the feather, and the piece of flesh to the piece of flesh, while he watched that, then he called them, and they came hastening upon their feet, each bird throwing its head toward him. Regarding the number of mountains over which they were divided, there are two sayings. One: he divided them over four mountains, said by Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and Qatadah. It is related from Ibn Abbas that he said: he made them four portions at the quarters of the earth, as if he meant the four directions of the human being. The second: he divided them into seven portions over seven mountains, said by Ibn Jurayj and al-Suddi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then call them, they will come to you running﴾ Ibn Qutaybah said: It is said: "running (ʿadwan)," and it is said: "walking (mashyan) upon their feet." And one does not say of a bird when it flies: "sa'a" (it hastened). ﴿And know that Allah is Mighty﴾ That is: Invincible, not overcome, ﴿Wise﴾ in what He arranges. Muqatil claims that this story occurred to Ibrahim in Syria before he had a son, and before the scrolls were sent down to him, when he was seventy-five years old.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 261:

﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain that grows seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains, and Allah multiplies for whom He wills, and Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾

(p-316) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾. Tha'lab related to us from him that he said: "The likeness, and Allah knows best, is for the expenditure, not for the men. But when the meaning makes clear what they intend, the Arabs omit words, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they were made to drink the calf into their hearts﴾. So 'the love' was omitted because the meaning is known. Likewise here." He intended: "the likeness of the expenditure of those who spend their wealth." A similar example is His saying: ﴿And let not those who withhold what Allah has given them of His bounty think that it is better for them﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 18]. He means: "the stinginess of the stingy," so "stinginess" was omitted.

Regarding what is meant by "the way of Allah" there are two views. The first is that it is jihad (struggle in the cause of God). The second is that it encompasses all avenues of righteousness (al-birr). Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: The verse is linked back to His saying: ﴿O you who believe, spend of what We have provided you﴾. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has informed, by the coining of this parable, that a good deed in spending in His way is multiplied seven hundred fold.

al-Sha'bi said: A man's expenditure on himself and his household is multiplied seven hundred fold.

Ibn Zayd said: ﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾ means: He increases it beyond the seven hundred.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 262:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾. Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Uthman ibn Affan regarding his expenditure in the Battle of Tabuk, and his purchase of the Well of Rumah (bi'r Rumah), a well (rakiyyah) in Medina, which he gave in charity to the Muslims. And it was revealed concerning Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf when he gave in charity four thousand dirhams, which was half of his wealth.

As for "al-mann" (reminding of one's favour), there are two opinions. The first: it is reminding the poor person of one's favour, such as saying, "I have done good to you and supported you," and this is the view of the majority. The second: it is reminding Allah of one's charity, narrated from Ibn Abbas. If it is asked: how did He praise them for abandoning al-mann, while He described Himself as al-Mannan (the Bestower of favours)? The answer: it is said, "min fulan 'ala fulan" (so-and-so bestowed a favour upon so-and-so) when he confers a benefit upon him, and this is the praiseworthy sense. The poet said:

"So bestow upon us (fa-munni 'alayna) with greeting, for your speech is rubies and strung pearls."

He meant by al-mann the bestowal of favour. As for the blameworthy sense, it is said, "min fulan 'ala fulan" when he regards what he gave as great and boasts of it. A poet said concerning this:

"You gave a little, then you quickly made it a favour (minna), so your bounty is burdensome and likewise it is little."

Abu Bakr al-Anbari mentioned this. As for "al-adha" (harm), there are two opinions. One: it is confronting the poor person with what hurts him, such as saying to him, "You are always poor, I have been afflicted with you, and Allah has relieved me of you." The second: (p-318) it is informing others of one's kindness to the poor person in the presence of those whom the poor person dislikes to know of it. Both opinions cause harm to the poor person, and this is not a characteristic of those who are sincere in charity.

And indeed, he related to us from Hassan ibn Abi Sinan that he used to buy a man's household and dependents, then free them all, without making himself known to them or telling them who he was.

"Qawlun ma'ruf" (﴿a kind word﴾): that is, a good word to the poor person, such as saying to him, "May God widen [His provision] for you." "Wa maghfirah" (﴿and forgiveness﴾): that is, he conceals from a Muslim his need and his poverty. It was also said that by "forgiveness" is meant overlooking the one who asks if he behaves arrogantly toward the one being asked at the time of refusing him. "Khayrun min sadaqatin yatba'uha adha" (﴿is better than a charity followed by injury﴾), and its explanation has already passed.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 264:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do not nullify your charities﴾, meaning: do not nullify their reward, just as the reward of the charity of the show-off (mura'i) who does not believe in God is nullified, and he is the hypocrite (munafiq). ﴿So his example﴾, meaning: the likeness of his expenditure, ﴿is like a smooth rock﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-Safwan is a rock, al-Wabil is the heaviest rain, and al-Saldu is the smooth one. Al-Zajjaj said: al-Safwan is a smooth rock, and likewise al-Safa. Tha'lab said: al-Saldu is the pure one. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah regarding ﴿and leaves it bare, smooth﴾ that they both said: there is nothing upon it. This is a parable God, the Exalted, struck for the show-off with his expenditure, who on the Day of Resurrection is unable to obtain the reward of anything of what he spent.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 265:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the example of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾, i.e., seeking His good pleasure.

Regarding the meaning of "tathbit" (firm establishment), there are two views. The first: it is spending with certainty and affirmation of faith. This is the view of al-Sha'bi, Qatadah, and al-Suddi, among others. The second: it is firmness in choosing the place of spending, so they look into where they place it. This is the view of al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Abu Salih.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿like a garden﴾. Al-jannah is the orchard. Mujahid and Asim al-Jahdari read "habbah" (a grain) with a ḥā'. Al-rabwah is that which is elevated. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "bi-rubwah" with a ḍammah on the rā'. Asim and Ibn 'Amir read it with a fatḥah on the rā'. Al-Hasan and al-A'mash read it with a kasrah on the rā'. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Razin read "birabawah," with an added alif and a fatḥah on the rā'. Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Asim al-Jahdari read it likewise, except that they put a ḍammah on the rā'. Their disagreement over "al-mu'minin" is similar. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said rabwah, rubwah, ribwah, and rabawah. It is a place of raised ground that has water to irrigate it, so it yields more abundantly than the low ground. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-rabwah is elevation, and everything that rises and increases has raba (grown), and from this comes riba (usury) in trade.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿so it brought forth its produce﴾. Ibn Kathir and Nafi' read "uklaha." The word "ukl" is with a sukun on the kaf wherever it occurs, and Abu 'Amr agreed with them in what is attached to a feminine noun, such as: ﴿its produce is lasting﴾. As for what is attached to a masculine noun, such as "ukuluhu," or what is not attached to a pronoun, such as "ukli khamt" (the produce of tamarisk), Abu 'Amr read it with a heavy (emphatic) form. Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read all of that in the heavy form. "Uklaha" means its fruit. ﴿Double﴾ means twofold.

As for "al-tall" (light rain), Ibn Qutaybah said: it is the weakest rain. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the constant rain, of fine drops, from which the channels barely flow. Tha'lab said: this is a future form, but it refers to a past matter, so its meaning is: if a heavy rain (wabil) has not struck it, then a light rain (tall) will.

The meaning of this example is that the owner of this garden does not lose out: if the light rain reaches it, it is good, and if the heavy rain reaches it, its yield is doubled. Likewise is the spending of the sincere believer.

"Al-Basir" among the names of Allah, Exalted is He, means the All-Seeing (al-Mubsir). Al-Khattabi said: it is on the pattern of fa'il in the sense of muf'il, as in the saying "alim" in the sense of "mu'lim" (painful).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 266:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Would any of you like⦆ This verse is connected to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do not nullify your charities⦆. The meaning of "ayawaddu" (would he like) is "ayuhibbu" (would he love). He mentioned the date palms and grapevines because they are among the most valuable things in orchards, and he specified that (case) to the elderly, because he has despaired of the striving of youth in their earning.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And he has offspring, weak⦆ meaning weak (dhi'af), and when offspring are weak, he is more tender toward them and more concerned for them. ﴿Then there strikes it⦆ meaning the garden ﴿a whirlwind⦆, which is a severe wind that blows with force, lifting dust toward the sky so that it looks like a pillar.

The poet said:

؎ If you are a wind, then you have met a whirlwind
