That is: you have met one stronger than you. If it is asked: how is it permissible in speech that he has a garden and it is struck (fa-asabaha), and he did not say (fa-yusibuha)? Is it permissible to say: "Would you like to obtain wealth, and it perished," meaning "and it perishes"? The answer: that is permissible after "wadidtu" (I loved), because the Arabs use it sometimes with "an" and sometimes with "law" (p-321), so they say: "I loved that you would leave us" and "I loved that you leave us," as reported by al-Farra' and Tha'lab.

Section

This verse is like a parable that God Exalted struck regarding the regret of having a blessing removed at the time of greatest need. Regarding whom it is intended there are three views. The first: that it is like the one whose end is sealed with corruption at the close of his life, reported by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: that it is a parable for one who is negligent in obedience to God Exalted until he dies, reported by Mujahid. The third: that it is a parable for one who shows off in spending, whose benefit is cut off from him when he is most in need of it, reported by al-Suddi.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 267:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, spend from the good things you have earned﴾. Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are two reports. The first: the Ansar, whenever they cut the dates from the palm trees, each man would bring some of it and hang it in the mosque, and the poor among the Muhajirun would eat from it. Some people who did not care for good would bring a cluster containing worthless dates (al-hashf) and inferior dates (al-shis), (p-322) and hang it up, so this verse was revealed. This is the statement of al-Bara' ibn Azib. The second: "The Prophet ﷺ commanded the zakat al-fitr, and a man brought inferior dates, so this verse was revealed." This is the statement of Jabir ibn Abdullah. Regarding what is meant by this expenditure there are two views. The first: it is the obligatory charity, as said by Ubaydah al-Salmani and others. The second: it is voluntary charity. Regarding what is meant by "good" here there are two views. The first: it is the best of souls (i.e., the finest quality), as said by Ibn Abbas. The second: it is the lawful (halal), as said by Abu Ma'qil and others.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not aim at the bad﴾. That is: do not intend. Al-tayammum in the language means intending. Maymun ibn Qays al-A'sha said:

I aimed for Qays, though between me and him lay a land of a wide desert with rough terrain.

Regarding "the bad" (al-khabith) there are two views. The first: it is the inferior, as stated by most scholars, and the occasion of revelation points to it. The second: it is the forbidden (haram), as said by Ibn Zayd.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you would not take it except with reluctance (ghamd) in it﴾. Ibn Abbas said: if one of you were to demand from another a right owed to him, and then the other paid it, but he would not accept it except after seeing that he had overlooked some of his right. Ibn Qutaybah said: the origin of this is that a person turns his gaze away from something and closes his eyes to it, so leniency (tarakhkhus) was called ighmad. From this is the people's saying to the seller: "Ighmid," that is: do not stare, and act as if you do not see. Others said: since a man, when he sees what he dislikes, closes his eyes so that he does not see all of what he dislikes, he made overlooking and leniency in everything into ighmad.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And know that Allah is Ghani﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: He did not command you to give charity out of need, but He tests your states, so He is Hamid (Praiseworthy) in that. It is said: Zayd has become ghaniy (self-sufficient), yaghna ghina' (maqsur), when he became independent; and the people became ghaniy when they alighted in a place that suffices them, and the place where they alight is maghan. Al-ghawani are the women; it is said they were so named because they were self-sufficient by their beauty, and it is said by their husbands. As for "al-Hamid," al-Khattabi said: it means al-mahmud (the Praised), fa'il in the sense of maf'ul.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 268:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Shaytan threatens you with poverty﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said: wa'adtuhu a'iduhu wa'dan, wa'idatan, wa maw'idan, wa mu'idatan, wa maw'udan (the verbal forms of al-wa'd, "to promise/threaten"). It is said: al-faqr and al-fuqr (both forms of "poverty"). The meaning of the statement is: he drives you to pay the bad in the charities, frightening you with poverty if you give the good. The meaning of yaʿidukumu al-faqra is: with poverty, and the preposition (bāʾ) has been omitted. The poet said:

I commanded you to good, so do what you were commanded, for I have left you possessing wealth and property.

Regarding "al-fahsha'" (indecency) there are two views. One: stinginess. The other: sins. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "And Allah promises you forgiveness for your indecencies, and bounty in provision."

(p-324) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾. Concerning the meaning of this wisdom there are eleven opinions. The first: it is the Qur'an, said by Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Muqatil, and others. The second: knowledge of the abrogating (nasikh) and abrogated (mansukh) verses of the Qur'an, its clear (muhkam) and allegorical (mutashabih) verses, its preceding and succeeding verses, and the like; this was transmitted by Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas. The third: prophethood; transmitted by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. The fourth: understanding of the Qur'an, said by Abu al-Aliya, Qatada, and Ibrahim. The fifth: knowledge and jurisprudence (fiqh); transmitted by Layth from Mujahid. The sixth: correctness in speech; transmitted by Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid. The seventh: scrupulousness (wara') in the religion of Allah, said by al-Hasan. The eighth: fear of Allah, said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas. The ninth: intellect in religion, said by Ibn Zayd. The tenth: understanding, said by Sharik. The eleventh: knowledge together with action, since a man is not called wise (hakim) unless he combines the two; said by Ibn Qutayba.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And none will be reminded except those of understanding﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, none will reflect in a way that is reminded by what has been related of the verses of the Qur'an except those possessing intellects. Ibn Qutayba said: "Ulu" (أُولُو) means "dhu" (ذَوُو, possessors of), and the singular of "ulu" is "dhu," and of "ulat" is "dhat."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 270:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Or whatever vow you have vowed﴾. The nadhr (vow) is what a person makes obligatory upon himself. It may be unconditional, and it may be conditional upon a stipulation. ﴿Indeed, Allah knows it﴾. Mujahid said: He counts it. Al-Zajjaj said: He will recompense for it. Regarding who is meant by the wrongdoers (al-zalimin) here, there are two opinions. The first: they are the polytheists, as said by Muqatil. The second: (p-325) the hypocrites, through reminders of favor (al-mann), harm (al-adha), and showing off (al-riya'), and those who give warning in disobedience, as said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. And al-ansar (helpers): those who prevent. So its meaning: they have no preventer who would protect them from the punishment of Allah.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 271:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you disclose your charities, then how excellent they are﴾. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: "When His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And whatever you spend of expenditure﴾ was revealed, they said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is the charity given in secret better, or openly?' Then this verse was revealed." Al-Zajjaj said: It is said: "badā al-shay'u yabdū" means the thing appeared (became manifest), and "abdaytuhu ibdā'an" means I made it manifest, and "badā lī badā'an" means my opinion changed from what it had been.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿fa-ni'immā hiya﴾. In "ni'imma" there are four dialects: "na'imma" with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the ayn, like "ʿalima"; "ni'imma" with a kasra on it; "na'mma" with a fatha on the nun and sukun on the ayn; and "ni'ma" with a kasra on the nun and sukun on the ayn. As for His saying ﴿fa-ni'immā hiya﴾, Nafi' (except the narration of Warsh), Abu 'Amr, and 'Asim (in the narration of Abu Bakr), and al-Mufaddal read "fa-na'immā" with a kasra on the nun and the ayn silent. Ibn Kathir, 'Asim (in the narration of Hafs), Nafi' (in the narration of Warsh), and Ya'qub read with a kasra on the nun and the ayn. Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read "fa-na'immā" with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the ayn, and all of them doubled the mim. Their difference in Surat al-Nisa' is similar. Al-Zajjaj said: "mā" is in the sense of "thing," i.e., "then excellent is the thing it is." Abu 'Ali said: "excellent is the thing, its disclosure."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿it is better for you﴾, meaning the concealment. The scholars agreed that concealing voluntary charity is better than disclosing it, and regarding obligatory charity there are two opinions. The first: its disclosure is better, as said by Ibn 'Abbas and others, and chosen by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la. Al-Zajjaj said: concealing zakat was better in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, but today people think ill, so disclosing it is better. The second: concealing it is better, as said by al-Hasan, Qatada, and Yazid ibn Abi Habib. Those who held the first opinion took the charities in the verse to refer to obligatory charity and took ﴿and if you conceal them﴾ to refer to voluntary charity, and this is a strange view. The concealment of charity is preferred for two reasons. The first relates to the giver: it keeps him far from showing off, closer to sincerity, and turned away from what the soul desires of public display. The second relates to the recipient: concealing his condition protects him from humiliation, for in public he would be made to feel abased.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He will remove from you of your misdeeds﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "wa-nukaffiru 'ankum" with a nun and a raf', meaning: "and We remove from you," and it may be taken as a new sentence. Nafi', Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read "wa-nukaffir" with a nun and a jazm on the ra'. Abu 'Ali said: this is based on treating the words as having the place of His saying ﴿it is better for you﴾, because ﴿it is better for you﴾ is in the place of a jussive; do you not see that if He had said "and if you conceal them, it will be greater for your reward," it would be jussive. A similar case is ﴿Were it not that You delay me to a near term, so I would give charity and be among the righteous﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 10], where "wa-akun" is taken in the place of "fa-asaddaq." Ibn 'Amir read "wa-yukaffiru" with a ya' and a raf', and likewise from Hafs from 'Asim, as a reference to Allah, mighty and majestic. Aban from 'Asim read "wa-tukaffiru" with a raised ta' and a fatha on the fa' with sukun on the ra'.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿of your misdeeds﴾. Regarding "min" there are two views. The first: it is superfluous. The second: it is used for partition. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: the wisdom in this is that the servants remain in fear and trepidation.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 272:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you do not spend except seeking the Face of Allah﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: This is specific to the believers. Allah informed them that He knows their intention is what is with Him, and when He informed them of the soundness of their intention, He informed them of the reward for it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿It will be repaid to you in full﴾, meaning: you will be given its reward in full. The meaning of the verse is: it is not incumbent upon you that they be guided, so that you withhold charity from them in order that they enter Islam. Rather, if you give charity to them, you will be rewarded. The verse is to be understood as referring to voluntary charity (sadaqat al-tatawwu'), since it is not permissible to give a disbeliever anything from obligatory charity (al-sadaqah al-mafrudah) at all.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 273:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For the poor who are confined in the way of Allah﴾. When He urged them to give charity and expenditure, He guided them to a better recipient than whoever is given charity. The explanation of ihsar (being confined, restricted) has already been given at His saying: ﴿But if you are prevented﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196]. Regarding the intended meaning of "those who are confined," there are four opinions. The first: they are the People of the Suffah (ahl al-Suffah), who confined themselves to obedience to Allah and had nothing. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil. The second: they are the poor among the Muhajirun (Emigrants). This was said by Mujahid.

(p-328) The third: they are a people who confined themselves to military campaigning (ghazw), so they cannot earn a living. This was said by Qatadah. The fourth: they are a people who were wounded while with the Prophet ﷺ and became disabled. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and al-Kisa'i chose it and said: "They were confined by illness (ihsar min al-maradh). Had he meant confinement by imprisonment, it would have said hussiru (ḥuṣirū). Ihsar is only from fear or illness. Ḥaṣr is confinement in other than these two."

Regarding "in the way of Allah," there are two opinions: one is that it means jihad, and the second is that it means obedience. Regarding "striking through the land," there are two opinions: one is that it means jihad, which they could not undertake because of their poverty; this is reported from Ibn 'Abbas. The second is earning a living (al-kasb), said by Qatadah. Regarding what prevented them from that, there are three opinions: the first is poverty, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second is their illnesses, said by Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Zayd. The third is their commitment to jihad, said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The ignorant one thinks them﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read "yahsabuhum" and "yahsabna" with a kasra on the sin throughout the Qur'an. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah and Abu Ja'far read them with a fatha on the sin in all instances. Abu 'Ali said: the fatha on the sin is more analogical (aqyas), because when the past tense is on the pattern "fa'ila" such as "hasiba," the present tense is on the pattern "yaf'alu," like "fariqa yafraqu" and "shariba yashrabu." The kasra is good for the sake of what is heard. Ibn Qutaybah said: he did not mean ignorance (jahl) which is the opposite of intellect, but rather the ignorance which is the opposite of information; it is as if he said: "He thinks them to be one whose state is not informed of."

Al-ta'affuf is abstaining from asking; it is said: "'affa 'an al-shay' and ta'affafa." Al-simа (al-sima) is the mark by which a thing is recognized, and its origin is from al-simah (the mark). Regarding the intended meaning of "their mark," there are three opinions: the first is that it is their adornment, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second is their humility (khushu'), said by Mujahid. The third is the effect of poverty upon them, said by al-Suddi and al-Rabi' ibn Anas. This indicates that the mark has a ruling connected to it. Our Imam Ahmad said regarding a dead person found in the land of war whose situation is unknown: his mark is examined; if he bears the mark of the disbelievers, such as being uncircumcised, he is judged by their ruling, so he is not buried in the graveyards of the Muslims and is not prayed over; and if he bears the mark of the Muslims, he is judged by their ruling.

As for al-ilhaf, it is al-ilhah (insistence). Ibn Qutaybah said: it is said "alhafa fi al-mas'alah" when he insisted. al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of alhafa is that he enveloped (shamila) with the request, and from it is derived al-lihaf (blanket), because it envelops the person with covering. If it is said: did they ask without insistence? The answer: no; rather the meaning of the statement is that there was no asking from them, so there would be insistence.

Al-A'sha said:

"He does not press his shin from weariness, nor from ailment, nor does he bite on his chest-bone, the yellowed one."

Its meaning: his shin has no weariness nor ailment, so that he would press it for that reason. Al-Farra' said: similar to this is that you say: "Rarely have I seen the like of this man," and perhaps you have not seen a little or much of his likes; so they do not ask people with insistence, nor without insistence. al-Zajjaj, Ibn al-Anbari, and others among others went to a similar view.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 274:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly﴾. The scholars differed concerning who it was revealed about, into three opinions.

The first: it was revealed concerning those who tie horses (yartabitūn) in the way of Allah, mighty and majestic. This was related by Hanash al-San'ani from Ibn 'Abbas (p-330), and it is the saying of Abu al-Darda', Abu Umamah, Makhul, al-Awza'i, and others.

The second: it was revealed concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him. He had four dirhams: he spent one dirham at night, one by day, one secretly, and one openly. This was related by Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid, Ibn al-Sa'ib, and Muqatil also said so.

The third: it was revealed concerning 'Ali and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf. 'Ali sent a wasq of dates to the People of the Suffah (Ahl al-Suffah) at night, and 'Abd al-Rahman sent them many dinars by day. This was related by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

**The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 2, verse 275:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who consume riba (al-ribā)⦈. Al-ribā, in linguistic origin (aṣl fi al-lughah), means increase. From it come *al-rabwah* (a raised mound) and *al-rābiyah* (a hill). Fulān *arbā* over Fulān means he exceeded him. This threat includes the one who consumes it and the one who deals in it. The consumer was singled out for mention because he is the principal concern. It is authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he "cursed the one who consumes riba, the one who pays it, its two witnesses, and its scribe."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They will not stand⦈. Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, on the Day of Resurrection, from the graves. *Al-mass* means madness; it is said, "a man who is *mamsūs*" (one afflicted by madness). When people come out of their graves, they hasten, as He, may He be exalted, says: ﴿On the Day they emerge from the graves rapidly⦈ [al-Ma'arij: 43]. Except the consumers of riba, for they will stand and fall, because God has made the riba swell in their bellies on the Day of Resurrection until it weighs them down, so they cannot hasten. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: that is the sign of the consumer of riba if he regards it as lawful on the Day of Resurrection.

(p-331) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That⦈, that is: this which was mentioned of their punishment, ﴿because they said, "Trade is only like riba."⦈ It was said that the Thaqif were the most prone of the Arabs to riba, and when they were forbidden from it, they said, "It is only like trade."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever has received an admonition from his Lord⦈. Al-Zajjaj said: every feminine form that is not *ḥaqīqī* (of real, natural gender) may be made masculine. Do you not see that *al-waʿẓ* and *al-mawʿiẓah* express one meaning?

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then for him is what has preceded⦈, that is: what he consumed of riba.

Regarding His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And his affair is up to God⦈, there are two opinions. The first: the pronoun (*al-hāʾ*) refers to the one who deals in riba, so the meaning is: if He wills, He protects him from it, and if He wills, He does not. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Muqatil. The second: it refers to riba, so the meaning is: God pardons what He wills of it and punishes for what He wills of it. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever returns⦈. Ibn Jubayr said: whoever returns to riba, regarding it as lawful, arguing with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Trade is only like riba⦈.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verses 276–277:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah destroys interest﴾ (yamhaqu Allahu al-riba). There are two opinions on this. The first: the meaning of its mahq (destruction) is its diminishing and its vanishing, and from this comes mahaq al-shahr (the waning of the moon), due to the decrease of the crescent in it. Abu Salih narrated this meaning from Ibn Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said likewise. The second: it is the nullification of what is given from it in charity and the like; al-Dahhak narrated this from Ibn Abbas.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and He causes charities to grow﴾ (wa yurbi al-sadaqat). Ibn Jubayr said: He multiplies them. And kaffar (the ungrateful/disbelieving one): the one who frequently commits that by which he disbelieves; and athim (the sinner): the one who persists in committing sin and insists upon it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verses 276–277:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah destroys interest﴾ (yamhaqu Allahu al-riba). There are two opinions on this. The first: the meaning of its mahq (destruction) is its diminishing and its vanishing, and from this comes mahaq al-shahr (the waning of the moon), due to the decrease of the crescent in it. Abu Salih narrated this meaning from Ibn Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said likewise. The second: it is the nullification of what is given from it in charity and the like; al-Dahhak narrated this from Ibn Abbas.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and He causes charities to grow﴾ (wa yurbi al-sadaqat). Ibn Jubayr said: He multiplies them. And kaffar (the ungrateful/disbelieving one): the one who frequently commits that by which he disbelieves; and athim (the sinner): the one who persists in committing sin and insists upon it.

(p-332) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and give up what remains of interest (riba)﴾. Concerning its revelation there are three opinions.

The first: it was revealed concerning the Banu Amr ibn Umayr ibn Awf of Thaqif, and the Banu al-Mughirah of the Banu Makhzum. The Banu al-Mughirah used to take interest (riba) from Thaqif. When Allah abolished interest, Thaqif demanded from the Banu al-Mughirah what was owed to them, and this verse and the one after it were revealed. This is the saying of Ibn Abbas.

The second: "It was revealed concerning Uthman ibn Affan and al-Abbas, who had both advanced loans against dates. When the time of harvesting (al-jidhadh) arrived, the owner of the dates said: 'If you take your money, there will be nothing left for me and my dependants to suffice us. Would you accept taking half and I will double it for you?' They did so. When the term came due, they sought the increase, and this reached the Prophet (ﷺ), who forbade them, and this verse was revealed." This is the saying of Ata and Ikrimah.

The third: it was revealed concerning al-Abbas and Khalid ibn al-Walid, who were partners in the Jahiliyyah and used to lend on interest. Then Islam came, and they had great wealth in interest, so this verse was revealed. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed every interest of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic era) is annulled, and the first interest I annul is the interest of al-Abbas." This is the saying of al-Suddi.

Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah and al-Dahhak said: He said "what remains of interest" because all interest had been abandoned, so only the interest of Thaqif remained.

Others said: The verse applies to one who practised interest before his Islam and received part of it while in disbelief, then embraced Islam. It is obligatory upon him to leave what remains and be pardoned for what has passed. As for practising interest after Islam, what he received is returned, and what remains is dropped.

(p-333) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if you do not, then be informed of war﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read (fa-adhanu), with a short alif and an open dhal. Hamza and Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read "fa-ādhinū", with a long alif and a kasra on the dhal. Al-Zajjaj said: As for the one who reads fa-adhanu, with a short alif and an open dhal, the meaning is "be certain" (aydaqu). As for the one who reads with a long alif and a kasra on the dhal, its meaning is: "inform everyone who has not abandoned usury that he is at war." Ibn 'Abbas said: On the Day of Resurrection it will be said to the one who consumed usury: "Take your weapon for war."

(p-334) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you repent, then for you is your principal; you do not wrong and you are not wronged﴾. That is, the principal you lent out: you do not wrong (by taking more than it) and you are not wronged (by having it reduced). The majority read the first "ta'" of tazlimuna with an open fatha and the second "ta'" with a damma. Al-Mufaddal related from 'Asim: a damma on the first and a fatha on the second.

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 280:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if someone is in hardship﴾. Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil mentioned that when the saying of the Exalted was revealed, ﴿and abandon what remains of interest (riba)﴾, the Banu 'Amr ibn 'Umayr said to the Banu al-Mughira: "Bring us the principal of our money, and we will leave the interest to you." The Banu al-Mughira complained of hardship, and this verse was revealed. As for ʿusra (hardship), it is poverty and constraint. The majority read the sin with a sukun (silent), while Abu Ja'far read it with a damma here and in ﴿the hour of hardship﴾. The majority read the sin of "maysara" (ease) with a fatha, while Nafi' read it with a damma, and Zayd, on the authority of Ya'qub, followed him in the damma of the sin, except that he added a kasra to the ra' and changed the ta' into a ha' and joined it with a ba'. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "wa-in kana" is "and if it occurs." And al-nazira is postponement. So He commanded them to postpone the principal after the abolition of interest when the creditor is in hardship, and He informed them that giving charity to him by this is better, by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and that you give charity (tasaddaqu)﴾. Most read the sad with a shadda, while ʿAsim lightened it along with a shadda on the dal. Ibn Abi ʿAbla read it with a sukun together with a damma on the dal, making it derive from al-sidq (truthfulness).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 281:

﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah; then every soul will be paid in full what it earned, and they will not be wronged.﴾ His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah.﴾ Abu 'Amr read the "ta" of "turja'un" with a fatha, while the rest read it with a damma. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Atiyyah, Muqatil, and others: this is the last verse to be revealed of the Qur'an. Ibn 'Abbas said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) died eighty-one days after it. Ibn Jurayj said: he died nine nights after it. Muqatil said: seven nights after it. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then every soul will be paid in full what it earned.﴾ That is: it will be given the recompense for what it earned.

The poet says:

*"I lent to Arwa, and debts are repaid; she delayed some and paid back some."*

The meaning: if one of you has a debt owed to him by another until a specified term, then write it down. Allah the Exalted commanded that debts be written down and witnessed, as a protection of wealth from Him and of people from injustice, because whoever has the evidence in hand seldom entertains the thought of denying it out of greed. Ibn 'Abbas said: this verse was revealed specifically concerning the salam (advance-payment) contract.

If it is asked: what is the benefit of His saying "with a debt" when "you deal" (tadayantum) would suffice? The answer: "tadayantum" applies to two meanings. The first is trade, exchange and lending. The second is recompense for deeds. For the first one says *al-dayn* with a fatha on the dal; for the second one says *al-din* with a kasra on the dal. He the Exalted said: ﴿They ask: when is the Day of Recompense?﴾ [al-Dhariyat 51:12], meaning the Day of Judgment.

They also recited:

*"We repaid them as they repaid."*

So His saying "with a debt" indicates the intended sense of "you deal." Ibn al-Anbari mentioned this. As for *al-'adl* (justice), it is the truth. Qatada said: do not leave out any right, and do not add any falsehood.

His saying: ﴿And let no scribe refuse﴾ means: let him not refuse to write as Allah has taught him. On this there are two views. The first: as Allah taught him the writing, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Al-Sha'bi said: writing is an obligation of sufficiency (fard kifaya), like jihad. The second: as Allah commanded him, with truth; said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying: ﴿And let the one upon whom the obligation lies dictate﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: meaning the debtor. He says: let him dictate what he owes of the creditor's right to the scribe, ﴿and let him not diminish from it anything﴾, meaning: let him not reduce it during the dictation. Our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi said: it is said "amlaltu umillu" and "amlaytu umli" are two dialectal forms. "Amlaytu" comes from *al-imla'* (dictation), and "amlaltu" comes from *al-malal* and *al-mulal* (weariness), because the one who dictates lengthens his speech to the scribe and repeats it.

His saying: ﴿But if the one upon whom the obligation lies is a fool (safih)﴾. Regarding the meaning of "safih" here there are four views. First: he is ignorant of finances and ignorant of dictation; said by Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr. Second: he is a child or a woman; said by al-Hasan. Third: he is a minor; said by al-Dahhak and al-Suddi. Fourth: he is a squanderer (mubadhdhir); said by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la. Regarding the meaning of "da'if" (weak) there are three views. First: he is incapable, or mute, or one who has imbecility; said by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr. Second: he is a fool; said by Mujahid and al-Suddi. Third: he is a minor; said by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la.

His saying: ﴿Or he is unable to dictate himself﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he is unable because of his inability to speak. Ibn Jubayr said: he does not know well how to dictate what is upon him. Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la said: he is the insane person.

His saying: ﴿then let his guardian dictate﴾. Regarding the pronoun there are two views. First: it refers to the right, so the estimate is: let the guardian of the right dictate. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, and Muqatil, (p-338) and Ibn Qutayba chose it. Second: it refers to the one upon whom the obligation lies. This is the view of al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd, and al-Zajjaj chose it and criticized the first view, saying: how would he accept the claim of the claimant? And what need would there be for scribes and witnesses if his word were accepted? This is also the choice of al-Qadi Abu Ya'la. And "al-'adl" means fairness.

Regarding His saying: ﴿from among your men﴾ there are two views. First: it means free men; said by Mujahid. Second: the people of Islam; this is the choice of al-Zajjaj and al-Qadi Abu Ya'la, and what supports it is that He addressed the believers at the beginning of the verse.

His saying: ﴿But if there are not two men﴾. He intended: if the two witnesses are not two men, ﴿then a man and two women﴾, and He did not mean by it: if two men are not found.

His saying: ﴿of those whom you accept as witnesses﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: from among the people of virtue and religion.

His saying: ﴿that if one of them errs, the other may remind her﴾. Al-Zajjaj mentioned that al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and all the trustworthy grammarians said: its meaning is: call two women as witnesses, because one of them reminds the other, and so that one of them reminds the other. Hamza read "in tadilla" with a kasra on the alif. The "dalal" here is forgetfulness, said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, al-Rabi', Muqatil, Abu 'Ubayda, and Ibn Qutayba. As for His saying "fa-tudhakkira": Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with the lightened form and a fatha on the ra'; Hamza read it with a damma and a shadda on the kaf; and the rest read it with a fatha and a shadda on the kaf. Whoever read it with a shadda intended the remembering after forgetfulness. As for the reading of whoever lightened it, there are two views. First: it has the same meaning as the emphatic form, and this is the view of the majority. Al-Dahhak, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, and al-Suddi said: the meaning of the two readings is one. Second: it means: makes her testimony equal to the testimony of a man. This is the position of Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, and al-Asma'i reported something similar from Abu 'Amr, and al-Qadi Abu Ya'la chose it, but a group rejected it, among them Ibn Qutayba. Abu 'Ali said: the view of Ibn 'Uyayna is not strong, because if women reached whatever they reached, their testimony would not be valid unless a man were with them; and because "dalal" here is forgetfulness, so it should be matched by what is its equivalent, which is reminding.

(p-339) His saying: ﴿And let not the witnesses refuse when they are called﴾. Qatada said: a man would go around a great gathering, where the people were, and call them to testimony, and none of them would follow him, so this verse was revealed. To what is this calling? There are three views. First: to bearing witness and recording it in writing; said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Atiyya, Qatada, and al-Rabi'. Second: to its establishment and delivery before the judges after their testimony had been given earlier; said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Tawus, Mujahid, 'Ikrima, 'Ata', al-Sha'bi, Abu Mijlaz, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Zayd. It was also related by al-Maymuni from Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Third: to bearing it and to delivering it; reported from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan, and al-Zajjaj chose it. Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la said: the witness is only obligated not to refuse when called to establish testimony if no one else who can testify is found; but if a group has already borne it, it does not become binding on him, and likewise during its bearing, because it is an obligation of sufficiency like jihad, so it is not permissible for all people to refrain from it.

His saying: ﴿And do not be weary (tas'amu)﴾, meaning: do not become tired or impatient in writing down the small and the large, whose deferral to its term is customary, that is, to the time of its term. ﴿That is more just in the sight of Allah﴾, meaning: more equitable; ﴿and more suitable as testimony﴾, because the document mentions all that the witnesses testified to; ﴿and nearer﴾, meaning closer; ﴿to preventing doubt﴾, meaning: that you not doubt. ﴿Except that it be﴾ the wealth ﴿trade﴾, meaning: except that it occurs as trade. 'Asim read "tijaratan" with a fatha, meaning: except that the wealth be ready trade (tijara hadira), which means sales in which each of the two parties is entitled from the other to the immediate delivery of what was contracted on his side without deferral. So He permitted leaving off writing in these as a relaxation, lest a matter become burdensome for them when you deal in food or drink.

His saying: ﴿And take witnesses when you sell﴾. Calling witnesses is recommended in matters for which calling witnesses is customary.

(p-340) * Section

This verse contains a command to record debts in a document, and to establish testimony in sale and debt. The scholars disagreed whether this is a command of obligation or of recommendation. The majority held that it is a command of recommendation and preference (nadb wa istihbab); on this view it is muhkam (not abrogated). A group held that writing and witnessing are obligatory; this was reported from Ibn 'Umar, Abu Musa, Mujahid, Ibn Sirin, 'Ata', al-Dahhak, Abu Qilaba, al-Hakam, and Ibn Zayd. Then these disagreed among themselves whether this ruling remains in force or is abrogated (mansukh). Most of them held that it is muhkam and not abrogated; but a group held that it is abrogated by His saying: ﴿But if one of you trusts another, let the one who is trusted fulfill his trust﴾.

His saying: ﴿And let no scribe or witness be harmed﴾. Abu Ja'far read "yudarru" with a lightened rā' and sukūn. Regarding the meaning of the statement there are three views. First: its meaning is that he should not be harmed by being claimed upon while he is occupied; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrima, al-Suddi, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, al-Farra', and Muqatil. al-Rabi' said: one of them would come to the scribe and say: write for me; he would say: I am occupied; so he would press him and say: you were ordered to write; so he would harm him and not leave him, while he could find someone else; and the witness would do likewise; so this verse was revealed. Second: its meaning is a prohibition on the scribe harming the one who engages him by writing something other than what was dictated to him, and on the witness testifying to what he was not called to testify to; this is the view of al-Hasan, Tawus, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd, and Ibn Qutayba and al-Zajjaj chose it. Al-Zajjaj argued for its soundness by His saying: ﴿And if you do, then it is defiance (fusuq) in you﴾, and said: one who calls a scribe to write while he is occupied, or a witness, is not called a defiant (fasiq); he is called defiant only if he distorts the document or lies in testimony. Third: the meaning of harming is that the scribe refuses to write, or the witness refuses to testify; this is the view of 'Ata' and others.

His saying: ﴿And if you do﴾ means: the harming.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 283:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you are on a journey﴾. The journey is singled out because usually there is no scribe (katib) and no witness on it. The intended meaning of the speech is: if you lack assurance through writing and witnessing, then take a pledge (rahn).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿then a pledge (fa-rihanun)﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and 'Abd al-Warith read (fa-ruhnun) with a damma on the ra' and the ha' and without an alif, and 'Abd al-Warith made the ha' sukun. Its basis is lightening (al-takhfif). Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read (fa-rihanun) with a kasra on the ra' and a fatha on the ha', with the alif retained. Ibn Qutaybah said: whoever reads (fa-rihanun) intends the plural of rahn (pledge), and whoever reads (fa-ruhnun) intends the plural of rihan, so it is as if it is the plural of a plural.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿taken into possession (maqbudhah)﴾. This indicates that among the conditions for the binding nature of the pledge is possession (al-qabd). Taking possession of the pledge is receiving it from the one who pledged it (rahin) when it is movable. If it is something that cannot be moved, such as houses and lands, its possession is the pledgor (rahin) leaving it between him and the pledgee (murtahin).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if one of you trusts another (fa-in amina ba'dukum ba'dan)﴾. That is: if the creditor (rabb al-dayn) trusts the honesty of the debtor (gharim) and hands over his property without writing, without witnesses, and without a pledge, ﴿then let him who has been entrusted (alladhi ౯ui'tumina)﴾, who is the debtor (al-madin), ﴿fulfill his trust (amanatahu) and let him fear Allah, his Lord﴾ by not betraying the one who entrusted him.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿his heart is sinful (fa-innahu athimun qalbuhu)﴾. Al-Suddi related from his teachers: "His heart is wicked (fajir)." Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la said: He attributed the sin to the heart only because sins are connected to the commitment of the heart, and concealing testimony is nothing but the resolve of intention to abandon its delivery.

The Qur'anic verse: ﴿If you show what is in your souls or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it﴾.

As for showing what is in the soul, it is acting upon what the servant has harboured, or speaking it. This is something for which the servant is called to account and held responsible. As for what he conceals within himself, the scholars differed over what is meant by the concealed matter in this verse, on two views.

The first view: it is general, covering all concealed matters. This is the view of the majority. They then differed over whether this ruling still holds regarding accountability or has been abrogated (*naskh*, the cancellation of a earlier ruling by a later one), on two views. The first: it has been abrogated by the words of Allah, ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:286). This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayrah, Ibn 'Abbas in one narration, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Ibn Sirin, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, 'Ata' al-Khurasani, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, and Muqatil. The second: it holds regarding accountability in general, so He calls to account whomever He wills and forgives whomever He wills. This is narrated from Ibn 'Umar and al-Hasan, and was chosen by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi and al-Qadi Abu Ya'la.

Ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "This verse has not been abrogated. Rather, when Allah gathers the creatures, He will say to them: 'I will inform you of what you concealed in your souls, which My angels did not witness.' As for the believers, He will inform them and forgive them what they merely thought in their souls. This is the meaning of His words, ﴿Allah will call you to account for it﴾, meaning: Allah will inform you of it. As for the people of association and doubt, He will inform them of what they concealed of denial." This is the meaning of His words, ﴿So He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills﴾.

(p. 344) Most readers, including Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i, read *fa-yaghfiru* and *yu'adhdhibu* with a sukun (silent vowel) on the *ra'* and the *ba'*. They did so to make these follow what precedes them, namely *yuhasibukum* (He calls you to account). Abu Ja'far, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, and Ya'qub read both with a damma (*raf'*, nominative) on the *ra'* and the *ba'*. These readers thereby make the sentence a new clause, separate from the first.

Ibn al-Anbari said: Some people hold that the accounting here is Allah making the servant aware, on the Day of Resurrection, of what he had spoken to himself about in the world, so that he knows nothing escaped Him. He said: What we choose is that the verse is *muhkamah* (definitive, not abrogated), because abrogation only applies to commands and prohibitions. It has been narrated from 'A'ishah that she said: "As for what you make public, Allah will call you to account for it. As for what you conceal, it is the punishment in this world that is hastened for you because of it."

The second view: it is a specific ruling concerning one kind of concealed matter, and the proponents of this view have two opinions regarding it. The first: it is concealing testimony, said by Ibn 'Abbas in one narration, 'Ikrimah, and al-Sha'bi. The second: it is doubt and certainty, said by Mujahid. According to this view, the verse is *muhkamah*.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 2, verse 285:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord﴾. Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated in their two Sahihs, from the hadith of Abu Mas'ud al-Badri, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The two verses at the end of Surah al-Baqarah: whoever recites them in a night, they will suffice him." Abu Bakr al-Naqqash said: its meaning is that they suffice him from performing the night prayer (qiyam al-layl).

(p-345) It has also been said: they were revealed because of a cause, which is what al-'Ala' narrated from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿And whether you show what is in your souls or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it﴾, this was difficult for the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) [so they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then knelt upon their knees] and said: 'This verse has been revealed to you and we cannot bear it.' He said: 'Do you want to say as the two peoples of the Book before you said: we hear and we disobey? Say: We hear and we obey, Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the final return.' When they said it and their tongues were subdued by it, Allah revealed after it: ﴿The Messenger believes﴾." Al-Zajjaj said: when He had mentioned what this surah contains of narratives and rulings, He concluded it with the affirmation of His Prophet and the believers. Ibn 'Abbas recited (wa-kitabihi, "and His Book," in the singular), and when he was asked about this, he said: "Kitab is more general than kutub (books)," taking it as a collective noun (ism al-jins), just as you say: "the dirham has become abundant in the hands of people." Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf agreed with Ibn 'Abbas in his recitation, and likewise in (al-Tahrim). Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and 'Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr, and Ibn 'Amir recited (wa-kutubihi, "and His Books," in the plural) here, and in (al-Tahrim) in the singular. Abu 'Amr recited the plural in both places.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾. Abu 'Amr read what is attached to a pronoun of two letters, such as "rusulina" and "rusulukum," with a sukun on the sin, and made heavy (tashdid-less, i.e., read with the full vowel) everything other than that. On his authority, regarding His saying (ʿala rusulika), there are two transmissions: lightening and heavying. The rest read every instance of this type in the Qur'an with heaviness. The meaning of His saying ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ is: we do not do as the People of the Book did, who believed in some and disbelieved in others. Ya'qub read (lā yufarriqu, "he does not distinguish," with the ya') and with a fatha on the ra'.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Ghufranaka﴾ means: we ask You for Your forgiveness. And al-masir means: the return.

(p-346) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾. Al-wus‘ (capacity) means ṭāqah (ability). This is what Ibn ‘Abbas and Qatadah said. Its meaning is: He does not burden it with what it has no power over, because that is impossible for it, such as burdening the disabled with running and the blind with seeing. As for burdening a person with what becomes impossible for him due to the lack of the instruments, it is permissible, such as burdening the disbeliever whom the eternal knowledge has predetermined will not believe in faith. Thus the verse is to be understood according to the first view. From the evidence for what we have said is His saying, exalted is He, in the context of the verse: ﴿Our Lord, do not burden us with what we have no ability to bear﴾. So if burdening with what cannot be borne were impermissible, the supplication would be meaningless. Allah, exalted is He, has commanded His Prophet to call a people about whom He said: ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they will never be guided, ever﴾ [al-Kahf: 57]. Ibn al-Anbari said: The meaning is: Do not burden us with what is heavy for us to perform, even though we are able to do it with exertion and by enduring something disliked. He addressed the Arabs according to what they understand, for a man among them says to someone he hates: "I cannot bear to look at you," while he is able to do so, but it is burdensome for him. Similar to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They were not able to hear﴾.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It has what it has earned﴾. Ibn ‘Abbas said: It has what it has earned of obedience, ﴿and against it what it has acquired﴾ of disobedience. Abu Bakr al-Naqqash said: His saying "lahā" (for it) is an indication of good, and "‘alayhā" (against it) is an indication of evil. Some scholars held that kasabat is used for a single act or several acts, while iktasabat is used only for something occurring after another. According to others, the two are dialectal variants with one meaning, like His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿So give respite to the disbelievers; give them time, a little﴾ [al-Tariq: 17].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, do not take us to task﴾. This is a teaching from Allah to the creation that they should say this. Ibn al-Anbari (p-347) said: What is meant by forgetting here is abandoning with intention, because forgetting in the sense of heedlessness has had its sins removed on its account. Error (khaṭa’) here also refers to intention, not to inadvertence. It is said: "akhṭa’a al-rajul" when he does something deliberately, just as it is said "akhṭa’a" when he is heedless.

Regarding "al-iṣr" (the burden) there are two views. One: it is the covenant, said by Ibn ‘Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi. The second: it is the heavy weight, meaning: Do not make heavy upon us from the obligations what You made heavy upon the Children of Israel, said by Ibn Qutaybah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not burden us with what we have no ability to bear﴾. Concerning this there are five views. One: it is what is difficult and arduous of deeds, said by al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, and the majority. The second: it is love (maḥabbah), (p-348) narrated by al-Thawri from Mansur from Ibrahim. The third: it is sexual desire, said by Makhul. The fourth: it is the inner speech and its whisperings. The fifth: it is the punishment of the Fire.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You are our Protector﴾, that is, You are our Guardian. ﴿So help us﴾, that is, assist us. Mu‘adh, when he finished this surah, used to say: Amin.
